AI.method: The 3rd MAC expands upon the first two editions by introducing a new task—fine-grained micro-action understanding—evaluated with multimodal large language models (MLLMs), moving from recognition/detection to deeper semantic interpretation.
AI.result: The paper summarizes datasets, task settings, evaluation protocols, competition results, and representative solutions from top-performing teams in the 3rd MAC challenge.
AI.conclusion: The authors discuss future directions for micro-action analysis and its broader role in human-centric video understanding, emphasizing the shift toward fine-grained semantic understanding of subtle human behaviors.

title: Feature-Guided Diffusion for Non-Differentiable Inverse Rendering
summary: Inverse rendering is traditionally solved via differentiable renderers and gradient descent, which requires substantial problem-specific engineering and is prone to getting stuck in local minima due to ambiguities. Derivative-free approaches alleviate engineering requirements, but often heavily depend on a good problem initialization. In this work, we propose Feature-Informed Diffusion Evolution (FIDE), a fully black-box framework that requires no gradients or specific initialization: the renderer is treated as an opaque function whose only requirement is to produce images. Our key insight is feature guiding: rather than reducing each candidate rendering to a scalar loss value, we use a Vision Transformer (ViT) to extract dense visual features from it. We subsequently use these features to train a diffusion-based candidate proposal model, allowing the network to use visual cues to predict parameters that would match the target image. The candidate solutions proposed by this diffusion model are then refined in a closed loop with a CMA evolution strategy, continuously narrowing the proposal region as optimization progresses. We validate across diverse inverse problems from path tracing, vector splines, Voronoi shaders, and robotics, and demonstrate that feature-guiding substantially improves convergence over scalar-loss baselines and reliably escapes local minima where gradient-based methods stall.

AI.tldr: FIDE is a black-box inverse rendering framework that uses Vision Transformer features to guide a diffusion-based candidate proposal model, refined via CMA evolution strategy, achieving robust convergence without gradients or special initialization across diverse inverse problems.
AI.motivation: Traditional inverse rendering requires differentiable renderers and gradient descent, which needs problem-specific engineering and often gets stuck in local minima due to ambiguities. Derivative-free methods reduce engineering needs but rely heavily on good initialization.
AI.method: FIDE treats the renderer as an opaque function (black-box), uses a Vision Transformer (ViT) to extract dense visual features from candidate renderings instead of reducing them to scalar loss, trains a diffusion-based candidate proposal model using these features, and refines proposals in a closed loop with CMA evolution strategy to narrow the proposal region.
AI.result: Validated across diverse inverse problems (path tracing, vector splines, Voronoi shaders, robotics). Feature-guiding substantially improves convergence over scalar-loss baselines and reliably escapes local minima where gradient-based methods stall.
AI.conclusion: FIDE provides a fully black-box, gradient-free, initialization-free framework for inverse rendering that effectively leverages visual features to escape local minima and improve convergence.

title: A Step Forward Towards Trustworthy Risk-Aware Facial Retrieval (RA-FR)
comment: Accepted at the 28th International Conference on Pattern Recognition (ICPR 2026). Extended version with additional citations and expanded sections
summary: Facial image retrieval in unconstrained surveillance environments is a high-stakes challenge where missing a subject of interest -- a single false negative -- is simply not an option. Despite near-perfect performance on curated benchmarks, current recognition systems falter under real-world domain shifts such as low resolution, motion blur, and uncontrolled illumination (e.g., SCFace). Addressing this reliability gap, we propose Risk-Aware Facial Retrieval (RA-FR), a framework that moves beyond fixed Top-$k$ retrieval to adaptive set generation, guaranteeing ground truth inclusion within a user-specified risk level ($α$) and confidence level ($1 - δ$). Our approach integrates three core contributions: (1) reducing aleatoric uncertainty via a hybrid blind face restoration technique coupling Latent Consistency Models (InterLCM) and DiffBIR; (2) extracting discriminative, restoration-robust features via self-supervised DINOv1 ViT-B with GGeM pooling; and (3) employing conformal prediction with Hoeffding's inequality to dynamically calibrate retrieval set sizes based on query uncertainty. On the IMFDB benchmark, it consistently satisfies a 5% risk target with an average retrieval set size of approximately 10 images. By unifying domain-specific restoration, robust representation learning, and provable decision rules, RA-FR offers a pipeline that makes facial retrieval in surveillance both reliable and auditable. The code is available at: https://github.com/MuhammadEmmadSiddiqui/RA-FR.

AI.tldr: RA-FR is a risk-aware facial retrieval framework for unconstrained surveillance that guarantees ground truth inclusion within specified risk and confidence levels by combining blind face restoration (InterLCM + DiffBIR), self-supervised DINOv1 ViT-B features with GGeM pooling, and conformal prediction with Hoeffding's inequality, achieving 5% risk target with ~10 average retrieval set size on IMFDB.
AI.motivation: Current facial recognition systems achieve near-perfect performance on curated benchmarks but fail under real-world domain shifts (low resolution, motion blur, uncontrolled illumination) where missing a subject (false negative) is unacceptable. Fixed Top-k retrieval cannot provide reliability guarantees in such unconstrained surveillance environments.
AI.method: (1) Hybrid blind face restoration (InterLCM + DiffBIR) to reduce aleatoric uncertainty; (2) Self-supervised DINOv1 ViT-B with GGeM pooling for discriminative, restoration-robust features; (3) Conformal prediction with Hoeffding's inequality to dynamically calibrate retrieval set sizes based on query uncertainty.
AI.result: On the IMFDB benchmark, RA-FR consistently satisfies a 5% risk target with an average retrieval set size of approximately 10 images.
AI.conclusion: By unifying domain-specific restoration, robust representation learning, and provable decision rules, RA-FR provides a reliable and auditable pipeline for facial retrieval in surveillance, moving beyond fixed Top-k to adaptive, risk-aware set generation.

title: When to Use Which? Benchmarking Optimisers for Configurable Systems under Varying Budgets
summary:
Software configuration tuning is crucial for optimising system performance, and various optimisers have emerged over the last decade. Yet, the time required during the tuning process may vary across systems. In some systems (e.g., PostgreSQL), it may take a few minutes to measure a configuration, whereas in some others (e.g., MariaDB), it can take several hours. Moreover, even within the same system, users may have varying budgets and preferred settings. This naturally raises a question -- Given a budget level, which optimiser is the best choice for SE practitioners? This matters because optimisers usually have their own ``comfort zone'' and may perform very differently under distinct budgets.
  In this paper, we aim to answer this question. We systematically evaluate eight well-established optimisers across 22 configurable systems under varying budget levels. We find that, unsurprisingly, model-based optimisers (e.g., SMAC) are well-suited under tight budgets, and model-free optimisers (e.g., GAs) become superior with more generous budgets. However, interestingly, there is one optimiser, FLASH, that performs consistently well on most systems regardless of budgets. We lastly investigate the reasons behind this phenomenon and find that many systems possess good local optima (with large basins of attraction), allowing greedy optimisers (e.g., FLASH) to achieve strong performance.
  Source code, data, and supplementary materials of this work are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Config-W2W-98B2.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates eight optimisers across 22 configurable systems under varying budget levels, finding that model-based optimisers (e.g., SMAC) work best under tight budgets, model-free optimisers (e.g., GAs) excel with generous budgets, and FLASH performs consistently well across most systems and budgets due to many systems having good local optima with large basins of attraction.
AI.motivation: Software configuration tuning time varies across systems and even within the same system users have different budgets and preferences. The key question is: given a budget level, which optimiser is the best choice for SE practitioners? This matters because optimisers have their own "comfort zone" and perform very differently under distinct budgets.
AI.method: Systematically evaluate eight well-established optimisers across 22 configurable systems under varying budget levels. Investigate reasons behind performance differences by analyzing system properties such as basins of attraction for local optima.
AI.result: Model-based optimisers (e.g., SMAC) are well-suited under tight budgets; model-free optimisers (e.g., GAs) become superior with more generous budgets. FLASH performs consistently well on most systems regardless of budgets. Many systems possess good local optima with large basins of attraction, benefiting greedy optimisers like FLASH.
AI.conclusion: The choice of optimiser for software configuration tuning should consider budget levels, but FLASH offers robust performance across diverse budgets and systems due to the prevalence of systems with favourable local optima landscapes.

title: LLM Unlearning for Cyber Defense: A Survey on Methods, Challenges, and Emerging Threats
summary: LLMs are increasingly deployed in security-critical systems across healthcare, finance, education, and decision support, yet their inability to forget creates serious cybersecurity, privacy, and safety risks. Sensitive personal information, copyrighted material, hazardous domain knowledge, and memorized training data remain encoded across billions of parameters long after deployment, leaving models vulnerable to extraction, jailbreak attacks, membership inference, and regulatory non-compliance. Real-world incidents, from chatbots regenerating private information to fabricated legal citations producing direct legal and financial cost, place the problem at the center of the emerging-threats landscape rather than the realm of speculation. Because retraining billion-parameter models on revised corpora is computationally infeasible, and because knowledge within an LLM is distributed and entangled across parameters rather than localized to identifiable units, LLM unlearning has emerged as the principal cyber defense response, aiming to remove or suppress targeted knowledge from a trained model without retraining and without eroding what the model should still know. A central question, however, remains unresolved. Do current methods genuinely remove knowledge, or do they only stop the model from expressing it under ordinary prompting conditions? This survey examines LLM unlearning through the lens of security, robustness, and verifiable forgetting, with primary focus on gradient-based methods, which have come to dominate the field due to their compatibility with existing training pipelines and their scalability to billion-parameter models.

AI.tldr: This survey examines LLM unlearning—the challenge of removing specific knowledge from trained models without retraining—focusing on gradient-based methods and questioning whether current approaches genuinely delete knowledge or merely suppress its expression under normal prompting.
AI.motivation: LLMs deployed in security-critical systems retain sensitive data (personal information, copyrighted material, hazardous knowledge) post-deployment, creating risks of extraction, jailbreak attacks, membership inference, and regulatory non-compliance. Retraining is computationally infeasible for billion-parameter models, and knowledge is distributed and entangled rather than localized, necessitating targeted unlearning as a cyber defense.
AI.method: This is a survey paper focusing on gradient-based LLM unlearning methods, which dominate the field due to their compatibility with existing training pipelines and scalability. The survey evaluates these methods through the lens of security, robustness, and verifiable forgetting.
AI.result: The paper identifies a central unresolved question: whether current unlearning methods genuinely remove knowledge or merely suppress its expression under ordinary prompting conditions. Real-world incidents (e.g., chatbots regenerating private information, fabricated legal citations causing financial harm) demonstrate the practical urgency of this problem.
AI.conclusion: The survey concludes that LLM unlearning is a critical but unresolved cyber defense mechanism, with gradient-based methods being the dominant approach. The core open challenge remains achieving verifiable forgetting—ensuring knowledge is truly removed rather than hidden—while preserving model utility for retained knowledge.

title: A Survey on GNN-based Link Prediction: Techniques, Applications, and Challenges
comment: Submmit to WIREs: Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery. This version of the article has been accepted, after peer review but is not the version of record. The final version will be available at: https://doi.org/10.1002/widm.70093. Paper list at Github: https://github.com/sunxiaobei/awesome-gnn-based-link-prediction
summary: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as the leading paradigm for link prediction, enabling the inference of missing connections and the anticipation of potential future links. However, existing reviews lack systematic exploration specifically targeting underlying GNN architectures and diverse graph structures. To address this critical gap, this paper provides a comprehensive review of GNN-based link prediction from a novel and dedicated GNN perspective. We propose an innovative taxonomy that categorizes recent advancements based on techniques and applications. From a technique perspective, we focus on key GNN encoder architectures, including GCN-based, GAE-based, GAT-based, and GFormer-based methods, discussing their strengths and limitations. From an application perspective, we highlight prominent use cases of link prediction in knowledge graphs and recommendation systems, demonstrating their real-world impact. In addition, we examine the current challenges and discuss promising future directions.

AI.tldr: This paper provides a comprehensive review of GNN-based link prediction, proposing a novel taxonomy based on GNN encoder architectures (GCN, GAE, GAT, GFormer) and applications (knowledge graphs, recommendation systems), while discussing challenges and future directions.
AI.motivation: Existing reviews lack systematic exploration specifically targeting underlying GNN architectures and diverse graph structures for link prediction, creating a critical gap that this paper aims to fill.
AI.method: The authors propose an innovative taxonomy categorizing recent advancements from two perspectives: (1) technique perspective focusing on key GNN encoder architectures (GCN-based, GAE-based, GAT-based, GFormer-based), and (2) application perspective highlighting use cases in knowledge graphs and recommendation systems.
AI.result: The paper systematically categorizes and discusses GNN-based link prediction methods across different encoder architectures and application domains, analyzing their strengths and limitations.
AI.conclusion: The review examines current challenges and discusses promising future directions for GNN-based link prediction research.

title: SSTMark: Robust Training-Free Semantic-Level Speech Watermarking
summary: As speech generation models become increasingly realistic and widely accessible, concerns about the misuse, attribution, and governance of synthetic speech continue to grow. Watermarking provides a practical way to make synthesized speech traceable and verifiable. Most existing speech watermarking methods embed watermark information into signal-level representations, such as waveforms or spectrograms. Under sufficiently strong distortions, the embedded watermark may be weakened or destroyed, leading to degraded detectability. In this paper, we propose SSTMark, a training-free speech watermarking framework that operates at the semantic level through text watermarking. Unlike conventional signal-level watermarking methods, SSTMark encodes watermark information into the semantic content conveyed by generated speech, and detects the watermark from the recovered linguistic content. Experiments on AudioMarkBench demonstrate that SSTMark exhibits the strongest average robustness. Compared with the state-of-the-art baselines at a fixed false positive rate of 1\%, SSTMark improves the average detection rate by 4.6\% and 16.9\% on signal-processing edits and compression edits, respectively.

AI.tldr: SSTMark is a training-free semantic-level speech watermarking framework that embeds watermarks into the linguistic content of generated speech rather than signal-level representations, achieving stronger robustness against distortions compared to existing methods.
AI.motivation: Growing realism and accessibility of speech generation models raise concerns about misuse, attribution, and governance of synthetic speech; existing signal-level watermarking methods suffer from degraded detectability under strong distortions.
AI.method: SSTMark operates at the semantic level by encoding watermark information into the semantic content (text) of generated speech, and detects watermarks from recovered linguistic content—a training-free approach unlike conventional waveform/spectrogram-based methods.
AI.result: On AudioMarkBench, SSTMark achieves the strongest average robustness; at a fixed 1% false positive rate, it improves average detection rate by 4.6% on signal-processing edits and 16.9% on compression edits over state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: Semantic-level watermarking offers a more robust alternative to signal-level methods for synthetic speech attribution, particularly under distortion-heavy conditions.

title: From Modalities to Propositions: A Language-Centric Framework for Multimodal Intelligence
summary: We propose a language representation for multimodal data in which any observation, whether image, video, or text, is expressed as a bag of atomic propositions, simple statements about the entities, actions, and relations in a scene. A global semantic codebook unifies these into a shared vocabulary of canonical atomic propositions, placing every modality and observation into one interpretable space that spans fine grained facts to high level concepts and composes into richer ones. This brings interpretability with reasoning, cross-modal understanding and retrieval, and compositionality that enables complex multimodal understanding, rich data curation and complex structured retrieval. We demonstrate the framework on autonomous driving and open-world data.

AI.tldr: Proposes a language representation for multimodal data using atomic propositions in a shared semantic codebook, enabling interpretability, reasoning, cross-modal understanding, compositionality, and structured retrieval across images, video, and text.
AI.motivation: To unify multimodal observations (image, video, text) into a single interpretable representation that supports reasoning, cross-modal retrieval, and compositionality, overcoming the lack of shared semantics between modalities.
AI.method: Represents any observation as a bag of atomic propositions (simple statements about entities, actions, relations) using a global semantic codebook of canonical propositions spanning fine-grained to high-level concepts, enabling composition into richer structures.
AI.result: Demonstrated on autonomous driving and open-world data, showing effectiveness for interpretability, reasoning, cross-modal understanding and retrieval, complex multimodal understanding, data curation, and structured retrieval.
AI.conclusion: A unified atomic proposition representation with a shared semantic codebook effectively bridges modalities and supports complex multimodal tasks while maintaining interpretability.

title: Fast VEM Fluid Simulation
summary: The intricate motion arising from fluid--boundary interactions is visually compelling, yet notoriously difficult and computationally expensive to simulate in the presence of complex boundaries. Accurately resolving boundary geometry requires body-fitted grids constructed via cut-cell methods, which often leads to poorly conditioned linear systems in the pressure projection stage and, consequently, prohibitive computational cost. We present FastVEM, an efficient boundary-conforming fluid simulation framework that enables high-fidelity flow--boundary interaction at substantially reduced cost. Computational efficiency is achieved through a coordinated, top-down design spanning numerical discretization, grid construction, and linear solvers. FastVEM adopts a Virtual Element Method (VEM) discretization to robustly enforce incompressibility and boundary conditions on irregular body-fitted grids, and employs a VEM polynomial-space Particle-in-Cell scheme for advection. Complementing this discretization, a convexity-preserving cut-cell strategy is introduced to construct simulation-friendly body-fitted grids. To accelerate pressure projection, we develop a Galerkin geometric multigrid solver featuring a diffusion-free prolongation operator that prevents coarse-level matrix densification, along with a nested, boundary-aware grid hierarchy that ensures well-posed placement of coarse-level degrees of freedom. Compared to prior cut-cell--based fluid simulators, FastVEM speeds up the computationally dominant pressure projection stage by up to 100x, while robustly handling even more challenging boundary geometries.

AI.tldr: FastVEM is an efficient boundary-conforming fluid simulation framework that speeds up pressure projection by up to 100x compared to prior cut-cell methods, using Virtual Element Method discretization, a convexity-preserving cut-cell grid strategy, and a diffusion-free Galerkin geometric multigrid solver.
AI.motivation: Fluid-boundary interactions are computationally expensive with traditional cut-cell methods due to poorly conditioned linear systems in pressure projection, making high-fidelity simulation with complex boundaries prohibitive.
AI.method: FastVEM combines VEM discretization for robust boundary conditions and incompressibility enforcement, a convexity-preserving cut-cell strategy for grid construction, a VEM polynomial-space PIC scheme for advection, and a Galerkin geometric multigrid solver with diffusion-free prolongation and nested boundary-aware grid hierarchy for pressure projection.
AI.result: Up to 100x speedup in the pressure projection stage compared to prior cut-cell-based fluid simulators, while handling more challenging boundary geometries robustly.
AI.conclusion: The coordinated top-down design over discretization, grid construction, and linear solvers enables substantial computational gains for high-fidelity flow-boundary interaction simulations.

title: 3D FaceShell: Attribute Transfer in 3D Face Avatars as a VLM Defense Mechanism
summary: Photorealistic 3D face avatars are increasingly deployed as reusable digital assets across applications such as telepresence, animation, and personalized media. At the same time, vision-language models (VLMs) can infer sensitive attributes from rendered images with open-ended semantic reasoning without any fine-tuning. This creates a new privacy challenge: once a 3D face avatar is shared, any of its renderings can be analyzed to extract high-level facial attributes. Existing defenses largely operate in 2D image space and do not address identity-preserving semantic manipulation of 3D facial representations. We propose 3D FaceShell, a framework for steering VLM interpretations of faces rendered from 3D models while preserving geometric fidelity and facial identity. 3D FaceShell augments the original 3D representation with a learnable Gaussian shell that produces subtle, spatially distributed perturbations optimized through multi-view embedding alignment. The perturbations are designed to be visually inconspicuous yet sufficient to redirect VLM-based attribute inference in a view-consistent manner. Extensive experiments on reconstructed celebrity face avatars and multiple black-box VLMs demonstrate that 3D FaceShell significantly increases attribute injection and mismatch rates while maintaining high perceptual similarity and identity consistency. Our results show that it is possible to manipulate VLM-level semantic interpretation of 3D faces without compromising their human-recognizable appearance.

AI.tldr: 3D FaceShell is a framework that adds learnable, subtle perturbations to 3D face avatars (via a Gaussian shell) to steer vision-language model (VLM) attribute inference, preserving geometric fidelity and identity while enabling semantic manipulation against privacy attacks.
AI.motivation: VLMs can infer sensitive attributes from rendered 2D images of 3D face avatars without fine-tuning, posing a privacy risk once avatars are shared. Existing defenses are limited to 2D image space and fail to address identity-preserving semantic manipulation of 3D facial representations.
AI.method: 3D FaceShell augments the original 3D representation with a learnable Gaussian shell, which produces subtle, spatially distributed perturbations optimized through multi-view embedding alignment. The perturbations are visually inconspicuous yet sufficient to redirect VLM-based attribute inference in a view-consistent manner.
AI.result: Experiments on reconstructed celebrity face avatars and multiple black-box VLMs show that 3D FaceShell significantly increases attribute injection and mismatch rates while maintaining high perceptual similarity and identity consistency.
AI.conclusion: It is possible to manipulate VLM-level semantic interpretation of 3D faces without compromising human-recognizable appearance, offering a viable privacy defense for 3D facial representations.

title: Personalized Assessments from Personal Artifacts
summary: The rapid development and popularization of AI-enabled coding agents have meant software engineering students and professionals cannot be assumed to understand their own code, which risks academic integrity and professional accountability. We developed a method called Personalized Probing Puzzles ($p^3$) to evaluate students' understanding of their own code, and tested $p^3$ in a graduate-level cloud computing course. Our pilot study shows that $p^3$ can help identify potential gaps in students' understanding of their own code. The puzzles are automatically generated, asynchronously administered, and finished in minutes. Future work is needed to correlate puzzle results with code understanding and to embed $p^3$ in a professional code review process.

AI.tldr: A pilot study on Personalized Probing Puzzles ($p^3$) that automatically generates puzzles to evaluate students' understanding of their own AI-generated code, showing potential to identify comprehension gaps.
AI.motivation: The rise of AI-enabled coding agents means students and professionals cannot be assumed to understand their own code, posing risks to academic integrity and professional accountability.
AI.method: Developed Personalized Probing Puzzles ($p^3$) to automatically generate, asynchronously administer, and quickly evaluate students' understanding of their own code; tested in a graduate-level cloud computing course.
AI.result: The pilot study shows $p^3$ can help identify potential gaps in students' understanding of their own code, with puzzles being finished in minutes.
AI.conclusion: Future work is needed to correlate puzzle results with code understanding and to embed $p^3$ in a professional code review process.

title: Operator-Aware Mixed-Precision Tolerance Calibration for Tensor Kernels
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, LNCS format. Companion paper: arXiv:2606.20128 (P1). Additional companions (P3, P4) to follow on arXiv this week; IDs will be added in a v2 replace
summary:
Most tensor-kernel correctness tests go through a fixed-shape all close-style check with hand-picked absolute and relative tolerances. The thresholds are copied across the corpus and rarely revisited. We mine the element-wise error distribution of every test case from accumulated cloud GPU runs across the 26-entry gpuemu corpus and 2 dtypes (8,076 result rows). We then ask one empirical question: what absolute tolerance would the kernel itself, observed under its correct implementation, justify?
  The answer is much tighter than the current hand-picked atol. The largest tightening is attention_triton fp16 at $2{,}184\times$. Restricted to the seven LLM-style buggy variants for which the corpus ships a paired correct counterpart, calibrated per-(op, dtype) tolerances raise bug-detection recall from 73.2% (1,805 of 2,467) to 82.4% (2,034 of 2,467), an absolute gain of 9.3 percentage points (+229 new detections). The control false-positive count rises from 0 to 20 out of 1,882 correct-control cases (+1.1 percentage points).

AI.tldr: By mining element-wise error distributions from 8,076 GPU runs across 26 kernels and 2 dtypes, the paper finds that data-driven calibrated tolerances are up to 2,184× tighter than hand-picked ones, improving LLM bug-detection recall from 73.2% to 82.4% with only a 1.1 pp false-positive increase.
AI.motivation: Current tensor-kernel correctness tests use fixed-shape all-close checks with hand-picked tolerances that are copied arbitrarily and rarely revisited, leading to imprecise thresholds.
AI.method: Mine element-wise error distributions from cloud GPU runs across the 26-entry gpuemu corpus with 2 dtypes (8,076 result rows); calibrate per-(op, dtype) absolute tolerances based on the kernel's own observed behavior under its correct implementation.
AI.result: Calibrated tolerances are up to 2,184× tighter (attention_triton fp16). On 7 LLM-style buggy variants, bug-detection recall improves from 73.2% (1,805/2,467) to 82.4% (2,034/2,467), a 9.3 pp gain (+229 detections), with false positives increasing from 0 to 20 out of 1,882 correct-control cases (+1.1 pp).
AI.conclusion: Data-driven tolerance calibration substantially improves bug detection sensitivity while maintaining low false-positive rates, suggesting that hand-picked tolerances should be replaced by empirically justified ones.

title: PlanFlip: Attacking Multi-Agent LLM Systems via Planning-Phase Prompt Injection
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly rely on a Planner to decompose goals into sub-task sequences that downstream Executor and Critic agents execute and audit. We identify the planning phase as a critical attack surface: a single injection into the Planner's context achieves cascade amplification, corrupting all downstream sub-tasks simultaneously. We introduce PlanFlip, a framework comprising four planning-phase prompt injection attacks -- GoalSubstitution (PF-1), PriorityInversion (PF-2), ContextPollution (PF-3), and RoleConfusion (PF-4) -- each disguised as plausible tool outputs to evade keyword filters. Evaluating nine frontier LLMs across 3,479 episodes, we uncover three findings: (1) capability amplifies vulnerability -- GPT-5 achieves the highest attack success rate (ASR = 0.68), contradicting the assumption that stronger models are inherently more secure; (2) homogeneous pipelines exhibit a correlated-agent blind spot -- GPT-4o and Llama-3.3-70B show ASR near 0 yet Stealth = 1.00 and StepShift > 0, with attacks restructuring plans while the same-backbone Critic reports alignment (two independent judges confirm -0.20 to -0.32 semantic deviation, r = 0.943); (3) reasoning-augmented models resist injections -- DeepSeek-R1 achieves StepShift = 0.00 across all attacks. We propose GoalAnchorCheck (D1) and CrossAgentConsensus (D2), achieving detection rates up to 1.00 and outperforming same-backbone baselines in 15 of 16 cells. Our key insight: heterogeneous model diversity is a security prerequisite for multi-agent systems; redundancy within a homogeneous backbone provides no protection against planning-phase attacks.

AI.tldr: PlanFlip introduces four planning-phase prompt injection attacks on multi-agent LLM systems, showing that stronger models are more vulnerable (GPT-5 ASR=0.68), homogeneous pipelines have correlated-agent blind spots, and reasoning-augmented models resist injections. Proposed defenses (GoalAnchorCheck, CrossAgentConsensus) achieve up to 1.00 detection rate, demonstrating that heterogeneous model diversity is a security prerequisite.
AI.motivation: The planning phase in multi-agent LLM systems (where a Planner decomposes goals into sub-tasks) is identified as a critical but underexplored attack surface. A single injection into the Planner's context can corrupt all downstream sub-tasks simultaneously via cascade amplification.
AI.method: PlanFlip framework: four planning-phase prompt injection attacks (GoalSubstitution PF-1, PriorityInversion PF-2, ContextPollution PF-3, RoleConfusion PF-4) disguised as plausible tool outputs. Evaluated on nine frontier LLMs across 3,479 episodes. Proposed defenses: GoalAnchorCheck (D1) and CrossAgentConsensus (D2).
AI.result: (1) Capability amplifies vulnerability: GPT-5 achieves highest ASR (0.68). (2) Homogeneous pipelines show correlated-agent blind spot: GPT-4o and Llama-3.3-70B have ASR near 0 but Stealth=1.00 and StepShift>0, with Critic reporting alignment despite restructured plans (-0.20 to -0.32 semantic deviation, r=0.943). (3) Reasoning-augmented models resist: DeepSeek-R1 achieves StepShift=0.00 across all attacks. Defenses achieve detection rates up to 1.00, outperforming baselines in 15/16 cells.
AI.conclusion: Heterogeneous model diversity is a security prerequisite for multi-agent systems; redundancy within a homogeneous backbone provides no protection against planning-phase attacks.

title: Re-Sonance: A Dysarthric Asynchronous Real-Time Speech Conversion System Based on a Three-Stage Cascaded ASR-LLM-TTS Architecture
summary: Individuals with dysarthria face significant challenges in professional speaking scenarios such as conferences, presentations, and meetings, where real-time communication is crucial. While existing Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) systems provide basic support, they often fail to meet the demands of professional speaking environments due to high latency and unnatural speech patterns. This paper presents Re-Sonance, a novel LLM-enhanced speech-driven AAC system designed for real-time professional speaking scenarios. By integrating Whisper ASR, Qwen LLM, and CosyVoice TTS, Re-Sonance achieves improved speech intelligibility and naturalness while maintaining real-time performance. Both subjective and objective evaluations using a Mandarin dysarthric speech dataset demonstrate that our speech reconstruction approach significantly improved intelligibility while preserving semantic coherence for speakers with mild to moderate dysarthria. Although performance remains limited for severe dysarthria cases, our findings validate the potential of LLM-based methods for enhancing speech-driven AAC systems, paving the way for more effective and accessible communication technologies.

AI.tldr: Re-Sonance is an LLM-enhanced speech-driven AAC system that integrates Whisper ASR, Qwen LLM, and CosyVoice TTS to improve speech intelligibility and naturalness for individuals with dysarthria in real-time professional speaking scenarios, showing significant improvements for mild-to-moderate cases but limited performance for severe dysarthria.
AI.motivation: Existing AAC systems fail to meet the demands of professional speaking environments (conferences, presentations, meetings) for individuals with dysarthria due to high latency and unnatural speech patterns, motivating the need for a real-time, intelligible, and natural solution.
AI.method: The system integrates three components: Whisper ASR for speech recognition, Qwen LLM for language enhancement, and CosyVoice TTS for speech synthesis, forming a pipeline that reconstructs dysarthric speech into clearer, more natural output in real time.
AI.result: Subjective and objective evaluations on a Mandarin dysarthric speech dataset showed significantly improved intelligibility and preserved semantic coherence for mild-to-moderate dysarthria, but performance remained limited for severe cases.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based methods show strong potential for enhancing speech-driven AAC systems, paving the way for more effective and accessible communication technologies, though further work is needed for severe dysarthria.

title: Packet-Loss Robust 3D Gaussian Compression via Atomic Packaging and GNN-based Error Concealment
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) and recent compression schemes such as HAC++ enable high-fidelity real-time neural rendering, but their bitstreams are fragile under packet loss during network streaming. Existing compression methods often separate correlated anchor attributes into independent streams, so losing one packet can create attribute-inconsistent broken anchors and severe rendering artifacts. We propose a packet-loss robust 3DGS transmission and error concealment framework. On the encoder side, anchor-level atomic packaging jointly encapsulates all attributes of each anchor, converting corrupted-attribute failures into clean missing-anchor erasures. Stratified random grouping further disperses packet losses across the spatial domain to avoid large contiguous voids. On the decoder side, we formulate recovery as prior-aware attribute inpainting. A Context-Aware Residual Interpolation (CARI) branch uses hash-grid prior predictions and neighboring residuals to build a robust baseline, while a lightweight two-layer graph neural network with cross-attention over hash-grid priors refines high-frequency attribute residuals. Attribute-wise confidence control falls back to interpolation when learned predictions are unreliable. Experiments under 20 percent random packet loss on BungeeNeRF, Mip-NeRF 360, and Tanks and Temples show that the proposed method substantially improves over no-concealment transmission and limits average PSNR degradation to about 3 dB relative to the lossless HAC++ reference.

AI.tldr: Proposes a robust 3DGS transmission framework with anchor-level atomic packaging and stratified random grouping on the encoder side, plus a Context-Aware Residual Interpolation and lightweight graph neural network for error concealment on the decoder side, limiting PSNR degradation to ~3 dB under 20% packet loss.
AI.motivation: 3DGS bitstreams are fragile under packet loss during network streaming because existing compression methods separate correlated anchor attributes into independent streams, causing attribute-inconsistent broken anchors and severe rendering artifacts.
AI.method: Encoder: anchor-level atomic packaging (joint encapsulation of all attributes per anchor) + stratified random grouping to spatially disperse packet losses. Decoder: prior-aware attribute inpainting via Context-Aware Residual Interpolation (CARI) using hash-grid priors and neighboring residuals, plus a lightweight two-layer graph neural network with cross-attention for high-frequency residual refinement, with attribute-wise confidence control.
AI.result: Under 20% random packet loss on BungeeNeRF, Mip-NeRF 360, and Tanks and Temples, the method substantially improves over no-concealment transmission and limits average PSNR degradation to about 3 dB relative to lossless HAC++ reference.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively mitigates packet-loss-induced rendering artifacts in 3DGS streaming, achieving robust performance close to lossless quality.

title: Moving Like a Human: Ego-Motion-Normalized Temporal Signatures for Real-Time Aerial Person Tracking on Milliwatt-Class Hardware
summary: Follow-me person tracking must run on the drone itself, where affordable companion computers offer only a few effective int8 GFLOP/s. At typical follow distances a person spans 10-60 pixels, indistinguishable from clutter and beyond the reach of single-frame appearance detectors. The missing evidence is temporal and belongs in the input representation, computed analytically, rather than in learned temporal machinery. EMTS-Det is a five-stage system that estimates ego-motion, converts each frame into ego-motion-normalized residual-motion channels, detects person centers with a 22k-parameter, 7.6-MFLOP network, tracks a locked target with a Kalman filter in stabilized coordinates, and verifies tracks with a 1-D convolutional classifier of human motion (ROC AUC 0.941). Training uses a synthetic-motion curriculum with motion channels generated by the deployed ego-motion code. Multi-seed ablations locate the value in generalization: on held-out VisDrone-DET a luminance-only variant collapses to 0.051 AP25 versus 0.415, as does YOLOv8n fine-tuned identically despite 1,100 times the compute, while the deployed int8 detector reaches 0.694 AP25 in-domain and 0.444 on this split. Temporal-shift modules lower accuracy, so the deployed detector is stateless. Silent int8 calibration failures are documented; min-max calibration with propagated caches matches float within 0.008 AP. On a Raspberry Pi Zero 2W the pipeline runs at 31.85 FPS with 0.462 AP25 and 0.714 recall over 1,000 real-world UAV videos, versus 1.95 FPS and 0.172 AP25 for YOLOv8n. A 57-second field sequence shows auto-lock at 1.3 s, 97.9% lock recall, and recovery from all nine occlusions with zero false re-locks.

AI.tldr: EMTS-Det is a lightweight, stateless detector for drone-based person tracking that uses ego-motion-normalized residual-motion channels and a tiny 22k-parameter network to achieve real-time performance (31.85 FPS) on a Raspberry Pi Zero 2W, with significantly higher accuracy (0.462 AP25) than YOLOv8n (0.172 AP25) despite using 1,100x less compute.
AI.motivation: Person tracking on drones must run on-board with limited compute (few int8 GFLOP/s), but at typical follow distances persons appear as tiny 10-60 pixel targets indistinguishable from clutter, making single-frame appearance detectors ineffective. The missing temporal evidence should be incorporated into the input representation analytically rather than through learned temporal mechanisms.
AI.method: A five-stage system: (1) ego-motion estimation, (2) conversion of each frame into ego-motion-normalized residual-motion channels, (3) detection of person centers using a 22k-parameter, 7.6-MFLOP network, (4) Kalman filter tracking in stabilized coordinates, and (5) track verification via a 1-D convolutional classifier of human motion. Training uses a synthetic-motion curriculum with motion channels from deployed ego-motion code.
AI.result: On VisDrone-DET: luminance-only variant collapses to 0.051 AP25 vs 0.415; deployed int8 detector achieves 0.694 AP25 in-domain and 0.444 on held-out split. On Raspberry Pi Zero 2W: 31.85 FPS with 0.462 AP25 and 0.714 recall vs YOLOv8n at 1.95 FPS and 0.172 AP25. Field test: auto-lock at 1.3s, 97.9% lock recall, recovery from 9 occlusions with zero false re-locks.
AI.conclusion: Temporal evidence belongs in the input representation (motion channels computed analytically) rather than in learned temporal modules, as temporal-shift modules lower accuracy and the stateless detector outperforms compute-heavy alternatives. Silent int8 calibration failures are documented and mitigated with min-max calibration using propagated caches.

title: ReqGenX: An Empirical Study of Atomic Decomposition, Artifact Regeneration, and Reconstruction for Legacy SRS Documents
comment: Accepted at the International Symposium on Empirical Software Engineering and Measurement (ESEM) technical papers (main) track 2026
summary: Background: Evaluating automated Software Requirements Specification (SRS) generation is challenging because few datasets provide fine-grained traceability between source requirements, intermediate elicitation artifacts, and generated specifications. Aims: We aim to study whether legacy SRS documents can be transformed into traceable synthetic pre-SRS artifacts that support fine-grained evaluation of LLM-based SRS generation. Method: We conduct an empirical study using ReqGenX, a controlled pipeline that decomposes SRS sections into source-grounded atomic statements, routes atoms to standards-inspired artifact types through multi-LLM plurality voting, and generates artifacts using constrained prompts with iterative judge-guided refinement. We evaluate ReqGenX on seven PURE SRS documents using grounding, quality, information retention, and downstream reconstruction analyses. Results: ReqGenX produces faithful and usable atoms, with median AlignScore values typically between 0.96 and 0.99 and Prometheus scores ranging from 4.34 to 4.85. Generated artifacts remain strongly grounded in their source atoms, with AlignScore values typically between 0.80--0.94 and judge pass rates near 100%; stricter Prometheus evaluation yields pass rates from 54.8% to 97.1%. In a downstream SRS reconstruction case study, artifact-backed atoms remain recoverable from generated SRSs, with SBERT means between 0.69 and 0.75 and AlignScore medians between 0.76 and 0.84. Conclusions: Traceable synthetic pre-SRS artifacts can support more fine-grained evaluation of LLM-based SRS generation, while exposing tradeoffs among faithfulness, information retention, and artifact completeness.

AI.tldr: ReqGenX transforms legacy SRS documents into traceable synthetic pre-SRS artifacts using a controlled pipeline with atomic decomposition, multi-LLM voting, and iterative refinement. Evaluated on seven PURE documents, it achieves high faithfulness (AlignScore 0.96-0.99) and downstream recoverability (SBERT 0.69-0.75), enabling fine-grained evaluation of LLM-based SRS generation while exposing tradeoffs among faithfulness, information retention, and artifact completeness.
AI.motivation: Evaluating automated SRS generation is difficult due to the lack of datasets with fine-grained traceability between source requirements, elicitation artifacts, and generated specifications.
AI.method: ReqGenX pipeline decomposes SRS sections into source-grounded atomic statements, routes atoms to standards-inspired artifact types via multi-LLM plurality voting, and generates artifacts using constrained prompts with iterative judge-guided refinement.
AI.result: Median AlignScore 0.96-0.99 for atoms, Prometheus scores 4.34-4.85. Generated artifacts have AlignScore 0.80-0.94, judge pass rates near 100%, Prometheus pass rates 54.8%-97.1%. Downstream SBERT means 0.69-0.75, AlignScore medians 0.76-0.84.
AI.conclusion: Traceable synthetic pre-SRS artifacts enable more fine-grained evaluation of LLM-based SRS generation while exposing tradeoffs among faithfulness, information retention, and artifact completeness.

title: RouteCost: A Production-Inspired Multi-Stage Framework for Pre-Order Shipping Cost Estimation in E-Commerce
summary: Accurate pre-order shipping cost estimation is important in e-commerce because it affects price presentation, margin planning, and conversion. In practice, shipping cost is shaped not only by distance but also by destination demand mix, billable weight, dimensional pricing, surcharge triggers, and latent operational effects such as shipment consolidation. Static lookup methods therefore miss important sources of variation, while monolithic regressors may exploit strong but non-causal correlations. We propose RouteCost, a production-inspired multi-stage framework that decomposes the problem into time-aware demand forecasting, fee-card-informed baseline pricing, Stage 2 residual correction, and proxy-based box-consolidation inference. Route-level cost estimates are aggregated through a route-weighted expectation formulation to produce product-level shipping cost predictions. Across over 250,000 orders, 260 products, and 18 months of order history, the framework improves predictive quality and aggregate calibration while preserving route-level interpretability.

AI.tldr: RouteCost is a multi-stage framework for e-commerce shipping cost estimation that decomposes the problem into demand forecasting, fee-card-based baseline pricing, residual correction, and box-consolidation inference, improving predictive quality and calibration across 250K+ orders and 260 products.
AI.motivation: Accurate pre-order shipping cost estimation is critical for price presentation, margin planning, and conversion in e-commerce, but static lookup methods miss important cost variation sources and monolithic regressors exploit non-causal correlations.
AI.method: A production-inspired multi-stage framework (RouteCost) decomposing the problem into: (1) time-aware demand forecasting, (2) fee-card-informed baseline pricing, (3) Stage 2 residual correction, and (4) proxy-based box-consolidation inference. Route-level estimates are aggregated via route-weighted expectation formulation for product-level predictions.
AI.result: Across over 250,000 orders, 260 products, and 18 months of history, the framework improves predictive quality and aggregate calibration while preserving route-level interpretability.
AI.conclusion: The multi-stage decomposition approach outperforms both static lookup methods and monolithic regressors for shipping cost estimation, achieving better accuracy and calibration with inherent interpretability.

title: Deterministic Replay for AI Agent Systems
summary:
AI agent systems that couple large language models (LLMs) with external tools and APIs are inherently non-deterministic: LLM sampling variance, external API state, CDN infrastructure headers, and execution-environment noise collectively prevent any prior agent run from being faithfully re-executed. Existing observability platforms capture execution logs but cannot reproduce a run in isolation. We present agrepl, a developer-first CLI framework for deterministic replay of agent executions. agrepl intercepts all external interactions at the transport layer via a man-in-the-middle (MITM) proxy, serialises them as structured execution traces, and replays them in a strictly isolated environment with zero outbound network access. We formalise the agent execution model, define the request-key matching function K(s), and prove the determinism invariant. We introduce a noise-aware diff algorithm classifying HTTP header divergence into signal and noise tiers. Empirical evaluation across five workloads (n = 250 replay instances) demonstrates replay fidelity F = 1.0 and a median per-step latency reduction of 98.3%. agrepl is implemented in Go, ships as a single static binary, and is released under the MIT licence.
  Keywords: AI agents, deterministic replay, LLM debugging, reproducibility, MITM proxy, execution tracing, record/replay systems.

AI.tldr: agrepl is a CLI framework for deterministic replay of LLM-based AI agent executions. It uses a MITM proxy to intercept and record all external interactions at the transport layer, then replays them in an isolated environment with zero network access. It achieves perfect replay fidelity (F=1.0) and 98.3% median per-step latency reduction across five workloads.
AI.motivation: AI agent systems coupling LLMs with external tools are inherently non-deterministic due to LLM sampling variance, external API state, CDN infrastructure headers, and execution-environment noise. Existing observability platforms capture logs but cannot reproduce runs in isolation, making debugging and reproducibility difficult.
AI.method: agrepl intercepts all external interactions at the transport layer via a MITM proxy, serializes them as structured execution traces, and replays them in a strictly isolated environment with zero outbound network access. It formalizes the agent execution model with a request-key matching function K(s) and a noise-aware diff algorithm for classifying HTTP header divergence into signal and noise tiers.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across five workloads (n=250 replay instances) demonstrates replay fidelity F=1.0 and median per-step latency reduction of 98.3%.
AI.conclusion: agrepl enables fully deterministic replay of AI agent executions despite the non-deterministic nature of the underlying systems. It is implemented in Go as a single static binary and released under the MIT license.

title: Time-Frequency Consistency Learning for Robust Speech Deepfake Detection
summary: Recently, speech deepfake detection (SDD) has achieved significant progress. However, its robustness evaluation remains largely confined to controlled additive noise scenarios, lacking systematic investigation of the complex distortions introduced by acoustic front-end (AFE) processing pipelines in real-world deployments. In this work, we simulate a unified AFE pipeline comprising acoustic echo cancellation, noise suppression, automatic gain control, and voice activity detection (VAD), and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of current state-of-the-art models. The results show that the nonlinear and time-frequency coupled distortions introduced by AFE significantly degrade detection performance. To address this issue, we propose a Time-Frequency Consistency Learning (TFCL) framework, which aims to learn invariant spoofing representations that remain stable before and after AFE processing. We observe that AFE not only introduces temporal misalignment (e.g., segment-level shifts caused by VAD), but also weakens or distorts critical frequency-domain cues. To this end, TFCL employs an attention-driven soft alignment mechanism to capture cross-temporal dependencies, along with frequency-domain structural consistency constraints to enforce feature invariance. As a result, the model is able to maintain stable representations under both temporal perturbations and spectral distortions. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively mitigates the performance degradation caused by AFE processing, significantly improving the robustness of SDD in real-world scenarios. The code is available at https://github.com/JunXue-tech/TFCL.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how real-world acoustic front-end (AFE) processing (echo cancellation, noise suppression, AGC, VAD) degrades speech deepfake detection (SDD) performance, and proposes a Time-Frequency Consistency Learning (TFCL) framework using attention-driven soft alignment and frequency-domain structural consistency to learn AFE-invariant spoofing representations, significantly improving robustness.
AI.motivation: Existing SDD robustness evaluation is limited to controlled additive noise scenarios, lacking systematic study of complex nonlinear, time-frequency coupled distortions introduced by real-world AFE processing pipelines.
AI.method: Proposes Time-Frequency Consistency Learning (TFCL) framework with: (1) an attention-driven soft alignment mechanism to handle temporal misalignment (e.g., VAD-induced segment shifts), and (2) frequency-domain structural consistency constraints to enforce feature invariance against spectral distortions caused by AFE.
AI.result: AFE processing significantly degrades state-of-the-art SDD performance; the proposed TFCL effectively mitigates this degradation and improves SDD robustness in real-world scenarios.
AI.conclusion: TFCL enables stable spoofing representations under both temporal perturbations and spectral distortions from AFE processing, offering a practical solution for deploying SDD in real-world acoustic environments.

title: Look Clearly Before Answering: Mitigating Hallucinations in LVLMs via Saliency-Driven Perceptual Realignment
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in multimodal understanding. However, they remain prone to hallucinations, generating responses that are inconsistent with the visual evidence. Existing mitigation methods largely address language-prior bias or cross-modal imbalance, while progressive visual degradation across perception and memory remains underexplored. In this work, we propose Saliency-Driven Perceptual Realignment (SDPR), a training-free framework that mitigates the degradation of visual awareness throughout inference. Specifically, we first introduce saliency-driven attention redistribution to release attention hijacked by non-semantic sink tokens, thereby recovering critical visual evidence. Second, we identify spatial distortion in the KV cache and propose saliency-driven cache alignment to preserve query-relevant visual features during generation. Finally, we introduce prior-constrained contrastive decoding to penalize unfaithful predictions induced by dominant language priors. Our proposed SDPR is robust against hallucinations due to its holistic alignment of visual awareness across the entire generative trajectory. Extensive experiments across diverse LVLM architectures show that SDPR outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both hallucination and general-purpose benchmarks, requiring no additional training and incurring minimal runtime overhead. The code is available \href{https://github.com/PengSyuChen/SDPR}{\color{blue}{here}}.

AI.tldr: SDPR is a training-free framework that mitigates hallucinations in LVLMs by realigning visual awareness through saliency-driven attention redistribution, cache alignment, and contrastive decoding, outperforming SOTA methods on both hallucination and general benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LVLMs hallucinate due to progressive visual degradation across perception and memory during inference, which is underexplored by existing methods that mostly address language-prior bias or cross-modal imbalance.
AI.method: SDPR consists of three components: (1) saliency-driven attention redistribution to release attention hijacked by non-semantic sink tokens; (2) saliency-driven cache alignment to preserve query-relevant visual features in the KV cache; (3) prior-constrained contrastive decoding to penalize unfaithful predictions from dominant language priors.
AI.result: SDPR outperforms state-of-the-art methods on both hallucination and general-purpose benchmarks across diverse LVLM architectures, requiring no additional training and minimal runtime overhead.
AI.conclusion: Holistic alignment of visual awareness across the entire generative trajectory is effective for robust hallucination mitigation, and training-free approaches can achieve SOTA performance.

title: EVOLVE: Efficient Learned Volume Compression with Variable-Rate Encoding on a Cross-Domain Database
comment: To be published in Proceedings of IEEE VIS 2026, IEEE Transactions on Visualization and Computer Graphics
summary: Large-scale scientific simulations generate volumetric data at rates that far outpace advances in storage and network bandwidth, making effective lossy compression increasingly critical. However, conventional compressors often struggle to preserve fine structural details at high compression ratios (CRs), and implicit neural representations (INRs) require costly per-volume optimization and produce models with fixed CRs. To respond, we present EVOLVE, an autoencoder (AE)-based volume-compression framework that targets high CRs for offline compression, with three key contributions. First, we construct a large-scale cross-domain database of 6,376 volumes from 21 scientific simulations, curated via perceptual hashing to ensure diversity, enabling the optimized model to extract features that generalize across volumes within the covered scientific simulation domains. Second, we reexamine the design space of AE-based compressors and incorporate several macro- and micro-designs into a vanilla AE to develop EVOLVE, which substantially improves the expressive power and compression capability. Third, we develop a learnable gain mechanism with a three-stage training strategy to enable variable-rate encoding, allowing a single model to support continuous CR adjustment at inference time. Experiments on multiple unseen scientific simulation datasets demonstrate that EVOLVE achieves substantially higher CRs than conventional compressors at comparable reconstruction quality, while delivering compression speeds that are orders of magnitude faster than INR-based methods, highlighting its promise as a strong alternative for compressing scientific data. The code, model weights, and results are available on our project page at https://evolve-vis.github.io.

AI.tldr: EVOLVE is an autoencoder-based volume compression framework for scientific simulations that, by leveraging a large curated cross-domain training database, enhanced AE architecture designs, and a learnable variable-rate mechanism, achieves substantially higher compression ratios than conventional methods with reconstruction quality comparable to or better than existing approaches, and runs orders of magnitude faster than INR-based methods.
AI.motivation: Large-scale scientific simulations produce volumetric data far exceeding storage and network bandwidth capacities, making effective lossy compression critical. Existing compressors struggle to preserve fine structural details at high compression ratios, and implicit neural representations require costly per-volume optimization with fixed compression ratios, motivating a need for a more efficient and flexible approach.
AI.method: The method consists of three key components: (1) construction of a large-scale cross-domain database of 6,376 volumes from 21 scientific simulations, curated via perceptual hashing for diversity; (2) reexamination of autoencoder design space with macro- and micro-designs to build EVOLVE, enhancing expressive power and compression capability; (3) a learnable gain mechanism with a three-stage training strategy enabling variable-rate encoding, allowing a single model to support continuous CR adjustment at inference time.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple unseen scientific simulation datasets show EVOLVE achieves substantially higher compression ratios than conventional compressors at comparable reconstruction quality, with compression speeds orders of magnitude faster than INR-based methods.
AI.conclusion: EVOLVE demonstrates strong promise as an alternative for compressing scientific data, offering a favorable trade-off between compression ratio, reconstruction quality, and speed. The code, model weights, and results are publicly available.

title: GenSyn10: A Multi-Generative AI Dataset For Benchmarking Image Classification
summary: The rapid advancement of generative AI has outpaced our ability to reliably detect its outputs, particularly when detectors encounter generators they have not seen before. We introduce GenSyn10, a CIFAR-10-aligned synthetic image dataset of 60,000 images (10 classes, 32$\times$32, 50k/10k split) generated using three architecturally diverse state-of-the-art models: FLUX.2-dev (Rectified Flow Transformer), HunyuanImage-3.0 (MoE Transformer), and Qwen-Image-2512 (Multimodal Diffusion Transformer), to advance research in AI-generated image detection. A central challenge in this domain is that detectors perform well on known generators but degrade on unseen ones. GenSyn10 addresses this limitation by curating data from multiple contemporary architectures under a standardized generation protocol, enabling controlled and systematic evaluation of out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization to novel generators. Images are generated using a template-based prompt engine and downsampled to ensure consistency. We evaluate 17 image classification models under a four-stage protocol: real-data baseline, zero-shot transfer, fine-tuning, and retention. Despite a measurable domain gap, CIFAR-10-trained models achieve up to 96.86\% zero-shot accuracy on GenSyn10, increasing to 99.88\% after fine-tuning. In binary real-vs-synthetic classification, fine-tuned models achieve 97-99.9\% accuracy on seen generators but drop to 79-96\% on images from an unseen generator, highlighting persistent limitations in OOD generalization. These results establish GenSyn10 as a controlled benchmark for studying synthetic image detection beyond single-generator settings, supporting research on robustness, domain adaptation, and cross-generator generalization.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces GenSyn10, a CIFAR-10-aligned synthetic image dataset (60k images, 10 classes, 32×32) generated by three architecturally diverse models (FLUX.2-dev, HunyuanImage-3.0, Qwen-Image-2512) to benchmark AI-generated image detection, particularly studying generalization to unseen generators. Evaluations on 17 classifiers show high accuracy on seen generators (97-99.9%) but significant degradation on unseen ones (79-96%), highlighting persistent OOD generalization challenges.
AI.motivation: Generative AI has advanced faster than detection methods; detectors fail on unseen generators, and existing benchmarks lack controlled, multi-architecture settings to study this OOD generalization problem systematically.
AI.method: GenSyn10 dataset created using three architecturally distinct SOTA models with a template-based prompt engine, downsampled to 32×32 for CIFAR-10 alignment. Evaluated 17 image classifiers under four stages: real-data baseline, zero-shot transfer, fine-tuning, and retention (binary real-vs-synthetic classification).
AI.result: Zero-shot accuracy on GenSyn10 reaches 96.86%, improves to 99.88% after fine-tuning. Binary classification achieves 97-99.9% on seen generators but drops to 79-96% on unseen generators, demonstrating a persistent OOD generalization gap.
AI.conclusion: GenSyn10 serves as a controlled benchmark for synthetic image detection beyond single-generator settings, enabling research on robustness, domain adaptation, and cross-generator generalization.

title: From Discussion to Execution: Replicating Buggy and Correct Data Science Code
comment: accepted at the 37th IEEE International Symposium on Software Reliability Engineering (ISSRE 2026)
summary: Reproducing reliable data science code from informal sources is challenging due to ambiguous problem specifications, missing dependencies, and performance bottlenecks. Although developer Q&A forums provide rich discussions on diagnosing and fixing real-world issues, the information is often incomplete and unstructured, limiting its use for automated debugging and verification. In this paper, we introduce Reprodgen, a large language model (LLM) based framework for automatically replicating executable buggy and patched data science programs from Q&A forum posts. Given a question and its corresponding answer, Reprodgen reconstructs the buggy behavior described in the question and the intended fix described in the answer, producing executable buggy and patched code pairs that reflect the original discussion. The framework builds structured representations of code intent (CI), functional requirements (FR), and Structured Chain of Thought (SCoT), and iteratively refines code using an LLM-based reviewer until it is executable and semantically consistent. We evaluate Reprodgen on Stack Overflow (SO) and GitHub Issues (GI) across seven data science libraries, including pandas, numpy, and scikit-learn, and construct a benchmark of runnable buggy and patched programs validated by human experts. Our pipeline uses LLMs for semantic assessment, while executability is verified through actual execution. Results show reliable replication with clear differences in model performance.

AI.tldr: Reprodgen is an LLM-based framework that automatically generates executable buggy and patched data science code pairs from Q&A forum posts by reconstructing buggy behavior and intended fixes using structured representations (CI, FR, SCoT) and iterative LLM-based refinement.
AI.motivation: Reproducing reliable data science code from informal sources (e.g., Q&A forums) is challenging due to ambiguous problem specifications, missing dependencies, and performance bottlenecks. The information in developer forums is often incomplete and unstructured, limiting its use for automated debugging and verification.
AI.method: The framework uses LLMs to build structured representations of Code Intent (CI), Functional Requirements (FR), and Structured Chain of Thought (SCoT), then iteratively refines code via an LLM-based reviewer until executable and semantically consistent. Evaluation uses LLMs for semantic assessment and actual execution for executability verification.
AI.result: Evaluated on Stack Overflow and GitHub Issues across seven data science libraries (pandas, numpy, scikit-learn, etc.), producing a human-validated benchmark of runnable buggy and patched programs. Results show reliable replication with clear differences in model performance.
AI.conclusion: Reprodgen demonstrates that automated replication of executable code pairs from informal Q&A discussions is feasible, enabling more systematic use of forum content for debugging and verification tasks in data science.

title: Orthogonal Gradient Constraints Shape Noisy-Label Memorization Dynamics
comment: 7 pages, accepted into the ICML HiLD workshop 2026 @Seoul
summary: Modern neural networks can fit corrupted training labels, making noisy-label learning a useful setting for studying memorization-driven overfitting. Most regularization methods modify the objective, architecture, or data distribution; here we instead study a geometric intervention on the optimizer update itself. We evaluate OrthoGrad, which removes the component of each weight gradient parallel to the current weight vector, in noisy-label image classification. On MNIST with small-data regimes, OrthoGrad improves test accuracy most clearly for CNNs while reducing corrupted-label fitting. Mechanism diagnostics based on weight norms and gradient-weight cosine similarity suggest that the projection has the strongest effect when the raw gradient contains a nontrivial radial component, and becomes weaker in larger-data regimes where gradients are already nearly orthogonal to weights. Additional CIFAR-10 ResNet-18 experiments show that the method can alter memorization trajectories but does not prevent eventual noisy-label memorization. These results support orthogonal update constraints as a useful diagnostic for studying learning dynamics, while showing that OrthoGrad is regime-dependent rather than universally regularizing.

AI.tldr: This paper studies OrthoGrad, a geometric intervention on optimizer updates that removes the radial component of gradients, showing it can reduce memorization of corrupted labels in small-data CNN regimes but is not universally regularizing.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether a geometric constraint on optimizer updates—removing the gradient component parallel to weights—can serve as an alternative to traditional regularization methods for mitigating memorization-driven overfitting in noisy-label learning.
AI.method: OrthoGrad projects gradients onto the subspace orthogonal to the current weight vector, removing the radial component. Evaluated on noisy-label image classification with MNIST (CNNs, small-data regimes) and CIFAR-10 (ResNet-18), comparing test accuracy and corrupted-label fitting against baselines. Mechanism diagnostics via weight norms and gradient-weight cosine similarity.
AI.result: OrthoGrad improves test accuracy most clearly for CNNs on MNIST in small-data regimes while reducing corrupted-label fitting. The effect is strongest when raw gradients have nontrivial radial components, and weaker in larger-data regimes where gradients are already nearly orthogonal to weights. On CIFAR-10 ResNet-18, OrthoGrad alters memorization trajectories but does not prevent eventual noisy-label memorization.
AI.conclusion: Orthogonal update constraints serve as a useful diagnostic tool for studying learning dynamics. However, OrthoGrad is regime-dependent rather than a universally effective regularizer; its benefit diminishes in larger-data settings.

title: Generative Ontology Induction: Domain-Agnostic Schema Discovery from Document Corpora Using Large Language Models
summary:
Ontology engineering remains a critical bottleneck in knowledge-intensive AI systems. Existing automated approaches either depend on predefined schemas, operate within narrow domains, or produce unstructured outputs unsuitable for downstream pipelines.
  We introduce Generative Ontology Induction (GOI), a domain-agnostic framework that induces a generative blueprint - entities, dimensions, properties, relationships, and constraints - from a corpus of examples and exports it as a typed graph (six node types, seven edge types) in YAML/JSON. We introduce the Node Coverage Score, a novel evaluation metric that measures the fraction of structural ontology nodes (classes, properties, and dimensions) appearing in generated outputs.
  A controlled generative validation on four contrasting ontologies - a familiar Software Services Invoice schema, a custom Job Description Ontology, a confidential Pain-Management Clinical Visit Record Ontology, and a Professional Services Contract & Statement of Work Ontology - shows that GOI-prompted generation covers 95-100% of the structural backbone in every case; a generic three-field template holds at 97.8% on the invoice schema but drops to 52.2% on the Job Description Ontology, 62.2% on the Pain-Management ontology, and 78.3% on the Professional Services Contract ontology. The structural coverage holds regardless of how familiar the document type is to the model.

AI.tldr: GOI induces a typed graph ontology from a corpus and achieves 95-100% structural node coverage across four diverse domains, far outperforming a generic template baseline (52-78%).
AI.motivation: Ontology engineering is a bottleneck: existing methods rely on predefined schemas, narrow domains, or produce unstructured outputs unsuitable for downstream pipelines.
AI.method: GOI is a domain-agnostic framework that induces a generative blueprint (entities, dimensions, properties, relationships, constraints) from example corpora, exports it as a typed graph (6 node types, 7 edge types) in YAML/JSON, and evaluates via Node Coverage Score.
AI.result: Across four ontologies (Invoice, Job Description, Clinical Visit, Contract), GOI achieves 95-100% structural backbone coverage; a generic three-field template drops to 52.2-78.3% on unfamiliar domains.
AI.conclusion: GOI robustly covers ontology structure regardless of document familiarity, outperforming generic templates on diverse, unfamiliar domains.

title: Harness TTS: Towards Context-Aware Expressive Speech Synthesis with Harness Layer
summary: Expressive speech synthesis for voice assistants requires flexible style control that adapts to explicit requests and broader interaction context. We propose Harness TTS, a lightweight control layer that wraps around a TTS engine to externalize and govern its expressive behavior. It reformulates style control as closed-set prompt-tool routing: offline, a compact registry of stylistic prompt tools is constructed with structured metadata; online, an LLM planner selects the appropriate tool based on a priority-aware observation schema, and the TTS executor synthesizes speech using the corresponding prompt audio. We evaluate Harness TTS on both routing and synthesis tasks. In routing, Qwen3-4B achieves Top-1 accuracies of 74.3%, 43.0%, and 64.6% on explicit, implicit, and conflict subsets. For synthesis, experiments on CosyVoice3 and VoxCPM2 show that Harness TTS outperforms instruction-only control, achieving higher instruction-following win rates (margins of 23.1-35.6 points on CosyVoice3 and 13.8-20.0 points on VoxCPM2) and improving UTMOSv2 scores by 0.11-0.38. Moreover, the 4B planner delivers its first tool recommendation in under 50 ms in standard mode, introducing negligible latency for real-time interaction. These results demonstrate that equipping TTS engines with a dedicated Harness layer offers a practical, auditable, and context-aware solution for voice assistant expression control.

AI.tldr: Harness TTS is a lightweight control layer for TTS engines that externalizes expressive behavior via closed-set prompt-tool routing, where an LLM planner selects style prompts based on context. Evaluated on routing (e.g., Qwen3-4B achieves 74.3% Top-1 on explicit subset) and synthesis (outperforms instruction-only control by 13.8-35.6 points win rate), it adds minimal latency (<50ms) for real-time voice assistant use.
AI.motivation: Expressive speech synthesis for voice assistants needs flexible style control that adapts to both explicit requests and broader interaction context, which existing TTS systems lack.
AI.method: A lightweight control layer wrapping a TTS engine. Style control is reformulated as closed-set prompt-tool routing: offline, a compact registry of stylistic prompt tools is built with structured metadata; online, an LLM planner selects the appropriate tool via a priority-aware observation schema, then the TTS executor synthesizes speech using the corresponding prompt audio.
AI.result: Routing: Qwen3-4B achieves 74.3%, 43.0%, 64.6% Top-1 accuracy on explicit, implicit, and conflict subsets. Synthesis: Harness TTS outperforms instruction-only control on CosyVoice3 (23.1-35.6 point win margins) and VoxCPM2 (13.8-20.0 points), with UTMOSv2 improvements of 0.11-0.38. Latency: first tool recommendation under 50ms.
AI.conclusion: Equipping TTS engines with a dedicated Harness layer offers a practical, auditable, and context-aware solution for voice assistant expression control with negligible latency overhead.

title: Semantic Context Matters: Analysis of Color Names Across Domains
comment: Submitted to 2026 Joint 14th International Conference on Soft Computing and Intelligent Systems and 27th International Symposium on Advanced Intelligent Systems (SCIS&ISIS 2026)
summary: Color naming is influenced not only by physical color values but also by the semantic context in which colors are used. This paper investigates context-dependent color naming by mapping color-name datasets from Cosmetics, Crayola, and Car-color vocabularies onto the 86 fuzzy color categories of the COLIBRI color model. Contextual variation is analyzed using category coverage, Shannon entropy, and maximum lift. The results show that the three contexts occupy the COLIBRI color space differently: Cosmetics covers 48 of 86 fuzzy categories, Crayola covers 50, and Car colors cover 40. The results demonstrated that Crayola provides the broadest and most balanced use of the fuzzy color space, Cosmetics is mainly concentrated around warm-tone regions, and Car colors are more specialized around blue and achromatic regions. These findings show that color naming cannot be fully explained by numerical color similarity alone and that semantic context plays an important role in human color interpretation. The proposed framework supports the development of context-aware color models for design analytics, product search, recommendation systems, and human-centered artificial intelligence.
