AI.tldr: This paper analyzes how color naming varies across three contexts (Cosmetics, Crayola, Car colors) by mapping them onto the COLIBRI color model's 86 fuzzy color categories, finding that Crayola provides the broadest coverage, Cosmetics concentrates on warm tones, and Car colors specialize in blue/achromatic regions, demonstrating that semantic context significantly influences color naming beyond physical color values.
AI.motivation: To demonstrate that color naming is influenced not only by physical color values but also by semantic context, and to provide a framework for understanding context-dependent color variation.
AI.method: Mapped color-name datasets from Cosmetics, Crayola, and Car-color vocabularies onto the 86 fuzzy color categories of the COLIBRI color model, then analyzed contextual variation using category coverage, Shannon entropy, and maximum lift.
AI.result: Cosmetics covers 48/86 categories, Crayola covers 50/86, and Car colors cover 40/86. Crayola has the broadest and most balanced use of fuzzy color space; Cosmetics concentrates on warm-tone regions; Car colors specialize in blue and achromatic regions.
AI.conclusion: Color naming cannot be fully explained by numerical color similarity alone; semantic context plays an important role. The framework supports context-aware color models for design analytics, product search, recommendation systems, and human-centered AI.

title: Clarify Before Executing: A Self-Evolving Agent for Resolving Intent Asymmetry in 3D Tool Orchestration
comment: Accepted to ACM Multimedia 2026 (ACM MM 2026). 26 pages including appendix, 8 figures. Code: https://github.com/xyzhu1225/CLARE
summary: A fundamental intent asymmetry plagues modern 3D asset creation: while state-of-the-art 3D toolchains demand precise, executable parameters, ordinary users typically provide vague, underspecified instructions. Current 3D agents treat this ambiguity as noise, defaulting to blind execution under a single-turn assumption. To address this limitation, we introduce CLARE, a clarification-aware and evolutionary 3D agent that treats intent asymmetry not as an execution error, but as an opportunity for strategic dialogue. By decoupling the generation pipeline into four specialized cognitive roles, CLARE intercepts and resolves underspecified instructions before invoking computationally expensive 3D tools to seamlessly execute tasks across five diverse domains: text-to-3D generation, single-view reconstruction, multi-view reconstruction, point cloud editing, and post-processing. Crucially, rather than relying on rigid manual rules, CLARE self-evolves its clarification policy via simulated multi-turn interactions. By optimizing a Multi-turn Reward, the agent internalizes the delicate balance between interaction efficiency and task completion. To rigorously test this, we construct 3D-Clarify, a comprehensive benchmark comprising 620 interaction scenarios with systematically injected ambiguity, missing information, and mistaken details. CLARE achieves state-of-the-art performance, with 60.40% and 43.34% success rates on single-step and multi-step tasks, respectively, more than doubling existing baselines. Both quantitative and qualitative results demonstrate that proactive clarification is the missing key to robust 3D execution. Code is available at https://github.com/xyzhu1225/CLARE.

AI.tldr: CLARE is a clarification-aware 3D agent that resolves underspecified user instructions through strategic multi-turn dialogue before executing 3D generation tasks, achieving over double the success rates of existing baselines.
AI.motivation: There is a fundamental intent asymmetry in 3D asset creation: users provide vague, underspecified instructions while 3D tools require precise parameters. Existing agents treat ambiguity as noise and blindly execute under single-turn assumptions.
AI.method: CLARE decouples the generation pipeline into four specialized cognitive roles, uses simulated multi-turn interactions with a Multi-turn Reward to self-evolve its clarification policy, and proactively resolves underspecified instructions before invoking expensive 3D tools. A benchmark (3D-Clarify) with 620 scenarios was constructed for evaluation.
AI.result: CLARE achieves 60.40% and 43.34% success rates on single-step and multi-step tasks respectively, more than doubling existing baselines.
AI.conclusion: Proactive clarification is the critical missing component for robust 3D execution; treating intent asymmetry as an opportunity for dialogue rather than noise significantly improves performance.

title: DataFlow-Harness: A Grounded Code-Agent Platform for Constructing Editable LLM Data Pipelines
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, and 5 tables. Technical report
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to automate data-processing workflows, yet coding agents typically produce scripts that are not automatically materialized as persistent, editable platform artifacts. We call this disconnect the \textit{NL2Pipeline gap}. To bridge it, we introduce \textsc{DataFlow-Harness}, a platform that guides an LLM agent to construct platform-native directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) through typed, incremental mutations rather than free-form scripts. The platform combines \textsc{DataFlow-Skills} for procedural guidance, a Model Context Protocol (MCP) layer that exposes the live operator registry and current pipeline state, and \textsc{DataFlow-WebUI}, which synchronizes conversational authoring with a visual DAG editor. On a 12-task data-engineering benchmark, \textsc{DataFlow-Harness} achieves a 93.3\% observed end-to-end pass rate. Relative to Vanilla Claude Code, it reduces measured monetary cost by 72.5\% and generation latency by 49.9\%; its observed pass rate is within 0.9 percentage points of the Context-Aware Claude Code baseline while its cost is 42.8\% lower. Per-task analysis indicates that Skills are most useful when construction depends on implicit procedural knowledge. These results show that live platform grounding can produce persistent, editable workflow artifacts with an observed reliability close to script-generation baselines and with lower measured construction cost and latency.

AI.tldr: DataFlow-Harness bridges the NL2Pipeline gap by guiding LLMs to construct persistent, editable DAG-based data pipelines through typed incremental mutations, achieving 93.3% pass rate with 72.5% cost reduction and 49.9% latency reduction vs. vanilla code generation.
AI.motivation: LLM-based coding agents produce scripts that are not automatically materialized as persistent, editable platform artifacts—termed the NL2Pipeline gap.
AI.method: DataFlow-Harness combines DataFlow-Skills (procedural guidance), an MCP layer (live operator registry and pipeline state), and DataFlow-WebUI (conversational + visual DAG editor), using typed incremental mutations rather than free-form scripts.
AI.result: 93.3% end-to-end pass rate on 12 data-engineering tasks; 72.5% cost reduction and 49.9% latency reduction vs. Vanilla Claude Code; within 0.9 pp of Context-Aware baseline with 42.8% lower cost.
AI.conclusion: Live platform grounding produces persistent, editable workflow artifacts with reliability close to script-generation baselines and lower construction cost and latency.

title: From Weights to Words: Expressing and Editing Preference Model Inferences in Natural Language
comment: 42 pages, 22 figures, 14 tables; main text 11 pages, remainder appendices
summary: The growing use of statistical learning algorithms to infer human preferences from high-dimensional choice data runs up against a fundamental challenge: choice alternatives typically differ in many ways simultaneously, so it is generally unclear which factors actually drove an observed decision and should be credited as preferences. Compounding this problem, the opacity of these methods leaves human operators unable to inspect, contest, or correct models when they err. We introduce \emph{weights to words}, a method that takes a dataset of choice problems as input and automatically discovers a collection of domain-relevant preference dimensions, each described in natural language and paired with a vector in the model's representational space. These dimensions address both under-determination and opacity: they can be applied to concentrate attribution on a small set of meaningful factors, and they can externalize the model's inferences in natural language so that users can inspect and edit them in real time. We first qualitatively illustrate the method's versatility on four diverse domains: moral dilemmas, movies, wines, and free-form LLM responses. We then report two pre-registered human-subjects experiments, on moral dilemmas ($N=450$) and movie selection ($N=449$), that demonstrate its benefits for learning preference models: (1) regularizing a preference model toward the learned basis increases prediction accuracy on held-out choices, and (2) incorporating participants' structured edits further improves accuracy. In head-to-head comparisons, participants prefer the method's inferred preference profiles and endorse its predictions as more accurate.

AI.tldr: Introduces "weights to words," a method that automatically discovers natural language preference dimensions from choice data, addressing under-determination and opacity in preference learning. Demonstrated across four domains with two human-subject experiments showing improved prediction accuracy and user preference over baselines.
AI.motivation: Statistical learning algorithms inferring human preferences from high-dimensional choice data face two key challenges: (1) under-determination—it's unclear which factors drove observed decisions when alternatives differ in many ways; (2) opacity—model inferences cannot be inspected, contested, or corrected by human operators.
AI.method: The method ("weights to words") takes choice problem datasets and automatically discovers domain-relevant preference dimensions, each described in natural language and paired with a vector in the model's representational space. These dimensions enable concentrated attribution on meaningful factors and externalize model inferences for real-time user inspection and editing.
AI.result: Qualitative illustrations on four domains (moral dilemmas, movies, wines, free-form LLM responses). Two pre-registered experiments (N=450 for moral dilemmas, N=449 for movies) show: (1) regularizing preference models toward the learned basis improves held-out prediction accuracy; (2) incorporating participant edits further improves accuracy; (3) participants prefer the inferred preference profiles and endorse predictions as more accurate in head-to-head comparisons.
AI.conclusion: The method successfully addresses both under-determination and opacity in preference learning, yielding more accurate and interpretable models that users can inspect and edit, with demonstrated advantages over baselines in both predictive performance and user preference.

title: Democratizing AI with Small Language Models: Structured Benchmarking and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Local Deployment
summary: AI democratization is not primarily a question of matching frontier-scale generality; it is a question of whether capable models can be selected, audited, and specialized under hardware and governance constraints that ordinary institutions can actually satisfy. This paper studies that problem through a controlled evaluation of nine open-weight language models between 135M and 3B parameters on a 1,085-example, 16-topic multiple-choice benchmark designed for structured local deployment. The benchmark emphasizes symbolic precision, constrained formatting, extraction, and short-horizon semantic decision making under a strict one-letter output protocol. A shared parameter-efficient fine-tuning pipeline then adapts a subset of models using 4-bit NF4 quantization with DoRA/LoRA-style adapters on an NVIDIA L4-class budget. In base evaluation, Qwen Coder 3B leads at 75.67% strict accuracy, followed by Qwen2.5 1.5B at 67.10%, Qwen3.5 2B at 64.98%, and Granite 3.3 2B at 64.61%. On the shared 108-example held-out fine-tuning split, adaptation improves Qwen Coder 3B by +26.85 points, SmolLM2 1.7B by +25.92, Qwen2.5 1.5B by +19.44, SmolLM2 360M by +10.18, and SmolLM2 135M by +5.55. Across ranking, topic-level heterogeneity, difficulty strata, failure composition, efficiency frontiers, and topic-conditioned transfer, the same conclusion recurs: a disciplined workflow of benchmark construction, cross-model evaluation, and low-cost specialization already makes a subset of sub-3B models viable as local experts for structured niche workloads.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that AI democratization for structured niche workloads is achievable with sub-3B open-weight models when combined with disciplined benchmark construction, cross-model evaluation, and low-cost parameter-efficient fine-tuning (4-bit NF4 with DoRA/LoRA) on a limited hardware budget. Qwen Coder 3B achieves 75.67% base accuracy and gains +26.85 points after fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: AI democratization should not require frontier-scale general models; the goal is to determine whether capable models can be selected, audited, and specialized under hardware and governance constraints ordinary institutions can satisfy.
AI.method: Controlled evaluation of nine open-weight LMs (135M–3B params) on a 1,085-example, 16-topic multiple-choice benchmark for structured local deployment, using strict one-letter output protocol. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning with 4-bit NF4 quantization and DoRA/LoRA adapters on an NVIDIA L4-class budget.
AI.result: Qwen Coder 3B leads base evaluation at 75.67% strict accuracy. Fine-tuning improves Qwen Coder 3B by +26.85, SmolLM2 1.7B by +25.92, Qwen2.5 1.5B by +19.44. Sub-3B models are viable as local experts for structured niche workloads.
AI.conclusion: A disciplined workflow of benchmark construction, cross-model evaluation, and low-cost specialization makes sub-3B models viable for structured niche workloads under realistic constraints.

title: Dense-Sparse Dynamic Time Warping for Customizing Piano Concerto Accompaniments
summary: In this study, we explore how pianists can customize Music Minus One (MMO) concerto accompaniments to match their playing style. Bypassing the need for a symbolic score, often not available digitally, we use three types of audio data: solo piano recordings, MMO orchestra-only recordings, and mixed recordings of both piano and orchestra (e.g., from YouTube). The mixed recording serves as an intermediary reference to align the solo and orchestra parts, with only the orchestral part being adjusted through time-scale modification to synchronize with the user's playing. The main challenge with estimating these alignments is the spectral mismatch between recordings containing different musical parts. Motivated by this application scenario, we introduce Dense-Sparse DTW, a variant of Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) that is designed to improve robustness of alignments to spectral mismatch by focusing on aligning a selected subset of audio frames containing prominent timing cues. We collect and annotate data from four piano concerto movements and establish a framework for generating and evaluating customized accompaniment recordings. On this benchmark, we show that Dense-Sparse DTW has better or comparable performance than more complex approaches based on source separation and spectral subtraction techniques.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Dense-Sparse DTW, a variant of Dynamic Time Warping, to align solo piano recordings with orchestra accompaniments for customizable Music Minus One (MMO) concerto performances, achieving robust alignment despite spectral mismatch between recordings containing different musical parts.
AI.motivation: To enable pianists to customize MMO concerto accompaniments to match their playing style without needing symbolic scores, by using only audio data (solo piano, orchestra-only, and mixed recordings).
AI.method: Proposes Dense-Sparse DTW, a DTW variant that improves alignment robustness to spectral mismatch by focusing on a selected subset of audio frames containing prominent timing cues, using mixed recordings as an intermediary reference.
AI.result: On four piano concerto movements, Dense-Sparse DTW achieves better or comparable performance than more complex approaches based on source separation and spectral subtraction techniques.
AI.conclusion: Dense-Sparse DTW provides an effective solution for customizing MMO accompaniments, outperforming or matching more complex methods while being simpler in approach.

title: LFM: Leveraging Foundation Models for Source-Free Universal Domain Adaptation
comment: Accepted by IEEE Transactions on Multimedia (2026)
summary: Source-free universal domain adaptation (SF-UniDA) adapts a pre-trained source model to an unlabeled target domain under both covariate and label shifts, without access to source data. However, existing SF-UniDA methods rely on inefficient techniques such as threshold tuning and clustering. Foundation models (FMs), known for their generalization and zero-shot capabilities, remain underexplored in SF-UniDA. In this paper, we propose a framework that leverages foundation models (LFM) for SF-UniDA. We use a vision-language model (VLM) to compute similarities between target samples and text labels, including those for unknown classes generated by prompting a large language model. The label shift type is determined by analyzing the coefficient of variation of a similarity-based sample-level score. Unknown samples are identified using a binary Gaussian mixture model fitted to another similarity-based metric. Under a consensus strategy, the pseudo-labels generated by the VLM are refined by the target model initialized with the pre-trained source model, integrating knowledge from both the source domain and foundation models. Finally, these refined pseudo-labels are used to train the target model. Extensive experiments across all possible label shifts and multiple benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness and superiority of our proposed LFM framework. Our code is available at https://github.com/iamjingli/LFM.

AI.tldr: LFM leverages vision-language foundation models (VLMs) and large language models (LLMs) for source-free universal domain adaptation by generating pseudo-labels from text similarities, detecting label shift types via coefficient of variation, identifying unknown samples with Gaussian mixture models, and refining pseudo-labels through a consensus strategy between VLM and target model initialized from source.
AI.motivation: Existing SF-UniDA methods rely on inefficient threshold tuning and clustering, while foundation models with strong generalization and zero-shot capabilities remain underexplored for this task.
AI.method: (1) Use VLM to compute similarities between target samples and text labels (including LLM-generated unknown class labels). (2) Determine label shift type by analyzing the coefficient of variation of a similarity-based sample-level score. (3) Identify unknown samples using a binary Gaussian mixture model on another similarity-based metric. (4) Refine VLM pseudo-labels via consensus with target model initialized from pre-trained source model. (5) Train target model with refined pseudo-labels.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across all possible label shifts and multiple benchmarks demonstrate effectiveness and superiority of LFM over existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging foundation models (VLMs and LLMs) provides a more effective and efficient alternative to traditional threshold tuning and clustering approaches for SF-UniDA.

title: CNS-Edit++: Category-Agnostic 3D Editing with Coupled Neural Shape Representation
summary: This paper presents a latent-space 3D shape editing framework built upon a coupled neural shape (CNS) representation and a neural feature volume optimization. This work extends CNS-Edit, built on Coupled Neural Shape optimization, to CNS-Edit++, by generalizing the category-specific coupled representation to category-agnostic 3D shape editing with foundation models. The Coupled Neural Shape (CNS) representation couples a global latent code that captures high-level shape semantics with a 3D neural feature volume that provides spatial context for local shape manipulation. Then we formulate a coupled neural shape optimization procedure that co-optimizes these two components subject to a given editing operation. Our framework can be instantiated on both the category-specific 3D inversion model and category-agnostic 3D foundation models. We provide various shape editing operators, including copy, resize, delete, mix, point-wise drag, and region-wise drag, each of which is formulated as an objective to guide the CNS optimization. To preserve regions outside the editing area, we further introduce two complementary region-wise control mechanisms, i.e., KV-cache replacement and latent feature regularization. Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations across different 3D generative models demonstrate the strong capabilities of our approach over state-of-the-art solutions.

AI.tldr: This paper presents CNS-Edit++, a latent-space 3D shape editing framework that extends the category-specific CNS-Edit to category-agnostic editing by leveraging foundation models. It uses a Coupled Neural Shape (CNS) representation combining a global latent code with a 3D neural feature volume, co-optimized via a coupled optimization procedure. The framework supports diverse editing operations (copy, resize, delete, mix, point-wise drag, region-wise drag) and introduces KV-cache replacement and latent feature regularization for region-preserving control. Extensive evaluations demonstrate superiority over state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: To extend category-specific 3D shape editing to a category-agnostic setting by generalizing the coupled neural shape representation with foundation models, enabling more flexible and generalizable 3D editing.
AI.method: The method uses a Coupled Neural Shape (CNS) representation that couples a global latent code (high-level semantics) with a 3D neural feature volume (spatial context). A coupled optimization procedure co-optimizes both components under editing operations. The framework works with both category-specific inversion models and category-agnostic foundation models. Editing operators include copy, resize, delete, mix, point-wise drag, and region-wise drag. Region preservation is achieved via KV-cache replacement and latent feature regularization.
AI.result: Extensive quantitative and qualitative evaluations across different 3D generative models demonstrate strong capabilities over state-of-the-art solutions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CNS-Edit++ framework successfully generalizes category-specific 3D editing to category-agnostic settings, achieving superior editing quality and flexibility through coupled neural shape optimization and region-aware control mechanisms.

title: A Shared Latent for Partially-Labeled Multi-Task Facial Affect Recognition
summary: Facial affect in the wild is naturally multi-task: valence-arousal, discrete expressions, and facial action units describe the same face. Yet real corpora annotate these tasks only partially and unevenly, so most systems mask the missing labels or impute pseudo-labels and forgo the cross-task signal. We instead cast partially-labeled multi-task learning as marginalization over a shared affect latent: one variational bottleneck mediates all three task decoders, so a frame annotated for one task shapes the representation the others use, and the masked objective reappears as the reconstruction term of an evidence lower bound. On s-Aff-Wild2, where only 37% of frames carry all three labels, the classes are severely imbalanced, and pretraining on the source data is disallowed, we isolate where this coupling acts. On a single backbone it lifts expression macro-F1 from 0.403 for a dedicated specialist to 0.446, which the masked-loss model does not reach; a second, near-peer backbone with decorrelated errors then breaks an action-unit ceiling that external action-unit data could not, while valence-arousal stays within noise. Every gain is disciplined by a matched-control negative; together these controls indicate that the rare-class failure is representational, not a matter of loss shaping. As each task's source is chosen on the evaluation split, we report the assembled result, a combined multi-task score of 1.679 on validation, as an in-sample endpoint and rest our conclusions on the controlled comparisons; a small, regime-dependent transfer of the expression advantage to AffectNet and RAF-DB is presented as exploratory rather than conclusive.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a variational marginalization approach for partially-labeled multi-task facial affect learning, where a shared latent bottleneck enables cross-task signal propagation. This method improves expression recognition (macro-F1 from 0.403 to 0.446) and breaks action-unit ceilings without external data, while controlled experiments show gains stem from representational improvements, not loss shaping.
AI.motivation: Real facial affect corpora are annotated only partially and unevenly across tasks (valence-arousal, expressions, action units), causing most systems to either mask missing labels or impute pseudo-labels, thereby discarding valuable cross-task supervisory signals.
AI.method: Cast partially-labeled multi-task learning as marginalization over a shared affect latent variable using a variational bottleneck. The ELBO reconstruction term subsumes the masked objective, enabling a frame labeled for any one task to shape the shared representation used by all three task decoders.
AI.result: On s-Aff-Wild2 (only 37% frames fully labeled), the method lifts expression macro-F1 from 0.403 (specialist) to 0.446, surpassing masked-loss baselines. A second near-peer backbone with decorrelated errors breaks an action-unit ceiling unattainable with external AU data. Valence-arousal stays within noise. Combined multi-task score: 1.679 on validation.
AI.conclusion: Rare-class failure in multi-task facial affect is representational, not a loss-shaping issue. Controlled negative experiments confirm that gains come from the shared latent representation. Expression benefits show regime-dependent transfer to AffectNet/RAF-DB (exploratory, not conclusive).

title: CLOSER-Bench: Evaluating Budgeted Cross-Stage Design Closure for Hardware Agents
summary: Hardware engineering exposes coding agents to a form of long-horizon work that is difficult to capture with pass-at-k: progress is continuous, tool feedback is delayed and heterogeneous, and a backend failure may require revising RTL rather than tuning another physical-design parameter. Existing benchmarks measure RTL generation, repository repair, verification, PPA evolution, or physical implementation, but their different designs and oracles make it hard to determine where an agent succeeds or fails across abstraction boundaries. We introduce CLOSER-Bench, a controlled evaluation protocol for budgeted cross-stage design closure. For one design and one hidden objective, it pairs spec-to-RTL, RTL-to-GDS, and spec-to-GDS tasks, records every simulator, synthesis, STA, and place-and-route invocation, and measures final quality, anytime progress, tool cost, and cross-stage recovery. The benchmark is built on open-source Verilator, Yosys, OpenROAD, KLayout, Sky130, and the Harbor agent harness. A ten-task pilot spanning RTL repair, mutation-based verification, coverage, PPA optimization, design-space exploration, cross-model debugging, and security establishes the executable harness and exposes a sharp completion--closure gap: three agents solve a localized AXI repair task, while the matched verification-closure task separates a frontier agent from two otherwise successful baselines. We further validate a full RTL-to-GDS flow and construct a macro-based AXI/DMA streaming accelerator for the stage-paired evaluation. These results motivate treating hardware closure as a budgeted sequential decision problem rather than a collection of independent code generation tasks.

AI.tldr: CLOSER-Bench introduces a controlled evaluation protocol for budgeted cross-stage hardware design closure, pairing spec-to-RTL, RTL-to-GDS, and spec-to-GDS tasks with cost-aware metrics, revealing a sharp completion-closure gap that motivates treating hardware closure as a sequential decision problem rather than independent code generation.
AI.motivation: Hardware engineering involves long-horizon work with continuous progress, delayed heterogeneous feedback, and cross-abstraction failures that existing benchmarks (RTL generation, verification, PPA, physical implementation) fail to capture due to inconsistent designs and oracles, making it impossible to determine where agents succeed or fail across abstraction boundaries.
AI.method: CLOSER-Bench pairs spec-to-RTL, RTL-to-GDS, and spec-to-GDS tasks for one design with one hidden objective, records every tool invocation (simulator, synthesis, STA, PnR), and measures final quality, anytime progress, tool cost, and cross-stage recovery, built on open-source tools (Verilator, Yosys, OpenROAD, KLayout, Sky130) and the Harbor agent harness.
AI.result: A ten-task pilot spanning RTL repair, mutation-based verification, coverage, PPA optimization, design-space exploration, cross-model debugging, and security reveals a sharp completion-closure gap: three agents solve a localized AXI repair task, while the matched verification-closure task separates a frontier agent from two otherwise successful baselines. A full RTL-to-GDS flow with a macro-based AXI/DMA streaming accelerator is validated for stage-paired evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Hardware closure should be treated as a budgeted sequential decision problem rather than a collection of independent code generation tasks, as the completion-closure gap demonstrates that pass-at-k metrics are insufficient for capturing the continuous, recovery-oriented nature of hardware engineering.

title: Token-Level Cross-Modal Transformer with Contrastive Multi-Task Learning for Breast Cancer Subtype Classification and Survival Prediction
summary: Integrating heterogeneous genomic and clinical modalities for joint cancer subtype classification and survival prediction remains a key challenge in precision oncology. Existing approaches suffer from three limitations: (1) they treat each modality as a monolithic feature vector, precluding fine-grained token-level interactions across modalities; (2) cross-modal fusion is typically performed through linear weighting or late averaging rather than structured token exchange; and (3) survival and classification objectives are optimized independently, missing a joint regularization signal.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a new approach for joint cancer subtype classification and survival prediction by integrating heterogeneous genomic and clinical data, addressing limitations of existing methods that treat modalities as monolithic features, use simple fusion techniques, and optimize objectives independently.
AI.motivation: To overcome three key limitations in existing multimodal methods for cancer analysis: (1) inability to perform fine-grained token-level interactions across modalities, (2) reliance on simplistic fusion strategies (linear weighting or late averaging) rather than structured token exchange, and (3) independent optimization of survival and classification objectives without joint regularization.
AI.method: The paper introduces a structured token exchange mechanism for cross-modal fusion that enables fine-grained token-level interactions between genomic and clinical modalities, along with a joint optimization framework that regularizes both survival prediction and cancer subtype classification objectives.
AI.result: Expected improvements in cancer subtype classification and survival prediction accuracy through enhanced multimodal integration and joint learning.
AI.conclusion: Structured token-level cross-modal fusion with joint optimization can better capture complementary information from heterogeneous modalities, improving performance on both tasks simultaneously.

title: Masked Diffusion Language Models are Strong and Steerable Text-Based World Models for Agentic RL
summary: Recent growth in reinforcement learning (RL) has surfaced a need for diverse, specialized training environments. Hand-curated environments with fixed task and reward difficulties become ineffective signals as model performance improves, and sparse rewards over long horizons induce mode collapse on specific workflows or tool structures. World models that simulate environment states have matched pure rollout performance, making them promising for scaling diversity on-demand. However, autoregressive (AR) world models suffer from a left-to-right bias preventing conditioning on globally interdependent state anchors such as tool schemas, prior turns, and expected outcomes. We (i) formalize text-based world modeling as a steerable transition-dynamics problem decomposed into initial state, task context, tool schemas, domain rules, and steering directives, and (ii) curate 239,403 grounded state-action trajectories spanning nine open-source environments and twelve frontier model families. We compare AR LMs and masked diffusion language models (MDLMs), showing MDLMs, via bidirectional anchor-aware denoising, achieve better coherence, groundedness, and empirically validated rollout diversity than LLMs over 4x their parameter size, at comparable inference latency. We introduce a plug-and-play GRPO training framework with deterministic state checks, and perform zero-shot transfer ablations on three OOD environments (ScienceWorld, ALFWorld, AppWorld) across three 1.2B-7B agent backbones (LFM2.5, Qwen3, Mistral), achieving up to 47% absolute gains over baselines without environment-specific fine-tuning. We further conduct behavioral analysis of failure modes under adversarial scenarios and human evaluation on realism, outcome correctness, and training utility. We open-source our work to encourage research in this direction.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a steerable text-based world modeling framework using masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) to overcome autoregressive biases in RL training environments, achieving better coherence, diversity, and up to 47% absolute gains in zero-shot transfer across OOD environments compared to larger LLMs.
AI.motivation: Hand-curated RL training environments with fixed task/reward difficulties become ineffective as models improve; sparse rewards over long horizons cause mode collapse. There is a need for diverse, on-demand scalable training environments that world models can provide, but autoregressive models suffer from left-to-right bias preventing conditioning on globally interdependent state anchors.
AI.method: (i) Formalize text-based world modeling as steerable transition-dynamics decomposed into initial state, task context, tool schemas, domain rules, and steering directives. (ii) Curate 239,403 grounded trajectories from 9 environments and 12 model families. (iii) Compare AR LMs vs masked diffusion language models (MDLMs) for bidirectional anchor-aware denoising. (iv) Introduce plug-and-play GRPO training with deterministic state checks. (v) Perform zero-shot transfer ablations on 3 OOD environments across 3 agent backbones (1.2B-7B).
AI.result: MDLMs achieve better coherence, groundedness, and rollout diversity than LLMs 4x their parameter size at comparable inference latency. Zero-shot transfer ablations on ScienceWorld, ALFWorld, AppWorld across LFM2.5, Qwen3, Mistral backbones achieve up to 47% absolute gains over baselines without environment-specific fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: MDLMs with bidirectional anchor-aware denoising outperform much larger autoregressive models for steerable world modeling in RL, enabling effective zero-shot transfer to unseen environments. The work is open-sourced to encourage further research.

title: Audio Cross Verification Using Dual Alignment Likelihood Ratio Test
summary: This paper explores a way to verify that audio has not been maliciously tampered in a specific context: short viral videos taken from news recordings. Rather than trying to detect artifacts of tampering (internal inconsistency), we focus on positively verifying a query against a trusted source such as a news recording (external consistency). We propose a method for cross verifying a short audio query against a reference recording from which it was taken. Our approach is to define two hypotheses (non-tampered vs tampered), calculate the most likely alignment between query and reference for each hypothesis, and then perform a likelihood ratio test on the two alignments. We show that this method is fast to compute, much more robust than using MFCC features with Euclidean distance, and has the key benefit of explainability. Our cross verification approach provides an alternative perspective and complementary tool to existing tampering detection methods.

AI.tldr: Proposes a cross-verification method for detecting audio tampering in short viral news clips by aligning a query against a trusted reference and performing a likelihood ratio test between tampered vs. non-tampered hypotheses.
AI.motivation: Existing tampering detection focuses on internal artifacts (inconsistencies within the audio itself), which may be insufficient. This paper seeks a complementary approach that positively verifies a query's authenticity against an external trusted source (e.g., original news recording).
AI.method: Defines two hypotheses (non-tampered vs. tampered), computes the most likely alignment between query and reference for each hypothesis, then performs a likelihood ratio test on the two alignments to decide which hypothesis holds.
AI.result: The method is computationally fast, significantly more robust than using MFCC features with Euclidean distance, and offers the key advantage of explainability.
AI.conclusion: Cross verification provides an alternative perspective and a complementary tool to existing audio tampering detection methods, particularly suited for verifying short viral clips against trusted news recordings.

title: OrientSAM: Mitigating Camera-Centric Shortcut in Multimodal Spatial Reasoning via Orientation-Aware Spatial Alignment
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) still struggle with spatial reasoning that requires perspective transformation. In particular, they often rely on camera-centric cues rather than reasoning from the reference object's viewpoint, leading to systematic errors in non-camera reference settings. In this paper, we first analyze this failure mode and show that object orientation is a key factor underlying such camera-centric shortcut behavior. To address this issue, we propose OrientSAM, an orientation-aware spatial alignment framework for multimodal models. OrientSAM injects explicit orientation information into multimodal representations through orientation-aware tokens and Fourier-based angle encoding, and further adopts a curriculum learning strategy to progressively improve perspective-aware reasoning. In addition, we build a spatial data construction pipeline to generate orientation-aware spatial supervision from large-scale images. Experiments on Spatial-MM, ViewSpatial, and 3DSRBench show that OrientSAM consistently outperforms strong baselines, especially on non-camera-view, person-centric, and orientation-sensitive tasks. The results further demonstrate that explicit orientation modeling is important for mitigating camera-centric shortcut behavior and enabling more robust allocentric spatial reasoning in multimodal models.

AI.tldr: OrientSAM addresses camera-centric shortcut bias in MLLMs by injecting explicit orientation information via orientation-aware tokens and Fourier angle encoding, using curriculum learning and a spatial data pipeline; it outperforms baselines on spatial reasoning benchmarks, especially for non-camera-view and person-centric tasks.
AI.motivation: MLLMs fail at perspective transformation-based spatial reasoning, relying on camera-centric cues instead of reasoning from the reference object's viewpoint. Object orientation is identified as a key factor underlying this shortcut behavior.
AI.method: OrientSAM framework injects explicit orientation information via orientation-aware tokens and Fourier-based angle encoding, adopts curriculum learning for progressive perspective-aware reasoning, and uses a spatial data construction pipeline for supervision from large-scale images.
AI.result: Consistent outperformance over strong baselines on Spatial-MM, ViewSpatial, and 3DSRBench, especially on non-camera-view, person-centric, and orientation-sensitive tasks.
AI.conclusion: Explicit orientation modeling is crucial for mitigating camera-centric shortcut behavior and enabling robust allocentric spatial reasoning in multimodal models.

title: TopoGS: Planar Reconstruction via Topology-aware 3D Gaussian Splatting
comment: European Conference on Computer Vision (Proceedings of ECCV 2026); Project page: https://vcc.tech/research/2026/TopoGS
summary: Extracting structured, parametric 3D representations from raw images remains a fundamental challenge in computer vision and graphics. While recent advancements in the 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) pipeline integrate planar primitives to yield compact and editable geometry, these approaches typically treat planes as isolated, discrete sets. This lack of topological connectivity hinders robust geometric reasoning, leading to fragmented reconstructions and misaligned boundaries that fall short of the precision for rigorous spatial analysis and professional design workflows. To address this, we introduce TopoGS, the first 3DGS framework to explicitly integrate both planar and topological constraints for coherent 3D reconstruction. Specifically, we extract global 2D topological relationships from multi-view image segmentations and anchor Gaussian primitives to these structural elements. This formulation enables the joint optimization of plane parameters, rendering fidelity, and topological adjacency. By enforcing strict multi-view consistency alongside these topological constraints, our method significantly mitigates geometric misalignments and produces connected, structured 3D models. Extensive evaluations on the ScanNet++ dataset demonstrate that TopoGS achieves state-of-the-art performance, providing a highly robust solution for generating accurate, topologically sound, and visually faithful scene representations.

AI.tldr: TopoGS is a 3D Gaussian Splatting framework that integrates planar and topological constraints to produce connected, structured 3D models with improved geometric alignment and rendering fidelity.
AI.motivation: Existing 3DGS methods with planar primitives treat planes as isolated discrete sets without topological connectivity, leading to fragmented reconstructions, misaligned boundaries, and insufficient precision for spatial analysis and professional design workflows.
AI.method: TopoGS extracts global 2D topological relationships from multi-view image segmentations, anchors Gaussian primitives to these structural elements, and jointly optimizes plane parameters, rendering fidelity, and topological adjacency under strict multi-view consistency constraints.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on the ScanNet++ dataset, producing accurate, topologically sound, and visually faithful scene representations with significantly mitigated geometric misalignments.
AI.conclusion: Enforcing topological connectivity alongside planar constraints in 3DGS yields coherent, connected 3D models that outperform prior approaches in both geometric accuracy and visual quality.

title: Depth Estimators Are Implicit Neural Fields for 3D Scene Geometry Inpainting and Reconstruction
summary: The 3D geometry of real-world scene data is often incomplete. Mainstream methods use depth estimators to inpaint missing structure. However, their prediction results can be inconsistent with observed geometry, or unreliable on out-of-distribution data. To solve these problems, we propose Neural Depth Field (NDF). Our key insight is that a depth estimator can also be a scene-level implicit field. As an estimator, it adapts to the target domain by learning observed depth data. As an implicit field, it fits the existing geometry to maintain consistency. Under this view, NDF addresses both problems through a single test-time optimization. Experiments show that NDF produces high-fidelity and globally consistent geometry across diverse scene data, ranging from indoor scans to satellite imagery. It reduces cross-view inconsistency by 63.3\% and improves inpainting accuracy by 23.1\%, achieving state-of-the-art performance in 3D scene geometry inpainting. The code is available at: https://github.com/Shadow-Dream/Neural-Depth-Field.

AI.tldr: Neural Depth Field (NDF) proposes a unified approach that treats a depth estimator as a scene-level implicit field, enabling test-time optimization to produce consistent and high-fidelity 3D geometry inpainting across diverse real-world scenes.
AI.motivation: Existing depth estimators for 3D geometry inpainting often produce predictions inconsistent with observed geometry and are unreliable on out-of-distribution data.
AI.method: NDF treats a depth estimator as a scene-level implicit field: as an estimator it adapts to the target domain by learning observed depth data, and as an implicit field it fits existing geometry to maintain consistency, all through a single test-time optimization.
AI.result: Reduces cross-view inconsistency by 63.3%, improves inpainting accuracy by 23.1%, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on diverse scenes from indoor scans to satellite imagery.
AI.conclusion: NDF produces high-fidelity and globally consistent 3D geometry across diverse scene data, addressing both inconsistency and unreliability issues of prior depth-based inpainting methods.

title: Falsification-Based Verification of LLM-Generated Optimization Models: Sound Test Batteries and Their Detection Limits
summary: Large language models now translate natural-language descriptions of decision problems into solver-ready optimization models, but they fail silently. A generated model often runs and still formulates the wrong problem. This paper develops a theory of falsification-based verification for this setting. Every numeric quantity in the description is a typed slot, and a candidate model is tested only through solver calls on slot-transformed instances; no reference model or label is consulted. From duality, comparative statics, and polyhedral limit arguments we derive a battery of test classes covering directions, curvature, crush probes, prohibitive limits, annihilation, and exchange. Every test is sound, so a violation certifies unfaithfulness and the false-positive rate is zero by design. We characterize what such verification can never see, give conditions under which the canonical error classes are detected with certainty, and prove that no fixed-threshold perturbation tester is simultaneously sound and nontrivial. Experiments on 326 ground-truth models from NL4OPT and four benchmark families confirm the theory. The battery attains a 0.0% false-positive rate against 54.9% for a threshold tester, detects 70.0% of certified conditional-class mutants, convicts 40.4% of the mutants invisible to execution-accuracy scoring, and reproduces the predicted detectability pattern including its zeros.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a falsification-based verification theory for optimization models generated by LLMs, using solver calls on slot-transformed instances without reference models. It derives sound test classes from duality, comparative statics, and polyhedral limits, proving zero false-positive rate and characterizing detection limits, with experimental validation on 326 models.
AI.motivation: LLMs translating natural language into optimization models fail silently—generated models run correctly but formulate the wrong problem. Without reference models or labels, existing methods cannot detect these unfaithful translations.
AI.method: Each numeric quantity is a typed slot; tests are derived from duality, comparative statics, and polyhedral limit arguments, covering directions, curvature, crush probes, prohibitive limits, annihilation, and exchange. Tests are sound by construction (zero false positives).
AI.result: On 326 ground-truth models, the battery achieves 0.0% false-positive rate (vs. 54.9% for threshold testers), detects 70.0% of certified conditional-class mutants, convicts 40.4% of mutants invisible to execution-accuracy scoring, and reproduces predicted detectability patterns.
AI.conclusion: Falsification-based verification via slot-transformed solver calls is a provably sound approach for detecting unfaithful optimization models, with theoretical guarantees on what can and cannot be detected.

title: HantaWatch: Federated Learning for Hantavirus Genomic Surveillance
summary: Hantavirus genomic surveillance is limited by the distribution of sequence data, non-IID source heterogeneity, and constrained expert-review capacity. We propose HantaWatch, a federated learning framework that enables laboratories and surveillance sites to collaboratively train sequence-based models without sharing raw data. HantaWatch integrates k-mer feature extraction, source-aware federated client construction, adaptive DU-FedProx optimization, surveillance-specific model selection, and prediction-only triage. Experiments on binary and multi-class tasks show that HantaWatch supports high-risk screening, outbreak-associated prediction, clade classification, and clinical-syndrome categorization while balancing predictive performance, false-negative risk, and update stability. The framework converts model output into risk scores, confidence estimates, uncertainty flags, and ranked expert-review priorities. HantaWatch therefore provides a practical federated decision-support layer for decentralized Hantavirus surveillance, supporting expert prioritization without replacing laboratory or public-health interpretation.

AI.tldr: HantaWatch is a federated learning framework for decentralized Hantavirus genomic surveillance that enables collaborative model training across labs without sharing raw data, supporting risk screening, outbreak prediction, clade classification, and clinical categorization while balancing performance and stability.
AI.motivation: Current Hantavirus genomic surveillance is limited by sparse sequence data distribution, non-IID source heterogeneity across sites, and constrained capacity for expert review, necessitating a privacy-preserving collaborative approach.
AI.method: HantaWatch integrates k-mer feature extraction, source-aware federated client construction, adaptive DU-FedProx optimization, surveillance-specific model selection, and prediction-only triage to train sequence-based models without sharing raw data.
AI.result: Experiments on binary and multi-class tasks demonstrate HantaWatch supports high-risk screening, outbreak-associated prediction, clade classification, and clinical-syndrome categorization while balancing predictive performance, false-negative risk, and update stability.
AI.conclusion: HantaWatch provides a practical federated decision-support layer for decentralized Hantavirus surveillance that aids expert prioritization without replacing laboratory or public-health interpretation.

title: It Takes 8 Tokens: Weak-to-Strong Off-Policy RL via Auxiliary Branches
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has emerged as a standard approach for enhancing reasoning in large language models, which typically optimizes the policy by contrasting multiple self generated rollouts. However, we identify a critical support limited bottleneck in this paradigm: on challenging reasoning tasks, the target model's samples often exhibit semantic redundancy, converging into the same erroneous "reasoning basins" that offer negligible reward contrast for policy updates. In this paper, we propose to overcome this limitation through a weak to strong learning paradigm, where a policy's exploration is informed by a weaker but computationally efficient auxiliary model. We introduce W2SPO, an off policy RL method that injects short auxiliary segments often as brief as 8 tokens into intermediate target model trajectories and the target model then completes the reasoning path from these diverted states. Policy updates are restricted to these short inserted segments based on final verifiable rewards. Empirically, W2SPO achieves superior performance among evaluated 4B scale models on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, outperforming evaluated post trained baselines. Compared with vanilla GRPO under the same sampling budget, W2SPO improves Pass@1 from 62.3% to 64.2% while achieving a 3.55 times training speedup. These results suggest that weak auxiliary branches can induce stronger target reasoning policies by expanding local exploration support.

AI.tldr: W2SPO is an off-policy RL method that uses a weaker auxiliary model to inject short token segments into the target model's reasoning trajectories, expanding exploration support and overcoming the "reasoning basins" bottleneck in verifiable reward RL for LLMs, achieving 64.2% Pass@1 with 3.55x training speedup over GRPO.
AI.motivation: The standard RL with verifiable rewards suffers from a "support limited bottleneck": on challenging reasoning tasks, the target model's self-generated samples are semantically redundant and converge into the same erroneous "reasoning basins," providing negligible reward contrast for meaningful policy updates.
AI.method: W2SPO is an off-policy RL method that leverages a weaker but computationally efficient auxiliary model to inject short segments (as few as 8 tokens) into intermediate states of the target model's trajectories. The target model then completes the reasoning path from these diverted states. Policy updates are restricted to the injected segments based on final verifiable rewards, enabling local exploration without disrupting the main reasoning structure.
AI.result: Among 4B-scale models on mathematical reasoning benchmarks, W2SPO outperforms post-trained baselines. Compared to vanilla GRPO under the same sampling budget, W2SPO improves Pass@1 from 62.3% to 64.2% while achieving a 3.55x training speedup.
AI.conclusion: Weak auxiliary branches can induce stronger target reasoning policies by expanding local exploration support, suggesting an effective weak-to-strong learning paradigm for overcoming the reasoning basin bottleneck in RL-based LLM reasoning enhancement.

title: SciForma: Structure-Faithful Generation of Scientific Diagrams
summary: Structural fidelity is essential to scientific methodology diagrams. To communicate research logic, these diagrams must faithfully render components, directional relations, and textual annotations. Since a single error, such as a reversed arrow or an unreadable equation, can invalidate the entire figure, structural fidelity is inherently conjunctive: correctness on one axis cannot compensate for failure on another. Current open-source models fail to satisfy this criterion. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) learns plausible layouts but cannot reliably ensure structural correctness, while scalar reward-based post-training obscures which structural dimension has failed. To address this, we introduce SciForma, a framework for the structure faithful generation of scientific methodology diagrams. Specifically, SciForma decomposes diagram quality into three structural axes: Component, Arrow, and Text, guided by a structural inventory. Built on this foundation, we curate SciFormaData-700K for structured training and SciFormaBench-2K for logic-verified evaluation. To close the gap left by SFT, we develop Multi-Dimensional Conjunctive Preference Optimization (M-DPO), which enforces simultaneous correctness across all axes and adaptively routes gradients to the most deficient dimension in post-training. The same structural inventory also enables iterative editing at inference time to correct residual errors. This combination allows SciForma-9B to exceed all open-source baselines and GPT-Image-1.5 on both SciFormaBench-2K and AIBench, bringing open scientific diagram generation close to proprietary-level structural fidelity. Our code and data will be available at: https://github.com/microsoft/SciForma.

AI.tldr: SciForma is a framework for generating structurally faithful scientific methodology diagrams by decomposing quality into three axes (Component, Arrow, Text), using a multi-dimensional preference optimization (M-DPO) and iterative editing to achieve near-proprietary-level structural fidelity.
AI.motivation: Current open-source models fail to generate structurally faithful scientific diagrams; SFT learns plausible layouts but cannot ensure structural correctness, and scalar reward-based post-training cannot identify which structural dimension has failed, making structural fidelity a conjunctive requirement that existing approaches cannot satisfy.
AI.method: SciForma decomposes diagram quality into three structural axes (Component, Arrow, Text) guided by a structural inventory; curates SciFormaData-700K for training and SciFormaBench-2K for evaluation; proposes Multi-Dimensional Conjunctive Preference Optimization (M-DPO) that enforces simultaneous correctness across all axes and adaptively routes gradients to the most deficient dimension; plus iterative editing at inference time to correct residual errors.
AI.result: SciForma-9B exceeds all open-source baselines and GPT-Image-1.5 on both SciFormaBench-2K and AIBench benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: The combination of multi-dimensional conjunctive preference optimization and iterative editing brings open-source scientific diagram generation close to proprietary-level structural fidelity.

title: Identity-Consistent Expression Fields: A Disentangled Neural Radiance Field Framework for Few-Shot Facial Expression Synthesis
summary: Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) have enabled photorealistic novel-view synthesis of 3D scenes and, in the facial domain, have been extended to reconstruct and animate 3D face models from a small number of images. However, existing few-shot dynamic NeRF methods for facial expression editing typically warp a single learned feature volume conditioned on target expression parameters, which can cause identity-specific appearance details (skin texture, fine geometric structure) to drift when the model is driven toward expressions far from those seen in the few-shot input set. We propose Identity-Consistent Expression Fields (ICEF), a framework that explicitly disentangles a static, identity-specific radiance component from a dynamic, expression-conditioned deformation component, and introduces an identity preservation regularizer that constrains the deformation network to modify only expression-relevant regions while leaving identity-specific canonical appearance untouched. ICEF further incorporates a confidence-weighted conditional feature warping step that down-weights unreliable warps for target expressions that are far, in parameter space, from the observed few-shot inputs, mitigating artifacts observed in prior few-shot dynamic NeRF methods when extrapolating to novel expressions. We relate ICEF to prior few-shot dynamic NeRF, static 3D-aware face generation, and disentangled face-editing radiance field methods, and describe an evaluation protocol measuring both novel-expression rendering quality and, specifically, identity-consistency metrics across a range of expression-parameter extrapolation distances.

AI.tldr: ICEF explicitly disentangles static identity-specific radiance from dynamic expression-conditioned deformation, using an identity preservation regularizer and confidence-weighted feature warping to maintain identity consistency when extrapolating to novel expressions in few-shot dynamic NeRF.
AI.motivation: Existing few-shot dynamic NeRF methods for facial expression editing suffer from identity-specific appearance details drifting when driving the model toward expressions far from the few-shot input set, due to warping a single learned feature volume conditioned on target expression parameters.
AI.method: (1) Explicit disentanglement of static identity-specific radiance from dynamic expression-conditioned deformation; (2) Identity preservation regularizer constraining the deformation network to modify only expression-relevant regions; (3) Confidence-weighted conditional feature warping that down-weights unreliable warps for target expressions far from observed few-shot inputs in parameter space.
AI.result: Novel-expression rendering quality and identity-consistency metrics measured across a range of expression-parameter extrapolation distances, with reduced artifacts compared to prior few-shot dynamic NeRF methods.
AI.conclusion: ICEF improves identity consistency in few-shot dynamic NeRF for facial expression editing by disentangling identity and expression components and introducing regularization and confidence-weighted warping to mitigate drift and artifacts during expression extrapolation.

title: How Do You Choose Your AI Component? An Interview Study of Secure AI Integration in Practice
summary:
The increasing adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) as AI components in modern software systems introduces distinct security risks to the software supply chain. While many considerations and safety mechanisms are in place for components of the traditional software supply chain, the recent rapid adoption of AI components and platforms has overlooked these hard learned lessons. Selecting and integrating AI models without clear guidance on how these choices affect system security may leave applications vulnerable to threats, such as malicious components, data leakage, and unintended behavior. The goal of this study is to understand practitioners' decision making process and security considerations in selecting and integrating AI components through an exploratory semi-structured interview study. Toward this goal, we conducted semistructured interviews with 22 software developers, architects, and AI practitioners across diverse organizations about how they integrate AI components into their software.
  Our analysis finds that practitioners' model selection is predominantly driven by functional criteria, including performance, accuracy, cost, and specific features, e.g., tool calling or multimodal support, while security is rarely considered as an evaluation criterion. We observe a consistent lack of security concern throughout the AI component integration process, with established software supply chain lessons overlooked or ignored. The industry is repeating the historically costly mistakes of early software dependency management, prioritizing rapid reuse and availability over security and provenance. We distill our findings into actionable recommendations for AI adopters, model providers, and researchers, advocating for a proactive, security-by-design approach that integrates security evaluation into component selection and sustains it throughout the software development lifecycle.

AI.tldr: This interview study with 22 practitioners reveals that AI component selection is driven by functional criteria (performance, accuracy, cost) while security is rarely considered, causing the software industry to repeat early dependency management mistakes by prioritizing rapid reuse over security. The authors recommend a security-by-design approach integrated throughout the AI software development lifecycle.
AI.motivation: The rapid adoption of LLMs as AI components in software systems introduces distinct security risks to the supply chain, yet lessons from traditional software security are being overlooked. The study aims to understand practitioners' decision-making and security considerations when selecting and integrating AI components.
AI.method: Exploratory semi-structured interview study with 22 software developers, architects, and AI practitioners across diverse organizations about how they integrate AI components into their software.
AI.result: Practitioners' model selection is predominantly driven by functional criteria (performance, accuracy, cost, specific features like tool calling or multimodal support), while security is rarely considered. There is a consistent lack of security concern throughout the AI component integration process, with established software supply chain lessons overlooked or ignored.
AI.conclusion: The industry is repeating historically costly mistakes of early software dependency management by prioritizing rapid reuse over security. The authors provide actionable recommendations advocating for a proactive, security-by-design approach that integrates security evaluation into component selection and sustains it throughout the software development lifecycle.

title: OpenMHC: Accelerating the Science of Wearable Foundation Models
summary: Mobile and wearable devices offer an unprecedented opportunity for continuous, passive health monitoring and active health coaching. However, the largest wearable datasets are not publicly available for research, and leading wearable foundation models trained on such datasets are rarely open-weight or come with reproducible training code. To accelerate open science in wearable health, we release OpenMyHeartCounts (OpenMHC), the largest and most comprehensive open-access wearable health dataset to date, alongside open-source implementations of recent wearable foundation models. OpenMHC, derived from over a decade of data collected through the My Heart Counts study app, includes >60 million hours of wearable data across 19 sensor channels (e.g., step count, heart rate, sleep, workouts) and up to 169 linked variables, including health, lifestyle, mood, and behavior from 11,894 consenting participants. Furthermore, we introduce a unified, open benchmark that enables standardized comparison of wearable health models across three tracks: health and behavior downstream prediction, multivariate data imputation, and time-series forecasting. We benchmark classical methods alongside recent wearable and multivariate time series foundation models. By open-sourcing data, code, and model weights at this unprecedented scale, we aim to democratize wearable health AI research and enable the community to drive open progress in this domain.

AI.tldr: OpenMHC is the largest open-access wearable health dataset (>60M hours, 19 channels, 11,894 participants) with open-source implementations of wearable foundation models and a unified benchmark for downstream prediction, imputation, and forecasting tasks.
AI.motivation: Largest wearable datasets and foundation models are not publicly available or reproducible, hindering open science in wearable health AI research.
AI.method: Released OpenMHC dataset from the My Heart Counts study (>10 years, 60M+ hours, 19 sensor channels, 169 variables); implemented open-source wearable foundation models; created a unified benchmark with three tracks (downstream prediction, imputation, forecasting) comparing classical and modern methods.
AI.result: Achieved unprecedented scale of open-access wearable data including step count, heart rate, sleep, workouts, health, lifestyle, mood, and behavior from 11,894 participants; provided reproducible code and model weights.
AI.conclusion: Democratizes wearable health AI research by releasing data, code, and models at scale, enabling the community to drive open progress in this domain.

title: PPO-HSC: An Exploratory Reinforcement Learning Framework Based on Wide-Area Policy Coverage Optimization
summary: This paper introduces PPO-HSC (Proximal Policy Optimization with High-order Sampling Coverage), an exploratory reinforcement learning framework designed to address the "Invisible Shackles" of mode collapse in Large Language Model (LLM) fine-tuning. While standard Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) effectively reinforces high-reward trajectories, it often leads models to over-optimize known solutions, sacrificing curiosity and the ability to explore broader solution manifolds. To overcome this, PPO-HSC incorporates a High-order Sampling Coverage (HSC) reward that incentivizes the discovery of "low-similarity yet high-validity" reasoning patterns. By maintaining a dynamic trajectory library of verified unique solutions, the framework provides a differentiable signal that rewards semantic novelty while ensuring structural rationality through a plausibility constraint. Empirical evaluations on mathematical reasoning (GSM8K, SVAMP) and code generation tasks demonstrate that PPO-HSC significantly enhances solution diversity and state-space coverage while maintaining or surpassing the accuracy and syntax integrity of state-of-the-art RL baselines.

AI.tldr: PPO-HSC introduces a High-order Sampling Coverage reward to incentivize diverse yet valid reasoning patterns in LLM fine-tuning, preventing mode collapse while maintaining or improving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Standard RLVR fine-tuning of LLMs causes mode collapse — models over-optimize known high-reward trajectories at the expense of exploration, losing curiosity and the ability to discover broader solution manifolds.
AI.method: PPO-HSC extends PPO with a High-order Sampling Coverage (HSC) reward that uses a dynamic trajectory library of verified unique solutions to reward semantically novel but structurally valid reasoning patterns, enforced via a plausibility constraint.
AI.result: Empirical results on GSM8K, SVAMP (math reasoning), and code generation tasks show PPO-HSC significantly improves solution diversity and state-space coverage while matching or exceeding SOTA RL baselines in accuracy and syntax integrity.
AI.conclusion: PPO-HSC effectively breaks the "Invisible Shackles" of mode collapse by balancing exploitation of high-reward trajectories with exploration of diverse, valid reasoning paths.

title: Keyframe-Anchored Identity Preservation for Sequential-Action Video Generation
summary: Identity-preserving text-to-video generation aims to synthesize a video that accurately follows a textual description while maintaining the recognizability of a user-specified subject throughout. The IPVG26 challenge extends this framework from a single holistic prompt to a temporally structured specification. The model additionally receives a sequence of timestamped action captions and must render the subject performing these actions in the specified order. This temporal structure presents a challenge not encountered in previous identity-preserving generation tasks, as the subject must continuously perform a scripted sequence of distinct actions while maintaining a consistent identity. However, end-to-end video generators are prone to appearance drift as motion accumulates and the depicted actions change. We address this challenge with a training-free, three-stage pipeline framework. An action-aware prompt polishment stage first rewrites the inputs into image-generation prompts that specify the terminal state of each action. An identity-preserving generation stage then produces the keyframe sequence by conditioning each frame jointly on the reference identity and its predecessor, thereby decoupling time-invariant appearance from time-varying pose. Finally, an identity-aware inference enhancement stage synthesizes the intermediate segments using multi-reference guidance and identity-driven noise searching, both of which reinforce identity fidelity during sampling. Our method ranked third on the official Track 2 leaderboard, demonstrating competitive performance and strong generality.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a training-free, three-stage pipeline for identity-preserving text-to-video generation with temporally structured action sequences, achieving third place on the IPVG26 Track 2 leaderboard by addressing appearance drift through prompt polishing, keyframe generation with predecessor conditioning, and inference-time identity enhancement.
AI.motivation: Existing identity-preserving text-to-video generation handles single holistic prompts but fails when faced with temporally structured specifications where a subject must perform a sequence of timestamped actions. End-to-end generators suffer from appearance drift as motion accumulates and actions change over time.
AI.method: A training-free three-stage pipeline: (1) Action-aware prompt polishment rewrites inputs into image-generation prompts specifying the terminal state of each action; (2) Identity-preserving generation produces keyframes by conditioning each frame jointly on reference identity and its predecessor, decoupling time-invariant appearance from time-varying pose; (3) Identity-aware inference enhancement synthesizes intermediate segments using multi-reference guidance and identity-driven noise searching to reinforce identity fidelity during sampling.
AI.result: The method ranked third on the official IPVG26 Track 2 leaderboard, demonstrating competitive performance and strong generality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed training-free pipeline effectively handles temporally structured identity-preserving video generation, mitigating appearance drift without requiring additional training data or fine-tuning.

title: SGA: Plug&Play Geometric Verification for Educational Video Synthesis
summary: Recent work leverages Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate executable code for pedagogical animations using libraries such as Manim. However, ensuring spatial correctness and visual legibility remains challenging, as existing frameworks emphasize pedagogical content while overlooking geometric occlusions. We propose the Symbolic Geometric Agent (SGA), a plug-and-play module for code-centric animation pipelines that intercepts LLM-generated code, performs partial execution to extract symbolic scene graphs, and applies targeted refinement when spatial conflicts are detected. We further introduce the Manim Visual Quality Score (MVQS), a deterministic rendering-free proxy for spatial integrity. Experiments on the MMMC-Code benchmark across four LLM backbones and two agentic pipelines show that SGA achieves a peak MVQS of 73.11 (Code2Video + GPT-5.1), corresponding to a 16.1% relative improvement over the raw baseline, and improves MVQS in 7 of 8 backbone x pipeline configurations.

AI.tldr: SGA is a plug-and-play module that improves spatial correctness of LLM-generated Manim animations by intercepting code, extracting symbolic scene graphs, and refining spatial conflicts. It also introduces MVQS, a rendering-free metric for spatial integrity. SGA achieves up to 73.11 MVQS (16.1% improvement) on the MMMC-Code benchmark.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based animation pipelines emphasize pedagogical content but overlook geometric occlusions and spatial correctness, leading to visually illegible animations.
AI.method: SGA intercepts LLM-generated code, partially executes it to extract symbolic scene graphs, detects spatial conflicts, and applies targeted refinement. MVQS serves as a deterministic rendering-free proxy for spatial integrity.
AI.result: Peak MVQS of 73.11 (16.1% relative improvement) achieved with Code2Video + GPT-5.1; improvements in 7 of 8 backbone × pipeline configurations.
AI.conclusion: SGA effectively enhances spatial correctness in LLM-generated animations without requiring full rendering, offering a lightweight, plug-and-play solution for code-centric animation pipelines.

title: A Synthetic 3D Gear Dataset for Manufacturing Quality Inspection (MFGNet-Gear)
summary: Quality control in smart manufacturing increasingly relies on data-driven methods, particularly deep learning, to automate the inspection of manufactured parts. Recent advances in three-dimensional (3D) metrology have enabled fine-scale assessment of dimensional accuracy, surface quality, and shape conformity. However, deep learning methods for point-cloud-based inspection require large volumes of labeled data covering part designs and defect types, which are costly and time-consuming to obtain. Moreover, defective parts are intrinsically rare in mass production, and the resulting class imbalance can degrade model performance and make rare defect types difficult to detect. Synthetic data generation (SDG) offers a promising approach to address these challenges by producing large, balanced, and fully annotated datasets. Yet, applying SDG to precision components requires representing part geometry and defect morphology parametrically, so that design and quality can be co-varied. This article describes MFGNet-Gear, a publicly available synthetic 3D dataset comprising 24,000 paired polygon meshes and point clouds across 12 gear designs and 4 quality classes, with 500 instances per design-quality combination. Gear geometries are generated with parametric computer-aided design software, with dimensional parameters perturbed by $\pm$0.0254 mm and defect parameters sampled from distributions representing defect morphologies. For each mesh, 100,000 points are uniformly sampled using Open3D and stored as N $\times$ 3 coordinate text files. Metadata labels identify the gear design and quality class, supporting part design classification, geometric defect detection, representation learning, and dataset benchmarking. MFGNet-Gear provides an open-source dataset for deep learning-based 3D metrology, with a reproducible generation pipeline extensible to additional part designs.

AI.tldr: MFGNet-Gear is a synthetic 3D dataset of 24,000 paired meshes and point clouds across 12 gear designs and 4 quality classes, designed to address data scarcity and class imbalance in deep learning-based quality inspection for smart manufacturing.
AI.motivation: Deep learning for point-cloud-based quality inspection in smart manufacturing requires large labeled datasets, but obtaining real-world annotated data is costly, time-consuming, and suffers from class imbalance due to the rarity of defective parts in mass production.
AI.method: Parametric CAD generation of 12 gear designs with dimensional perturbations (±0.0254 mm) and defect morphology distributions; 4 quality classes; 500 instances per design-quality combination; 100,000 points uniformly sampled per mesh via Open3D; stored as N×3 coordinate text files with metadata labels.
AI.result: 24,000 paired polygon meshes and point clouds; balanced dataset (500 per design-quality class); reproducible open-source generation pipeline; supports classification, defect detection, representation learning, and benchmarking.
AI.conclusion: MFGNet-Gear provides a publicly available, extensible synthetic dataset and pipeline to enable deep learning-based 3D metrology for quality control, overcoming data scarcity and imbalance challenges in smart manufacturing.

title: Specification-Driven Development as the Foundation of AI-Native Enterprise Software Engineering
summary: Large language models (LLMs) and agentic AI are shifting software engineering from manual coding toward intent specification, architecture, and governance. Two paradigms have emerged: vibe coding, an intuition-driven approach accepting AI artifacts via observed behavior, and Specification-Driven Development (SDD), which uses structured specifications as the authoritative source of truth. This article makes three contributions.
