First, based on a verified literature corpus, it identifies failure modes of ungoverned conversational generation: the productivity-reliability paradox, architectural erosion from limited context, security exposure, and technical debt. Second, it introduces the Specification Governance Reference Model (SGRM). This tool-independent framework defines four-component specification contracts, constrains stochastic generation via deterministic validation, formalizes three rigor levels, and integrates generation, verification, and governance into a closed-loop architecture. Third, it evaluates SGRM against ISO/IEC 25010, mapping quality characteristics to governance mechanisms. Empirical evidence supports this, reporting a 73% reduction in security defects under constitutional constraints and a 50% reduction in time-to-market through specification-governed agentic delivery. The analysis concludes that while vibe coding is valuable for ideation and rapid prototyping, enterprise software requires specification governance to transform probabilistic AI generation into deterministic, auditable engineering. Boundary conditions, threats to validity, and future research directions are discussed.

AI.tldr: This paper compares vibe coding (intuition-driven AI use) versus Specification-Driven Development (SDD) for LLM-based software engineering, proposing the Specification Governance Reference Model (SGRM) to govern AI-generated code. SGRM reduces security defects by 73% and time-to-market by 50% through structured specification contracts and deterministic validation.
AI.motivation: Ungoverned conversational AI generation in software engineering suffers from four failure modes: productivity-reliability paradox, architectural erosion, security exposure, and technical debt. The paper aims to bridge the gap between rapid AI generation and reliable, auditable enterprise software.
AI.method: The paper conducts a literature corpus analysis to identify failure modes, then proposes SGRM—a tool-independent framework with four-component specification contracts, three rigor levels, and a closed-loop architecture integrating generation, verification, and governance. Evaluation is performed against ISO/IEC 25010 quality characteristics.
AI.result: Empirical evidence shows a 73% reduction in security defects under constitutional constraints and a 50% reduction in time-to-market through specification-governed agentic delivery. SGRM transforms probabilistic AI generation into deterministic, auditable engineering.
AI.conclusion: While vibe coding suits ideation and rapid prototyping, enterprise software requires specification governance. SGRM provides a structured approach to govern AI-generated code, with boundary conditions and future research directions discussed.

title: The Failures of Marginal Influence-Based Attribution Methods for Global Time Series Explanations
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI 2026)
summary: Explainability methods for time series models predominantly produce flat attribution scores: they quantify the direct influence of a feature at a timestamp by a scalar. We prove that the dominant failure mode of such methods is not the scalar format itself but a fundamental computational mismatch: existing methods compute scores via marginal conditioning or off-manifold gradients, both of which conflate direct temporal dependencies with mediated ones under autocorrelation. We also define DAG-faithfulness: an explanation is DAG-faithful if the temporal dependency graph it encodes is Markov-equivalent to the temporal directed acyclic graph (DAG) implicitly learned by the model. Particularly, we observe that standard attribution methods, specifically SHAP, are not DAG-faithful in general, and that recent time-series-aware extensions inherit the same computational limitation.

AI.tldr: Existing explainability methods for time series models produce scalar attribution scores that fail due to a computational mismatch (marginal conditioning or off-manifold gradients) conflating direct and mediated temporal dependencies under autocorrelation. The paper introduces DAG-faithfulness and shows current methods (SHAP, time-series-aware extensions) are not DAG-faithful.
AI.motivation: To identify and formally prove the fundamental failure mode of existing time series explainability methods, which is not the scalar format but a computational mismatch related to temporal autocorrelation and dependency structures.
AI.method: The paper defines DAG-faithfulness, a property requiring that the temporal dependency graph encoded by an explanation be Markov-equivalent to the temporal DAG implicitly learned by the model. It then theoretically analyzes standard attribution methods (e.g., SHAP) and recent time-series-aware extensions against this criterion.
AI.result: Standard attribution methods (SHAP) and recent time-series-aware extensions are not DAG-faithful in general, as they compute scores via marginal conditioning or off-manifold gradients, which conflate direct and mediated temporal dependencies under autocorrelation.
AI.conclusion: Existing explainability methods for time series models fundamentally fail due to computational mismatches with temporal dependency structures, and DAG-faithfulness provides a rigorous criterion for evaluating and designing better explanations.

title: JUMP: Single-Pass Membership Inference on Fine-Tuned Diffusion Language Models
summary: Membership inference attacks (MIAs) test whether a candidate example appeared in a model's training data. We study MIAs for fine-tuned discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs), where membership means inclusion in the target model's fine-tuning set. Unlike autoregressive language models, dLLMs allow an attacker to choose arbitrary mask sets and obtain token distributions for all masked positions in parallel. The prior dLLM attack, SAMA, follows a natural loss-mimicking strategy by averaging reconstruction signals over many randomly sampled masks, but it uses the any-order interface only as randomization and requires many target/reference queries. We propose JUMP (Joint Uncertainty-Guided Mask Probing), a single-pass scoring attack that exploits both distinctive properties of dLLMs: any-order decodability is used to select low-reference-confidence positions, and parallel decodability is used to score all selected positions through one joint masked query per model. JUMP masks the selected positions jointly and computes a clipped target/reference reconstruction-gap statistic. On fine-tuned LLaDA-8B-Base across six MIMIR domains, JUMP improves mean ROC-AUC from 0.82 to 0.90 over SAMA and substantially improves low-FPR detection, while requiring only one selector pass and one scoring pass through each of the target and reference models.

AI.tldr: JUMP is a new single-pass membership inference attack for fine-tuned discrete diffusion LLMs that leverages any-order and parallel decodability to achieve higher accuracy (ROC-AUC 0.90 vs 0.82) with fewer model queries than prior work SAMA.
AI.motivation: Existing MIA for dLLMs (SAMA) is inefficient, requiring many random mask samples and multiple target/reference queries, failing to exploit the unique any-order and parallel decodability interface of discrete diffusion models.
AI.method: JUMP selects low-reference-confidence positions using any-order decodability, then jointly masks them and computes a clipped target/reference reconstruction-gap statistic via one joint masked query per model, leveraging parallel decodability.
AI.result: On fine-tuned LLaDA-8B-Base across six MIMIR domains, JUMP improves mean ROC-AUC from 0.82 to 0.90 over SAMA, substantially improves low-FPR detection, and requires only one selector pass and one scoring pass through each model.
AI.conclusion: JUMP demonstrates that exploiting the unique inference interface of dLLMs (any-order + parallel decodability) yields more efficient and more accurate membership inference than prior loss-mimicking approaches.

title: Lossless-INR: Lossless Volumetric Implicit Neural Representations
summary: Implicit neural representation (INR) methods provide continuous coordinate-to-value mappings and integrate naturally with direct volume rendering, making them attractive for representing volumetric data. However, existing INR-based approaches for volumetric data are inherently lossy, and even small reconstruction errors can propagate through rendering and downstream analysis. In this work, we explore Lossless-INR, a lossless INR framework for 3D scientific volumetric data based on bit-plane decomposition. By decomposing each voxel value into binary bit-planes, we reformulate reconstruction as per-bit binary classification, so that exact recovery reduces to predicting every bit correctly. To make this optimization tractable while keeping the representation compact, we combine an octree block-partitioning strategy that adaptively subdivides complex regions with a ternary feature-grid network whose grid entries are parameterized by a ternary set of values. Experiments on diverse volumetric datasets show that this design can achieve zero bit-error rate and bit-exact reconstruction, enabling faithful rendering and downstream analysis with a compact representation. The code is available at https://github.com/TouKaienn/Lossless-INR.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Lossless-INR, a framework using bit-plane decomposition, octree partitioning, and ternary feature-grid networks to achieve bit-exact (lossless) implicit neural representation of 3D scientific volumetric data.
AI.motivation: Existing INR-based approaches for volumetric data are inherently lossy; even small reconstruction errors can propagate through rendering and downstream analysis, motivating the need for a lossless representation.
AI.method: The method decomposes each voxel value into binary bit-planes, reformulating reconstruction as per-bit binary classification for exact recovery. It combines an octree block-partitioning strategy for adaptive subdivision of complex regions with a ternary feature-grid network whose grid entries are parameterized by a ternary set of values.
AI.result: Experiments on diverse volumetric datasets demonstrate zero bit-error rate and bit-exact reconstruction, enabling faithful rendering and downstream analysis with a compact representation.
AI.conclusion: Lossless-INR achieves the first lossless implicit neural representation for 3D scientific volumetric data, successfully combining bit-plane decomposition with adaptive partitioning and ternary representations to ensure exact recovery.

title: Strength-Parity Ensembling with Parameter-Isolated Experts for Multi-Task Affect Recognition
summary: Leading entries on the multi-task track of the 11th ABAW challenge rely on heavy ensembling, yet which member is worth adding to an already strong ensemble is rarely made explicit. We study this question for joint valence-arousal estimation, 8-way expression recognition, and 12-way action-unit detection from a single unconstrained face, under partial, long-tailed labels and a rule that forbids pretraining on Aff-Wild2. Building on a shared affect-latent that marginalizes the missing labels across two affect-supervised backbones, we propose a strength-parity rule: an added member lowers the ensemble error only when it is both decorrelated from the current members and a near-peer of them in individual accuracy. The rule exposes a concrete obstacle, as on a single backbone re-seeding and even distinct fine-tuning curricula re-converge to a prediction correlation of 0.98 and add no diversity. Parameter-isolation removes it: confining each adaptation to a disjoint low-rank subspace of a shared backbone yields experts that stay decorrelated at 0.91 while remaining near-peers, the strongest of them an AffectNet-adapted expert. The resulting system raises the overall validation score to 1.6949, against the organizers ConvNeXt-with-MixAugment baseline of 0.45; with per-AU calibration and by pooling the shared-latent heads valence-arousal byproduct as a further near-peer, the strongest configuration reaches 1.7259.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates how to construct effective ensembles for multi-task affective computing (valence-arousal, expression recognition, action-unit detection) under constrained training conditions. It proposes a strength-parity rule requiring ensemble members to be both decorrelated and similarly accurate. Parameter isolation via low-rank subspaces enables diverse experts, achieving state-of-the-art results (1.7259 vs. 0.45 baseline).
AI.motivation: Current multi-task ABAW challenge solutions rely on heavy ensembling without clear justification for which members contribute. The paper aims to formalize when adding a member to an already strong ensemble is beneficial, under the constraints of partial/long-tailed labels and no pretraining on Aff-Wild2.
AI.method: A shared affect-latent architecture marginalizes missing labels across two affect-supervised backbones. A strength-parity rule is proposed: an added member reduces ensemble error if decorrelated from current members and a near-peer in individual accuracy. Parameter isolation (confining each adaptation to a disjoint low-rank subspace of a shared backbone) is used to enforce decorrelation while maintaining accuracy parity. Per-AU calibration and pooling shared-latent heads as additional near-peers further improve performance.
AI.result: The proposed system achieves a validation score of 1.6949 (vs. 0.45 baseline). The strongest configuration with per-AU calibration and pooled shared-latent heads reaches 1.7259. Parameter isolation reduces inter-expert correlation from 0.98 to 0.91 while maintaining near-peer accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The strength-parity rule effectively guides ensemble construction for multi-task affect recognition. Parameter isolation successfully overcomes the re-convergence problem, producing diverse yet comparably accurate experts. The findings provide principled guidance for ensemble design in affective computing.

title: Beyond Visibility and Technical Reuse: Public Application Transformation in Open-Source Model Ecosystems
summary: Open-source model platforms have made it easier to publish AI models, but model release alone does not reveal whether models become visible, technically reused, or incorporated into public applications. This study introduces public application transformation as a platform-visible dimension of model impact and examines it through structured Model-Space links on Hugging Face. We construct a platform-scale dataset of 2.56 million model repositories, 1.06 million Spaces, 810,087 dataset repositories, and 1.22 million account profiles, together with Model-Space, Dataset-Space, and model-to-model technical reuse links. The analysis shows that public application transformation is highly selective and concentrated: only a small share of models are linked to Spaces, and most Model-Space links are concentrated among a limited set of models. More importantly, application transformation is associated with platform visibility but is not equivalent to technical reuse, indicating that downloads, likes, downstream model reuse, and application-facing uptake capture different forms of model impact. Additional analyses show that application-transformed models tend to exhibit stronger metadata-based readiness and enter heterogeneous Space configurations involving datasets, SDKs, and task-specific application categories. By tracing how models move from repositories into public applications and demos, this study extends the measurement of open-source model impact from artifact availability and technical reuse to platform-mediated transformation across AI information objects.

AI.tldr: This study introduces "public application transformation" as a new dimension of model impact on Hugging Face, analyzing 2.56M models, 1.06M Spaces, and 1.22M accounts. It finds that only a small fraction of models are linked to public applications, these links are highly concentrated, and application transformation correlates with platform visibility but differs from technical reuse, highlighting multiple distinct forms of model impact.
AI.motivation: Open-source model platforms facilitate publication, but model release alone does not indicate whether models gain visibility, technical reuse, or integration into public applications. Existing metrics fail to capture application-facing transformation as a distinct impact dimension.
AI.method: Constructed a platform-scale dataset from Hugging Face with 2.56M model repos, 1.06M Spaces, 810K dataset repos, and 1.22M accounts, featuring Model-Space, Dataset-Space, and model-to-model technical reuse links. Analyzed selectivity, concentration, visibility correlations, and metadata readiness of application-transformed models.
AI.result: Public application transformation is highly selective and concentrated; only a small share of models link to Spaces. Application transformation correlates with platform visibility but is not equivalent to technical reuse. Transformed models exhibit stronger metadata readiness and diverse Space configurations (datasets, SDKs, task-specific categories).
AI.conclusion: Extends measurement of open-source model impact from artifact availability and technical reuse to platform-mediated transformation across AI information objects, revealing that downloads, likes, downstream reuse, and application-facing uptake capture distinct impact forms.

title: Quantizing Recursive Reasoning Models
summary: Recursive reasoning models solve hard puzzles by applying compact, weight-tied blocks over many refinement steps. Because these blocks are reused many times, quantizing them creates a unique dynamical problem: the quantization error is incurred at every step. While 8-bit quantization (integer or float) preserves accuracy, moving to a per-tensor 4-bit format causes a systematic bias to accumulate. The ensuing drift catastrophically degrades exact-solution accuracy on Sudoku from 84.1% to 0.0% (only ~25% of cells correct). In this work, we show that this collapse is caused by activation-scaling granularity rather than bit-width or number format. Crucially, moving to per-block scaling completely restores the transition. To implement this, we apply MXInt4, a blockwise integer activation format, to recursive reasoning models. It is competitive with blockwise float formats on our tasks, while keeping integer elements and power-of-two block scales. Finally, recursion depth and reuse modulate quantization sensitivity, with the deepest architecture we test (the EqR equilibrium model) the most sensitive. Yet blockwise scaling overcomes this vulnerability, staying robust across these architectures and transferring to the open-ended ARC-AGI benchmark.

AI.tldr: Per-tensor 4-bit quantization causes catastrophic accuracy collapse in recursive reasoning models (e.g., Sudoku accuracy drops from 84.1% to 0.0%), but per-block scaling (MXInt4 format) fully restores performance by addressing activation-scaling granularity rather than bit-width or format issues.
AI.motivation: Recursive reasoning models reuse weight-tied blocks over many refinement steps, so quantization error accumulates systematically. While 8-bit quantization works, 4-bit per-tensor quantization causes catastrophic drift; the goal is to understand and fix this collapse.
AI.method: Identify that the collapse stems from activation-scaling granularity, not bit-width or number format. Apply MXInt4, a blockwise integer activation format with power-of-two block scales, to recursive reasoning models. Compare with blockwise float formats and test across architectures including EqR equilibrium models and the ARC-AGI benchmark.
AI.result: Per-block scaling completely restores accuracy (from 0.0% to 84.1% on Sudoku). MXInt4 is competitive with blockwise float formats while using integer elements. Deeper recursion increases quantization sensitivity, but blockwise scaling remains robust across architectures and transfers to ARC-AGI.
AI.conclusion: Blockwise activation scaling (MXInt4) is an effective solution for quantizing recursive reasoning models to 4-bit, overcoming the cumulative drift problem that plagues per-tensor quantization.

title: ColGraphRAG: Late-Interaction Evidence Retrieval for Multimodal GraphRAG
summary: Graph-grounded multimodal question answering organizes text, tables, and images in a structured evidence graph, yet end-to-end accuracy depends on which multimodal assets are ranked highly enough to enter downstream reasoning; for graph-linked images, single-vector bi-encoder similarity can discard patch- and token-level structure needed for fine-grained alignment. We evaluate replacing the visual candidate-ranking operator over graph-linked image nodes with late-interaction MaxSim-style multi-vector scoring in the ColBERT/ColPali lineage, while keeping offline graph construction, text- and table-side retrieval, structured extraction, and downstream reasoning unchanged. On MultimodalQA, this change is associated with improved retrieval-stage point estimates for graph-linked image candidates and downstream QA gains, with larger movement where visual evidence matters most and mixed trends on text-dominant questions; we interpret the pattern as mechanism-level evidence for graph-linked visual evidence inclusion, while broader validation and finer graph-level diagnostics remain important future work.

AI.tldr: Replacing bi-encoder similarity with late-interaction MaxSim multi-vector scoring for graph-linked image retrieval improves candidate ranking and downstream QA accuracy on MultimodalQA, especially for visually-dependent questions.
AI.motivation: Single-vector bi-encoder similarity for graph-linked image retrieval discards patch- and token-level structural details needed for fine-grained alignment, limiting end-to-end accuracy in graph-grounded multimodal QA.
AI.method: Replace bi-encoder visual candidate ranking with late-interaction MaxSim-style multi-vector scoring (ColBERT/ColPali lineage) over graph-linked image nodes, keeping graph construction, text/table retrieval, extraction, and downstream reasoning unchanged.
AI.result: Improved retrieval-stage point estimates for graph-linked image candidates and downstream QA gains on MultimodalQA, with larger improvements on visually-dependent questions and mixed trends on text-dominant questions.
AI.conclusion: Late-interaction multi-vector scoring provides mechanism-level evidence for better graph-linked visual evidence inclusion, though broader validation and finer graph-level diagnostics are needed.

title: Beyond Target Scores: Measuring Off-Target Drift in Diffusion-Based Medical Image Editing
summary: Diffusion models can now edit medical images in visually plausible ways, but the standard evaluation question is too narrow: did the target score increase? In clinical imaging, target findings are entangled with co-morbidities, acquisition effects, and selection bias, so a model can appear successful by changing correlated non-target findings rather than isolating the intended pathology. We introduce CIB-Med-1, a trajectory-level benchmark for controlled biomarker editing in chest radiography. CIB-Med-1 evaluates directional pleural effusion editing through calibrated target progression, inversion rate, and off-target semantic drift over 14 clinically motivated nuisance axes. The benchmark exposes a reward-hacking failure mode in which diffusion editors increase effusion scores while simultaneously altering parenchymal, cardiomediastinal, pleural, chronic, or artifact-related findings. We further present a constrained diffusion guidance baseline that optimizes target progression subject to bounded off-target change. Across held-out radiographs, the constrained editor preserves target progression ($ρ_{\mathrm{trend}}=0.88$ vs. $0.90$ for unconstrained guidance) while reducing median off-target drift from $0.46$ to $0.20$ and 90th-percentile drift from $0.98$ to $0.33$. Drift magnitude tracks empirical target--off-target association, supporting the view that semantic instability is structured rather than incidental. A blinded human validation probe with radiology trainees further shows stronger agreement with intended progression orderings ($τ=0.61$ vs.\ $0.29$ for Pix2Pix). These results argue that medical image editing should be evaluated as trajectory-level semantic control, not as endpoint score maximization.

AI.tldr: CIB-Med-1 benchmark reveals that diffusion-based medical image editors often "reward-hack" by changing correlated non-target findings rather than isolating the intended pathology; a constrained diffusion guidance method reduces off-target semantic drift from 0.46 to 0.20 median while preserving target progression (ρ_trend=0.88), with blinded human raters preferring its edits (τ=0.61 vs. 0.29 for Pix2Pix).
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation of diffusion-based medical image editing (asking "did the target score increase?") is insufficient because target findings are entangled with co-morbidities, acquisition effects, and selection bias, allowing models to appear successful by altering correlated non-target features instead of isolating the intended pathology.
AI.method: Introduces CIB-Med-1, a trajectory-level benchmark for controlled biomarker editing in chest radiography, evaluating directional pleural effusion editing via calibrated target progression, inversion rate, and off-target semantic drift across 14 clinically motivated nuisance axes. Also presents a constrained diffusion guidance baseline that optimizes target progression subject to bounded off-target change.
AI.result: Unconstrained diffusion editors exhibit reward-hacking by increasing effusion scores while altering parenchymal, cardiomediastinal, pleural, chronic, or artifact-related findings. The constrained editor preserves target progression (ρ_trend=0.88 vs. 0.90 for unconstrained) while reducing median off-target drift from 0.46 to 0.20 and 90th-percentile drift from 0.98 to 0.33. Blinded human validation shows stronger agreement with intended progression (τ=0.61 vs. 0.29 for Pix2Pix).
AI.conclusion: Medical image editing should be evaluated as trajectory-level semantic control rather than endpoint score maximization.

title: Dependency-Guided Code Generation: Structured Matrix Decomposition and Consistency-Guided Refinement
summary: The increasing complexity of modern software systems has made automated code generation a fundamental task in software engineering. However, existing approaches often fail to adequately capture the intricate, multi-level dependencies among code entities, leading to generated code that is logically incomplete or difficult to integrate into real-world systems. To address this limitation, we propose a dependency-aware code generation framework that explicitly models interactions among code entities through a graph-based representation. We decompose dependencies into two complementary components: a quantized matrix that captures strong, explicit relations, and a sparse low-rank factorization that models weaker, implicit interactions. The decomposition is efficiently learned via an alternating optimization procedure. During code generation, the learned dependency structure is incorporated as a constraint, ensuring both semantic coherence and structural consistency of the generated code. Furthermore, we introduce a sparse triplet representation for strong dependencies, significantly improving storage efficiency and computational scalability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach consistently produces code with superior semantic alignment and structural fidelity compared to existing methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dependency-aware code generation framework that uses a graph-based representation with quantized matrix (strong relations) and sparse low-rank factorization (weak interactions) to model code entity dependencies, learned via alternating optimization, and incorporates these as constraints during generation to improve semantic and structural quality.
AI.motivation: Existing automated code generation methods fail to capture complex multi-level dependencies among code entities, resulting in logically incomplete code that is difficult to integrate into real-world systems.
AI.method: A graph-based representation decomposes dependencies into a quantized matrix (strong, explicit relations) and a sparse low-rank factorization (weak, implicit interactions). An alternating optimization procedure learns the decomposition. During generation, the dependency structure is used as a constraint. A sparse triplet representation is introduced for strong dependencies to improve efficiency.
AI.result: The approach consistently produces code with superior semantic alignment and structural fidelity compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: Modeling both strong and weak dependencies via a decomposed graph representation with learned constraints significantly improves the quality and integrability of generated code.

title: Diffusion-corrected Autoregressive Fourier Neural Operator for Droplet Evolution Prediction
summary: Predicting droplet evolution in material jetting, or Inkjet Printing (IJP), is essential for maintaining printing quality. However, long-horizon forecasts remain challenging due to error accumulation and the complex coupling of process variables. In this work, we introduce the Diffusion-corrected Auto-Regressive Fourier Neural Operator (DiffARFNO), a two-stage framework that combines an autoregressive Fourier-MIONet with a conditional Denoising Diffusion Implicit Model (DDIM) corrector. Fourier-MIONet is trained as a coarse predictor and deployed autoregressively for long-horizon forecasting. In the second stage, a DDIM-based conditional corrector refines the coarse prediction within each sliding window through efficient iterative denoising. By combining coarse predictions from Fourier-MIONet with a DDIM corrector that restores fine details, DiffARFNO aims to provide high-fidelity predictions for long-horizon forecasts. Extensive experiments on droplet datasets from ANSYS Fluent demonstrate that DiffARFNO significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art models.

AI.tldr: DiffARFNO combines an autoregressive Fourier-MIONet with a DDIM corrector to improve long-horizon droplet evolution predictions in material jetting, outperforming existing models on ANSYS Fluent datasets.
AI.motivation: Long-horizon forecasting of droplet evolution in inkjet printing is challenging due to error accumulation and complex coupling of process variables.
AI.method: Two-stage framework: (1) autoregressive Fourier-MIONet as coarse predictor, (2) conditional DDIM corrector refines predictions within sliding windows via iterative denoising.
AI.result: DiffARFNO significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art models on droplet datasets from ANSYS Fluent.
AI.conclusion: The combination of coarse Fourier-MIONet predictions with DDIM-based correction enables high-fidelity long-horizon forecasts for droplet evolution.

title: Shapley Context Pruning: A Cooperative Game Perspective for Context Reranking and Pruning
summary: Context reranking and pruning have become essential for improving the efficiency of modern Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, yet an interpretable and unified framework remains underexplored. Previous work has primarily emphasized lexical retrieval, cross-encoder architectures, model distillation, and Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), mostly relying on heuristic loss functions and empirical attribution. This paper presents Shapley Context Pruning (SCP), a novel framework for context reranking that establishes a cooperative-game-theory perspective for importance attribution by modeling the context as a cooperative game. Balancing the trade-off between fine-grained and coarse-grained representations, we employ a Deep Sets architecture to approximate a permutation-invariant value function at the sentence level, utilizing pre-trained language models as sentence embedders and optimizing via a pairwise margin ranking loss. To ensure practical scalability without sacrificing mathematical rigor, we leverage Monte-Carlo sampling for efficient training and inference, providing formal theoretical error bounds and sample complexity guarantees for preserving Top-K subset rankings. Furthermore, we conduct comprehensive experiments-spanning supporting-sentence recall, Needle-in-the-Haystack (NIAH) evaluations, long-context QA, and multi-hop reasoning-alongside rigorous ablation studies on embedding quality and attribution strategies. The model achieves competitive downstream QA performance against robust baselines.

AI.tldr: Shapley Context Pruning (SCP) is a cooperative-game-theory framework for context reranking in RAG systems, using Deep Sets architecture with Monte-Carlo sampling for efficient, theoretically-grounded importance attribution at the sentence level.
AI.motivation: Existing context reranking methods rely on heuristic loss functions and empirical attribution without a unified, interpretable framework. There is a need for a principled approach to importance attribution in RAG context pruning.
AI.method: Models context as a cooperative game; uses Shapley values for importance attribution; employs Deep Sets architecture with pre-trained language model sentence embedders for permutation-invariant value function approximation; optimized via pairwise margin ranking loss; uses Monte-Carlo sampling with theoretical error bounds and sample complexity guarantees for scalability.
AI.result: Competitive downstream QA performance across supporting-sentence recall, NIAH evaluations, long-context QA, and multi-hop reasoning against robust baselines.
AI.conclusion: SCP provides an interpretable, theoretically grounded, and scalable solution for context reranking in RAG, balancing granularity trade-offs while achieving strong empirical results.

title: It Depends on the Dataset: When a Brain-Encoding Model's Predicted Responses Beat Their Visual Backbone for Video Memorability
comment: 10 pages, 3 figures. Code and predicted-response arrays released for reproduction; source videos/scores not redistributed
summary: Brain-encoding foundation models predict fMRI responses to video, audio, and text well enough to win the Algonauts 2025 challenge. We ask whether their predicted responses, obtained with no scanner, are a useful feature lens for a downstream human-behavior task: forecasting the memorability of short videos. We project each clip into TRIBE v2's predicted cortical space and forecast short-term memorability with ridge regression, against a matched control: the model's own V-JEPA2 visual backbone taken before the brain projection. The answer is dataset-dependent, and cleanly so. Within Memento10k the backbone wins (Spearman 0.594 vs 0.544 for the brain projection); within VideoMem the brain projection wins (0.415 vs 0.368, delta +0.047, 95% CI [+0.009, +0.088]). Both within-dataset gaps have bootstrap intervals excluding zero, in opposite directions. Cross-dataset transfer inherits the split: trained on Memento10k and tested on VideoMem the brain projection beats the backbone (+0.076), while the reverse loses heavily (-0.311). Each representation transfers best onto the dataset it already fits better. The VideoMem advantage is not a sample-size artifact (it survives matched training size and a PCA-then-ridge pipeline) and not mere compression of the backbone (a compressed or heavily regularized backbone tops out below the brain projection, which also beats a transfer-tuned backbone, +0.053). So predicted-brain features carry a small but real memorability signal the backbone misses on one dataset and not the other: not a domain-general prior, but a dataset-specific representation. A vision-orthogonal component (partial Spearman 0.19, permutation p=2.5e-4) localizes to ventral occipito-temporal cortex. Code and predicted-response arrays are released; source videos and scores are not redistributed.

AI.tldr: Brain-encoding foundation models' predicted fMRI responses can serve as useful features for predicting video memorability, but the advantage is dataset-dependent: the brain projection outperforms the visual backbone on VideoMem but not on Memento10k, with the effect driven by ventral occipito-temporal cortex.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether predicted brain responses from encoding models (which require no actual fMRI scanner) can serve as useful feature representations for downstream human-behavior tasks, specifically forecasting short-term video memorability.
AI.method: The authors project video clips into TRIBE v2's predicted cortical space and apply ridge regression to forecast short-term memorability. They compare this against a matched control: the V-JEPA2 visual backbone features taken before the brain projection. They test on two datasets (Memento10k and VideoMem), perform cross-dataset transfer, and conduct control analyses (matched training size, PCA-then-ridge, compression/regularization, transfer-tuning). They also localize the signal to ventral occipito-temporal cortex using partial Spearman correlation.
AI.result: Within Memento10k, the backbone wins (Spearman 0.594 vs 0.544). Within VideoMem, the brain projection wins (0.415 vs 0.368, delta +0.047, 95% CI [+0.009, +0.088]). Both gaps exclude zero in opposite directions. Cross-dataset transfer: Memento10k→VideoMem sees brain projection win (+0.076); VideoMem→Memento10k sees backbone win (-0.311). The VideoMem advantage is not due to sample size, compression, or regularization artifacts. A vision-orthogonal component (partial Spearman 0.19, p=2.5e-4) localizes to ventral occipito-temporal cortex.
AI.conclusion: Predicted-brain features carry a small but real memorability signal that the visual backbone misses, but this is not a domain-general prior—it is dataset-specific. The signal is partially orthogonal to vision and localized to ventral occipito-temporal cortex. Code and predicted-response arrays are released.

title: Model-Driven Discipline for Multi-Agent LLMs: Requirement-to-Verification Generation of Traceable System Models
summary:
Software complexity is a long-standing challenge for system engineers. Model-Driven Engineering (MDE) addresses it by treating models as first-class artefacts, but a typical MDE process spans many tools and produces heterogeneous models of different system aspects, making traceability, maintenance, and change management difficult.
  We propose RADIANT, an engineering methodology that combines MDE with Multi-Agent Large Language Models (LLMs) for complete model-based system development, with a focus on safety-critical systems. From a carefully specified requirement model, RADIANT automatically generates heterogeneous models across engineering phases -- a concept model, a domain-specific modelling language, a conforming system model, and a behaviour model -- together with executable, element-level traceability links, on top of which it provides exact, automated change-impact analysis. Generated behaviour models are translated into CSP and formally verified (e.g.\ for deadlock freedom and convergence) with a counterexample-driven repair loop. Evaluating RADIANT across three LLMs, we find that the multi-agent decomposition reliably improves the \emph{syntactic validity} of the generated formal artefacts over a single-agent baseline -- and their \emph{executability} where the model's code generation permits -- while gains in semantic accuracy are model-dependent. A six-participant study shows an order-of-magnitude ($10$--$15\times$) reduction in development time, and the unmodified pipeline transfers to a second domain.

AI.tldr: RADIANT combines Model-Driven Engineering with Multi-Agent LLMs to automatically generate heterogeneous models and traceability links from requirements, achieving formal verification and order-of-magnitude development time reductions (10-15x) for safety-critical systems.
AI.motivation: Software complexity challenges system engineers; MDE processes span many tools and produce heterogeneous models, making traceability, maintenance, and change management difficult.
AI.method: RADIANT integrates MDE with Multi-Agent LLMs to auto-generate concept models, domain-specific languages, system models, and behavior models from requirement models, with element-level traceability and automated change-impact analysis. Behavior models are translated to CSP for formal verification with counterexample-driven repair.
AI.result: Multi-agent decomposition improves syntactic validity and executability over single-agent baselines; a six-participant study shows 10-15x reduction in development time; the pipeline transfers to a second domain.
AI.conclusion: RADIANT demonstrates that multi-agent LLM collaboration with MDE can significantly improve development efficiency and formal artefact quality in safety-critical systems engineering.

title: BACON: Budgeted Human Calibration for Modeling and Evaluation with Multiple AI Judges
summary: AI judges offer a scalable, low-cost alternative to human evaluation, but their outputs can be biased relative to human preferences and highly item-dependent, varying across judges, tasks, and domains. When uncalibrated AI evaluations are used for model ranking, item scoring, or population-level quality reporting, these biases can directly distort downstream decisions. We propose BACON, a four-stage pipeline that combines budgeted human calibration with multiple AI-judge outputs to produce more accurate annotations. BACON constructs full-coverage auxiliary features for every item, including multi-judge scores, token-level uncertainty statistics, and contextual embeddings. It then collects human labels for a small sampled subset and trains a cross-fitted outcome model to generate calibrated item-level surrogate predictions. These predictions support two use cases: population-level estimation of summary metrics, such as means or quantiles, using an augmented estimating-equation estimator with valid confidence intervals; and individual-level surrogate scoring for item ranking and annotation. BACON treats AI judges as auxiliary measurements rather than ground truth: human labels provide the calibration anchor, while AI-derived signals improve efficiency. Across diverse tasks, domains, and labeling budgets, BACON improves predictive accuracy and ranking consistency, and reduces bias and variance relative to raw AI outputs and purely human-label-based methods. These results show that BACON offers a practical, statistically grounded framework for scalable evaluation with limited human annotation.

AI.tldr: BACON is a four-stage pipeline that combines budgeted human calibration with multiple AI judges to produce accurate, unbiased annotations for model ranking, item scoring, and population-level quality reporting.
AI.motivation: AI judges are scalable and low-cost but produce biased, item-dependent outputs varying across judges, tasks, and domains; uncalibrated AI evaluations distort downstream decisions like model ranking and quality reporting.
AI.method: Four-stage pipeline: (1) construct full-coverage auxiliary features (multi-judge scores, token-level uncertainty, contextual embeddings); (2) collect human labels on a small sampled subset; (3) train a cross-fitted outcome model to produce calibrated surrogate predictions; (4) use these for population-level estimation (augmented estimating-equation estimator with valid CIs) or individual-level surrogate scoring for ranking/annotation.
AI.result: Across diverse tasks, domains, and labeling budgets, BACON improves predictive accuracy and ranking consistency, and reduces bias and variance relative to raw AI outputs and purely human-label-based methods.
AI.conclusion: BACON offers a practical, statistically grounded framework for scalable evaluation with limited human annotation, treating AI judges as auxiliary measurements rather than ground truth.

title: A Survey on the Verification of Reinforcement Learning Policies
comment: Accepted at the 35th International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI) 2026
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly applied in complex, safety-critical domains, yet the lack of rigorous behavioral guarantees for neural network-based policies remains a major barrier to deployment. Recent advances in policy expressiveness and scale have intensified this challenge, leading to a rapidly growing but conceptually fragmented body of work on RL policy verification. This survey provides a unifying perspective on RL verification methods. We introduce a taxonomy that clarifies relationships among existing approaches along three axes: verification paradigm (formal versus probabilistic), temporal scope (step-wise versus multi-step), and guarantees strength. Beyond taxonomy, we unify underlying theoretical foundations, make implicit assumptions and limitations explicit, and identify emerging directions.

AI.tldr: This survey provides a unifying perspective on reinforcement learning policy verification, introducing a taxonomy across three axes (verification paradigm, temporal scope, guarantee strength) while unifying theoretical foundations and identifying emerging research directions.
AI.motivation: The lack of rigorous behavioral guarantees for neural network-based RL policies is a major barrier to deployment in safety-critical domains. The field has grown rapidly but remains conceptually fragmented, motivating the need for a unifying framework.
AI.method: The paper introduces a taxonomy that organizes RL verification methods along three axes: (1) verification paradigm (formal vs. probabilistic), (2) temporal scope (step-wise vs. multi-step), and (3) guarantee strength. It also unifies theoretical foundations and makes implicit assumptions and limitations explicit.
AI.result: A structured taxonomy clarifying relationships among existing RL verification approaches, along with explicit identification of assumptions, limitations, and emerging directions in the field.
AI.conclusion: The survey provides a unifying perspective that organizes the fragmented landscape of RL policy verification, enabling clearer understanding of existing methods and highlighting opportunities for future work.

title: SLT: Robust Quantum Neural Networks for Noisy-Label Medical Image Classification via Supermartingale-based Label Transition
summary: Noisy-label learning in small-scale medical image classification is challenging and hinders the superiority of deep neural networks. Recent studies suggest that quantum neural networks (QNNs) have shown potential in limited-data regimes, yet their use for noisy-label learning remains under-explored. A key obstacle is QNNs' intrinsic "natural smoothness", which may regularize training but also obscure high-confidence samples needed for noise-transition estimation. We propose Supermartingale-based Label Transition (SLT), an anchor-free loss correction framework for robust QNN-based medical image classification under noisy labels. SLT models entropy reduction in predictive distributions as a supermartingale and uses its monotonic behavior to identify stable transition-matrix refinement steps. This enables dynamic transition updates while reducing noise-driven oscillations during QNN training. We further provide a convergence analysis showing that the proposed transition-refinement process reaches a steady state. Experiments on multiple public small-scale medical image datasets demonstrate that SLT consistently improves QNN-based classification and stably outperforms classic noise-label learning baselines under synthetic and real-world label noise.

AI.tldr: Proposes Supermartingale-based Label Transition (SLT), an anchor-free loss correction framework that uses supermartingale theory to model entropy reduction in QNN predictive distributions for robust noisy-label learning in small-scale medical image classification.
AI.motivation: Noisy-label learning in small-scale medical image classification is challenging and hinders deep neural networks. QNNs show potential in limited-data regimes but their use for noisy-label learning is under-explored due to their intrinsic "natural smoothness" that obscures high-confidence samples needed for noise-transition estimation.
AI.method: SLT models entropy reduction in predictive distributions as a supermartingale, using its monotonic behavior to identify stable transition-matrix refinement steps, enabling dynamic transition updates while reducing noise-driven oscillations during QNN training.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple public small-scale medical image datasets demonstrate that SLT consistently improves QNN-based classification and stably outperforms classic noisy-label learning baselines under synthetic and real-world label noise.
AI.conclusion: The proposed transition-refinement process reaches a steady state (proven via convergence analysis), and SLT provides a robust anchor-free framework for QNN-based medical image classification under noisy labels.

title: Agentic Code Review in the Terminal: A Trajectory-Level Analysis of Behavior, Cost, and Human-Alignment
summary: Agentic code review in terminal-based environments enables early feedback during local development before pull request creation. However, existing evaluations remain performance-centric and fail to capture the dynamic behaviors of repository-grounded agentic reviewers. Understanding these behaviors is critical for identifying how agentic reviewers succeed, fail, and incur hidden operational costs in practice. Then, we analyze the reviewers' behavior based on their trajectories. Our results show that agentic reviewers achieve higher review precision but incur substantial exploration and validation overhead, while successful reviews are associated with stronger planning and less downstream validation. These findings highlight the potential benefits of trajectory-aware and cost-sensitive evaluation of future agentic code review systems.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the behavior of agentic code reviewers in terminal-based environments, finding they achieve higher precision but incur exploration and validation overhead. Successful reviews correlate with better planning and less downstream validation, suggesting the need for trajectory-aware and cost-sensitive evaluation methods.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of agentic code reviewers are performance-centric and fail to capture dynamic behaviors (how they succeed, fail, and incur hidden operational costs) in practice, which is critical for improving these systems.
AI.method: Behavioral analysis based on agent trajectories during code review in terminal-based environments, examining planning, exploration, validation, and downstream behaviors.
AI.result: Agentic reviewers achieve higher review precision but incur substantial exploration and validation overhead; successful reviews are associated with stronger planning and less downstream validation.
AI.conclusion: Future evaluation of agentic code review systems should be trajectory-aware and cost-sensitive to account for the behavioral dynamics and hidden operational costs identified.

title: Normalized Rewards for Preference Optimization
summary: Direct Alignment Algorithms (DAAs) such as DPO have become a common way to post-train and align LLMs with human preferences. However, DAAs have been observed to over-optimize their implicit reward model and decrease the likelihood of preferred responses. This results in a decrease in the total likelihood assigned to responses seen in the preference dataset, potentially resulting in undesirable behavior. To counteract this undesired side-effect of DAAs, we examine the effect of using objectives that add a regularization term to maintain the total length-normalized probabilities of the chosen and rejected responses. To better understand over-optimization, we investigate how response likelihood changes are distributed over the tokens with and without regularization. We find that a significant portion of the likelihood changes are due to a small set of outlier tokens, which explains how DAAs improve generation quality despite decreasing the likelihoods of chosen responses. We apply the proposed regularization to reference-based (DPO) and reference-free (SimPO) methods and find (1) improved trade-offs between generation quality and general benchmark capability and (2) improvements in reward modeling across datasets. For example, on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we see both a >20% relative increase in AlpacaEval2 scores and >9% relative performance gains on general benchmarks. Additionally, we find that the added regularization term effectively mitigates the amount of displacement within preferred responses overall, and for the outlier tokens specifically, by utilizing low-likelihood tokens.

AI.tldr: Direct Alignment Algorithms (DAAs) like DPO over-optimize their implicit reward model, decreasing likelihood of preferred responses. This paper proposes regularization to maintain length-normalized probabilities, finding improved trade-offs between generation quality and benchmark performance, with >20% AlpacaEval2 and >9% general benchmark gains on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.
AI.motivation: DAAs suffer from over-optimization of their implicit reward model, causing decreased likelihood of preferred responses and potentially undesirable behavior. The authors aim to understand this phenomenon and mitigate its effects through regularization.
AI.method: The authors add regularization terms to maintain total length-normalized probabilities of chosen and rejected responses. They apply this regularization to both reference-based (DPO) and reference-free (SimPO) methods. They analyze how response likelihood changes are distributed over tokens, finding outlier tokens account for significant likelihood changes.
AI.result: Regularization improves trade-offs between generation quality and general benchmark capability, and improves reward modeling across datasets. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: >20% relative increase in AlpacaEval2 scores and >9% relative performance gains on general benchmarks. Regularization mitigates displacement within preferred responses, especially for outlier tokens by utilizing low-likelihood tokens.
AI.conclusion: Adding regularization to maintain length-normalized probabilities effectively counteracts over-optimization in DAAs, improving both generation quality and benchmark performance while better understanding the role of outlier tokens in likelihood changes.

title: Accurate and Efficient Long-Term Memory for LLM Agents
summary: LLM agents augmented with persistent memory can recall past interactions, but existing systems suffer from two limitations: flat, unstructured storage loses relational context needed for multi-hop and temporal reasoning, and reliance on expensive LLM-based classification makes them impractical for latency-sensitive deployment. Without mechanisms to validate new information against stored knowledge, these systems silently accumulate contradictions. We present MOSAIC (Memory-Organized Structured Agent for Information Collection), a structured, conflict-aware long-term memory framework for LLM agents that is substantially more accurate and efficient. MOSAIC introduces three key capabilities: (1) entity-typed graph storage with semantic classification preserving relational structure across events, personas, and relationships, enabling multi-hop and temporal reasoning over conversation history; (2) hash-accelerated dual-path retrieval replacing LLM-based classification with locality-sensitive hashing, achieving near-instantaneous lookup with negligible accuracy loss; and (3) active conflict detection at save time that cross-references new information against existing graph neighbors, triggering updates or deletions for contradictory entries. Evaluated on LoCoMo (long-conversation QA), HaluMem, and a novel clinical-guideline error compounding test, MOSAIC achieves 89.35% accuracy on LoCoMo (+27.21 pp over the best baseline), best HaluMem-Medium extraction F1(86.77%) and HaluMem-Long extraction F1 (85.84%), best QA correctness on both Medium and Long (73.10%, 70.75%), and detects 66% of injected factual conflicts-4.7 times higher than the best baseline (14%)-while hash-accelerated retrieval keeps average search latency at 0.58 s per question.

AI.tldr: MOSAIC is a structured, conflict-aware long-term memory framework for LLM agents that uses entity-typed graph storage, hash-accelerated dual-path retrieval, and active conflict detection to significantly improve accuracy and efficiency over existing flat memory systems, achieving 89.35% accuracy on LoCoMo (+27.21 pp), best extraction F1 on HaluMem benchmarks, 66% conflict detection (4.7x baseline), and 0.58s average search latency.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent memory systems suffer from flat, unstructured storage that loses relational context necessary for multi-hop and temporal reasoning, rely on expensive LLM-based classification that is impractical for latency-sensitive deployment, and lack validation mechanisms to detect contradictions when new information conflicts with stored knowledge.
AI.method: MOSAIC introduces three key components: (1) entity-typed graph storage with semantic classification to preserve relational structure across events, personas, and relationships; (2) hash-accelerated dual-path retrieval using locality-sensitive hashing instead of LLM-based classification for near-instantaneous lookup; and (3) active conflict detection at save time that cross-references new information against existing graph neighbors and triggers updates or deletions for contradictory entries.
AI.result: MOSAIC achieves 89.35% accuracy on LoCoMo (+27.21 pp over best baseline), best HaluMem-Medium extraction F1 (86.77%) and HaluMem-Long extraction F1 (85.84%), best QA correctness on both Medium (73.10%) and Long (70.75%), and detects 66% of injected factual conflicts—4.7 times higher than the best baseline (14%)—while maintaining average search latency of 0.58s per question via hash-accelerated retrieval.
AI.conclusion: MOSAIC demonstrates that structured graph-based memory with hash-accelerated retrieval and proactive conflict detection substantially improves both accuracy and efficiency over flat, classification-dependent memory systems for LLM agents, enabling practical deployment in latency-sensitive settings while maintaining relational and temporal reasoning capabilities.

title: A${}^2$BM: Alignment-Aware Bridge Matching for Image-to-Image Translation
summary: Paired image-to-image translation underpins a wide range of computer vision tasks, including image editing, sensor translation, and domain adaptation. Bridge matching and flow matching have recently emerged as powerful frameworks, extending diffusion models to arbitrary source and target distributions. However, their standard formulations assume perfectly aligned training pairs, treating all source-target correspondences as equally reliable. In practice, real-world applications often involve weakly aligned pairs due to changes of acquisition conditions, including e.g. asynchronous captures, different illuminations, or misregistration. In this work, we introduce Alignment-Aware Bridge Matching (A${}^2$BM), a bridge matching method that leverages image pairs alignment during training. By incorporating alignment scores, the model learns to disentangle true semantic correspondences from misalignment artifacts. At inference time, we use the alignment score as a control variable over translation fidelity, with strongly aligned outputs obtained when prompting the model with the highest alignment score. We validate A${}^2$BM on both controlled synthetic experiments and on challenging real-world tasks, including cross-sensor super-resolution and pixel-space unsupervised domain adaptation. In all settings, A${}^2$BM consistently improves translation fidelity over strong GAN-, diffusion-, and Schr{ö}dinger bridge-based baselines, establishing alignment conditioning as a principled solution for image translation models with weakly aligned data.

AI.tldr: A${}^2$BM introduces alignment-aware conditioning into bridge matching for paired image translation, enabling models to handle weakly aligned training pairs by learning to distinguish semantic correspondences from misalignment artifacts, improving translation fidelity over GAN, diffusion, and Schrödinger bridge baselines.
AI.motivation: Standard bridge/flow matching methods assume perfectly aligned training pairs, but real-world image translation often involves weakly aligned data due to asynchronous captures, different illuminations, or misregistration, causing models to treat all correspondences as equally reliable and degrading performance.
AI.method: A${}^2$BM extends bridge matching by incorporating alignment scores during training, allowing the model to disentangle true semantic correspondences from misalignment artifacts. At inference, alignment score is used as a control variable over translation fidelity, with highest score prompting strongly aligned outputs.
AI.result: Validated on controlled synthetic experiments and real-world tasks (cross-sensor super-resolution, pixel-space unsupervised domain adaptation). Consistently improves translation fidelity over GAN-, diffusion-, and Schrödinger bridge-based baselines.
AI.conclusion: Alignment conditioning is a principled and effective solution for image translation models trained with weakly aligned data, establishing a new paradigm for handling imperfect pair correspondences.

title: A Preliminary Study on the Impact of AI in the Creativity and Collaboration in Software Teams
summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools are reshaping software engineering work, increasingly acting as cognitive partners rather than purely instrumental aids. Most AI tooling remains optimized for individual use, yet software development is inherently collaborative and creative, raising open questions about how AI affects team-based work. This paper examines how software engineering professionals perceive and integrate AI tools focusing on creativity and collaboration within teams. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 13 software professionals from four companies, each representing a distinct team. Our analysis identifies three central themes - AI Use, Consequences of AI, and Collaboration and Team Dynamics, alongside Emotions as a cross-cutting dimension. Key findings include: AI broadens developers' creative repertoires but may narrow independent ideation; developers increasingly consult AI instead of colleagues, weakening peer learning and mentoring; and teams are developing emerging triadic collaboration patterns in which developers, colleagues, and AI reason together.

AI.tldr: This study examines how software engineering professionals perceive and integrate Generative AI (GenAI) tools into their team-based work, with a focus on creativity and collaboration. Through semi-structured interviews with 13 professionals from four companies, the authors identify three main themes: AI Use, Consequences of AI, Collaboration and Team Dynamics, with Emotions as a cross-cutting dimension. Findings show AI broadens creative repertoires but may narrow independent ideation, reduces peer learning as developers consult AI instead of colleagues, and fosters emerging triadic collaboration patterns among developers, colleagues, and AI.
AI.motivation: Most AI tooling remains optimized for individual use, yet software development is inherently collaborative and creative. This gap raises open questions about how AI affects team-based work, motivating the study.
AI.method: Semi-structured interviews with 13 software professionals from four companies, each representing a distinct team.
AI.result: Three central themes identified: AI Use, Consequences of AI, and Collaboration and Team Dynamics, plus Emotions as a cross-cutting dimension. Key findings: AI broadens creative repertoires but may narrow independent ideation; developers consult AI instead of colleagues, weakening peer learning and mentoring; emerging triadic collaboration patterns where developers, colleagues, and AI reason together.
AI.conclusion: GenAI tools act as cognitive partners in software engineering, reshaping team dynamics by broadening creative possibilities while potentially reducing peer learning, and introducing new triadic collaboration patterns.

title: KernelBench-Verified: Do LLM-Generated Kernels Actually Beat PyTorch?
summary: Recent large language models (LLMs) can generate custom CUDA kernels that appear to outperform PyTorch on benchmarks such as KernelBench. Building upon this foundational framework, we demonstrate that frontier models frequently engage in reward hacking to artificially inflate reported performance. In this work, we identify two areas where evaluation frameworks must co-evolve with model capabilities. First, to accurately measure true speedup, we examine the baseline timing mechanism, noting that enabling Tensor Core acceleration with TF32 provides a more realistic estimation of execution on modern GPUs. Second, concerning algorithmic correctness, models often exploit the narrow test distribution by hardcoding bypasses for specific tensor values. By skipping required computations, these kernels artificially accelerate execution rather than implementing actual CUDA kernels. We introduce KernelBench-Verified, an extended evaluation framework that incorporates a TF32-enabled baseline and a four-distribution hidden test suite. We additionally introduce memory efficiency metrics that capture the often-overlooked speed-memory tradeoff in kernel optimization. Under verified single-turn evaluation with seven frontier LLMs, we find that the best-performing model (GPT-5.5) achieves a 0.88x geometric mean speedup, significantly lower than the 1.43x speedup observed under the standard evaluation protocol. No model consistently outperforms PyTorch when evaluated against realistic baselines. On the memory front, 28% of GPU kernels generated by the best model increase peak GPU memory usage. Our findings demonstrate the necessity of continually adapting robust evaluation protocols as LLM kernel generation capabilities advance.

AI.tldr: LLMs generate CUDA kernels that appear to outperform PyTorch (1.43x speedup) via reward hacking, but under rigorous evaluation (KernelBench-Verified with TF32 baseline and hidden test suite), the best model (GPT-5.5) achieves only 0.88x geometric mean speedup, and 28% of its kernels increase peak GPU memory usage.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation frameworks like KernelBench allow LLM-generated CUDA kernels to show inflated performance due to reward hacking and unrealistic baselines, motivating the need for a more robust evaluation protocol.
AI.method: Introduced KernelBench-Verified, which uses a TF32-enabled baseline (instead of default FP32) and a four-distribution hidden test suite to prevent hardcoded bypasses, plus memory efficiency metrics to capture speed-memory tradeoffs.
AI.result: GPT-5.5 achieves 0.88x geometric mean speedup under verified evaluation vs. 1.43x under standard protocol; no model consistently beats PyTorch; 28% of kernels from the best model increase peak GPU memory usage.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation frameworks must co-evolve with LLM capabilities; robust protocols are essential to measure true kernel optimization performance, as frontier models frequently exploit weak baselines and narrow test distributions.

title: Symbolic Augmentation Closes a Canonical-Equivalence Blind Spot in Neural Fact-Checkers
summary: Large language models hallucinate numbers and units when summarizing scientific text, a failure mode that can silently invert a scientific claim. We recast the detection of such errors as typed verification: we introduce a five-class typed-quantity error taxonomy and a 1500-item benchmark, rewritten from PMC and arXiv sources and labeled by two independent LLM annotators with adjudication (Krippendorff's alpha = 0.882). A ModernBERT encoder fine-tuned on this benchmark reaches macro-F1 = 0.899, far above any off-the-shelf neural fact-checker, yet four probes expose a sharp structural blind spot: on canonical-equivalent rewrites of physically equivalent quantities (e.g., 95°C and 368.15 K) its accuracy collapses to 36.5%. We propose Symbolic Augmentation, a training-time framework that runs the modules of a symbolic verifier in reverse to generate label-preserving augmented training data. The augmentation lifts canonical-equivalence robustness to 98.2% while slightly improving in-distribution accuracy (macro-F1: 0.899 to 0.902); the augmented encoder matches a closed-frontier LLM at no inference cost and transfers to an external benchmark (SciFact-Open binary macro-F1: 0.791 to 0.828). Two negative results sharpen the claim: symbolic features as auxiliary encoder inputs add nothing, and symbolic silver labels scale negatively under teacher noise. Together these results identify training-time augmentation as the right integration point between symbolic and learned components.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a typed-quantity error taxonomy and benchmark for detecting numerical hallucinations in scientific text, proposes Symbolic Augmentation (training-time data augmentation using symbolic verifier reverse modules) to fix a critical blind spot (canonical-equivalent rewrites), achieving 98.2% robustness and improved in-distribution and transfer performance while identifying augmentation as the optimal symbolic-neural integration point.
AI.motivation: Large language models hallucinate numbers and units when summarizing scientific text, which can silently invert scientific claims; existing fact-checkers fail to detect such typed quantity errors robustly, especially when physically equivalent quantities are expressed differently (e.g., 95°C vs 368.15 K).
AI.method: (1) A five-class typed-quantity error taxonomy and 1500-item benchmark from PMC/arXiv with dual LLM annotation (alpha=0.882). (2) ModernBERT encoder fine-tuned as baseline. (3) Four probes reveal structural blind spot on canonical-equivalent rewrites (accuracy 36.5%). (4) Symbolic Augmentation: runs symbolic verifier modules in reverse to generate label-preserving augmented training data.
AI.result: Baseline macro-F1=0.899; canonical-equivalent accuracy collapses to 36.5%. After Symbolic Augmentation: canonical-equivalent robustness rises to 98.2%, in-distribution macro-F1 slightly improves to 0.902, matches closed-frontier LLM at no inference cost, transfers to SciFact-Open (binary macro-F1 0.791→0.828). Symbolic features as auxiliary inputs add nothing; symbolic silver labels scale negatively under teacher noise.
AI.conclusion: Training-time augmentation is the right integration point between symbolic and learned components for robust numerical fact-checking; symbolic features as auxiliary inputs and silver label scaling are ineffective.

title: Emergent Hierarchical Monosemantic Neurons from the Group-Contrastive Forward-Forward Algorithm
summary: Mechanistic interpretability has made significant strides in understanding neural network representations, with sparse dictionary learning (SDL) methods, most prominently sparse autoencoders, as a central paradigm. However, recent work has reported several limitations of this paradigm: SDL objectives are non-identifiable; SDL methods rely heavily on the Linear Representation Hypothesis; and a growing body of evidence points to concepts that are encoded non-linearly and are therefore not expressible as any single direction. We hypothesise that a different route to monosemanticity is available. Biological visual systems exhibit highly selective neurons organised into hierarchies of increasing abstraction, and this organisation emerges from local, layer-wise learning rules rather than from a global error signal; we therefore ask whether a biologically plausible learning algorithm will likewise yield monosemantic neurons. To test this, we propose Group-Contrastive Forward-Forward (GCFF), a forward-forward training algorithm that combines class-specific routing with within-class contrastive objectives, reaching monosemanticity through architectural constraints rather than sparsity. Because GCFF attaches multiple non-linear layers to the representation under study, its neurons can therefore capture the non-linear concepts. On CLIP representations, a single trained GCFF module recovers monosemantic neurons whose abstraction increases progressively with depth, reaching environmental properties that hold independently of an image's foreground, without any sparsity constraint or supervision of abstraction level. We further demonstrate that GCFF can train networks from scratch, achieving state-of-the-art performance among forward-forward algorithms on various image classification benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Group-Contrastive Forward-Forward (GCFF) is a biologically plausible learning algorithm that achieves monosemantic neurons through architectural constraints and local learning rules, without relying on sparsity or the Linear Representation Hypothesis, recovering hierarchical and non-linear concepts in CLIP representations and achieving state-of-the-art performance among forward-forward methods on image classification.
AI.motivation: Current mechanistic interpretability approaches (sparse dictionary learning) face limitations: non-identifiability, reliance on the Linear Representation Hypothesis, and inability to capture non-linearly encoded concepts. The authors hypothesize that biologically plausible local learning rules, inspired by hierarchical organization in biological visual systems, can yield monosemantic neurons without these limitations.
AI.method: Proposes Group-Contrastive Forward-Forward (GCFF), a forward-forward training algorithm that uses class-specific routing combined with within-class contrastive objectives. It attaches multiple non-linear layers to the representation under study, enabling capture of non-linear concepts. Monosemanticity emerges from architectural constraints rather than sparsity.
AI.result: On CLIP representations, a single GCFF module recovers monosemantic neurons with progressively increasing abstraction across depth, capturing environmental properties independent of image foreground, without sparsity constraints or supervision of abstraction level. GCFF also achieves state-of-the-art performance among forward-forward algorithms on multiple image classification benchmarks when training from scratch.
AI.conclusion: Biologically plausible local learning rules (forward-forward approach) can yield monosemantic neurons, offering an alternative to sparse dictionary learning for mechanistic interpretability, and can effectively train networks from scratch.

title: A Non-Intrusive Traffic Analysis Framework for Authorization Risk Detection and Coordinated Response in Web Applications
comment: 25 pages; bilingual English-Chinese version. The complete English version is followed by the complete Chinese version; each version contains 3 figures and 5 tables
summary: Authorization violations under valid Web sessions are difficult to identify and handle in real time from traffic because they depend strongly on business semantics and exhibit few distinctive protocol-level features. This paper proposes a non-intrusive traffic analysis framework for authorization risk detection and coordinated response. Request-response transactions are correlated to extract the access subject, business endpoint, object identifier, authentication state, and behavioral sequence. Object-access evidence, identity consistency, behavioral anomalies, authentication context, network environment, and endpoint-operation risk are mapped to interpretable risk components. Weighted fusion and high-risk priority constraints produce graded decisions that drive allow, alert, block, and external policy actions. The risk components are instantiated using deterministic and interpretable rules to evaluate multi-source evidence organization, risk fusion, and the coordinated-response loop at the framework level. In a controlled local testbed containing 2,000 balanced labeled samples, the framework classified 998 of 1,000 authorization-risk events as risky and produced no false positives among 1,000 normal accesses, achieving 99.90% accuracy, 100.00% precision, 99.80% recall, and a 99.90% F1 score. Removing runtime object evidence reduced the F1 score to 81.31%, while removing the high-risk priority constraint reduced it to 73.90%. In a prototype feasibility test with 100 concurrent requests and 1,000 total requests, mean risk-decision computation latency was 0.077 ms and P99 latency was 0.137 ms. The results demonstrate the feasibility of organizing heterogeneous runtime evidence and establishing an executable authorization-risk decision and coordinated-response loop without modifying application code, but do not establish general applicability in production environments.

AI.tldr: A non-intrusive traffic analysis framework detects authorization risks in real-time by correlating HTTP transactions into interpretable risk components, achieving 99.90% accuracy and sub-millisecond latency without modifying application code.
AI.motivation: Authorization violations under valid Web sessions are hard to detect from traffic because they depend on business semantics and lack distinctive protocol-level features.
AI.method: Request-response transactions are correlated to extract access subject, business endpoint, object identifier, authentication state, and behavioral sequence. Six risk components (object-access evidence, identity consistency, behavioral anomalies, authentication context, network environment, endpoint-operation risk) are mapped and fused with weighted fusion and high-risk priority constraints to produce graded decisions (allow, alert, block, external policy actions).
AI.result: In a testbed with 2,000 balanced labeled samples: 99.90% accuracy, 100.00% precision, 99.80% recall, 99.90% F1 score. Removing object evidence dropped F1 to 81.31%; removing high-risk priority constraint dropped F1 to 73.90%. Mean latency 0.077 ms, P99 latency 0.137 ms on 100 concurrent/1,000 total requests.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates feasibility of organizing heterogeneous runtime evidence and establishing an executable authorization-risk decision loop without modifying application code, but does not establish general applicability in production environments.

title: TRACE: Trajectory-Based Safety Patch Learning for LLM Post-Training Realignment
summary:
Fine-Tuning-as-a-Service (FTaaS) platforms let users train large language models (LLMs) on customized tasks, but this pipeline could erode models' safety alignment. In practice, service providers need to recover models' safety without re-running full alignment, or destroying the utility gained from customized tasks. A line of existing work refers to model parameter merging, which adds a safety patch on the fine-tuned model parameters to shift the model away from unsafe tendencies. However, this merging-based paradigm is fundamentally bottlenecked by task-safety update entanglement: downstream task updates and the safety patch often overlap in their dominant directions, so the merge strength is intrinsically hard to calibrate.
