If the safety vector is scaled too weakly, harmful components could still dominate, preventing the model from returning to a safe region; if it is scaled too aggressively, it suppresses task-relevant directions and degrades utility.
  To solve this problem, we shift the focus of merging-based methods from designing online merging operators to offline patch learning, and seek a safety patch that minimally interferes with task-relevant directions while retaining decisive control over unsafe behaviors. We propose TRACE, a trajectory-based safety patch learning framework that (i) simulates harmful tuning trajectories to generate progressively corrupted states, and (ii) optimizes a plug-in patch to recover safety while maintaining utility across varying corrupted base states.
  Across six benchmarks and two models, TRACE consistently dominates the safety-utility frontier. TRACE reaches nearly 100% safety on all settings, while maintaining comparable utility to the undefended fine-tuned model.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a trajectory-based safety patch learning framework that addresses the task-safety entanglement problem in FTaaS by learning a plug-in patch that recovers safety alignment without degrading task utility, achieving near 100% safety while maintaining comparable utility across six benchmarks and two models.
AI.motivation: Existing merging-based safety recovery methods for fine-tuned LLMs suffer from task-safety update entanglement, where the optimal merge strength between the safety patch and task updates is fundamentally hard to calibrate due to overlapping dominant directions.
AI.method: TRACE shifts from online merging operators to offline patch learning by: (i) simulating harmful tuning trajectories to generate progressively corrupted model states, and (ii) optimizing a plug-in safety patch that minimally interferes with task-relevant directions while retaining decisive control over unsafe behaviors across varying corrupted base states.
AI.result: Across six benchmarks and two models, TRACE achieves nearly 100% safety on all settings while maintaining utility comparable to the undefended fine-tuned model, consistently dominating the safety-utility frontier.
AI.conclusion: The trajectory-based offline patch learning paradigm effectively resolves the task-safety entanglement bottleneck, providing a practical solution for safety recovery in FTaaS without sacrificing task utility.

title: SelKV: Selective KV Cache Merging with Per-Token Merge-or-Drop and Attention Compensation
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) generate text autoregressively, relying on a key-value (KV) cache whose memory footprint grows linearly with context length, creating a major bottleneck. Recent compression methods mitigate this cost via token merging; however, these approaches often rely on indiscriminate aggregation, which degrades representations and introduces attention sag, a mismatch where merged tokens receive the same softmax mass as individual tokens despite encoding multiple inputs. We propose a training-free, dual-component framework for KV cache compression that addresses these limitations. First, a soft cosine gate adaptively modulates merging decisions based on value-vector similarity, suppressing or discarding dissimilar tokens to preserve semantic fidelity. Second, we introduce an attention-ratio compensation mechanism that applies a decoding-time logit bias derived from prefill attention statistics, correcting the softmax imbalance induced by merging. Evaluated on LongBench (16 English datasets) while retaining only 25% of the KV cache, our framework achieves strong compressed performance against representative one-shot baselines. It is especially robust on the evaluated grouped-query attention (GQA) models, maintaining nearlossless generation quality. Furthermore, the method outperforms the full-cache baseline on complex multi-document QA tasks and delivers a 3.3x decoding speedup at 100k tokens.

AI.tldr: A training-free KV cache compression framework using soft cosine gate and attention-ratio compensation achieves 25% cache retention with near-lossless quality, 3.3x decoding speedup at 100k tokens, and outperforms full-cache on multi-document QA.
AI.motivation: LLMs' autoregressive generation suffers from linearly growing KV cache memory footprint. Existing token merging methods use indiscriminate aggregation, which degrades representations and causes attention sag (merged tokens receiving same softmax mass as individual tokens despite encoding multiple inputs).
AI.method: Dual-component training-free framework: (1) Soft cosine gate that adaptively modulates merging decisions based on value-vector similarity, suppressing/discarding dissimilar tokens; (2) Attention-ratio compensation mechanism applying decoding-time logit bias derived from prefill attention statistics to correct softmax imbalance from merging.
AI.result: On LongBench (16 English datasets) with 25% KV cache retention, achieves strong performance against one-shot baselines. Especially robust on GQA models with near-lossless generation. Outperforms full-cache baseline on complex multi-document QA. Delivers 3.3x decoding speedup at 100k tokens.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively addresses limitations of prior token merging approaches for KV cache compression, achieving efficient compression with minimal quality degradation, particularly benefiting GQA models and long-context scenarios.

title: Rethinking Feature Reliance Evaluation with Semantically Matched Suppression
summary: Understanding whether visual recognition models rely on shape, texture, or color is central to interpreting their behavior. Prior cue-conflict studies have strongly influenced the view that CNNs are texture-biased, yet such tests measure cue preference under artificial conflicts rather than feature reliance during natural recognition. We revisit this question through controlled feature suppression and show that performance drops are difficult to interpret unless different suppression operations impose comparable category-level damage. We introduce a semantically matched evaluation framework that compares shape and texture suppression at matched levels of category separability loss. Under this framework, ImageNet-trained CNNs show stronger degradation under texture suppression than under shape suppression, revealing greater texture reliance than suggested by unmatched suppression analyses. Extending the comparison across architectures, we find that Vision Transformers retain higher accuracy than CNNs under both shape and texture suppression. Brain encoding further shows that ViT representations exhibit smaller suppression-induced decreases in neural prediction performance under the tested suppression settings. These findings indicate that semantic comparability is essential for interpreting feature reliance from suppression experiments, and suggest that the robustness advantage of ViTs may be related to representations more compatible with human visual cortex.

AI.tldr: CNNs rely more on texture than shape when evaluated using a semantically matched suppression framework. ViTs are more robust to both shape and texture suppression than CNNs, and their representations align better with human visual cortex.
AI.motivation: Prior cue-conflict studies suggest CNNs are texture-biased, but these tests measure preference under artificial conflicts rather than feature reliance during natural recognition. Controlled suppression experiments are difficult to interpret without ensuring comparable category-level damage.
AI.method: Introduced a semantically matched evaluation framework that compares shape and texture suppression at matched levels of category separability loss. Evaluated ImageNet-trained CNNs and Vision Transformers under this framework, and compared brain encoding with neural prediction performance.
AI.result: ImageNet-trained CNNs show stronger degradation under texture suppression than shape suppression when matched semantically, revealing greater texture reliance. ViTs retain higher accuracy than CNNs under both suppression types. ViT representations show smaller suppression-induced decreases in neural prediction performance.
AI.conclusion: Semantic comparability is essential for interpreting feature reliance from suppression experiments. ViTs' robustness advantage may be related to representations more compatible with human visual cortex.

title: When Post-Anchor Metrics Fail: Stabilization Regimes in AI-Evidence Open-Source Projects
summary: Repository mining studies increasingly analyze AI-evidence projects, yet it remains unclear how to measure whether architectural changes create deferred stabilization obligations. A natural metric, post-anchor stabilization density, counts tests, CI gates, documentation, and fixes appearing after a durable boundary is introduced. We show that this metric fails. In a diff-level study of 338 high-visibility 2026 GitHub repositories, anchors are common (321 of 338 contain real changed-file anchor evidence), but a controlled 308-event contiguous-window experiment finds no post-anchor uplift: broad and strict stabilization signals both yield median post/pre density ratios near 1.0, and non-anchor controls are equally dense. We introduce stabilization regimes, six recurring patterns that explain why the density metric fails, and use human validation to calibrate them. Two independent coders label 100 stratified candidate-anchor events from blinded packets (kappa = 0.50 on debt attribution). The validation exposes a two-layer trap: many candidate anchors are not durable boundaries (45 of 100), and even among valid anchors in this calibration sample the no-uplift result holds: only 3 of 100 events survive as attributable delayed obligations; the remaining 97 are explained by classifier error, anchor-local hardening, background maintenance, or pre-anchor hardening. Post-anchor density conflates pervasive maintenance with genuine debt; controlled designs with regime-aware attribution are necessary before repository mining can reliably identify stabilization obligations.

AI.tldr: A study of 338 GitHub repositories finds that post-anchor stabilization density fails as a metric for measuring deferred stabilization obligations, with controlled experiments showing no uplift and human validation revealing that only 3 of 100 candidate anchor events represent genuine delayed obligations.
AI.motivation: Repository mining studies need to measure whether architectural changes create deferred stabilization obligations, but existing metrics for this purpose are unreliable.
AI.method: Diff-level study of 338 high-visibility 2026 GitHub repositories with a controlled 308-event contiguous-window experiment, plus human validation using two independent coders on 100 stratified candidate-anchor events (kappa = 0.50).
AI.result: Anchors are common (321/338 repositories), but no post-anchor uplift is found (median post/pre density ratios ~1.0). Only 3 of 100 events survive as attributable delayed obligations; 97 are explained by classifier error, anchor-local hardening, background maintenance, or pre-anchor hardening.
AI.conclusion: Post-anchor density conflates pervasive maintenance with genuine debt; controlled designs with regime-aware attribution are necessary for reliable identification of stabilization obligations in repository mining.

title: RobustMAD: Evaluating Real-World Robustness of Multimodal Small Language Models for Deployable Anomaly Detection Assistants
comment: Accepted for publication in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026 at https://openreview.net/forum?id=skrA9UYNIZ
summary: Multimodal industrial anomaly inspection assistants are a critical component of next-generation smart factories, enabling interactive vision-language-based querying. However, multimodal large language models remain impractical for on-site deployment due to prohibitive computational demands and privacy risks from cloud-based inference. Compact multimodal small language models (MSLMs) offer a deployable alternative, yet progress is constrained by the lack of comprehensive robustness analyses and meaningfully challenging benchmarks that reflect real-world industrial conditions. To address this gap, we develop RobustMAD, the first deployment-motivated benchmark, designed to comprehensively evaluate model robustness through diverse open-ended queries spanning object understanding, anomaly detection, unanswerable problems, and visual quality degradations. Contrary to conventional assumptions, top-performing MSLMs exhibit promising capabilities, surprisingly outperforming even the larger GPT-5 Nano. However, they still fall short of safety-critical requirements, and RobustMAD reveals critical robustness gaps that pose operational risks. In particular, three recurring failure modes emerge: (i) fragile multimodal grounding under fine-grained distinctions or degraded visual conditions, (ii) insufficiently comprehensive responses, and (iii) weak logical grounding on unanswerable or ill-posed queries, leading to hallucinated outputs. Grounded in these insights, we provide actionable guidance for the design of next-generation multimodal industrial inspection assistants that leverage their promising competence. Code is available at https://github.com/en-research/RobustMAD.

AI.tldr: RobustMAD is the first deployment-motivated benchmark for evaluating robustness of multimodal small language models (MSLMs) in industrial anomaly inspection, revealing that while MSLMs can surprisingly outperform larger models like GPT-5 Nano, they exhibit critical failure modes in fine-grained grounding, response comprehensiveness, and logical reasoning on unanswerable queries, providing actionable guidance for next-generation industrial assistants.
AI.motivation: Multimodal large language models are impractical for on-site industrial deployment due to computational demands and privacy risks, while compact multimodal small language models (MSLMs) lack comprehensive robustness analyses and meaningful benchmarks reflecting real-world industrial conditions.
AI.method: Developed RobustMAD, a deployment-motivated benchmark evaluating MSLM robustness through diverse open-ended queries covering object understanding, anomaly detection, unanswerable problems, and visual quality degradations.
AI.result: Top-performing MSLMs surprisingly outperform even GPT-5 Nano, but still fall short of safety-critical requirements. Three recurring failure modes identified: (i) fragile multimodal grounding under fine-grained or degraded visual conditions, (ii) insufficiently comprehensive responses, (iii) weak logical grounding on unanswerable/ill-posed queries leading to hallucinations.
AI.conclusion: RobustMAD reveals critical robustness gaps posing operational risks; provides actionable guidance for designing next-generation multimodal industrial inspection assistants leveraging MSLMs' promising competence.

title: RAIL Guard: Closing the Evaluation-to-Remediation Gap in Responsible AI for LLM Agents
summary: Existing guardrail systems for large language model agents operate as binary classifiers that block unsafe content, leaving organizations to discard failing outputs and retry from scratch. We introduce RAIL Guard, a closed-loop responsible AI pipeline that evaluates LLM outputs across eight measurable dimensions and iteratively remediates failing outputs through an evaluate-rewrite-reevaluate loop. We evaluate the pipeline across three experiments on four frontier LLMs and 4,276 content outputs plus 6,400 agent tool-call scenarios. Closed-loop remediation achieves 96.9% convergence versus 49.1% for block-and-retry, though the highest-convergence method reduces utility by 22.3%; feedback-driven self-repair achieves 86.6% convergence on fixable dimensions with no significant utility loss (p = 0.177). Pre-tool-call evaluation reduces unsafe agent executions by 33% (p = 0.007) with zero impact on task completion. We identify a key distinction between fixable dimensions that respond to remediation and structural dimensions (Transparency at 93.0%, Accountability at 92.8%, and Inclusivity at 82.5% failure) that require architectural rather than algorithmic solutions. The system is available as open-source SDKs.

AI.tldr: RAIL Guard is a closed-loop responsible AI pipeline that evaluates and iteratively remediates LLM outputs across eight dimensions, achieving 96.9% convergence via closed-loop remediation vs 49.1% for block-and-retry, while identifying fixable vs structural dimensions that require architectural solutions.
AI.motivation: Existing guardrail systems operate as binary classifiers that block unsafe content, forcing organizations to discard failing outputs and retry from scratch, which is inefficient and lacks remediation capabilities.
AI.method: RAIL Guard implements an evaluate-rewrite-reevaluate loop across eight measurable dimensions, evaluated on four frontier LLMs with 4,276 content outputs and 6,400 agent tool-call scenarios.
AI.result: Closed-loop remediation achieves 96.9% convergence vs 49.1% for block-and-retry; feedback-driven self-repair achieves 86.6% convergence on fixable dimensions with no significant utility loss; pre-tool-call evaluation reduces unsafe agent executions by 33% with zero impact on task completion.
AI.conclusion: A distinction exists between fixable dimensions (responsive to remediation) and structural dimensions (Transparency, Accountability, Inclusivity) that require architectural rather than algorithmic solutions. The system is available as open-source SDKs.

title: FedDP-PALD: A Privacy-Preserving Federated Latent Diffusion Framework with Prototype Aggregation for Medical Data Synthesis
summary: Medical images and physiological signals provide valuable information for accurate diagnosis. Developing diagnostic models often requires patient data from multiple institutions, although strict privacy regulations limit the sharing of sensitive clinical records. Federated learning enables multiple hospitals to train a shared model without exchanging raw data. However, existing methods face two problems: the information exchanged during training can reveal whether a patient's data were used, and synthetic data meant to replace real records often fail to preserve their predictive structure, which limits clinical use. To address this issue, we propose FedDP-PALD, a privacy-preserving federated latent diffusion framework for multimodal medical data synthesis under formal privacy guarantees. It jointly processes chest X-ray images and electrocardiogram (ECG) signals through gated multi-head attention with modality-availability masks, remaining effective even when a modality is missing. We also introduce Differentially Private Prototype Mixture Aggregation (DP-PMA), which clips class-level latent prototypes and adds calibrated Gaussian noise before combining them on the server to maintain $(ε, δ)$ differential privacy. We evaluate FedDP-PALD on PneumoniaMNIST, ChestMNIST, and MIT-BIH datasets, where differential privacy reduced summary-level attack AUROC from 0.6229 $\pm$ 0.0026 to between 0.5016 and 0.5093 for privacy budgets from $ε= 1$ to $ε= 8$. On the test data, synthetic-latent training achieved an F1 score of 0.8993 $\pm$ 0.0006 and an AUROC of 0.9057 $\pm$ 0.0503, close to the 0.9747 $\pm$ 0.0132 real-latent training. These results show that FedDP-PALD generates private synthetic representations that preserve useful decision performance while strongly resisting membership inference.

AI.tldr: FedDP-PALD is a privacy-preserving federated latent diffusion framework for multimodal medical data synthesis that uses differentially private prototype mixture aggregation to generate synthetic data that preserves predictive performance while strongly resisting membership inference attacks.
AI.motivation: Existing federated learning methods face two problems: information exchanged during training can reveal patient data membership, and synthetic data meant to replace real records often fail to preserve their predictive structure, limiting clinical utility.
AI.method: Proposes FedDP-PALD, which jointly processes chest X-ray images and ECG signals through gated multi-head attention with modality-availability masks. Introduces Differentially Private Prototype Mixture Aggregation (DP-PMA) that clips class-level latent prototypes and adds calibrated Gaussian noise to maintain (ε, δ) differential privacy.
AI.result: On PneumoniaMNIST, ChestMNIST, and MIT-BIH datasets, DP reduced summary-level attack AUROC from 0.6229±0.0026 to between 0.5016-0.5093 for ε=1 to ε=8. Synthetic-latent training achieved F1 of 0.8993±0.0006 and AUROC of 0.9057±0.0503, close to real-latent training (0.9747±0.0132).
AI.conclusion: FedDP-PALD generates private synthetic representations that preserve useful decision performance while strongly resisting membership inference, enabling privacy-preserved multimodal medical data synthesis under formal guarantees.

title: Schema-Bound LLM Control of Scientific Instrumentation through Model Context Protocol Skills
comment: 36 pages, 8 figures, 7 tables. Open-source reference implementation, physics-plausible simulator, and validation suite. Software-only validation; live-instrument validation is not reported
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can plan tool-mediated scientific work, but scientific instruments remain difficult to connect to such agents: vendor APIs may load only inside acquisition host processes, facilities may prohibit cloud-hosted agents, and natural-language interfaces can emit physically unreasonable arguments. We present a method for connecting local LLMs to scientific instruments through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). It combines: (1) a schema-bound tool surface that validates requests against physical bounds before adapter dispatch; (2) a vendor-neutral, host-process adapter pattern separating language-side reasoning from instrument-side execution; (3) a persistent lifecycle for long-running live-processing jobs; and (4) MCP-prompt-registered skills that compose typed tools into reusable multi-step protocols. Our open-source reference server exposes 30 typed tools, 5 live-job types, and 6 skills through a physics-plausible simulator implementing the same protocol surface. Validation is software-only: all 120 hardware-independent tests pass deterministically, while 15 local-LLM integration tests pass 12-15 of 15 across runs because of model nondeterminism. A preliminary single-run probe across five open tool-calling LLMs indicates that the schema-bound interface can be driven locally by small open-weight models without cloud dependency; it is not a benchmark and has no confidence intervals. The method provides a bounded, testable, and reproducible foundation for closed-loop agentic instrumentation research.

AI.tldr: Presents a method for connecting local LLMs to scientific instruments via the Model Context Protocol (MCP), using schema-bound tools, vendor-neutral adapters, persistent live-processing jobs, and MCP-registered skills, validated with a simulator and local open-weight models.
AI.motivation: Scientific instruments are difficult to connect to LLM-based agents due to vendor-specific APIs, facility restrictions on cloud-hosted agents, and risk of physically unreasonable arguments from natural-language interfaces.
AI.method: Four components: (1) schema-bound tool surface with physical bounds validation; (2) vendor-neutral, host-process adapter pattern; (3) persistent lifecycle for live-processing jobs; (4) MCP-prompt-registered skills for multi-step protocols. Implemented as an open-source reference server with 30 typed tools, 5 live-job types, and 6 skills.
AI.result: All 120 hardware-independent tests pass deterministically; 15 local-LLM integration tests pass 12-15/15 across runs due to model nondeterminism; a preliminary single-run probe across five open tool-calling LLMs shows small open-weight models can drive the schema-bound interface locally.
AI.conclusion: The method provides a bounded, testable, and reproducible foundation for closed-loop agentic instrumentation research, enabling local LLM-driven scientific instrument control without cloud dependency.

title: CIGPO: Contextual Information-Gain Policy Optimization for Multi-Turn Evidence-Reading LLM Agents
summary: Training multi-turn evidence-reading agents with outcome-only reinforcement learning is unstable because intermediate turns receive little direct credit. In HotpotQA experiments with Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, GRPO initially improves (standard F1 0.430) but subsequently collapses to 100% format-violating outputs. Training-log diagnosis reveals a zero-advantage lock-in mechanism: all sampled trajectories receive the minimum format penalty (-2.0), group-relative advantages vanish, and the policy-gradient loss becomes zero--an optimization deadlock. We propose a variance-injection strategy: by assigning per-turn rewards to intermediate evidence-reading turns, we prevent the group reward distribution from collapsing to a single value--preserving the variation that GRPO's group-relative advantage requires. Contextual Information-Gain Policy Optimization (CIGPO) implements this strategy using the marginal increase in the frozen reference model's log-likelihood of the ground-truth answer as the per-turn signal. With separate normalization of IG and F1 rewards and an IG-weight curriculum, CIGPO reaches a standard F1 of 0.518 on HotpotQA at the 3B scale (from 0.252 base; +105%), compared with 0.430 for the best GRPO checkpoint and 0.000 for the final GRPO checkpoint. CIGPO maintains meaningful reward variance and avoids zero-advantage lock-in throughout training. These results identify reward-variance collapse as a concrete failure mode of outcome-only GRPO and show that turn-level IG rewards can prevent it in this HotpotQA setting.

AI.tldr: Outcome-only GRPO for multi-turn evidence reading collapses due to zero-advantage lock-in (all trajectories get the same format penalty, eliminating reward variance). CIGPO solves this by injecting per-turn information-gain rewards, achieving F1 0.518 on HotpotQA (+105% vs base, vs GRPO's 0.430 best and 0.000 collapse).
AI.motivation: Training multi-turn evidence-reading agents with outcome-only RL is unstable because intermediate turns receive little direct credit, leading to optimization deadlocks.
AI.method: CIGPO (Contextual Information-Gain Policy Optimization): assigns per-turn rewards based on the marginal increase in the frozen reference model's log-likelihood of the ground-truth answer, with separate normalization of IG and F1 rewards and an IG-weight curriculum.
AI.result: CIGPO achieves standard F1 0.518 on HotpotQA at 3B scale (from 0.252 base; +105%), compared to GRPO's best 0.430 and final 0.000 (collapse). CIGPO maintains meaningful reward variance throughout training.
AI.conclusion: Reward-variance collapse is a concrete failure mode of outcome-only GRPO; turn-level IG rewards can prevent it in HotpotQA settings.

title: Generalist AI Control: Towards Multi-purpose Adaptive Algorithms
summary: Traditional controllers are designed for specific systems and do not transfer across different system orders and dynamics. We present a Generalist Controller, a learning-based controller capable of controlling systems of varying orders and dynamics. The approach introduces a novel dynamic state-space representation using attention mechanisms with masking, enabling a single neural network, trained in one shot, to handle systems with different dimensions without architectural modifications by assigning a system tag to each system. We generated 314,630 demonstrations from 25 diverse systems, including stable, unstable, minimum-phase, and non-minimum-phase dynamics, spanning linear and nonlinear systems from autonomous underwater and aerospace vehicles to mechanical systems and chemical processes. The model learns cross-system control strategies through multi-scale temporal processing and a mixture-of-experts architecture. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed generalist controller achieves comparable performance to system-specific LQI controllers across all tested systems, including challenging cases such as non-minimum-phase and unstable dynamics, whilst generalising to unseen operating conditions including actuator saturation, noise, disturbance, and reference trajectories not encountered during training. This work represents a significant step towards generalist control policies within a defined family of dynamical systems, demonstrating effective control across a range of single-input single-output (SISO) systems of varying order and dynamics using a single learned policy without system-specific tuning.

AI.tldr: A single neural network controller trained on 314,630 demonstrations from 25 diverse dynamical systems generalizes across different system orders and dynamics without system-specific tuning, achieving comparable performance to LQI controllers.
AI.motivation: Traditional controllers are system-specific and do not transfer across different system orders and dynamics, necessitating a generalist approach.
AI.method: Uses a dynamic state-space representation with attention mechanisms and masking, system tags, multi-scale temporal processing, and a mixture-of-experts architecture; trained on 314,630 demonstrations from 25 SISO systems (stable, unstable, minimum-phase, non-minimum-phase, linear/nonlinear).
AI.result: Achieves comparable performance to system-specific LQI controllers across all tested systems, including challenging non-minimum-phase and unstable dynamics, and generalizes to unseen conditions (actuator saturation, noise, disturbance, novel reference trajectories).
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a significant step towards generalist control policies within a defined family of dynamical systems, enabling a single learned policy to control diverse SISO systems without system-specific tuning.

title: Med-OPD: Improving Medical Vision-Language Models via Evidence-Aware On-Policy Distillation
summary: Medical Vision-Language Models (Med-VLMs) require reliable reasoning from fine-grained visual evidence, yet existing models can produce plausible clinical answers by relying on language priors or medical templates rather than truly attending to diagnosis-critical regions. On-Policy Distillation (OPD) offers dense token-level supervision on student-generated trajectories and provides a privacy-compatible means of capability transfer without requiring the redistribution of raw patient data. However, standard OPD uniformly distills all tokens, causing sparse evidence-dependent tokens to be diluted by abundant clinical narrative tokens. Inspired by the success of OPD in the large language model community, we propose \textbf{Med-OPD}, to our knowledge the first unified post-training framework that integrates on-policy distillation with medical evidence-aware supervision for Med-VLMs. We introduce \textbf{Medical Evidence Advantage} (MEA), a teacher-grounded counterfactual signal that uses an answer-aware hint to focus teacher scoring on evidence supporting the target diagnosis, and measures each token's dependence on medical visual evidence by comparing teacher likelihoods under the original and evidence-degraded imaging modalities. Based on MEA, Med-OPD redistributes the distillation signal at both the token and trajectory levels, emphasizing diagnosis-critical tokens and evidence-reliant rollouts. Experiments on OmniMedVQA subsets show that Med-OPD consistently outperforms SFT and standard OPD across CT, MRI, Disease Diagnosis, and Lesion Grading. These results demonstrate that evidence-aware distillation can better strengthen medical VLMs' reliance on key visual evidence and improve reliable multimodal medical reasoning. The source code and data is publicly available at: https://github.com/yunhang8658/MedOPD.git

AI.tldr: Med-OPD is a unified post-training framework for Medical VLMs that integrates on-policy distillation with evidence-aware supervision using Medical Evidence Advantage (MEA) to emphasize diagnosis-critical tokens and evidence-reliant trajectories, outperforming SFT and standard OPD on OmniMedVQA subsets.
AI.motivation: Existing Med-VLMs can produce plausible answers using language priors or medical templates without truly attending to diagnosis-critical regions. Standard On-Policy Distillation (OPD) uniformly distills all tokens, causing sparse evidence-dependent tokens to be diluted by abundant clinical narrative tokens.
AI.method: Med-OPD introduces Medical Evidence Advantage (MEA), a teacher-grounded counterfactual signal that uses an answer-aware hint to focus teacher scoring on evidence supporting the target diagnosis. It measures each token's dependence on medical visual evidence by comparing teacher likelihoods under original and evidence-degraded imaging modalities. Based on MEA, distillation signals are redistributed at both token and trajectory levels.
AI.result: On OmniMedVQA subsets, Med-OPD consistently outperforms SFT and standard OPD across CT, MRI, Disease Diagnosis, and Lesion Grading tasks.
AI.conclusion: Evidence-aware distillation strengthens medical VLMs' reliance on key visual evidence and improves reliable multimodal medical reasoning.

title: Can LLM Code Explanations Adapt to Diverse Problem-Solvers' Needs?
comment: To be published in AAAI/ACM conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2026)
summary: Large language model (LLM) code explanations can support people in solving code-related problems, yet prior work has shown that people have diverse problem-solving styles. If explanations fail to meet people's problem-solving needs, they may be less productive in their occupations and miss opportunities to learn and grow. Although some research has examined how LLMs can adapt their outputs to a user's age or expertise, no prior work has examined how LLMs can adapt their code explanations to people's problem-solving styles. To address this gap, we developed prompts from an established inclusive design method that considers 5 types of problem-solving styles, and we generated 1,072 code explanations from six open-weight LLMs. Using natural language processing techniques, we uncovered a taxonomy of 13 linguistic adaptations, with each adaptation supported by evidence from the literature, the prompts, or the LLMs' outputs. They also show which LLMs adapted their code explanations more frequently than others. This paper is the first to investigate problem-solving style adaptations in LLM code explanation, contributing two problem-solving adaptation approaches: declarative statements for each adaptation and 10 problem-solving style prompts.

AI.tldr: First study to investigate how LLMs can adapt code explanations to users' problem-solving styles, developing prompts based on 5 problem-solving styles, generating 1,072 explanations from six LLMs, and uncovering a taxonomy of 13 linguistic adaptations via NLP techniques.
AI.motivation: LLM code explanations can support problem-solving, but people have diverse problem-solving styles. Prior work only adapted to age/expertise, not problem-solving styles; mismatched explanations may reduce productivity and learning opportunities.
AI.method: Developed prompts from an established inclusive design method covering 5 problem-solving styles; generated 1,072 code explanations from six open-weight LLMs; used NLP techniques to uncover a taxonomy of 13 linguistic adaptations.
AI.result: Identified a taxonomy of 13 linguistic adaptations, each supported by evidence from literature, prompts, or LLM outputs. Found variation in how frequently different LLMs adapted their explanations.
AI.conclusion: First paper to investigate problem-solving style adaptations in LLM code explanations; contributes two adaptation approaches: declarative statements for each adaptation and 10 problem-solving style prompts.

title: Learning Structural Manipulability in Gate-Level Netlists Using Graph Neural Networks
summary: Gate-level netlists exhibit intrinsic structural properties that influence signal propagation independently of functional simulation. We define a topology-driven structural manipulability score that characterizes node-level structural flexibility using path participation, k-core embedding, symmetry, and centrality. Modeling netlists as directed graphs, we formulate node-level regression to learn this topology-derived score using graph neural networks (GNNs). Experiments on ISCAS85 and EPFL benchmarks evaluate how effectively different GNN architectures approximate this metric across held-out circuits, with hierarchical models yielding the most consistent rankings. Component-level and ablation analyses examine the contribution of individual factors. As an illustrative case study, analysis of Trojan-injected circuits using TrustHub templates reveals statistically distinguishable structural patterns, indicating that topology-based scoring provides complementary structural insight.

AI.tldr: This paper defines a topology-driven structural manipulability score for gate-level netlists using path participation, k-core embedding, symmetry, and centrality, then uses GNNs to learn and predict this score. Experiments on ISCAS85 and EPFL benchmarks show hierarchical GNNs perform best, and Trojan-injected circuits exhibit distinguishable structural patterns.
AI.motivation: Gate-level netlists have intrinsic structural properties affecting signal propagation independent of functional simulation; there is a need to characterize node-level structural flexibility without relying on functional analysis.
AI.method: Define a topology-driven structural manipulability score combining path participation, k-core embedding, symmetry, and centrality; model netlists as directed graphs; formulate node-level regression using various GNN architectures (including hierarchical models) to learn the score.
AI.result: Hierarchical GNN models yield the most consistent rankings across held-out circuits on ISCAS85 and EPFL benchmarks; component-level and ablation analyses reveal individual factor contributions; Trojan-injected circuits (TrustHub) show statistically distinguishable structural patterns.
AI.conclusion: Topology-based scoring provides complementary structural insight beyond functional analysis, as demonstrated by its ability to distinguish Trojan-injected circuits.

title: LaCache: Exact Caching and Precision-Adaptive Inference for Diffusion Large Language Models
summary: Diffusion-based Large Language Models(DLLMs) enable parallel generation via Semi-Autoregressive (SAR) decoding in text generation. However, current methods suffer from severe operator-level redundancy: they recompute the entire sequence during denoising steps, ignoring that the prefix and masked suffix remain invariant within a block. We propose LaCache, a training-free acceleration framework that alleviates this redundancy through lossless caching and mixed precision. Specifically, LaCache employs Lossless State Memoization (LSM) by caching three types of intermediate results: (i) EmbedCache for embedding outputs, (ii) RoPECache for token-wise pre-attention states, and (iii) FACache for the online softmax statistics within FlashAttention. These caches allow the model to skip redundant computation on unchanged tokens without altering the output. To further alleviate memory-bandwidth bottlenecks, LaCache inegrates a per-group FP8 quantization strategy for FFN layers, tailored to step-dependent activation distributions across the diffusion process. Experiments demonstrate that LaCache alone achieves approximately 1.3X end-to-end speedup over vanilla DLLM. When combined with existing acceleration methods, LaCache reaches up to 40.2X end-to-end speedup while maintaining comparable task accuracy.

AI.tldr: LaCache is a training-free acceleration framework for Diffusion-based Large Language Models that reduces operator-level redundancy via lossless caching (EmbedCache, RoPECache, FACache) and per-group FP8 quantization, achieving up to 40.2X end-to-end speedup while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: Current Diffusion-based LLMs suffer from severe operator-level redundancy during denoising steps — they recompute the entire sequence despite the prefix and masked suffix remaining invariant within a block, leading to unnecessary computational cost.
AI.method: LaCache proposes two main techniques: (1) Lossless State Memoization (LSM) with three caches (EmbedCache for embedding outputs, RoPECache for token-wise pre-attention states, FACache for online softmax statistics in FlashAttention) to skip redundant computation on unchanged tokens; (2) per-group FP8 quantization strategy for FFN layers, tailored to step-dependent activation distributions across the diffusion process.
AI.result: LaCache alone achieves ~1.3X speedup over vanilla DLLM. When combined with existing acceleration methods, it reaches up to 40.2X end-to-end speedup while maintaining comparable task accuracy.
AI.conclusion: LaCache effectively eliminates operator-level redundancy in DLLMs through lossless caching and mixed precision, providing significant speedup without training requirements or accuracy degradation.

title: Dual-Domain Self-Supervised Artifact Removal Framework for Photoacoustic Computed Tomography
summary: Photoacoustic Computed Tomography (PACT) often faces severe challenges from reconstruction artifacts due to sparse detection conditions. In this work, based on the distinct differences in artifact patterns between back-projection-based and Fourier-based reconstruction algorithms, we propose a self-supervised artifact removal framework that employs a lightweight Siamese Neural Network and a composite loss function integrating cross-domain fidelity and uncertainty-weighted consistency, effectively decoupling dual-domain features and filtering artifacts. Comprehensive validations using simulations, phantoms, in vivo rat and human experimental data demonstrate that the proposed method can significantly suppress image artifacts. Furthermore, enabled by the acceleration of the spatial-domain and frequency-domain inverse operator, this end-to-end approach also achieves exceptional computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: Proposes a self-supervised Siamese neural network framework that leverages artifact pattern differences between back-projection and Fourier reconstruction algorithms to remove artifacts in sparse-view PACT, validated across simulations, phantoms, and in vivo data with high computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: PACT suffers from severe reconstruction artifacts under sparse detection conditions, which limits its practical imaging quality.
AI.method: A self-supervised artifact removal framework using a lightweight Siamese Neural Network with a composite loss function combining cross-domain fidelity and uncertainty-weighted consistency, exploiting artifact pattern differences between back-projection and Fourier-based reconstruction algorithms to decouple dual-domain features.
AI.result: Significantly suppresses image artifacts in simulations, phantoms, in vivo rat and human experimental data, with exceptional computational efficiency due to accelerated spatial-domain and frequency-domain inverse operators.
AI.conclusion: The proposed end-to-end self-supervised approach effectively removes PACT artifacts under sparse conditions while maintaining high computational efficiency, validated across multiple experimental settings.

title: Where Does Agent Reliability Come From? A Cross-Benchmark Decomposition of Verification Loops, Specialist Models, and Scaffolding in a Production Enterprise Agent
comment: 19 pages, 5 figures, 5 tables. Evaluations conducted March-April 2026. Run-level evaluation record and audit scripts: https://github.com/arnabdastidar/leni-agent-evals
summary: Multi-step enterprise agent tasks fail in a characteristic way: single-pass inference has no checkpoint between deciding an answer and committing to it. We study one production system (Leni) whose architecture installs such checkpoints: verification loops (execute, observe, compare, correct) staffed by lightweight task-specialized post-trained models. We evaluate the unmodified production configuration on three public benchmarks stressing distinct failure modes: SpreadsheetBench Verified (silent computation error), BullshitBench v2 (premise confabulation), and the GAIA validation split (cascade error over long tool chains). The full system improves over its frontier base model by +11.0 percentage points on SpreadsheetBench (91.25% vs 80.25%, n=400, p<0.001), +7 to +10 percentage points on BullshitBench (98% vs 91%, n=100), and roughly +15 points on GAIA validation (75.2% pass@1, n=165; 83.0% best-of-k). Our central contribution is a decomposition of that uplift: most of it comes from scaffolding, routing, and specialist models rather than from the verification step itself, whose isolated contribution is small (+1.5 points) but concentrated at the top of the score distribution, where it converts otherwise-failing tasks. We instrument the loop end-to-end, yielding an empirical verifier confusion matrix (catch rate about 0.20, fix rate 0.75, no false-alarm regressions) that grounds a compounding-reliability model. Specialist-swap ablations suggest that the loop's value depends on who observes it: replacing the small trained verifier with the generating frontier model eliminates most rescues. A valid-premise control shows zero over-rejections in 100 expert-level questions.

AI.tldr: The paper studies Leni, a production system that installs verification loops (execute, observe, compare, correct) with lightweight specialist models to add checkpoints in multi-step enterprise agent tasks. The system improves over frontier base models by +7 to +15 percentage points across three benchmarks, but most gains come from scaffolding, routing, and specialist models, not the verification step itself (+1.5 points). The verifier achieves ~0.20 catch rate, 0.75 fix rate, with no false-alarm regressions.
AI.motivation: Multi-step enterprise agent tasks fail because single-pass inference lacks checkpoints between deciding an answer and committing to it, leading to characteristic failure modes like silent computation errors, premise confabulation, and cascade errors.
AI.method: The Leni system architecture uses verification loops (execute, observe, compare, correct) staffed by lightweight task-specialized post-trained models. The study evaluates the unmodified production configuration on three benchmarks and decomposes the uplift through instrumentation, confusion matrix analysis, and specialist-swap ablations.
AI.result: Full system gains: +11.0 pp on SpreadsheetBench (91.25% vs 80.25%), +7-10 pp on BullshitBench (98% vs 91%), +15 pp on GAIA validation (75.2% pass@1). Verification step contributes only +1.5 points but at the top of the score distribution. Verifier confusion matrix: catch rate ~0.20, fix rate 0.75, no false-alarm regressions.
AI.conclusion: Most uplift comes from scaffolding, routing, and specialist models rather than the verification step itself. The loop's value depends on who observes it—replacing the trained verifier with the generating frontier model eliminates most rescues. A valid-premise control shows zero over-rejections in 100 expert-level questions.

title: Let the Data Decide: Supervision Analysis, Capability Trade-offs, and Adaptive Objective Routing in Continued Pre-Training via Off-Policy Distillation
summary: Off-policy distillation is now central to large language model pre-training, yet how training data, objective parameterization, and model capabilities interact remains poorly characterized. We studies top-$k$-truncated, temperature-scaled off-policy distillation by decomposing this problem into two questions: an \emph{objective-to-capability} analysis of how the training objective shapes token-level supervision and downstream performance, and a \emph{data-to-objective} analysis of how data heterogeneity should inform objective routing. We first show that the language-modeling objective ($L_{\mathrm{LM}}$) and the knowledge-distillation objective ($L_{\mathrm{KD}}$) induce systematically different capability profiles, and trace this divergence to a gradient-level tension between \emph{direct observed-token reinforcement} and \emph{teacher-supported alternative supervision}. To quantify this tension, we introduce diagnostic metrics -- support coverage, observed-token probability mass, and teacher-distribution concentration -- and show via controlled sweeps that the support size $k$ governs a coverage-sharpness trade-off, while distillation temperature controls within-support probability allocation. We then examine adaptive objective routing: a domain-level policy that applies $L_{\mathrm{LM}}$ to math and code and $L_{\mathrm{KD}}$ to general-domain data yields consistent gains over both single-objective baselines, whereas token-level routing based on observed-token probability mass or teacher entropy fails to consistently match the single-objective baseline. These results suggest that effective objective routing depends less on routing granularity than on the quality of the routing signal, reframing continued pre-training via off-policy distillation as a structured, data-conditional supervision-design problem rather than a global hyperparameter choice.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes off-policy distillation for LLM pre-training by decomposing it into objective-to-capability and data-to-objective mappings, introducing diagnostic metrics (support coverage, observed-token probability mass, teacher-distribution concentration), and showing that domain-level adaptive objective routing (LM for math/code, KD for general data) outperforms single-objective baselines while token-level routing fails, reframing the problem as structured data-conditional supervision design rather than global hyperparameter choice.
AI.motivation: To characterize how training data, objective parameterization (top-k truncation, temperature scaling), and model capabilities interact in off-policy distillation for LLM pre-training, given that these relationships remain poorly understood.
AI.method: Decomposes the problem into (1) objective-to-capability analysis comparing LM and KD objectives, introducing diagnostic metrics (support coverage, observed-token prob mass, teacher-distribution concentration); (2) data-to-objective analysis examining adaptive routing at domain-level and token-level, with controlled sweeps over support size k and temperature.
AI.result: Support size k governs coverage-sharpness trade-off; temperature controls within-support probability allocation. Domain-level routing (LM for math/code, KD for general data) yields consistent gains over single-objective baselines, while token-level routing based on observed-token prob mass or teacher entropy fails to consistently match baselines.
AI.conclusion: Effective objective routing depends less on routing granularity than on the quality of the routing signal; continued pre-training via off-policy distillation should be viewed as a structured, data-conditional supervision-design problem rather than a global hyperparameter choice.

title: Interactive Task Alignment as a POMDP
summary: Current benchmarks for language models primarily evaluate execution on fully specified tasks. However, real user tasks are often ambiguous. Users arrive with incomplete, exploratory, or even inconsistent goals, requiring the assistant to first determine the intended task before carrying it out. We study this problem as task alignment: the ability to align with a user on their intended task. We introduce a general framework for converting specified tasks into underspecified interactions, formalized as a POMDP in which the model must infer a latent task from partial and evolving user intent. We validate our user simulator post hoc with a human user study. Across shopping, coding, and professional work settings, we find that while models often perform well once the task is specified, models still struggle with task alignment: current models act prematurely, interact ineffectively, and fail to resolve ambiguous requests. Models on average recover the user's intended task only 22-32% of the time under ambiguity. In a human study in the same setting, humans reach 48%, outperforming all evaluated models. We show that post-training with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning improves task alignment, but models still lag behind humans in resolving uncertainty through interaction. Together, our results suggest that current models still lack key interaction abilities required for reliable agency.

AI.tldr: This paper studies task alignment, where models must infer a user's intended task from ambiguous, underspecified interactions. Models correctly infer the intended task only 22-32% of the time (vs. 48% for humans). Post-training improves alignment but still lags behind human performance.
AI.motivation: Real user tasks are often ambiguous (incomplete, exploratory, inconsistent goals), but current benchmarks evaluate models only on fully specified tasks. The authors aim to study whether models can align with users on the intended task under ambiguity.
AI.method: The authors formalize task alignment as a POMDP where the model must infer a latent task from partial and evolving user intent. They convert specified tasks into underspecified interactions and validate their user simulator with a human study. They evaluate models in shopping, coding, and professional settings.
AI.result: Models recover the intended task only 22-32% of the time under ambiguity. Humans achieve 48% in the same setting. Post-training (SFT + RL) improves alignment but models still lag behind humans in resolving uncertainty through interaction.
AI.conclusion: Current models lack key interaction abilities required for reliable agency. While they perform well once tasks are specified, they struggle with task alignment, acting prematurely, interacting ineffectively, and failing to resolve ambiguous requests.

title: LookME: Lookup-Based Multimodal Embeddings for Layer Injection in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong progress in multimodal understanding. However, scaling dense or sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models to improve performance limits deployment in resource-constrained environments due to the trade-off between high memory usage from full loading and increased latency from on-demand loading. Recently, the Per-Layer Embedding (PLE) architecture addresses this by scaling models with large external embedding tables stored in ROM and performing lightweight lookup to retrieve relevant embeddings to enhance token representations. Nevertheless, existing PLE-style methods are primarily designed for text embeddings due to the convenience of ID-based retrieval, limiting their effectiveness in VLMs where multimodal embeddings contain richer information for visual tasks. In this paper, we propose LookME, the first framework that enables lookup-based enhancement for multimodal embeddings in VLMs while supporting partitioned storage and on-demand loading. To efficiently lookup arbitrary continuous multimodal embeddings from large-scale embedding tables, we propose a hierarchical two-level lookup method employing a coarse-to-fine strategy that performs lookups from the scene-level to the intra-scene primitive-level. Furthermore, we integrate the lookup method with a sparse injection strategy, which adaptively prioritizes critical embeddings over voluminous multimodal embeddings within layers, and facilitates embedding table reuse across neighboring layers, improving the trade-off among efficiency, model size, and performance. Experiments on multiple visual benchmarks show that LookME outperforms text-only PLE-style methods, validating the effectiveness of lookup-based multimodal embedding enhancement.

AI.tldr: LookME is the first framework enabling lookup-based multimodal embedding enhancement for VLMs with partitioned storage and on-demand loading, using a hierarchical two-level coarse-to-fine lookup method and a sparse injection strategy to improve efficiency, model size, and performance trade-offs.
AI.motivation: Existing VLMs struggle with deployment in resource-constrained environments due to memory-latency trade-offs from dense or sparse MoE models. Current PLE-style methods only support text embeddings via ID-based retrieval, limiting their effectiveness for multimodal embeddings in visual tasks.
AI.method: LookME proposes (1) a hierarchical two-level lookup method (coarse-to-fine: scene-level to intra-scene primitive-level) for retrieving arbitrary continuous multimodal embeddings from large-scale tables, and (2) a sparse injection strategy that adaptively prioritizes critical embeddings and enables embedding table reuse across neighboring layers.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple visual benchmarks show LookME outperforms text-only PLE-style methods, validating the effectiveness of lookup-based multimodal embedding enhancement.
AI.conclusion: LookME demonstrates that lookup-based enhancement can be effectively extended to multimodal embeddings in VLMs, achieving better trade-offs among efficiency, model size, and performance compared to prior text-only PLE approaches.

title: MechMem-RTL: Reusing Verified Mechanism Memories for LLM-Based RTL Repair
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can automatically repair register-transfer-level (RTL) designs. However, fixing complex sequential logic errors requires reusing past debugging experience. Existing retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) relies on task-text similarity to provide this experience. This text-based approach often misguides the model because natural language poorly reflects cycle-level hardware execution semantics. To address this, we present MechMem-RTL, a repair framework that reuses verifier-confirmed repair records instead of text similarity. Each stored record strictly links trigger evidence, a diagnosed failure mechanism, a local repair action, preservation constraints, and a verification summary. For a new failure, MechMem-RTL injects a past record only when deterministic verifier evidence is strictly compatible with the stored trigger. Otherwise, the system uses only current verifier evidence. We evaluate MechMem-RTL on 48 public sequential RTL tasks across six repair models. With at most two repair attempts per task, MechMem-RTL successfully resolves 180 out of 288 task-model pairs, outperforming standard feedback repair (109 pairs) and task-similarity RAG (107 pairs).

AI.tldr: MechMem-RTL is a hardware repair framework that reuses verifier-confirmed repair records (based on trigger evidence, failure mechanism, repair action, constraints, verification) instead of text-similarity-based RAG. It retrieves past records only when verifier evidence is strictly compatible, otherwise uses current evidence alone. Evaluated on 48 sequential RTL tasks across 6 models, it resolves 180/288 task-model pairs, outperforming standard feedback repair (109) and text-similarity RAG (107).
AI.motivation: Existing RAG approaches for LLM-based RTL repair rely on task-text similarity, but natural language poorly captures cycle-level hardware execution semantics, often misleading the model. The goal is to reuse past debugging experience more effectively by using verifier-confirmed structural evidence rather than textual similarity.
AI.method: MechMem-RTL stores repair records that strictly link: trigger evidence, diagnosed failure mechanism, local repair action, preservation constraints, and verification summary. For a new failure, it retrieves a past record only when deterministic verifier evidence is strictly compatible with the stored trigger; otherwise, it uses only current verifier evidence.
AI.result: Evaluated on 48 public sequential RTL tasks across six repair models. With at most two repair attempts per task, MechMem-RTL resolves 180 out of 288 task-model pairs, outperforming standard feedback repair (109 pairs) and task-similarity RAG (107 pairs).
AI.conclusion: MechMem-RTL demonstrates that verifier-evidence-based record reuse significantly outperforms text-similarity-based RAG for sequential RTL repair, providing a more reliable mechanism for leveraging past debugging experience in hardware design automation.

title: Self-Evolving Just-In-Time Memory for Proactive Embodied Safety
summary: While Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have empowered embodied agents to execute complex household tasks, they struggle to proactively handle dynamically emerging hazards during closed-loop interactions. Existing safety approaches often rely on runtime guardrails to block unsafe actions or induce excessive caution, which severely stalls task progress instead of actively resolving the underlying risks. To break this safety-progress trade-off, we introduce the Self-Evolving Just-In-Time Memory framework, which reframes embodied safety from progress-stalling guardrails to proactive hazard mitigation. The framework consists of a Risk-Sufficient Topological Belief Graph (RSG) for persistent safety-relevant state tracking under partial observability, an Agency-Grounded Factual Memory for precise hazard anticipation, and an Experience Memory that injects procedural Meta-Skills to guide executable, progress-preserving mitigation. Furthermore, we propose an automated Test-Verify-Write loop, allowing agents to continually refine their mitigation Meta-Skills from execution traces at test time. Experiments on IS-Bench demonstrate that our framework substantially boosts the Safe-Success rate across multiple VLM backbones (e.g., +30.3% on Qwen3-VL-8B), enabling agents to proactively mitigate hazards without stalling task progress. Code is available at https://github.com/DyMessi/JIT-Memory.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Self-Evolving Just-In-Time Memory framework with RSG, Agency-Grounded Factual Memory, and Experience Memory to enable VLMs to proactively mitigate hazards during embodied tasks without stalling progress, achieving +30.3% Safe-Success rate on IS-Bench.
AI.motivation: Existing VLMs struggle to proactively handle dynamically emerging hazards during closed-loop task execution. Current safety approaches either block unsafe actions (guardrails) or induce excessive caution, both stalling task progress instead of actively resolving underlying risks. The safety-progress trade-off remains unsolved.
AI.method: The framework has three components: (1) Risk-Sufficient Topological Belief Graph (RSG) for persistent safety-relevant state tracking under partial observability; (2) Agency-Grounded Factual Memory for precise hazard anticipation; (3) Experience Memory that injects procedural Meta-Skills for executable, progress-preserving mitigation. An automated Test-Verify-Write loop refines mitigation Meta-Skills from execution traces at test time.
AI.result: Experiments on IS-Bench show substantial improvements in Safe-Success rate across multiple VLM backbones, e.g., +30.3% on Qwen3-VL-8B, enabling agents to proactively mitigate hazards without stalling task progress.
AI.conclusion: The Self-Evolving Just-In-Time Memory framework successfully reframes embodied safety from progress-stalling guardrails to proactive hazard mitigation, breaking the safety-progress trade-off.

title: When to Plan: Learning to Select Between Reactive Control and Deliberative Planning
summary: It has long been recognized that humans have the ability to switch between fast, reactive decision-making and slower, deliberative planning. In this paper, we study the question of how to learn this ability, known as meta-reasoning, in artificial agents. We model reactive decision-making as a policy that directly maps state observations to actions. Such policies can be trained with reinforcement learning (RL) or imitation learning, but may generalize poorly outside of their training distribution. Alternatively, model-based decision-time planning is more likely to produce good actions across a broader set of states but requires additional computation time, which delays acting. In this work, we introduce an RL method for training a meta-reasoning policy that allocates computation by conditioning on a reactive-policy uncertainty score. This score enables it to predict when the reactive policy is likely to perform poorly and when planning is needed. We conduct an empirical study on motion planning and navigation environments, showing that this design enables the meta-reasoning policy to learn when the reactive policy provides a good-enough action versus when decision-time planning is needed. Additionally, we show that our design enables the meta-agent to shift toward fully reactive control as the reactive policy improves.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a reinforcement learning method for training a meta-reasoning policy that learns to dynamically switch between fast reactive control and slower deliberative planning based on an uncertainty score from the reactive policy, enabling efficient computation allocation in artificial agents.
AI.motivation: Humans can switch between fast reactive decision-making and slower deliberative planning, but artificial agents lack this meta-reasoning ability. The goal is to learn when to rely on efficient but potentially brittle reactive policies versus costly but robust planning.
AI.method: An RL method trains a meta-reasoning policy that conditions on a reactive-policy uncertainty score to predict when the reactive policy is likely to perform poorly, thereby deciding whether to use the reactive action directly or engage in decision-time planning.
AI.result: Empirical studies in motion planning and navigation environments show the meta-reasoning policy successfully learns when to use reactive control versus planning, and can gradually shift toward fully reactive control as the reactive policy improves.
AI.conclusion: The uncertainty-based gating mechanism enables efficient computation allocation in artificial agents, allowing them to dynamically balance speed and deliberation like humans do.

title: CoBind: Stage-Aware Compositional Binding for Training-Free Text-to-Image Generation
summary:
Diffusion-based text-to-image models often fail on complex prompts involving multiple entities, attributes, and relations, producing object omissions, incorrect attribute assignments, or reversed spatial layouts. Existing training-free methods mainly strengthen token-level attention, but do not explicitly model which attributes belong to which entities or when different constraints should be enforced during denoising.
  We introduce \textbf{CoBind}, a training-free framework for stage-aware compositional binding. CoBind parses a prompt into a composition graph of entities, attributes, and relations. It first establishes the global layout using entity-completeness and relation constraints, then binds attributes to their target entities through contrastive cross-entity optimization. Structural guidance is gradually relaxed in later denoising steps to preserve textures and visual details. CoBind also adapts the guidance strength according to the current satisfaction of each constraint, reducing unnecessary latent updates.
  CoBind requires no retraining or additional annotations. Experiments on T2I-CompBench++, GenEval, and multiple diffusion backbones show consistent improvements in attribute binding, spatial relations, and complex compositional generation while maintaining competitive visual quality.

AI.tldr: CoBind is a training-free framework that improves diffusion-based text-to-image generation by parsing prompts into composition graphs and applying stage-aware constraints for entity-completeness, relations, and attribute binding, with adaptive guidance strength that relaxes over denoising steps.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based text-to-image models struggle with complex compositional prompts involving multiple entities, attributes, and relations, leading to object omissions, incorrect attribute assignments, or reversed spatial layouts. Existing training-free methods only strengthen token-level attention without explicitly modeling attribute-entity belonging or stage-appropriate constraint enforcement.
AI.method: CoBind parses a prompt into a composition graph of entities, attributes, and relations. It first establishes global layout using entity-completeness and relation constraints, then binds attributes to target entities via contrastive cross-entity optimization. Structural guidance is gradually relaxed in later denoising steps to preserve visual details, and guidance strength adapts based on current satisfaction of each constraint.
AI.result: Consistent improvements on T2I-CompBench++, GenEval, and multiple diffusion backbones in attribute binding, spatial relations, and complex compositional generation, while maintaining competitive visual quality. No retraining or additional annotations required.
AI.conclusion: CoBind effectively addresses compositional binding in text-to-image generation through a training-free, stage-aware framework that explicitly models entity-attribute relationships and adaptively controls guidance strength, outperforming previous methods on compositional benchmarks.

title: Teach it to stop, not just to click
comment: 15 pages, 3 figures. Reliability protocol and library (cua_reliability), completion verifier, and leakage-free held-out plus bootstrap evaluation harness are open-source
summary: Agentic computer-use RL is reported in single runs, and those numbers mislead. Using verifier-guided repair of a 35B computer-use agent (CUA) across five oracle-graded environments, we show a repaired policy's success rate is dominated by upstream variance: a variance-components decomposition across three cells (crossed data-draw $\times$ seed grid, bootstrap CIs) finds evaluation variance negligible ($σ_{\mathrm{eval}} \approx 0$) and the training-seed effect small everywhere ($\leq 10\%$); instead it splits between the data draw and run-to-run nondeterminism, the data draw's share rising to dominant ($48\%$) on the hardest cell. There the run-to-run distribution is bimodal (Hartigan dip $p=0.07$, $k=10$), so a single run has roughly a 30% chance of the failure mode and mean$\pm$std is the wrong summary. On that footing, two findings hold. First, repairability is two-tier in how constrained the corrective action is: a single fixed token installs reliably (done-detection $0.97\pm0.06$), while open-ended corrections are only partial -- spatial-coordinate clicks (grounding $0.53\pm0.35$) and a generative field-fill ($0.14\pm0.04$). Second, the frame-level repair transfers to task success only when the corrective action is the task's sole remaining blocker (LinkedIn 8/20 vs. base 0/15, Fisher $p=0.006$). We caught two of our own over-claims -- a sample-efficiency curve and a 'grounding cannot be bought' boundary -- only by replicating across seeds; a stress test makes the stakes external: a single-run improvement of the size this field publishes would have the wrong sign roughly one-third of the time in a comparable regime. We release a library (cua_reliability) for routine k-seed reporting. The apparatus is, to our knowledge, the first multimodal segment-aggregated on-policy self-distillation (SA-OPSD) update on a real 35B CUA policy.

AI.tldr: Single-run evaluation of agentic computer-use RL is unreliable; a variance-components analysis shows that evaluation noise is negligible while data-draw variance dominates (up to 48%), and run-to-run distributions can be bimodal. Repairability is two-tier: constrained fixes work reliably, open-ended ones only partially; frame-level repair transfers to task success only when it addresses the sole remaining blocker. The paper demonstrates that single-run improvements can have the wrong sign ~1/3 of the time, and releases a library for routine k-seed reporting, along with a novel multimodal SA-OPSD update on a 35B CUA policy.
AI.motivation: Agentic computer-use RL is typically reported with single-run results, which are misleading due to high variance from data draws and run-to-run nondeterminism. The paper aims to quantify this variance, expose the unreliability of single-run evaluations, and demonstrate proper multi-seed reporting practices.
AI.method: The authors use verifier-guided repair of a 35B computer-use agent (CUA) across five oracle-graded environments. They perform a variance-components decomposition (crossed data-draw × seed grid with bootstrap CIs) to attribute variance to evaluation noise, training seeds, data draws, and run-to-run nondeterminism. They also apply Hartigan dip test for bimodality. They introduce multimodal segment-aggregated on-policy self-distillation (SA-OPSD) update on a real 35B CUA policy.
AI.result: Evaluation variance is negligible (σ_eval ≈ 0); training-seed effect is small (≤10%); data-draw variance dominates (up to 48% on hardest cell). Run-to-run distribution is bimodal (Hartigan dip p=0.07). Repairability is two-tier: constrained fixes (single token install) are reliable (0.97±0.06), open-ended corrections are partial (grounding 0.53±0.35, generative field-fill 0.14±0.04). Frame-level repair transfers to task success only when it is the sole remaining blocker (LinkedIn 8/20 vs. base 0/15, Fisher p=0.006). Single-run improvements can have the wrong sign ~1/3 of the time.
AI.conclusion: Single-run reporting is unreliable for agentic computer-use RL. Multi-seed replication is necessary; the authors caught their own over-claims only by replicating across seeds. They release the cua_reliability library for routine k-seed reporting and demonstrate a novel SA-OPSD update on a 35B CUA policy.

title: High-accuracy Low-Bit KV-Cache Quantization via Local Distribution Restoration
summary:
Long-context large language model inference relies on the KV cache to avoid redundant attention computation, but incurs high memory and bandwidth overheads. Low-bit KV-cache quantization reduces this cost, yet it severely degrade quality; particularly, one-bit quantization reduces accuracy from 84.2% to 47.8% on Llama-3.1-8B under RULER.
  Rather than common beliefs that absolute error of logits, we find that the root cause is structured local misranking, where the distribution of logits in top-K region is drifted. We thereby propose local distribution restoration, a new technique that detects steps with high local distribution risk from quantized-logit features and restores only the selected top-K candidate distribution before token selection. We implement DGAP to achieve local distribution restoration, with efficient risk detcetors and correctors. Expeirments show that on Llama-3.1-8B, DGAP recovers K1V1 RULER accuracy from 47.8% to 83.2% and reduces distribution drift from 0.38 to 0.14; across Llama, Mistral, and Qwen models, it preserves the persistent low-bit KV-cache footprint with modest decode overhead.

AI.tldr: DGAP restores long-context LLM accuracy under 1-bit KV-cache quantization (from 47.8% to 83.2% on Llama-3.1-8B RULER) by detecting and correcting structured local misranking in top-K logits, rather than reducing absolute quantization error.
AI.motivation: KV-cache quantization reduces memory/bandwidth overhead in long-context LLM inference, but extreme low-bit (especially 1-bit) quantization severely degrades accuracy (e.g., 84.2% → 47.8% on Llama-3.1-8B RULER). Existing approaches focus on reducing absolute logit error but fail at 1-bit settings, motivating the need to identify the true degradation mechanism.
AI.method: The authors identify that degradation stems from structured local misranking (drift of top-K logit distribution), not absolute error. They propose local distribution restoration: detect risky steps via quantized-logit features, then selectively restore top-K candidate distribution before token selection. Implemented as DGAP with efficient risk detectors and correctors.
AI.result: On Llama-3.1-8B, DGAP recovers RULER accuracy from 47.8% to 83.2% and reduces distribution drift from 0.38 to 0.14. It generalizes across Llama, Mistral, and Qwen models with low-bit KV-cache footprint and modest decode overhead.
AI.conclusion: The root cause of 1-bit KV-cache quantization degradation is structured local misranking in top-K logits, not absolute logit error. DGAP's targeted local distribution restoration effectively recovers accuracy while maintaining the memory efficiency of extreme low-bit quantization.

title: Berkeley and Heiserman as an Unexhausted Architecture for Embodied Machine Intelligence
summary: Edmund C. Berkeley is usually remembered as a writer who helped connect symbolic logic to computing machinery. That description is correct, but incomplete. Read across Berkeley's machine-oriented writings and projects, the central concern is broader: to show that symbolic logic can serve as a practical design language for machines that acquire information, retain it, respond appropriately to changing conditions, and organize their behavior over time. This paper takes Symbolic Logic and Intelligent Machines as the principal text in that effort, while treating it as representative of a larger Berkeley program that links logical form, circuitry, control, and intelligent behavior. On this reading, Berkeley does not merely treat intelligence as abstract symbol manipulation. He repeatedly defines intelligent machines in operational terms, ties logic to hardware realization, and describes machine behavior through the coordinated interaction of inputs, outputs, memory, calculation, control, states, and events. His treatment of robots and machine activities accordingly moves beyond static logical form toward temporally extended, environment-coupled behavior. David L. Heiserman's machine-intelligence work extends this program toward adaptive creature architectures built around memory, confidence, and generalization. Taken together, Berkeley and Heiserman can be read not as exhausted historical episodes but as contributors to a still under-tested architectural approach to embodied robotic cognition.

AI.tldr: Edmund C. Berkeley's work on symbolic logic extended beyond logic-computing connections to a broader program treating logic as a design language for intelligent, environmentally-coupled machines. His work with Heiserman's adaptive architectures suggests an under-tested approach to embodied robotic cognition.
AI.motivation: To correct the incomplete view of Berkeley as merely connecting symbolic logic to computing machinery, and to show his broader vision of logic as a practical design language for intelligent machines that interact with their environment over time.
AI.method: Analysis of Berkeley's machine-oriented writings, focusing on *Symbolic Logic and Intelligent Machines* as a representative text, and connecting it to Heiserman's adaptive creature architectures involving memory, confidence, and generalization.
AI.result: Berkeley defined intelligent machines operationally, tied logic to hardware realization, and described behavior through coordinated inputs/outputs, memory, calculation, control, states, and events—moving beyond static logic to temporally extended, environment-coupled behavior. Heiserman extended this toward adaptive architectures.
AI.conclusion: Berkeley and Heiserman's work represents a still under-tested architectural approach to embodied robotic cognition, not merely historical footnotes.

title: DAUPNet: Domain-Aware Uncertainty Modeling for Reliable Prototype Discrimination in Cross-Domain Few-Shot Semantic Segmentation
