summary: Cross-domain few-shot semantic segmentation (CD-FSS) has predominantly been formulated as learning domain-invariant representations or improving support-query correspondence. Nevertheless, large domain shifts still make prototype matching unreliable: inconsistent hierarchical responses corrupt the support representation, deterministic prototypes cannot express boundary and appearance ambiguity, and treating prototypes with different reliability equally during optimization weakens foreground-background separation. We therefore propose DAUPNet, a unified framework that reformulates cross-domain prototype matching as uncertainty-aware prototype discrimination. DAUPNet first harmonizes hierarchical support-query features to provide stable evidence, then represents foreground and background prototypes probabilistically, and finally uses their estimated uncertainty to regulate contrastive optimization. On four standard target domains, DAUPNet achieves 72.6% and 76.7% average mIoU in the 1-shot and 5-shot settings, respectively, including substantial gains on the two medical domains. These results demonstrate that modeling prototype uncertainty and incorporating it into optimization provides a robust and interpretable approach to CD-FSS under severe domain shift. The code is available at https://github.com/madness-Lei/DAUPNet

AI.tldr: DAUPNet reformulates cross-domain few-shot semantic segmentation as uncertainty-aware prototype discrimination, harmonizing hierarchical features, probabilistically representing prototypes, and using uncertainty to regulate contrastive optimization, achieving 72.6% and 76.7% average mIoU on 1-shot and 5-shot settings across four target domains.
AI.motivation: Existing CD-FSS methods rely on domain-invariant representations or support-query correspondence but suffer from unreliable prototype matching under large domain shifts due to: (1) inconsistent hierarchical responses corrupting support representations, (2) deterministic prototypes failing to capture boundary/appearance ambiguity, and (3) treating prototypes with different reliability equally during optimization, which weakens foreground-background separation.
AI.method: DAUPNet proposes uncertainty-aware prototype discrimination with three components: (1) harmonizing hierarchical support-query features to produce stable evidence, (2) probabilistically representing foreground and background prototypes rather than deterministic ones, and (3) using estimated prototype uncertainty to regulate contrastive optimization.
AI.result: On four standard target domains, DAUPNet achieves 72.6% and 76.7% average mIoU in 1-shot and 5-shot settings respectively, with substantial gains on two medical domains.
AI.conclusion: Modeling prototype uncertainty and incorporating it into optimization provides a robust and interpretable approach to CD-FSS under severe domain shift.

title: SynH-Rank: Quality-Aware Code Search via Diverse Data Synthesis and Hierarchical Ranking Training
summary:
Code search enhances developer productivity by enabling efficient code reuse. Current code search systems often use a retrieve-then-rerank pipeline, where rerankers focus on modeling semantic relevance between queries and code. However, these rerankers overlook critical non-functional qualities like execution speed, memory usage, and maintainability, which are essential for practical software development. Studies reveal developers expect results to maintain high coding standards and satisfy specific needs, such as resource optimization, highlighting the importance of quality-aware code search.
  Achieving quality-aware code search faces two major challenges: the scarcity of quality-annotated datasets for effective training and the limitations of standard contrastive learning objectives, which fail to capture the ordinal relationships among high-quality, low-quality, and irrelevant code. Although contrastive learning excels in distinguishing relevant from irrelevant code, its binary objective does not support nuanced quality distinctions.To address these challenges, we propose SynH-Rank, a quality-aware code reranking framework that combines LLM-driven diverse data synthesis with hierarchical ranking training. SynH-Rank employs a three-level labeling scheme to explicitly model the hierarchy: high-quality relevant > low-quality relevant > irrelevant. Additionally, we introduce a new benchmark with 4,209 pairs and two novel metrics: Quality Preference Accuracy (QPA) for assessing prioritization of high-quality code and Multi-Condition Accuracy (MCA) for evaluating performance under complex constraints.Experimental results show SynH-Rank improves QPA by 20.15\% over backbone models and outperforms standard relevance-only contrastive training by 15.80\%, while simultaneously enhancing traditional relevance metrics and multi-condition generalizability.

AI.tldr: SynH-Rank is a quality-aware code reranking framework that uses LLM-driven data synthesis and hierarchical ranking training to prioritize code quality (execution speed, memory usage, maintainability) alongside relevance, improving Quality Preference Accuracy by 20.15% over backbone models.
AI.motivation: Current code search rerankers focus only on semantic relevance between queries and code, ignoring critical non-functional qualities (execution speed, memory usage, maintainability) that developers care about. Studies show developers expect results to meet high coding standards and specific optimization needs, motivating quality-aware code search.
AI.method: SynH-Rank combines LLM-driven diverse data synthesis to address quality-annotated data scarcity with hierarchical ranking training using a three-level labeling scheme (high-quality relevant > low-quality relevant > irrelevant). The paper also introduces a benchmark with 4,209 pairs and two metrics: Quality Preference Accuracy (QPA) and Multi-Condition Accuracy (MCA).
AI.result: SynH-Rank improves QPA by 20.15% over backbone models and outperforms standard relevance-only contrastive training by 15.80%, while simultaneously enhancing traditional relevance metrics and multi-condition generalizability.
AI.conclusion: Modeling ordinal quality distinctions beyond binary relevance significantly improves code search quality, and the proposed hierarchical ranking approach with synthetic data effectively addresses both data scarcity and the limitations of contrastive learning objectives.

title: Benchmarking Machine Learning Models for Multi-Omics-Based Breast Cancer Prediction
summary: Estrogen Receptor (ER) status is a critical biomarker in breast cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and treatment selection. Recent advances in high-throughput sequencing technologies have enabled the generation of multi-omics datasets that provide complementary molecular information for computational prediction tasks. This study presents a systematic benchmarking analysis of classical machine learning models for ER status prediction using transcriptomic (RNA expression), genomic (copy number variation; CNV), and proteomic (RPPA) data from the TCGA-BRCA cohort. A rigorous experimental framework incorporating stratified train-test splitting, stratified five-fold cross-validation, class imbalance handling, and fold-specific feature selection was employed to ensure reliable evaluation and prevent data leakage. Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, Support Vector Machines (SVM), and Logistic Regression were evaluated across single-omic and multi-omic settings. Results demonstrated that RNA expression provided the strongest predictive signal, while multi-omic integration yielded modest but consistent improvements over individual modalities. Among all evaluated approaches, Random Forest achieved the best overall performance in the integrated multi-omic setting, obtaining a balanced accuracy of 90.3\% and an ROC-AUC of 97.1\%. Furthermore, recurrent selection of biologically relevant genes, including \textit{ESR1}, \textit{PGR}, \textit{FOXA1}, and \textit{GATA3}, supported the biological validity of the learned models. These findings indicate that carefully regularized classical machine learning methods remain highly effective for small, high-dimensional genomic datasets and that multi-omic integration provides complementary information for breast cancer ER status prediction.

AI.tldr: This study benchmarks classical ML models (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, SVM, Logistic Regression) for ER status prediction using TCGA-BRCA multi-omics data (RNA, CNV, RPPA). RNA expression was the strongest predictor; multi-omic integration gave modest improvements. Random Forest achieved best performance (balanced accuracy 90.3%, ROC-AUC 97.1%). Biologically relevant genes (ESR1, PGR, FOXA1, GATA3) were recurrently selected.
AI.motivation: To systematically benchmark classical machine learning models for ER status prediction across single-omic and multi-omic settings, addressing issues of data leakage and class imbalance in a rigorous framework.
AI.method: Six classical ML models (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, SVM, Logistic Regression) were evaluated on transcriptomic (RNA), genomic (CNV), and proteomic (RPPA) data from TCGA-BRCA. A rigorous framework with stratified train-test splitting, stratified 5-fold CV, class imbalance handling, and fold-specific feature selection was used.
AI.result: RNA expression provided the strongest predictive signal. Multi-omic integration yielded modest but consistent improvements. Random Forest achieved best overall performance (balanced accuracy 90.3%, ROC-AUC 97.1%). Recurrent selection of ESR1, PGR, FOXA1, GATA3 confirmed biological validity.
AI.conclusion: Carefully regularized classical ML methods remain highly effective for small, high-dimensional genomic datasets; multi-omic integration provides complementary information for ER status prediction.

title: SEER: Supervised Learning to Control Energetic Reasoning
summary: One of the main strengths of Constraint Programming is the ability to reduce the search space via propagation. However, propagation is a double-edged sword, with more pruning power coming at the price of larger computation time. For each problem constraint, the best propagator depends on the specific instance and may change at search time. In the literature, Machine Learning (ML) techniques and activity-based heuristics have been applied respectively for choosing (statically) the propagators for a batch of problems and to adapt (dynamically) the propagation strength. We propose to merge those efforts by using an oracle function, obtained via ML, to decide whether to run complex propagators for a target constraint. A combination of design choices makes the approach flexible and easy to embed in state-of-the-art solvers. In this paper, we focus on investigating the feasibility of building an oracle for the Energetic Reasoning propagator. Our experiments show that high prediction accuracy can be obtained, provide suggestions for classification features, and highlight important issues to address when building such an oracle.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using a Machine Learning oracle to dynamically decide when to apply expensive propagators (specifically Energetic Reasoning) in Constraint Programming solvers, balancing propagation strength against computation cost.
AI.motivation: Propagation in Constraint Programming offers a trade-off: stronger pruning reduces search space but increases computation time. The best propagator depends on the instance and changes during search, making static or fixed choices suboptimal. Existing ML methods are static (per problem batch) and activity heuristics adapt strength but lack learning.
AI.method: The authors propose merging ML with dynamic adaptation by building an oracle function that predicts whether to invoke a complex propagator (Energetic Reasoning) for a target constraint. The oracle is trained via ML, using features extracted at search time, with design choices that ensure flexibility and easy integration into existing solvers.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate high prediction accuracy for the Energetic Reasoning oracle. The study also provides recommendations for useful classification features and identifies key challenges (e.g., feature engineering, labeling, overhead) that must be addressed when constructing such an oracle.
AI.conclusion: Building a learned oracle to dynamically control propagator strength is feasible and promising, but practical deployment requires careful attention to feature selection, prediction cost, and integration overhead to ensure net runtime improvements.

title: SaaF: Scene-Specific Ambiguity-Aware 3D Language Fields towards Interactive Real-World Object Retrieval
comment: 8 pages, accepted as a conference paper for IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS2026)
summary: We propose Scene-specific Ambiguity-aware 3D Language Fields (SaaF), a novel Gaussian Splatting-based 3D language field designed for interactive object retrieval in a given real-world scene. Interactive object retrieval using natural language is a crucial capability for service robots operating in complex real-world environments. While recent 3D language field methods for object retrieval establish associations between rendered pixels and autoencoder-compressed CLIP features, they suffer from two limitations: (1) reduced discriminability among similar objects due to feature compression, and (2) poor handling of ambiguous queries, often resulting in unstable or incorrect retrieval. To address these limitations, SaaF introduces a metric learning strategy to construct a unified feature space that is both instance-discriminative and ambiguity-aware. (i) To enhance instance-level visual discrimination, SaaF employs metric learning that pulls image features from multiple viewpoints of the same object closer together in the feature space. (ii) To establish ambiguity awareness, the model jointly trains on multiple text labels generated by the proposed method from each tracked object image sequence, including ambiguous descriptions, to learn the semantic relationships between ambiguous and specific features in a target scene. This feature space enables fine-grained visual understanding while allowing the system to estimate query ambiguity and interactively request clarification when needed. Experimental results demonstrate that SaaF not only improves retrieval accuracy over previous methods but also robustly detects and handles ambiguity in the user text queries under open-vocabulary settings.

AI.tldr: SaaF is a 3D language field using Gaussian Splatting with metric learning that creates instance-discriminative and ambiguity-aware feature spaces for interactive object retrieval, improving accuracy and handling ambiguous queries through clarification requests.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D language field methods for object retrieval suffer from reduced discriminability among similar objects due to feature compression and poor handling of ambiguous queries, leading to unstable or incorrect retrieval in real-world service robot applications.
AI.method: SaaF introduces a metric learning strategy that (1) pulls multi-view image features of the same object closer for instance-level visual discrimination, and (2) jointly trains on multiple text labels from tracked object sequences (including ambiguous descriptions) to learn semantic relationships between ambiguous and specific features, enabling ambiguity detection and interactive clarification.
AI.result: SaaF improves retrieval accuracy over previous methods and robustly detects/handles ambiguity in open-vocabulary user text queries.
AI.conclusion: The ambiguity-aware metric learning approach effectively addresses discriminability and ambiguity limitations, making interactive object retrieval more reliable for service robots in complex real-world scenes.

title: Prefactory: Automated Discovery and Application of Library-Adoption Refactorings
summary: Replacing hand-written code with library API calls is a common refactoring that can reduce code size, make code more idiomatic, and reuse well-tested implementations. Yet many library-adoption opportunities are hard to find automatically: the original code often does not mention the target library and may resemble the library API only in behavior, with little syntactic overlap. Existing tools, such as linters and static modernizers, cover only a small set of manually specified patterns. LLMs and LLM-based agents, on the other hand, can generalize to more patterns, but they are costly, difficult to reproduce and to apply systematically at scale. This paper introduces Prefactory, an automated approach for library-adoption refactoring in Python. The key idea is to use an LLM to synthesize executable search heuristics rather than relying on repeated LLM prompting over a codebase. Given a target project and a target library name, Prefactory collects library metadata and project vocabulary, then generates lexical and structural detectors. Prefactory executes the detectors during a scan phase to find candidate functions. It then heuristically ranks the candidate functions, generates refactorings for the highest-ranked ones using an LLM, and validates the results with project tests and newly generated differential tests. We evaluate Prefactory on PrefactoryBench, a benchmark of 100 real-world library-adoption refactorings from 61 open-source Python projects and 18 libraries. Prefactory detects 75 instances at the file level and 56 at the function level, compared with 35 and 32 for the strongest baseline (Codex CLI). From the 56 detected functions, Prefactory produces 40 test-validated refactorings.

AI.tldr: Prefactory is an automated approach for library-adoption refactoring in Python that uses LLMs to synthesize executable search heuristics, rather than repeatedly prompting LLMs. It generates lexical and structural detectors, scans for candidate functions, ranks them, generates refactorings via LLM for top candidates, and validates them with tests. On a benchmark of 100 real-world refactorings from 61 projects and 18 libraries, Prefactory detects 75 instances at file level and 56 at function level, outperforming Codex CLI (35 and 32), and produces 40 test-validated refactorings.
AI.motivation: Existing tools for library-adoption refactoring (linters, static modernizers) cover only manually specified patterns, while LLM-based approaches are costly, difficult to reproduce, and hard to scale. There is a need for an automated, systematic approach that generalizes beyond predefined patterns without incurring high LLM costs.
AI.method: Prefactory takes a target project and library name, collects library metadata and project vocabulary, then uses an LLM to generate lexical and structural detectors. These detectors are executed during a scan phase to find candidate functions. Candidates are heuristically ranked, and an LLM generates refactorings for the highest-ranked ones. Results are validated using project tests and newly generated differential tests.
AI.result: On PrefactoryBench (100 real-world refactorings from 61 Python projects, 18 libraries), Prefactory detects 75 instances at file level and 56 at function level, compared to 35 and 32 for Codex CLI. From the 56 detected functions, it produces 40 test-validated refactorings.
AI.conclusion: Prefactory demonstrates that combining LLM-generated search heuristics with systematic scanning and validation can effectively automate library-adoption refactoring at scale, outperforming both traditional tools and LLM-based agents in detection and producing validated code transformations.

title: Learning Spatio-Temporal Foundation Models from Pure Synthetic Data
summary: Spatio-Temporal Foundation Models (STFMs) aim to learn generalizable representations of complex dynamical systems across space and time. However, existing approaches suffer from distributional bias in real-world pre-training data, structural bottlenecks of autoregressive or diffusion-based paradigms, and objectives that overemphasize point-wise reconstruction in noisy observation space.We propose \textbf{NeoST}, the first spatio-temporal foundation model pre-trained solely on procedurally generated synthetic systems. NeoST introduces a scalable synthetic pre-training corpus to mitigate real-world bias, a latent-space reasoning architecture that generates and iteratively refines multiple future trajectories without sequential error accumulation, and latent-space objectives that emphasize structural dynamics and enable inference-time correction under distribution shifts.Extensive experiments across diverse real-world benchmarks show that NeoST consistently outperforms existing STFMs in diverse real-world spatio-temporal systems, achieves superior long-horizon stability and inference efficiency.

AI.tldr: NeoST is the first spatio-temporal foundation model pre-trained solely on procedurally generated synthetic systems, introducing synthetic pre-training to avoid real-world bias, a latent-space reasoning architecture with iterative refinement to avoid error accumulation, and latent-space objectives focusing on structural dynamics. It outperforms existing STFMs across diverse real-world benchmarks with better long-horizon stability and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing STFMs suffer from distributional bias in real-world pre-training data, structural bottlenecks of autoregressive/diffusion-based models, and objectives that overemphasize point-wise reconstruction in noisy observation space.
AI.method: 1) A scalable synthetic pre-training corpus of procedurally generated systems to mitigate real-world bias. 2) A latent-space reasoning architecture that generates and iteratively refines multiple future trajectories without sequential error accumulation. 3) Latent-space objectives emphasizing structural dynamics with inference-time correction under distribution shifts.
AI.result: NeoST consistently outperforms existing STFMs across diverse real-world spatio-temporal benchmarks, with superior long-horizon stability and inference efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Pre-training on procedurally generated synthetic data combined with latent-space iterative refinement is a viable and superior alternative to real-world pre-training for spatio-temporal foundation models.

title: Nonuniformity Principle in Human-AI Coworking
summary: As generative AI is increasingly applied to automate multi-step and high-stake workflows, human judgment and involvement remain essential for ensuring the quality of AI-generated outputs. In practice, while it is desirable for human experts to provide oversight on AI regularly, often by reviewing intermediate outputs, giving feedback, making corrections, and steering subsequent steps, such oversight is constrained by the time and resources that humans can afford. This creates a tension between the need for human oversight and AI's efficiency in delivering more output with less intervention. An important but underexplored question, then, is how to optimally engage humans in human-AI coworking. This work was originally motivated by our empirical observation that in long AI workflows, human oversight often improves user satisfaction while reducing unnecessary rework and token consumption. From there, we formulate the problem of where to place oversight stages in human-AI coworking. Under reasonable assumptions, we then develop the nonuniformity principle, which states that the optimal schedule places oversight stages with non-decreasing gaps along the workflow. We empirically validate this principle in two common AI agent workflows: writing literature reviews and constructing websites.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the tension between human oversight and AI efficiency in multi-step workflows. Motivated by empirical observations that oversight improves satisfaction and reduces waste, the authors formalize the problem of optimal oversight placement, develop the "nonuniformity principle" (where oversight gaps should be non-decreasing), and validate it in literature review writing and website construction tasks.
AI.motivation: To resolve the tension between the need for human oversight in high-stakes AI workflows and the efficiency goals of AI, by determining how to optimally allocate limited human intervention resources.
AI.method: The authors formulate the oversight placement problem, derive the nonuniformity principle (optimal oversight stages have non-decreasing gaps) under reasonable assumptions, and empirically validate in two AI agent workflows: literature reviews and website construction.
AI.result: The nonuniformity principle is validated: optimal oversight schedules place oversight stages with non-decreasing gaps along the workflow, improving user satisfaction while reducing rework and token consumption.
AI.conclusion: Optimal human oversight in AI workflows follows a nonuniform pattern where gaps between oversight stages increase as the workflow progresses, offering a principled approach to balancing quality and efficiency.

title: Seeing What Is Actually There: PriVE-Bench and PriVE-Tools for Counterfactual Evaluation of Agentic Visual Evidence in VLMs
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often answer visual questions using learned language and category priors rather than grounding their predictions in the image itself. Counterfactual images provide a natural diagnostic setting for this failure mode: when visible evidence contradicts what is usually true, a grounded model should answer from the pixels, while a prior-following model will produce a canonical but visually incorrect response. However, existing counterfactual benchmarks mainly ask whether such prior-following behavior exists. In this paper, we ask a further question motivated by the rise of tool-augmented and agentic vision systems: can additional visual evidence views help VLMs reason against their priors? We introduce PriVE-Bench, a Prior-vs-Visual Evidence Benchmark that uses paired original and counterfactual images to distinguish visually grounded answers from prior-consistent errors. We further introduce PriVE-Tools, a controlled agentic-vision-inspired extension that evaluates whether tool-derived visual evidence -- including bounding boxes, crops, zoom panels, and contours -- improves grounding under the same counterfactual conflicts. Across open- and closed-source VLMs, we compare raw, paired-image, and tool-conditioned inputs using accuracy, prior-following error rate, and other-response rate. Our results show that visual evidence tools can help in some settings, especially when models can use localized evidence effectively, but they are not a universal remedy: several models continue to follow language and category priors even when relevant visual evidence is explicitly provided.

AI.tldr: PriVE-Bench and PriVE-Tools evaluate whether VLMs can overcome language/category priors using counterfactual images and tool-derived visual evidence (boxes, crops, zoom panels, contours). Results show tools sometimes help but are not a universal remedy for prior-following errors.
AI.motivation: Existing counterfactual benchmarks only detect prior-following behavior; this work asks whether additional visual evidence (via tools) can help VLMs reason against their priors, motivated by the rise of tool-augmented and agentic vision systems.
AI.method: Introduces PriVE-Bench (paired original/counterfactual images) and PriVE-Tools (tool-derived evidence: bounding boxes, crops, zoom panels, contours). Evaluates open- and closed-source VLMs under raw, paired-image, and tool-conditioned inputs using accuracy, prior-following error rate, and other-response rate.
AI.result: Visual evidence tools help in some settings, especially when models use localized evidence effectively, but are not a universal remedy; many models still follow language/category priors even with explicit visual evidence provided.
AI.conclusion: Tool-derived visual evidence can improve grounding in counterfactual conflicts but does not fully resolve prior-following failures across VLMs.

title: Specifying the Delegated-Autonomy Boundary: Requirements Engineering for Agentic AI
summary: Agentic AI systems do not just predict or recommend; they plan, maintain state, and act in external environments with varying degrees of autonomy. This changes the requirements engineering problem in a specific and under-addressed way: it introduces what we call the delegated-autonomy boundary -- the set of decisions about what may be delegated to the system, under what graduated authority, with what oversight, and how control is returned. Current practices bury these decisions inside prompts, tool schemas, and runtime policies, even though they are requirements-level commitments. This paper proposes two complementary artifacts. First, an Agency Justification Record (AJR) helps teams decide when an agent is warranted over simpler alternatives. Second, an Agentic Delegation Policy (ADP) captures what must be specified for safe and effective development: purpose, authority, information, coordination, assurance, and evolution. Crucially, authority in the ADP is modelled as graduated, i.e., a tiered structure. We illustrate the framework with two contrasting examples: a safety-critical hospital discharge coordination agent and an automated code review agent.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces two artifacts—Agency Justification Record (AJR) and Agentic Delegation Policy (ADP)—to address the requirements engineering challenge posed by agentic AI systems, specifically the delegated-autonomy boundary defining what decisions can be delegated, with what authority and oversight.
AI.motivation: Agentic AI systems plan, maintain state, and act autonomously in external environments, introducing a "delegated-autonomy boundary" that current requirements engineering practices inadequately address, as critical decisions are buried in prompts, tool schemas, and runtime policies rather than treated as explicit requirements-level commitments.
AI.method: The paper proposes two complementary artifacts: (1) an Agency Justification Record (AJR) for deciding when an agent is warranted over simpler alternatives, and (2) an Agentic Delegation Policy (ADP) specifying purpose, authority, information, coordination, assurance, and evolution, with authority modelled as a graduated tiered structure. The framework is illustrated via two contrasting case studies.
AI.result: Two concrete artifacts (AJR and ADP) for requirements engineering of agentic AI systems, demonstrated on a safety-critical hospital discharge coordination agent and an automated code review agent.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI introduces a delegated-autonomy boundary that must be explicitly captured as requirements-level artifacts; the proposed AJR and ADP provide structured mechanisms for specifying when agency is justified and how delegation authorities, oversight, and control should be defined in a graduated manner.

title: SOS-LoRA: Static Orthogonal-Subspace Low-Rank Adaptation with Fixed Multi-Scale Scaling
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method for large language models. Under a fixed rank budget, LoRA parameterizes each adapted weight through a single low-dimensional input-side pathway, which may couple heterogeneous behaviors through shared input directions and induce interference during optimization. We propose Static Orthogonal Subspace LoRA (SOS-LoRA), a drop-in extension that reparameterizes a rank-rtot update as a sum of K static (always-on, non-routed) low-rank experts. SOS-LoRA (i) decomposes the total rank across experts, (ii) applies a fixed multi-scale scaling scheme to encourage scale-separated optimization dynamics, and (iii) promotes diverse input-side directions via cross-expert orthogonal initialization and a lightweight regularizer. SOS-LoRA remains fully mergeable, adding no inference-time parameters or latency after merging. Experiments on reasoning and knowledge-intensive benchmarks (Llama 2/3), encoder-based NLU (GLUE), and math reasoning (GSM8K/MATH) show consistent gains over matched-budget LoRA baselines and recent variants. Code is available at https://github.com/llm172/sos-lora.

AI.tldr: SOS-LoRA is a drop-in extension to LoRA that decomposes a rank-r update into K static orthogonal low-rank experts with multi-scale scaling and orthogonal regularization, achieving consistent gains across multiple benchmarks without adding inference cost.
AI.motivation: Standard LoRA under a fixed rank budget uses a single low-dimensional input-side pathway, which can couple heterogeneous behaviors through shared input directions and induce interference during optimization.
AI.method: SOS-LoRA reparameterizes a rank-r total update as a sum of K static (always-on, non-routed) low-rank experts by (i) decomposing total rank across experts, (ii) applying fixed multi-scale scaling for scale-separated dynamics, and (iii) using cross-expert orthogonal initialization with a lightweight regularizer.
AI.result: Consistent gains over matched-budget LoRA baselines and recent variants on reasoning and knowledge-intensive benchmarks (Llama 2/3), encoder-based NLU (GLUE), and math reasoning (GSM8K/MATH).
AI.conclusion: SOS-LoRA is a simple, fully mergeable extension that improves LoRA's optimization by encouraging diverse, scale-separated input directions without adding inference-time parameters or latency.

title: xperception -- Making Robotic Grasping Easier
summary: The transition toward high-mix low-volume manufacturing demands flexibility in robotic manipulation. However, conventional vision systems remain a bottleneck, requiring extensive data collection and model retraining whenever a new object is introduced to the production line. To overcome this rigidity, we present xperception, a zero-shot 6D pose estimation technology that eliminates the need for object-specific fine-tuning and laborious data annotation. By directly utilizing typical CAD models and integrating the rich semantic features of foundation models (e.g. DINOv2, GeDi), xperception achieves millimeter-accurate 6D pose estimation. xperception showed robustness against severe occlusions in industrial tasks like bin picking and is engineered for deployment on industrial edge hardware, such as NVIDIA Jetson Thor. Validated at a TRL of 6, the core methodology behind xperception is based on the FreeZe algorithm, which won the international BOP Challenge 2024, paving the way for scalable, plug-and-play robotic automation in unstructured high-mix low-volume manufacturing industries.

AI.tldr: xperception is a zero-shot 6D pose estimation technology for high-mix low-volume manufacturing that uses CAD models and foundation model features (DINOv2, GeDi) to achieve millimeter-accurate pose estimation without object-specific fine-tuning. Based on the FreeZe algorithm (winner of BOP Challenge 2024), it is robust to occlusions and deployable on edge hardware like NVIDIA Jetson Thor at TRL 6.
AI.motivation: Conventional vision systems require extensive data collection and model retraining for each new object, making them inflexible for high-mix low-volume manufacturing where frequent object changes occur.
AI.method: xperception leverages CAD models directly and integrates semantic features from foundation models (DINOv2, GeDi) to perform zero-shot 6D pose estimation, eliminating the need for object-specific fine-tuning or data annotation. The core methodology is based on the FreeZe algorithm.
AI.result: Achieves millimeter-accurate 6D pose estimation, shows robustness against severe occlusions in industrial tasks like bin picking, is deployable on edge hardware (NVIDIA Jetson Thor), and validated at TRL 6. The underlying FreeZe algorithm won the international BOP Challenge 2024.
AI.conclusion: xperception enables scalable, plug-and-play robotic automation for unstructured high-mix low-volume manufacturing by removing the retraining bottleneck associated with conventional vision systems.

title: A RFID Based Campus Wide Payment System
summary: This work titled "RFID Based Campuswide Payment System" introduces an innovative cashless payment solution for educational institutions. It uses RFID cards and a Raspberry Pi to enable hassle free payments for various campus services, such as cafeteria purchases, tuition fees, and library fines. A centralized database ensures real-time updates on transactions and account balances, accessible through a simple and user-friendly web interface. This work is involved in designing a secure system with object-oriented principles, setting up databases, and integrating hardware like RFID readers with a Raspberry Pi. The systems are proved to be a cost-effective and efficient alternative to traditional payment methods, enhancing convenience and security for students and administrators. The study also explored similar RFID applications, like smart parking and attendance systems, to identify challenges and improvements. Looking ahead, it envisions features like wearable RFID devices, voice-activated payments, and blockchain integration to boost security and usability. Results show that this system simplifies campus payments and has the potential for broader adoption in similar environments.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an RFID and Raspberry Pi-based cashless payment system for campuses, enabling secure, real-time transactions for services like cafeteria, tuition, and library fines via a centralized database and web interface.
AI.motivation: To replace traditional cash-based payment methods in educational institutions with a secure, convenient, and cost-efficient cashless alternative.
AI.method: The system uses RFID cards and a Raspberry Pi integrated with RFID readers, a centralized database for real-time transaction updates, and a user-friendly web interface. Design follows object-oriented principles.
AI.result: The system is cost-effective, efficient, and enhances convenience and security for both students and administrators, simplifying campus payments.
AI.conclusion: The RFID-based payment system simplifies campus transactions and shows potential for broader adoption, with future directions including wearable RFID, voice-activated payments, and blockchain integration.

title: Comprehensive Evaluation of Machine Learning for Type 2 Diabetes Risk Prediction: Large-Scale External Validation and Fairness Analysis
comment: Accepted and published at the IEEE EDS Technically Sponsored International Conference on Intelligent Processing, Hardware, Electronics, and Radio Systems (CIPHER-2026), 13-15 Feb 2026, NIT Jalandhar, India (IEEE Conference Record #70417, Paper ID: 155). 8 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables
summary: Machine learning-based Type 2 diabetes risk prediction models obtain good internal validation results but lose effectiveness in real-world applications due to deficient external testing and fairness assessment. We developed a multi-dimensional framework evaluating discrimination, calibration, interpretability, and algorithmic fairness on nationally representative populations. An XGBoost model was trained on NHANES 2015-2020 (n=15,685) using eight non-laboratory predictors: age, sex, race/ethnicity, BMI, smoking status, physical activity, history of heart attack, and history of stroke. External validation was performed on BRFSS 2020-2022 (n=1,285,783) under realistic distribution shift. Internal validation showed good discrimination (AUC=0.794, 95% CI 0.788-0.800), with performance loss on external validation (AUC=0.717, relative decrease: -9.7%, p<0.001). Fairness analysis revealed severe bias: elderly adults (>=60) showed AUC=0.607 vs 0.742 for young adults (difference=0.135, p<0.001); obese individuals showed AUC=0.698 vs 0.735 for normal weight (difference=0.037, p<0.001). Gender showed comparable performance (male=0.723 vs female=0.712, p=0.142). Calibration revealed risk overestimation (Brier score=0.123). SHAP analysis identified age, BMI, and physical activity as primary risk drivers. Populations with highest diabetes risk receive the worst algorithmic performance, underscoring the need for fairness-aware, age-stratified deployment strategies before clinical use.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an XGBoost-based Type 2 diabetes risk prediction model using eight non-laboratory predictors, and evaluates it across discrimination, calibration, interpretability, and algorithmic fairness on two large nationally representative datasets (NHANES internal, BRFSS external). The model shows significant performance degradation under distribution shift (AUC drop from 0.794 to 0.717), risk overestimation, and severe age-related and obesity-related bias, with the highest-risk populations receiving the worst predictions.
AI.motivation: Existing ML-based Type 2 diabetes risk models perform well in internal validation but fail in real-world deployment due to insufficient external testing and lack of fairness assessment. The authors aim to develop a comprehensive evaluation framework that captures not only discrimination but also calibration, interpretability, and algorithmic fairness across diverse, nationally representative populations.
AI.method: Trained an XGBoost classifier on NHANES 2015-2020 (n=15,685) with eight non-laboratory features: age, sex, race/ethnicity, BMI, smoking, physical activity, history of heart attack, history of stroke. External validation on BRFSS 2020-2022 (n=1,285,783) under realistic distribution shift. Multi-dimensional evaluation: AUC (discrimination), Brier score (calibration), SHAP (interpretability), and subgroup fairness analysis by age, obesity, and gender.
AI.result: Internal AUC=0.794; external AUC=0.717 (-9.7%, p<0.001). Brier score=0.123 (risk overestimation). Severe age bias: AUC=0.607 (elderly) vs 0.742 (young), difference=0.135 (p<0.001). Obesity bias: AUC=0.698 (obese) vs 0.735 (normal weight), diff=0.037 (p<0.001). Gender bias not significant (p=0.142). SHAP identified age, BMI, physical activity as top drivers.
AI.conclusion: The highest-risk populations (elderly, obese) receive the worst algorithmic performance. The model is unsuitable for clinical deployment without fairness-aware, age-stratified mitigation strategies. Highlights the necessity of incorporating fairness evaluation alongside external validation before real-world use of diabetes risk models.

title: Exact Network Surgery: Functional Invariance and Gradient Plasticity in Reactive Computational Graphs
comment: Companion paper: "Cost Accounting for Reactive Computational Graphs" (submitted concurrently)
summary: Function-preserving network growth techniques such as Net2Net and progressive stacking expand a model's capacity without destroying its learned function, but existing formulations either tolerate numerical perturbations or require a full rebuild of the training program. We formalize Exact Network Surgery: the in-place insertion of a residual block into a live computational graph such that (i) the network function is preserved -- bit-exactly under explicit floating-point hypotheses -- and (ii) inserted parameters remain trainable immediately after insertion. We prove an identity-morphism theorem for gated residual blocks, a structural-locality theorem showing that a reactive invalidation engine recomputes exactly the downstream cone of the insertion point, leaving every other node's value and optimizer state untouched, and an escape-from-initialization proposition showing that the Gradient Shadowing gate alpha, initialized at zero over a randomly initialized branch, receives a generically non-zero gradient at insertion time. We identify a degenerate configuration -- zero-initialized output projections combined with a zero gate -- that is an exact saddle point gradient descent cannot escape. Every claim is validated on the reference implementation in NeuroDSL, a reactive graph engine in Julia: grafting is bit-exact on every logit tested (0 mismatches out of 1600); the gate escapes zero at the first optimizer step and unlocks branch gradients at the second, exactly as predicted; the degenerate configuration exhibits gradients identically zero for the entire 600-step run; surgery cost tracks downstream cone size with r = 0.9992 while graft-plus-invalidation bookkeeping is constant (about 0.75 ms) across insertion depths; and training resumes bit-identically across a real process restart. A flagged preliminary appendix reports first single-seed observations on post-insertion gate dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Exact Network Surgery, a method for inserting residual blocks into live computational graphs that preserves network function bit-exactly and keeps inserted parameters trainable immediately. Key theoretical results include an identity-morphism theorem, structural-locality theorem, and escape-from-initialization proposition. A degenerate zero-initialized configuration is identified as an inescapable saddle point. All claims are validated on NeuroDSL, showing bit-exact grafting, predicted gate dynamics, and efficient surgery costs.
AI.motivation: Existing function-preserving network growth techniques (Net2Net, progressive stacking) either tolerate numerical perturbations or require full training program rebuilds. The paper aims to formalize a method for exact, in-place insertion of residual blocks into live computational graphs that preserves the network function bit-exactly and maintains trainability.
AI.method: The authors formalize Exact Network Surgery via: (1) an identity-morphism theorem for gated residual blocks ensuring bit-exact preservation under explicit floating-point hypotheses; (2) a structural-locality theorem where a reactive invalidation engine recomputes only the downstream cone of the insertion point; (3) an escape-from-initialization proposition showing Gradient Shadowing gate α receives non-zero gradient at insertion time. Implementation uses NeuroDSL, a reactive graph engine in Julia.
AI.result: Validation results: bit-exact grafting with 0 mismatches out of 1600 logits; the gate escapes zero at the first optimizer step and unlocks branch gradients at the second; degenerate configuration shows identically zero gradients for 600 steps; surgery cost correlates with downstream cone size (r=0.9992); graft-plus-invalidation bookkeeping is constant (~0.75ms) across insertion depths; training resumes bit-identically across process restarts.
AI.conclusion: Exact Network Surgery enables precise, in-place network growth with provable guarantees on function preservation, locality of recomputation, and trainability of inserted parameters. The identified degenerate saddle point warns against zero-initialized output projections with zero gates. The approach is validated empirically and supported by theoretical results.

title: Depth-Regularized JEPA World Models Learn More Transferable Representations from Real Outdoor Robot Data
summary: World models, especially based on JEPA architectures, have been shown to learn robust dynamics of various environments. However, learning from visually complex real-world data remains a challenge, especially in unpredictable outdoor environments. We introduce depth as a geometric prior during training in learning more robust latent dynamics directly from robot video data and handling visual complexity. This combines depth supervision with an isotropy-inducing latent regularizer (SIGReg), maximizing task-agnostic latent diversity while constraining how that diversity is organized, with the combined objective targeting the highest-entropy representation consistent with scene geometry. To satisfy this greater complexity without increasing inference time, we also add training-only overparameterization. Training an 18M-parameter model on video from a real agricultural robot, we evaluate with frozen-representation visual odometry probes, predictor-based surprise detection, and multi-step latent rollout fidelity. Compared to the baseline LeWM, our method lowers visual odometry probe error by 33%, substantially increases surprise-score separation both in-domain and on the out-of-domain TartanGround benchmark, and improves multi-step rollout fidelity under domain shift, with gains that grow with rollout horizon. Notably, we also see improvements in surprise-score separation on physics understanding that is not directly tied to 3D geometry, such as lighting and shadows. These results show that a lightweight training-time geometric prior makes a compact JEPA world model more useful and more transferable on real outdoor data with strong underlying representations, without adding inference overhead. Our work suggests that depth as a physically grounded prior can enhance world model generalization on a variety of tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces depth as a geometric prior during training, combined with an isotropy-inducing latent regularizer (SIGReg) and training-only overparameterization, to improve JEPA-based world model learning from visually complex real-world robot video data, achieving significant gains in visual odometry, surprise detection, and latent rollout fidelity without increasing inference time.
AI.motivation: Learning robust latent dynamics from visually complex real-world data (especially unpredictable outdoor environments) remains a challenge for JEPA-based world models, motivating the need for a lightweight geometric prior that improves representation quality without adding inference overhead.
AI.method: Depth is used as a geometric prior during training via depth supervision combined with an isotropy-inducing latent regularizer (SIGReg) that maximizes task-agnostic latent diversity while constraining its organization, targeting the highest-entropy representation consistent with scene geometry. Training-only overparameterization (18M parameters) is added to handle greater complexity without increasing inference time.
AI.result: Compared to baseline LeWM, the method reduces visual odometry probe error by 33%, improves surprise-score separation both in-domain and on out-of-domain TartanGround benchmark, and enhances multi-step rollout fidelity under domain shift with gains growing over rollout horizon. Improvements also extend to physics understanding not directly tied to 3D geometry (e.g., lighting and shadows).
AI.conclusion: A lightweight training-time geometric prior (depth) makes compact JEPA world models more useful and transferable on real outdoor data with strong underlying representations, without adding inference overhead, suggesting depth as a physically grounded prior can enhance world model generalization across tasks.

title: A Large-Scale Measurement of AI Bill of Materials Completeness in Hugging Face Models
summary: Pretrained machine learning (ML) models help developers build ML-intensive software systems without training models from scratch. However, model repositories often provide incomplete machine-readable documentation about model provenance, licenses, datasets, limitations, and external references, creating transparency and governance gaps across the AI supply chain. Artificial Intelligence Bills of Materials (AIBOMs) address these gaps by documenting AI artifacts, including models, metadata, licenses, datasets, model-card information, and external references. Taking public Hugging Face (HF) model repositories as a case study, this paper empirically investigates AIBOM completeness, defined as the extent to which repositories provide AIBOM-relevant information for machine-readable AI supply-chain documentation. We examine approximately 97.5K AIBOM artifacts to assess the extent to which generated AIBOMs: (i) contain required structural and metadata fields, (ii) represent model identity, license, and external-reference information, (iii) capture model-card documentation such as datasets, limitations, safety-risk assessment, and environmental information, and (iv) vary in documentation coverage across repository and artifact characteristics such as task, license availability, dataset declaration, model family, and paper reference. Results indicate that generated AIBOMs provide complete coverage of required AIBOM structure but limited AI-specific documentation completeness. Required fields are fully represented, but model-card, metadata, responsible-use, environmental, limitation, and meaningful-description fields remain weakly represented or missing across generated artifacts. Our findings motivate improved model-card practices, repository-level traceability, and automated AIBOM validation to advance the generation and adoption of more complete AIBOMs.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically evaluates the completeness of AI Bills of Materials (AIBOMs) generated from ~97.5K Hugging Face model repositories, finding that while structural fields are fully covered, critical AI-specific documentation (model cards, metadata, limitations, environmental info, responsible-use fields) remains largely missing or weak.
AI.motivation: Model repositories lack machine-readable documentation on provenance, licenses, datasets, limitations, and external references, creating transparency and governance gaps across the AI supply chain. AIBOMs aim to address these gaps, but their completeness is unknown.
AI.method: Empirical study of ~97.5K AIBOM artifacts generated from public Hugging Face model repositories; analyzes completeness across structural/metadata fields, model identity/license/external references, model-card documentation (datasets, limitations, safety, environmental), and variation across repository/artifact characteristics (task, license, dataset, model family, paper reference).
AI.result: Generated AIBOMs achieve full coverage of required structural fields, but model-card, metadata, responsible-use, environmental, limitation, and meaningful-description fields are weakly represented or missing. Completeness varies across task, license, dataset, model family, and paper reference characteristics.
AI.conclusion: The findings motivate improved model-card practices, repository-level traceability, and automated AIBOM validation to enhance the generation and adoption of more complete AIBOMs.

title: More Than Memory: Task-Conditioned Signed FFN Writes in Long-Context Retrieval
summary:
FFNs are often treated as parametric memories. In long-context retrieval, however, the sharper question is not only what they store, but whether their native residual writes push the current retrieval state toward or away from the correct answer. We test this by scaling the model's own FFN write one layer at a time, without editing weights or injecting external steering vectors.
  Across controlled literal and semantic retrieval suites, native FFN response surfaces are signed, layer-specific, and task-conditioned: the final FFN is a suppressor in 7 of 8 model-suite cases, and 60% of layers switch role between retrieval modes (95% CI [50%, 69%]). A local directional derivative along the native write separates the two monotone roles: suppressors have negative derivative in 34/35 cases, and amplifiers have positive derivative in 18/18 cases, so the roles are not reducible to write size. On a safety-filtered LongBench retrieval-QA probe, the same diagnostic predicts attenuation damage with raw R^2=0.796 on Qwen2.5-7B and 0.791 on Qwen3.5-9B; a held-out suppressor-attenuation policy improves retrieval margins over random and norm-matched controls. These results show that native FFN scaling exposes a signed, task-conditioned residual-write structure in retrieval, and that write-gradient alignment is a compact diagnostic for the two monotone roles.

AI.tldr: FFN residual writes in LLMs have signed, layer-specific, task-conditioned roles (amplifier vs. suppressor) in retrieval, and the sign of the local directional derivative along the native write can diagnose these roles, predicting retrieval performance degradation with high accuracy.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether FFN residual writes in long-context retrieval push the retrieval state toward or away from the correct answer, beyond treating FFNs merely as parametric memories.
AI.method: Scale the model's own FFN write one layer at a time (no weight editing or external steering vectors) across literal and semantic retrieval tasks; compute local directional derivatives to classify layers as suppressors or amplifiers.
AI.result: FFN writes are signed and task-conditioned: final FFN is a suppressor in 7/8 model-suite cases; 60% of layers switch roles between retrieval modes. Suppressors have negative derivative (34/35 cases), amplifiers positive (18/18). Write-gradient alignment predicts attenuation damage with R²≈0.79 on LongBench retrieval-QA.
AI.conclusion: Native FFN scaling reveals a signed, task-conditioned residual-write structure in retrieval; write-gradient alignment is a compact diagnostic for amplifier/suppressor roles, and a suppressor-attenuation policy improves retrieval margins.

title: FST.ai 2.5: Explainable and Uncertainty-Aware AI for Olympic and Para-Taekwondo Decision Support, Athlete Digital Twins, and Federation-Scale Analytics
summary:
The rapid digitalisation of elite sport has created new opportunities for integrating artificial intelligence (AI), performance analytics, and decision-support systems into athlete development and competition management. However, existing solutions remain fragmented, typically addressing isolated tasks such as performance analysis, athlete monitoring, or referee support. This paper presents \textbf{FST$\cdot$ai~2.5}, an explainable, uncertainty-aware, and secure AI framework for Olympic and Para-Taekwondo.
  \textbf{FST$\cdot$ai~2.5} introduces a unified digital ecosystem integrating athlete intelligence, competition analytics, federation-scale data management, AI-assisted decision support, athlete and event digital twins, explainable performance indicators, and adaptive training recommendations. The framework supports World Taekwondo (WT), Member National Associations (MNAs), coaches, referees, analysts, and athletes through transparent, secure, and federation-aware governance.
  By combining multi-source competition data, athlete-performance information, and contextual evidence, \textbf{FST$\cdot$ai~2.5} provides tactical diagnostics, longitudinal athlete monitoring, performance forecasting, personalised development planning, and federation-wide benchmarking using explainable and uncertainty-aware AI. Prototype deployments demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed framework. Although developed for Olympic and Para-Taekwondo, the methodology is broadly applicable to explainable AI, digital twins, and trustworthy decision support in combat sports and other high-performance sporting environments.

AI.tldr: FST·ai 2.5 is an explainable, uncertainty-aware, and secure AI framework for Olympic and Para-Taekwondo that integrates athlete intelligence, competition analytics, digital twins, and federation-wide governance into a unified digital ecosystem, with prototype deployments demonstrating feasibility.
AI.motivation: Existing digital solutions in elite sport are fragmented, addressing isolated tasks (performance analysis, athlete monitoring, referee support) without a unified framework. A coherent system integrating AI, performance analytics, and decision-support is needed for comprehensive athlete development and competition management.
AI.method: The paper presents FST·ai 2.5, a unified AI framework combining multi-source competition data, athlete-performance information, and contextual evidence. It features athlete and event digital twins, explainable performance indicators, adaptive training recommendations, federation-aware governance, and uncertainty-aware AI for tactical diagnostics, longitudinal monitoring, forecasting, and benchmarking.
AI.result: Prototype deployments demonstrate the feasibility of the proposed framework for Olympic and Para-Taekwondo, showing unified integration of previously fragmented tasks.
AI.conclusion: FST·ai 2.5 provides a broadly applicable methodology for explainable AI, digital twins, and trustworthy decision support in combat sports and other high-performance sporting environments, beyond its initial Taekwondo focus.

title: Eddy-VL 1.9B: Structural Pruning and Layered Distillation for Edge-Deployable Multimodal Embedding
comment: 11pages,4figures,Model weights and inference code are available on Hugging Face
summary: In this report, we introduce Eddy-VL 1.9B, a compressed multimodal embedding model built on Qwen3-VL-Embedding-2B for offline, edge-deployable vision-language retrieval. Eddy-VL targets air-gapped forensic and investigative settings where cloud APIs are unavailable and low latency is essential. Compression combines (i) probe-driven structural pruning that removes four redundant text-decoder layers (28 to 24) ranked by adjacent-layer linear CKA, and (ii) layered knowledge distillation with hole-covering teacher-student mappings, mid-layer attention-map 1-CKA, and final-layer MSE and cosine losses with Matryoshka dimensions {128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048}. The released model contains 1,926,188,032 parameters (3.85 GB bf16), representing approximately 9.5% fewer parameters than the 2.13B teacher model. Empirical evaluations on MMEB-V2 (78 tasks, VLM2Vec protocol) show that Eddy-VL achieves an overall score of 63.2 compared with 68.9 for the teacher, retaining 91.7% of the teacher's performance while recovering 6.4 of the 12.1 points lost through pruning alone (56.8). Compositional reasoning performance remains close to the teacher on SugarCrepe (86.1 vs. 86.4), MR2-Bench (24.5 vs. 24.7), and ARO (59.5 vs. 60.4), while Winoground group performance (6.8 vs. 8.5) remains the primary limitation. Depth pruning also reduces forward latency by approximately 10% (150.0 to 136.4 ms per image on NVIDIA DGX Spark using FlashAttention-2). We present the architecture, compression methodology, training procedures, and evaluation results, demonstrating the effectiveness of Eddy-VL for multimodal retrieval under constrained edge deployment. Model weights and inference code are publicly available on Hugging Face.

AI.tldr: Eddy-VL 1.9B is a compressed multimodal embedding model (pruned from 28 to 24 transformer layers via CKA-driven structural pruning and knowledge distillation) that retains 91.7% of its 2.13B teacher's performance (63.2 vs. 68.9 on MMEB-V2) while reducing parameters by ~9.5% and latency by ~10%, targeting offline edge-deployable vision-language retrieval.
AI.motivation: To enable offline, edge-deployable multimodal retrieval in air-gapped forensic/investigative settings where cloud APIs are unavailable and low latency is critical, by compressing a larger embedding model without catastrophic performance loss.
AI.method: (i) Probe-driven structural pruning — removing 4 redundant text-decoder layers (28→24) ranked by adjacent-layer linear CKA; (ii) Layered knowledge distillation with hole-covering teacher-student mappings, mid-layer attention-map 1-CKA loss, final-layer MSE and cosine losses, and Matryoshka embedding dimensions {128,256,512,1024,2048}.
AI.result: Eddy-VL (1.93B params, 3.85 GB bf16) achieves 63.2 on MMEB-V2 vs. teacher's 68.9 (91.7% retention); recovers 6.4 of the 12.1 points lost by pruning alone (56.8). Compositional reasoning near teacher on SugarCrepe (86.1 vs. 86.4), MR2-Bench (24.5 vs. 24.7), ARO (59.5 vs. 60.4). Winoground (6.8 vs. 8.5) remains primary weakness. Forward latency reduced ~10% (150.0→136.4 ms/image).
AI.conclusion: Eddy-VL demonstrates that targeted structural pruning combined with layered distillation can effectively compress multimodal embedding models for edge deployment while preserving strong retrieval and compositional reasoning capabilities, with model weights and code released publicly.

title: IssueExec: A Test-Driven Approach for Localizing Software Engineering Issues
summary: Issue localization, which identifies code locations requiring modification from issue descriptions, is a critical step in automated software maintenance. Existing approaches predominantly attempt to directly align issue descriptions with code elements, yet often struggle due to the inherent abstraction gap between the issue description and code implementation. Seeking alternative signals, our theoretical analysis suggests that test suites can serve as executable proxies for requirements, reducing localization uncertainty by 7.73 bits of entropy on average. A large-scale empirical study on 18 repositories validates this premise: existing tests cover 96.98\% of ground-truth files, and the two-hop pathway yields stronger semantic connectivity than direct matching in 82.4\% of cases. Despite their potential, leveraging tests for localization faces two key challenges: the semantic gap separating issue descriptions from test identifiers, and the substantial noise in execution traces from infrastructure code. To address these, we propose IssueExec, which bridges the semantic gap through domain-knowledge-enhanced test representations and filters noise via hierarchical trace analysis. Experiments on SWE-bench Lite show that IssueExec achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving function-level Recall@1 by 41.57\% over the strongest baseline. When integrated into the Agentless pipeline, IssueExec resolves 17.72\% more issues, demonstrating practical downstream benefits.

AI.tldr: IssueExec uses test suites as executable proxies to bridge the abstraction gap between issue descriptions and code, achieving state-of-the-art localization via domain-enhanced test representations and hierarchical trace noise filtering.
AI.motivation: Existing issue localization approaches struggle due to the abstraction gap between natural language issue descriptions and code. The authors hypothesize that test suites can serve as executable requirements proxies to reduce localization uncertainty.
AI.method: IssueExec bridges the semantic gap between issue descriptions and test identifiers using domain-knowledge-enhanced test representations, and filters noise from execution traces via hierarchical trace analysis.
AI.result: On SWE-bench Lite, IssueExec improves function-level Recall@1 by 41.57% over the strongest baseline. When integrated into Agentless pipeline, it resolves 17.72% more issues.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging test suites as proxies significantly improves issue localization accuracy and downstream issue resolution, validating that tests encode executable requirements reducing localization entropy by 7.73 bits on average.

title: Feature Generation Using LLMs: An Evolutionary Algorithm Approach
summary: A crucial step in machine learning pipelines is to present each entity with features or attributes that are representative of the characteristics of the processed entities. Feature engineering is an important step in finding a relation among attributes that otherwise may not be processed by the ML algorithms. Meanwhile, Large Language Models have shown promising abilities in coding, mathematical reasoning, and processing world knowledge. In this work, we utilize an LLM for the problem of feature generation from tabular data based on the previously given features. We have created a pipeline that takes a set of attributes and a prompt to generate new features. Then, our selection algorithm selects the best-performing sets of attributes. We apply our method to eight datasets from different domains and data types. Our results show that, in most cases, the language model can produce new features based on mathematical and logical operators that are useful for the given tasks and can improve classification results.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes using LLMs to generate new features from tabular data by applying mathematical and logical operations on existing attributes, followed by a selection algorithm to choose the best features, showing improved classification results across eight diverse datasets.
AI.motivation: Feature engineering is a crucial but challenging step in ML pipelines. LLMs have shown strong capabilities in coding, math reasoning, and world knowledge, motivating their use to automate and improve feature generation from tabular data.
AI.method: The authors build a pipeline that takes existing attributes and a prompt to generate new features using an LLM. A selection algorithm then picks the best-performing feature sets. The method is evaluated on eight datasets across different domains and data types.
AI.result: In most cases, the LLM-generated features (based on mathematical and logical operators) improved classification results compared to using the original features alone.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can effectively generate useful features for tabular data, enhancing classification performance through automated feature engineering.

title: Just A Rather Very Intelligent Spoken Agent
summary: Long-horizon AI agents are becoming increasingly capable, yet their interaction with users remains surprisingly thin. In most workflows, users give an initial instruction, receive only selective textual updates, and lose a clear sense of what the agent is doing or when to step in. This leaves a missing part in the current agent ecosystem: an always-on Jarvis-style mediator that keeps the agent continuously reachable to the user. Such a mediator should support real-time spoken interaction with the user, answer questions without interrupting the worker, proactively report progress or confusion, and inject user guidance back into the agent's execution when useful. In this work, we introduce JarvisBench, a benchmark for measuring the dual value of mediation in long-horizon agent workflows. JarvisBench contains two complementary tracks: an agent-collaboration track that measures whether mediation improves downstream task completion, and a user-interaction track that measures whether mediation makes ongoing execution more understandable, responsive, and accessible to users. We instantiate the benchmark with a modular reference Jarvis prototype and evaluate it on 34 text-only WildClaw tasks executed in OpenClaw. Preliminary results with GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini-based, and GPT-based worker agents suggest that Jarvis-style mediation can provide trace-grounded responses to user questions and improve task performance when sparse user guidance is injected at appropriate moments. The results also show that effectiveness depends strongly on the mediator's LLM brain, highlighting both the promise of this missing middle layer and the need for broader community effort. Demo page https://cchen1436.github.io/jarvis

AI.tldr: JarvisBench is a benchmark for evaluating an always-on mediation layer that enables real-time spoken interaction between users and long-horizon AI agents, tested on 34 WildClaw tasks with preliminary results showing improved task performance and user accessibility.
AI.motivation: Current long-horizon AI agents lack continuous, interactive communication with users, relying on thin initial instructions and selective textual updates. This creates a gap where users have poor situational awareness and limited ability to intervene — motivating the need for a "Jarvis-style" always-on mediator.
AI.method: The authors propose JarvisBench, a benchmark with two tracks: (1) agent-collaboration track measuring downstream task completion improvement via mediation, and (2) user-interaction track measuring understandability, responsiveness, and accessibility. A modular reference Jarvis prototype is evaluated on 34 text-only WildClaw tasks executed in OpenClaw using GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini-based, and GPT-based worker agents.
AI.result: Jarvis-style mediation enables trace-grounded responses to user questions and improves task performance when sparse user guidance is injected at appropriate moments. Effectiveness depends strongly on the mediator's LLM brain.
AI.conclusion: The missing mediation layer shows promise for improving long-horizon agent workflows, but its effectiveness is highly dependent on the mediator LLM, indicating a need for broader community effort to develop this direction.

title: Monte Carlo Dropout Uncertainty and Entropy-Thresholded Selective Prediction for Architecture-Agnostic Brain Tumor MRI Triage
summary: Deep networks now subtype brain tumors on MRI about as well as specialist readers, yet accuracy is not what keeps them out of the clinic. What matters at the point of care is whether a model's confidence can be trusted to flag the cases it is likely to misclassify and defer them to a human. Deterministic estimates cannot: an auxiliary confidence head trained alongside the classifier collapses to a near-constant output that says nothing about correctness. This study proposes an uncertainty-first pipeline for four-class brain tumor MRI (glioma, meningioma, pituitary, no tumor) that reads predictive uncertainty from Monte Carlo (MC) Dropout over T = 20 passes and turns the resulting entropy into an explicit rule for deferring uncertain cases to a radiologist. We partitioned 7,200 images by perceptual-hash cluster, closing the near-duplicate leakage that inflates accuracy under naive splitting, and evaluated the pipeline on ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50 across five seeds along three axes: discrimination, calibration, and selective prediction. Both discriminate strongly (macro-AUC 0.994; accuracy 0.962 and 0.964), and no seed separates them (0 of 5 significant, p < 0.05), so the result is driven by the uncertainty pipeline, not the network. A single temperature scalar pulls the deterministic softmax into tight calibration (expected calibration error 0.016-0.020), and deferring the most uncertain 5% of cases lifts accuracy on the rest to about 0.98 on both (area under the risk-coverage curve 0.010-0.011). MC-Dropout uncertainty here is thus calibrated, non-collapsing, and directly actionable through a concrete deferral rule, providing an architecture-agnostic basis for calibrated, defer-to-human brain tumor MRI triage under internal validation.

AI.tldr: Proposes an uncertainty-first pipeline for brain tumor MRI classification that uses MC Dropout entropy to defer uncertain cases to radiologists, achieving near-perfect discrimination and calibration while enabling selective prediction where deferring the top 5% uncertain cases lifts accuracy to ~0.98.
AI.motivation: Deep networks can classify brain tumors as well as specialists, but their confidence estimates are unreliable—deterministic confidence heads collapse to near-constant outputs that fail to indicate misclassification risk, preventing clinical deployment despite high accuracy.
AI.method: Uncertainty-first pipeline: (1) MC Dropout with T=20 passes on ViT-B/16 and ResNet-50; (2) convert predictive entropy into a deferral rule; (3) use perceptual-hash clustering to avoid near-duplicate leakage in train/test splits; (4) evaluate on discrimination (macro-AUC, accuracy), calibration (temperature scaling, ECE), and selective prediction (risk-coverage curves) across five seeds.
AI.result: Both networks achieve macro-AUC 0.994, accuracy ~0.963; no significant difference between them (0/5 seeds significant). Temperature scaling yields ECE 0.016-0.020. Deferring top 5% uncertain cases lifts accuracy to ~0.98 with risk-coverage AUC 0.010-0.011. MC-Dropout uncertainty is calibrated, non-collapsing, and directly actionable.
AI.conclusion: MC-Dropout entropy provides an architecture-agnostic, calibrated deferral mechanism for brain tumor MRI triage that can flag uncertain cases for human review, addressing the reliability gap that prevents deep networks from entering clinical use.

title: Portable models as a replacement for industrial heuristics in compiler optimizations
summary: The paper investigates the possibility of predicting function-inlining decisions in compact compilers, source-to-source tools, and interpreters where the reuse of GCC or LLVM optimization infrastructure is impractical. The relevance of this work is determined by the need to transfer mature inlining heuristics to systems with limited compiler infrastructure, restricted runtime dependencies, and reduced access to target-specific analysis. Existing production compilers already contain strong inliners, but their decisions depend on internal intermediate representations (IRs), pass ordering, target models, and analysis stacks that are difficult to reproduce in lightweight systems. To overcome these constraints, we propose a portable inlining-prediction framework. Production compiler diagnostics serve as supervision; a separate extractor reconstructs caller-callee callsites, prepares sterile source snippets, normalizes them into a universal AST, optionally lowers them to a lightweight structural IR, and exports scalar features for model training. Thus, a trained predictor can be emitted as ordinary C code without a compiler-runtime dependency. To evaluate the proposed framework, we constructed a dataset comprising 336,938 callsites from fifteen open-source C projects, including 79,287 compiler-reported inline events. A comparison of several tabular models is performed using project-aware validation. Under leave-one-project-out validation, CatBoost reaches ROC-AUC 0.928 and PR-AUC 0.713; after threshold tuning, F1 improves from 0.670 to 0.729 and the false-positive rate drops from 0.192 to 0.084. Feature analysis shows that most signal is concentrated in source locality, explicit inline intent, callee size, side effects, branch and call structure, signature shape, and callsite argument shape.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a portable framework for predicting function-inlining decisions in lightweight compilers and source-to-source tools, using production compiler diagnostics as supervision. The framework extracts callsites, normalizes them to a universal AST, and trains tabular models (CatBoost achieves ROC-AUC 0.928, PR-AUC 0.713) that can be exported as plain C code without compiler-runtime dependencies. Evaluation on 336,938 callsites from 15 open-source C projects demonstrates the approach's effectiveness.
AI.motivation: Mature inlining heuristics from production compilers like GCC and LLVM are difficult to reuse in compact compilers, source-to-source tools, and interpreters due to their reliance on internal IRs, pass ordering, target models, and complex analysis stacks that are hard to reproduce in lightweight systems.
AI.method: A portable inlining-prediction framework that uses production compiler diagnostics as supervision, reconstructs caller-callee callsites, prepares sterile source snippets, normalizes them into a universal AST, optionally lowers to a lightweight structural IR, and exports scalar features for model training. Trained predictors are emitted as ordinary C code.
AI.result: Dataset of 336,938 callsites from 15 open-source C projects (79,287 inline events). Under leave-one-project-out validation, CatBoost achieves ROC-AUC 0.928, PR-AUC 0.713. After threshold tuning, F1 improves from 0.670 to 0.729, false-positive rate drops from 0.192 to 0.084.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully transfers inlining heuristics from production compilers to lightweight systems without compiler-runtime dependencies. Most predictive signal comes from source locality, explicit inline intent, callee size, side effects, branch/call structure, signature shape, and callsite argument shape.

title: Discovery by Dreaming: Cross-Domain Recombination in Artificial Memory
summary: Dreams splice together people, places, and times that never met. Neuroscience suggests this recombination is not noise, but a function driving insight and creative discovery.
