Second, to bridge this gap and handle its heterogeneity, a Hindsight-Aware Distillation Network transfers privileged knowledge via the hindsight target, with Distillation Experts improving transfer under per-user variability. On a large-scale industrial dataset, SemRaD lifts +1.9% LTV (Gini) and +1.0% CVR (AUROC) over a production-grade base; a four-week online A/B at Keeta confirms +1.0% LTV / +0.43% CVR. SemRaD also matches the production system's LTV using only 9% of the training data while improving CVR by 0.8%.

AI.tldr: SemRaD is a Semantic Reasoning-aware Distillation framework that addresses new-user cold-start in e-commerce by combining structured semantic profiles (via a discover-curate-audit pipeline) with hindsight-aware distillation to bridge the heterogeneous information gap between privileged teacher and sparse student, achieving +1.9% LTV and +1.0% CVR gains on industrial data and matching production LTV with only 9% training data.
AI.motivation: New-user cold-start is a critical bottleneck for e-commerce platforms; prior approaches (LLM-based semantic augmentation and LUPI) suffer from noisy unstructured rationales and brittle student-teacher distillation due to heterogeneous information gaps.
AI.method: Proposes SemRaD with two components: (1) Structured Semantic Reasoning Pipeline that replaces free-form LLM rationales with a structured schema via discover-curate-audit workflow, producing a Densified Semantic Profile and a Hindsight Distillation Target; (2) Hindsight-Aware Distillation Network that transfers privileged knowledge using Distillation Experts to handle per-user variability.
AI.result: +1.9% LTV (Gini) and +1.0% CVR (AUROC) over production-grade baseline on large-scale industrial dataset; 4-week online A/B at Keeta confirms +1.0% LTV / +0.43% CVR; matches production LTV using only 9% training data while improving CVR by 0.8%.
AI.conclusion: SemRaD effectively solves the new-user cold-start problem by structuring semantic reasoning and adaptively bridging heterogeneous distillation gaps, achieving significant offline and online gains with substantial data efficiency improvements.

title: Spectral-Morphological Attention U-Net: An Efficient Network for Active Wildfire Detection
summary: Over the past decades, the frequency of global wildfires has been increasing steadily. Therefore, if the fire can be detected and precisely located at an early stage, the potential hazards caused by it can be minimized to the greatest extent. The machine learning methods based on satellite images, due to their ability to automatically monitor extremely remote and vast areas, have shown great potential for application in the field of wildfire detection. To address this challenge, we proposed a new model named spectral-morphological attention U-Net(SMA-UNet), which includes a spectral attention module, a residual attention UNet backbone, a channel-spatial modulator, and a pair of differentiable morphological gates. We trained and evaluated this model with two datasets. These modules, excluding the backbone, are used to detect active fire events for the first time, especially the pair of differentiable morphological gates, which is innovatively developed. The proposed model achieved the highest scores in both datasets (e.g., intersection over union 75.16% in TS-SatFire, 22.50% in Sen2Fire). By conducting ablation studies of each module, we compared their independent contributions and tested their combinations. Ultimately, the integration of these modules yields a highly robust framework that significantly improves segmentation consistency across diverse and complex environmental conditions. Future work will focus on validating the proposed architecture across large-scale, multi-regional datasets from different satellite sensors to establish its broader generalizability for global wildfire detection.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SMA-UNet, a deep learning model combining spectral attention, residual attention U-Net, channel-spatial modulator, and differentiable morphological gates for early wildfire detection from satellite imagery, achieving state-of-the-art results (75.16% IoU on TS-SatFire, 22.50% on Sen2Fire).
AI.motivation: Global wildfires are increasing in frequency, and early detection/precise localization can minimize hazards. Machine learning on satellite images offers automatic monitoring of vast remote areas but still faces challenges in detection accuracy and robustness across diverse conditions.
AI.method: Proposed SMA-UNet with: (1) spectral attention module, (2) residual attention UNet backbone, (3) channel-spatial modulator, and (4) a pair of differentiable morphological gates. These modules (except backbone) are novel for active fire detection. Evaluated on two satellite datasets (TS-SatFire and Sen2Fire) with ablation studies.
AI.result: Achieved best IoU scores: 75.16% on TS-SatFire and 22.50% on Sen2Fire. Ablation studies confirmed individual contributions of each module; their integration yields a highly robust framework that improves segmentation consistency across diverse environmental conditions.
AI.conclusion: The integrated modules form a robust framework for wildfire detection. Future work will validate on large-scale, multi-regional datasets from different satellite sensors to establish broader generalizability for global wildfire detection.

title: Learning from World Feedback: Why Model Uncertainty Fails as a Risk Signal in Model-Based RL
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Reinforcement Learning from X Feedback (RLxF). 14 pages
summary: The RLxF programme argues that learning signals should come from world feedback rather than from internal model proxies. We instantiate this position in safe model-based control and distil it into three concrete design principles. Empirically, across four world-model architectures spanning a 2x MSE range, MPC planning is statistically equivalent (TOST, n=200), and dynamics-based uncertainty penalties increase collision rates from 26% to 34%: the standard MBRL safety proxy is anti-correlated with safety in this regime. Replacing the model-internal proxy with three world-feedback signals (a sensor-derived margin via minimum lidar, a temporal signal via time-to-collision, and an outcome-supervised feedback model g_psi trained on prior collision labels, structurally analogous to outcome-trained reward models in RLHF) reduces collisions to 1-14% without retraining the world model or the planner. The mechanism is structural: model uncertainty has support over state-prediction space, whereas task risk has support over constraint boundaries, with empirical correlation r < 0.15. From this we extract three RLxF principles (ground risk in world outcomes, validate proxies before deployment, and substitute outcome-trained feedback models when direct world signals are unavailable) and argue they apply equally to model-based control and to verifier-based or RLHF approaches in LLM alignment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes RLxF principles emphasizing world feedback over internal model proxies for safe control. Empirically, standard MBRL safety proxies (model uncertainty) are anti-correlated with safety, increasing collisions from 26% to 34%. Replacing them with three world-feedback signals (lidar margin, time-to-collision, outcome-supervised feedback model) reduces collisions to 1-14%. The authors extract three RLxF principles and argue they apply to model-based control and LLM alignment.
AI.motivation: Current safe model-based control relies on model-internal proxies (e.g., dynamics-based uncertainty) for safety estimation, but these proxies may be misaligned with actual task risk. The paper aims to demonstrate this misalignment and propose alternatives grounded in world feedback.
AI.method: The authors instantiate three RLxF design principles in safe model-based control: ground risk in world outcomes, validate proxies before deployment, and substitute outcome-trained feedback models when direct signals are unavailable. They test across four world-model architectures, comparing MPC with standard uncertainty penalties vs. three world-feedback signals: minimum lidar distance (sensor-derived margin), time-to-collision (temporal signal), and an outcome-supervised feedback model g_psi trained on collision labels.
AI.result: MPC planning is statistically equivalent across architectures (TOST, n=200). Standard dynamics-based uncertainty penalties increase collision rates from 26% to 34%. World-feedback signals reduce collisions to 1-14% without retraining. Model uncertainty and task risk have low empirical correlation (r < 0.15) due to different support regions.
AI.conclusion: Internal model proxies (like model uncertainty) are structurally misaligned with safety — they have support over state-prediction space while task risk has support over constraint boundaries. The RLxF principles (ground risk in world outcomes, validate proxies, use outcome-trained substitutes) are generalizable beyond MBRL to verifier-based and RLHF approaches in LLM alignment.

title: Otap:Structure-Aware Optimal Transport for Evaluating Planning and Execution in Agent Trajectories
summary: Large language model agents solve tasks by generating trajectories that interleave planning, tool calls, and intermediate results. Current evaluation metrics reduce such a trajectory to a binary success flag or compare it against a reference by exact matching. A success flag cannot distinguish a sound solution from one that succeeds by luck, and says nothing about why a failed run went wrong. Exact matching penalizes plans that are valid but reordered or decomposed differently from the reference. We reframe trajectory evaluation as a distance between the agent's execution graph and a set of valid solution graphs, and instantiate it via an unbalanced fused Gromov-Wasserstein transport problem over attributed dependency graphs. The resulting score, termed \otap{} (Optimal Transport for Agentic Planning), is a pseudo-metric that is provably invariant to dependency-preserving reorderings and has bounded sensitivity to redundant steps. Its unbalanced marginals handle missing or hallucinated steps without forcing a match, and its soft coupling accommodates variation in plan granularity. On controlled perturbations and three public benchmarks, \otap{} separates valid from invalid trajectories in a regime where semantics-only metrics score below chance. Its accuracy is highest when the dependency graph is recovered exactly, and drops only when the graph is inferred heuristically from free-text traces.

AI.tldr: OTAP is a new evaluation metric for LLM agent trajectories that uses optimal transport over dependency graphs to measure distances between execution traces and valid solution graphs, offering invariance to reorderings and robustness to redundant, missing, or hallucinated steps.
AI.motivation: Current metrics (binary success flags or exact matching) fail to distinguish lucky successes from sound ones, cannot diagnose failures, and penalize valid but differently structured plans. A finer-grained evaluation that captures structural similarity is needed.
AI.method: The paper frames trajectory evaluation as a distance between the agent's execution graph and a set of valid solution graphs, instantiated via an unbalanced fused Gromov-Wasserstein transport problem over attributed dependency graphs. The resulting OTAP score is a pseudo-metric with invariance to dependency-preserving reorderings and bounded sensitivity to redundant steps, with unbalanced marginals handling missing/hallucinated steps and soft coupling handling plan granularity variation.
AI.result: On controlled perturbations and three public benchmarks, OTAP separates valid from invalid trajectories where semantics-only metrics perform below chance. Accuracy is highest when dependency graphs are recovered exactly, dropping only when inferred heuristically from free-text traces.
AI.conclusion: OTAP provides a principled, structurally-aware evaluation metric for agentic planning that overcomes the limitations of binary success flags and exact matching, with theoretical guarantees on invariance and robustness.

title: WeedExpert-R1: Incentivizing Botanical Reasoning in MLLMs with Reinforcement Learning for Precision Weed Grounding
summary: Precision weed control requires species-level identification and instance-level localization. However, conventional object detectors use a closed vocabulary, limiting their deployment across regions, and cannot explain their predictions in complex agricultural scenes. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer visual grounding and reasoning capabilities, but insufficient botanical knowledge can cause hallucinations in fine-grained weed identification. This study introduces WeedExpert-R1, a multimodal model that learns visually grounded botanical reasoning through verifiable rewards. A domain-specific Chain-of-Thought synthesis pipeline combines a human-curated botanical trait dictionary with an Auditor-Synthesizer LLM workflow to generate reasoning data for supervised fine-tuning. Group Relative Policy Optimization is then applied with rewards for format, accuracy, instance count, and response length. Across 37 weed species from six datasets, WeedExpert-R1-4B achieved 75.82 percent exact-set precision at an IoU threshold of 0.5, 89.30 percent precision, and 87.81 percent recall. It outperformed proprietary models, including GPT-5.4 and Gemini-3.1-Pro, and larger open-source models, including Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct and Gemma-4-31B-it. Results on unseen species further demonstrate its open-vocabulary capability and potential for deployment across diverse regions and crops without retraining.

AI.tldr: WeedExpert-R1 is a multimodal LLM that improves precision weed control by combining botanical reasoning with verifiable rewards, achieving 75.82% exact-set precision across 37 weed species and outperforming larger proprietary and open-source models.
AI.motivation: Conventional object detectors use closed vocabularies, limiting deployment across regions, and cannot explain predictions in complex agricultural scenes. MLLMs offer visual grounding but lack botanical knowledge, causing hallucinations in fine-grained weed identification.
AI.method: A domain-specific Chain-of-Thought synthesis pipeline combining a human-curated botanical trait dictionary with an Auditor-Synthesizer LLM workflow generates reasoning data for supervised fine-tuning. Group Relative Policy Optimization is applied with rewards for format, accuracy, instance count, and response length.
AI.result: WeedExpert-R1-4B achieved 75.82% exact-set precision at IoU=0.5, 89.30% precision, and 87.81% recall across 37 weed species from six datasets, outperforming GPT-5.4, Gemini-3.1-Pro, Qwen3-VL-30B-Instruct, and Gemma-4-31B-it.
AI.conclusion: The model demonstrates open-vocabulary capability on unseen species and potential for deployment across diverse regions and crops without retraining.

title: Privacy Cost as Equity Input: A Group Fairness Criterion for Differentially Private Machine Learning
summary: Differential privacy (DP) is increasingly deployed to limit membership inference risk in machine-learning systems. Prior work has shown that DP-SGD can widen accuracy disparities across demographic groups, but this framing treats fairness as a purely outcome-side concern. We argue that privacy cost, the information leakage borne by each group, is itself a form of harm, and adopt a compensatory-fairness framework in which a group that involuntarily bears greater privacy exposure is owed proportionally greater benefit from the system. From this principle we derive the \emph{Privacy-Cost Equity Ratio} (PCER), a group fairness metric defined as a group's positive prediction rate normalized by its per-group overfitting gap. By a standard membership inference bound, this overfitting gap upper-bounds each group's vulnerability to inference attacks, making PCER a conservative measure of benefit relative to exposure. PCER needs only per-group train and test accuracy (no shadow models), making it a practical post-hoc audit tool. We evaluate PCER alongside standard fairness metrics across six benchmark--attribute combinations spanning tabular and NLP domains, under DP-SGD at a range of privacy budgets, and validate the overfitting-gap proxy against a direct threshold membership-inference attack. The results reveal patterns that outcome-based metrics miss. On COMPAS, PCER uncovers a persistent double disadvantage: the protected group bears both greater privacy exposure and worse predictive outcomes, something demographic parity gap masks entirely. Sensitivity analysis shows very strong privacy guarantees collapse both groups' overfitting to a numerical floor, rendering exposure-based audits uninformative in that regime. Together, these findings show that fairness audits of privacy-preserving systems must account for who bears the cost of protection, not only who benefits from its outcomes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Privacy-Cost Equity Ratio (PCER), a fairness metric that measures a group's positive prediction rate normalized by its per-group overfitting gap (proxy for privacy exposure). Applying PCER to DP-SGD-trained models reveals patterns missed by outcome-only metrics, such as a "double disadvantage" on COMPAS where protected groups bear both greater privacy exposure and worse outcomes. The work argues fairness audits must account for who bears privacy costs, not just who benefits from outcomes.
AI.motivation: Prior fairness analyses of DP-SGD focus on outcome disparities (accuracy gaps), ignoring that privacy cost itself is a harm. The authors adopt a compensatory-fairness framework: groups involuntarily bearing more privacy exposure deserve proportionally greater benefit, motivating a metric that jointly accounts for privacy cost and predictive benefit.
AI.method: The authors derive PCER = group's positive prediction rate / per-group overfitting gap (train-test accuracy difference). The overfitting gap upper-bounds membership inference vulnerability via a standard privacy bound, requiring only per-group train/test accuracy (no shadow models). PCER is evaluated across six benchmark-attribute pairs (tabular and NLP) under DP-SGD at multiple privacy budgets, validated against a direct threshold membership inference attack.
AI.result: PCER reveals patterns outcome-based metrics miss. On COMPAS, it uncovers a persistent "double disadvantage": the protected group faces both higher privacy exposure and worse outcomes, a pattern demographic parity gap entirely masks. At very strong privacy guarantees, both groups' overfitting collapses to a numerical floor, making exposure-based audits uninformative.
AI.conclusion: Fairness audits of privacy-preserving systems must account for who bears the cost of protection, not only who benefits from outcomes. PCER provides a practical post-hoc audit tool for this purpose, but its utility is limited under very strong privacy guarantees.

title: Fourier Geometric Wind Power Forecasting with Numerical Weather Prediction
summary: Accurate short-term wind power forecasting is essential for grid stability and operational planning, yet remains challenging due to the complex interactions between atmospheric conditions and turbine dynamics. However, existing methods fail to effectively incorporate weather forecasting with wind turbine data (i.e., SCADA), leading to suboptimal solutions. To address this, we introduce a multimodal framework that integrates historical point-based SCADA data with grid-based Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) forecasts, which is challenging due to heterogeneous input and the complex physical wind-turbine interactions. Our approach first explicitly decomposes inputs into scalar and vector features to better capture both site-specific and geometric dependencies and then incorporates a geometric encoder to extract rotation-invariant features from wind vectors. We further leverages a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) architecture, which performs global convolutions in the frequency domain to efficiently model long-range spatiotemporal relationships. Extensive experiments on three real-world wind farms, with weather forecasting data, demonstrate that our model consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of its physically-informed design. The core implementation of our method is publicly available at: https://github.com/shawn-sypiao/GWPF.

AI.tldr: A multimodal framework integrating SCADA data with NWP forecasts using geometric encoding and Fourier Neural Operators for short-term wind power forecasting, consistently outperforming baselines on three real-world wind farms.
AI.motivation: Existing methods fail to effectively incorporate weather forecasting (NWP) with turbine SCADA data due to heterogeneous inputs and complex physical wind-turbine interactions, leading to suboptimal wind power forecasting solutions.
AI.method: A multimodal framework that (1) explicitly decomposes inputs into scalar and vector features, (2) incorporates a geometric encoder for rotation-invariant features from wind vectors, and (3) leverages Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) for global convolutions in the frequency domain to model long-range spatiotemporal relationships.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on three real-world wind farms with weather forecasting data.
AI.conclusion: The physically-informed design effectively integrates heterogeneous data sources for improved wind power forecasting, with public implementation available.

title: Geometry-Enhanced Portion Estimation for Multimodal LLMs
summary: Image-based dietary assessment promises to replace costly, bias-prone manual recalls, but portion estimation remains a major blocker. Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) recognize a wide range of foods zero-shot in uncontrolled photos, yet they are weak at portion estimation -- a gap we measure across the current frontier (Gemini, GPT, and Claude flagships alike). We present a method that enhances a frozen, commercial MLLM with an accurate portion head: a small geometry-enhanced network on a frozen DINOv2 backbone with a structured softmax-ownership volume, consuming the MLLM's per-food name, bounding box, and density range -- no depth sensor, no MLLM fine-tuning. Evaluated fully open-vocabulary on three real-world benchmarks, the head cuts per-food portion error by 33-41% relative to the MLLM alone, outperforms every flagship MLLM's direct estimates, and surpasses each benchmark's originally published image-only model at its own reported metric.

AI.tldr: Multimodal LLMs excel at zero-shot food recognition but struggle with portion estimation. The paper proposes a geometry-enhanced portion head (frozen DINOv2 backbone + softmax-ownership volume) that uses the MLLM's food name, bounding box, and density range to reduce portion estimation error by 33-41% relative to MLLM alone, outperforming flagship MLLMs and prior image-only models on three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Image-based dietary assessment is hindered by poor portion estimation in multimodal LLMs, despite their strong zero-shot food recognition.
AI.method: A geometry-enhanced portion head (small network on frozen DINOv2 backbone + structured softmax-ownership volume) is attached to a frozen commercial MLLM, using the MLLM's per-food name, bounding box, and density range without depth sensors or MLLM fine-tuning.
AI.result: The method reduces per-food portion error by 33-41% relative to MLLM alone, outperforms all tested flagship MLLMs (Gemini, GPT, Claude), and surpasses each benchmark's originally published image-only model.
AI.conclusion: Augmenting frozen MLLMs with a specialized geometry-aware portion head is an effective, lightweight strategy to bridge the portion estimation gap in image-based dietary assessment.

title: Multimodal Attention-based Deep Learning for Emergency Triage with Electronic Health Records
summary: Accurate emergency triage decision is critical to avoid clinical deterioration, morbidity, and mortality. Machine learning-based triage system involves acquiring the main presenting complaint in text form and assessing vital signs in numerical data, enabling an automated and efficient analysis of patient information for timely and accurate prioritization of medical attention. However, modelling the intricacies of both data types requires a comprehensive understanding of the temporal structure and dependencies within the data. Thus, the aim of this study is to propose a multimodal deep learning architecture that can effectively handle both tabular and textual data. Furthermore, the proposed model exploits self-attention to to capture both local and global relationships between the features. A dataset consisting of 11,102 triage data collected from emergency department of Hospital Universiti Sains Malaysia is used for model development and validation. The proposed model demonstrated an increase of 1.95% in accuracy, 2.49% in F1-score, and 1.41% in ROC AUC compared to the baseline model. The experimental results demonstrated the potential of the proposed model in predicting triage decisions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a multimodal deep learning architecture using self-attention to process both textual (chief complaints) and tabular (vital signs) data for emergency triage, achieving 1.95% accuracy improvement over baselines on 11,102 ED visits from Hospital Universiti Sains Malaysia.
AI.motivation: Accurate emergency triage is critical to prevent clinical deterioration, morbidity, and mortality. Existing ML-based triage systems struggle to model the temporal structures and dependencies inherent in both textual presenting complaints and numerical vital signs simultaneously.
AI.method: A multimodal deep learning architecture with self-attention mechanisms that jointly handles tabular (vital signs) and textual (chief complaints) data, capturing both local and global feature relationships.
AI.result: Accuracy improved by 1.95%, F1-score by 2.49%, and ROC AUC by 1.41% compared to the baseline model, using a dataset of 11,102 triage encounters.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multimodal approach with self-attention demonstrates significant potential for improving automated triage decision accuracy by effectively integrating heterogeneous clinical data types.

title: Evidence Interfaces Shape How Retrieval-Augmented Readers Use Support
summary: In multi-hop RAG evaluation, a top-k answer score can hide two different failures: the retrieval window may drop part of the support chain, or it may contain support in a form the adapted reader does not use well. We call this reader-facing form of retrieved evidence an evidence interface. Using three support-annotated multi-hop QA benchmarks, we compare matched adapted readers trained with raw context, retrieval windows, and gold-support diagnostic renderings. These comparisons distinguish support-availability failures from remaining reader-interface effects. Top-k windows become interpretable only after checking whether the complete annotated support chain survives: when it does, short ranked windows can match or improve over raw context; when it does not, missing support explains much of the loss. Gold support-first improves matched readers; on 2Wiki and MuSiQue, a support-supervised ranker raises coverage and recovers raw-context quality at lower prompt cost, while retaining gold headroom. Support-removal checks further show that the gains rely on exposed evidence, not only answer priors. On support-annotated evaluations, top-k answer scores should therefore be reported together with complete-support coverage.

AI.tldr: Top-k answer scores in multi-hop RAG conflate two distinct failures: missing support in the retrieval window vs. poor reader utilization of available evidence. By comparing readers trained on raw context, retrieval windows, and gold-support renderings, the paper shows that reporting complete-support coverage alongside answer scores makes top-k evaluations interpretable.
AI.motivation: Top-k answer scores alone cannot distinguish whether RAG failures stem from incomplete retrieval (missing evidence) or from the reader's inability to use available evidence (interface mismatch). The paper aims to disentangle these factors.
AI.method: Using three support-annotated multi-hop QA benchmarks, the authors compare matched adapted readers trained with raw context, retrieval windows, and gold-support diagnostic renderings. They also employ a support-supervised ranker and perform support-removal checks.
AI.result: When complete support survives in the window, short ranked windows match or improve over raw context. Missing support explains most performance loss. Gold-support-first improves readers; a support-supervised ranker raises coverage and recovers raw-context quality at lower cost. Gains depend on exposed evidence, not answer priors.
AI.conclusion: Top-k answer scores should be reported together with complete-support coverage for interpretable multi-hop RAG evaluation.

title: Do Vision Encoders Exhibit Human-like Color Thresholds?
summary: Understanding and characterizing human color perception is a longstanding research goal. One of the most traditional approaches is looking for the human color discrimination thresholds, the minimum chromatic differences perceptible to human observers. In recent years, deep neural networks have become the standard networks for computer vision tasks. In particular, deep vision encoders, foundation models trained on large-scale visual data, map images into latent feature representations. Despite the widespread use of deep vision encoders, few studies have investigated whether their internal representations exhibit human-like discrimination thresholds. In this work, we present a large-scale exploratory study probing the chromatic sensitivity of more than 50 pretrained vision encoders, including convolutional networks and vision transformers, against human discrimination thresholds. Using controlled chromatic stimuli at multiple chroma levels, we compare model-derived chromatic discrimination thresholds with human discrimination ellipses through a region-overlap metric (mIoU). Our analysis reveals generally weak alignment between model representations and human perceptual thresholds across all model families, with the best mIoU < 0.25. Moreover, we find that self-supervised encoders consistently outperform supervised ones, while language-supervised models show the most polarized behavior, occupying both the top and bottom of the ranking. These findings suggest that human-like chromatic sensitivity does not emerge naturally from current large-scale visual training objectives for any of the analyzed architectures.

AI.tldr: A large-scale study of over 50 pretrained vision encoders (CNNs and ViTs) finds weak alignment (best mIoU < 0.25) between model-derived chromatic discrimination thresholds and human perceptual thresholds. Self-supervised encoders outperform supervised ones, while language-supervised models show polarized results, indicating human-like chromatic sensitivity does not emerge naturally from current large-scale visual training objectives.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether deep vision encoders' internal feature representations exhibit human-like chromatic discrimination thresholds, a question underexplored despite the widespread use of these models.
AI.method: Probed chromatic sensitivity of over 50 pretrained vision encoders (CNNs and ViTs) using controlled chromatic stimuli at multiple chroma levels; compared model-derived discrimination thresholds with human discrimination ellipses using a region-overlap metric (mIoU).
AI.result: Weak alignment across all model families (best mIoU < 0.25); self-supervised encoders consistently outperform supervised ones; language-supervised models show the most polarized behavior (top and bottom of ranking).
AI.conclusion: Human-like chromatic sensitivity does not naturally emerge from current large-scale visual training objectives, regardless of architecture.

title: CLDRoute: Conditional Latent Diffusion for Routability Map Generation in Physical Design
summary: Accurate routability estimation during physical design is important for reducing costly post-routing iterations. Prior learning-based methods treat this task as deterministic prediction, mapping placement-stage features to a single congestion or DRC outcome. We instead formulate routability estimation as a conditional generation problem, where both routing congestion and DRC violations are modeled as spatially structured routability fields. Our framework, Conditional Latent Diffusion for Routeability estimation (CLDRoute), uses physics-aware conditioning and task-specific latent modeling to handle the different characteristics of congestion and DRC maps. This allows our method to supports sample-based inference, producing both a mean prediction and a spatial uncertainty estimate for the same input design. On CircuitNet 2.0 (N28), our method achieves, for DRC violation generation, an SSIM of 0.9678, an MAE of 0.0028, and a TopK@1% of 0.3494; for congestion generation, it achieves an SSIM of 0.9031, an MAE of 0.0286, and an NZ-Pearson of 0.3692. Overall, our framework provides a more practical view of routability at placement by generating both the expected outcome and its uncertainty.

AI.tldr: CLDRoute formulates routability estimation as a conditional generation problem using latent diffusion, producing both congestion/DRC predictions and spatial uncertainty estimates to improve physical design workflows.
AI.motivation: Accurate routability estimation during physical design is important for reducing costly post-routing iterations. Prior learning-based methods treat this task as deterministic prediction, failing to capture the uncertainty inherent in the problem.
AI.method: Formulates routability estimation as conditional generation using latent diffusion, with physics-aware conditioning and task-specific latent modeling to handle congestion and DRC maps differently, supporting sample-based inference for both mean prediction and spatial uncertainty.
AI.result: On CircuitNet 2.0 (N28): DRC generation achieves SSIM 0.9678, MAE 0.0028, TopK@1% 0.3494; congestion generation achieves SSIM 0.9031, MAE 0.0286, NZ-Pearson 0.3692.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a more practical view of routability at placement by generating both expected outcomes and their uncertainties, enabling better design decisions.

title: A Diagnostic Framework for AI Agent Behavior
summary: AI agents increasingly act within the same clinical, political, scientific, and social systems that behavioral scientists study. Evaluating these systems requires source-level diagnosis: the same behavioral pattern may arise from an agent representational substrate or from the roles, objectives, interaction structures, and governance rules that shape its expression. This Perspective proposes a diagnostic framework for AI agent behavior: layer attribution. The foundational computational layer defines what behaviors are possible through architecture, memory, perception, attention, and representation. The behavioral modulation layer shapes how those capacities are expressed through identity, resources, objectives, social interaction, institutional constraints, and governance. The framework clarifies three consequences: surrogate validity is a model-task-layer relation, human-AI divergence provides diagnostic evidence, and governance requires source attribution before intervention. Treating AI agents as behavioral actors therefore requires evaluation methods that determine where behavior originates before deciding how to explain, validate, or govern it.

AI.tldr: This Perspective proposes a diagnostic framework called "layer attribution" to evaluate AI agent behavior by distinguishing between what behaviors are possible (computational layer) versus how they are expressed (behavioral modulation layer), arguing that source-level diagnosis is necessary before explaining, validating, or governing AI systems.
AI.motivation: AI agents now operate within the same social, clinical, political, and scientific systems that behavioral scientists study, yet current evaluation methods often fail to distinguish whether a behavioral pattern originates from the agent's representational substrate or from the roles, objectives, interaction structures, and governance rules shaping its expression.
AI.method: The paper proposes a two-layer diagnostic framework: (1) the foundational computational layer (architecture, memory, perception, attention, representation) defines what behaviors are possible; (2) the behavioral modulation layer (identity, resources, objectives, social interaction, institutional constraints, governance) shapes how those capacities are expressed.
AI.result: The framework yields three consequences: surrogate validity is a model-task-layer relation; human-AI divergence provides diagnostic evidence for source attribution; and governance requires source attribution before intervention can be properly designed.
AI.conclusion: Treating AI agents as behavioral actors requires evaluation methods that determine where behavior originates—computational substrate or contextual modulation—before deciding how to explain, validate, or govern it.

title: AffectFuse: Cross-Task Feature Fusion with Temporal Modeling for Multi-Task Affective Behavior Analysis
summary: Affective behavior recognition in the wild requires joint prediction of continuous valence-arousal, categorical facial expression, and multi-label action units from unconstrained face images. We present our system for the Multi-Task Learning (MTL) track of the 11th Affective Behavior Analysis in-the-wild (ABAW) competition on s-Aff-Wild2, the static selected-frame version of Aff-Wild2. The method focuses on post-encoder adaptation: frozen AffectNet-supervised backbones provide multi-resolution features, while task-specific temporal heads and cross-task fusion modules select the useful signals for each target. For action-unit recognition, we adapt MAE-Face with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and use DISFA through per-unit expert routing rather than direct sequential transfer. Ablations over backbone, temporal, fusion, and AU-adaptation choices define the final configuration. The final system obtains P = 1.7302 on the official validation split, showing that post-encoder adaptation and task-wise modeling choices provide a strong MTL pipeline without training a new large-scale face foundation model.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a multi-task learning system for the ABAW 2025 competition that jointly predicts valence-arousal, facial expressions, and action units using frozen AffectNet-pretrained backbones with post-encoder adaptation, task-specific temporal heads, cross-task fusion, and LoRA-based MAE-Face adaptation, achieving P=1.7302 on the validation set.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of joint affective behavior recognition (valence-arousal, facial expressions, action units) from unconstrained face images without training a new large-scale face foundation model, using efficient post-encoder adaptation instead.
AI.method: Frozen AffectNet-supervised backbones provide multi-resolution features; task-specific temporal heads and cross-task fusion modules select task-relevant signals; AU recognition uses MAE-Face with LoRA and per-unit expert routing on DISFA rather than sequential transfer.
AI.result: The final system achieves P = 1.7302 on the official validation split of s-Aff-Wild2.
AI.conclusion: Post-encoder adaptation and task-wise modeling choices provide a strong MTL pipeline without requiring training a new large-scale face foundation model.

title: A Framework for Early Sepsis Prediction via Self-Supervised (JEPA) and Federated Representation Learning
summary: Early sepsis prediction from electronic health records is challenged by irregular sampling, high missingness, and class imbalance. We systematically compare four modeling paradigms -- self-supervised Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA) via masked latent prediction, self-supervised VICReg (variance-invariance-covariance regularization) with two-view augmentation, semi-supervised fine-tuning of a VICReg-pretrained encoder, and supervised Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) -- alongside raw-feature baselines. All models share a common preprocessing pipeline of hourly binning with forward-fill imputation applied to 7 biomarkers selected via sparsity analysis from the MIMIC-III dataset. Our best model (JEPA + XGBoost + mean pooling) achieves AUPRC 0.636 at the time of onset (H0), approaching the SupMix benchmark (0.667) while using 83\% fewer biomarkers. The Tier 1 pipeline -- VICReg pretraining followed by semi-supervised fine-tuning and XGBoost -- achieves AUPRC 0.510 at H0, a 3.1$\times$ improvement over the raw-feature baseline (0.165) and a 7.6\% improvement over the end-to-end supervised TCN (0.474). Crucially, the fine-tuned VICReg encoder exhibits the most temporally persistent representations, degrading only 16.8\% from H0 to H10 compared to 47.5\% for supervised TCN and 65.3\% for JEPA, demonstrating that self-supervised pretraining with task-aware fine-tuning yields features that are both sharp near onset and robust across prediction horizons.

AI.tldr: This paper compares four modeling paradigms (JEPA, VICReg, semi-supervised VICReg fine-tuning, supervised TCN) for early sepsis prediction from EHR data, using a common preprocessing pipeline on 7 biomarkers from MIMIC-III. JEPA+XGBoost achieves AUPRC 0.636 at H0 (near SupMix benchmark 0.667 with 83% fewer biomarkers). The semi-supervised VICReg pipeline achieves AUPRC 0.510 at H0, a 3.1× improvement over raw-feature baseline, and shows the most temporally persistent representations (only 16.8% degradation from H0 to H10 vs. 47.5% for TCN and 65.3% for JEPA).
AI.motivation: Early sepsis prediction from EHR data is challenged by irregular sampling, high missingness, and class imbalance. The study aims to systematically compare self-supervised, semi-supervised, and supervised paradigms to identify which approach yields the best predictive performance and temporal robustness.
AI.method: Four modeling paradigms were compared: self-supervised JEPA (masked latent prediction), self-supervised VICReg (two-view augmentation), semi-supervised fine-tuning of VICReg-pretrained encoder, and supervised TCN, plus raw-feature baselines. All used a common preprocessing pipeline (hourly binning, forward-fill imputation) on 7 biomarkers selected via sparsity analysis from MIMIC-III.
AI.result: JEPA+XGBoost+mean pooling achieved AUPRC 0.636 at H0, approaching SupMix benchmark (0.667) with 83% fewer biomarkers. Semi-supervised VICReg pipeline achieved AUPRC 0.510 at H0 (3.1× over raw baseline 0.165, 7.6% over supervised TCN 0.474). Fine-tuned VICReg encoder showed only 16.8% degradation from H0 to H10 vs. 47.5% for TCN and 65.3% for JEPA.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised pretraining with task-aware fine-tuning yields features that are both sharp near sepsis onset and robust across prediction horizons, outperforming purely supervised and purely self-supervised approaches in temporal representation persistence.

title: Is Your Model Thinking or Just Stagnating? PUMA: Diagnosing Reasoning Pathology via Phase-Momentum Alignment
summary: Test-time scaling empowers Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) to tackle complex tasks via extensive Chain-of-Thought (CoT). However, this often induces the "overthinking" paradox, where redundant reasoning increases computational overhead without guaranteeing accuracy. Existing test-time efficiency optimization methods primarily fall into two categories: information-theoretic approaches, which are prone to "deceptive convergence" where low uncertainty masks hallucinations, and latent representation analyses, which are often post-hoc, lacking the real-time sensitivity for dynamic reasoning. To bridge this gap, we first posit the Phase-Momentum Alignment Hypothesis, asserting that reasoning correctness hinges on the temporal synchronization between geometric momentum and uncertainty resolution. We then theoretically formulate the Cognitive-Energy Model to characterize these dynamics through two orthogonal dimensions: Geometric Cognitive Effort, quantified by latent velocity and tortuosity, and Entropic Cognitive Uncertainty. To operationalize this, we introduce PUMA (Phase-Uncertainty Momentum Alignment), a training-free framework employing a tiered diagnostic architecture. By coupling lightweight phase monitoring with event-triggered geometric analysis, PUMA effectively distinguishes active exploration from passive stagnation, enabling precise interventions through adaptive truncation or corrective measures. Extensive experiments on LRMs spanning 1.5B to 32B demonstrate that PUMA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks, achieving a superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off and robust cross-domain generalization.

AI.tldr: PUMA introduces a training-free framework that uses Phase-Momentum Alignment to detect and mitigate overthinking in Large Reasoning Models by distinguishing active exploration from passive stagnation, achieving better accuracy-efficiency trade-offs across 1.5B-32B LRMs.
AI.motivation: Existing test-time efficiency methods suffer from "deceptive convergence" (low uncertainty masking hallucinations) or lack real-time sensitivity for dynamic reasoning, motivating a need for real-time, sensitive diagnostic approach to address the "overthinking" paradox in LRMs.
AI.method: Proposes Phase-Momentum Alignment Hypothesis and Cognitive-Energy Model with two orthogonal dimensions (Geometric Cognitive Effort via latent velocity/tortuosity, and Entropic Cognitive Uncertainty). Operationalized via PUMA—a training-free, tiered diagnostic architecture coupling lightweight phase monitoring with event-triggered geometric analysis for adaptive truncation or correction.
AI.result: PUMA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across diverse benchmarks on LRMs spanning 1.5B to 32B, achieving superior accuracy-efficiency trade-off and robust cross-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: PUMA effectively resolves the overthinking paradox by enabling precise, real-time interventions during Chain-of-Thought reasoning, offering a training-free solution that generalizes across model scales and domains.

title: Building a Neural Network from Scratch: Implementation, Evaluation, and Optimization
summary: The widespread adoption of high-level deep learning libraries, while accelerating model development, has increasingly abstracted away the internal mechanics of neural networks, creating a gap between practical usage and fundamental understanding. To address this, the paper presents a self-contained neural network framework implemented entirely from scratch -- without relying on automatic differentiation or pre-built deep learning modules. The implementation encompasses all essential components, including multi-layer architectures, diverse activation functions, regularization techniques, and state-of-the-art optimizers. Beyond serving as a pedagogical instrument that demystifies forward/backward propagation, gradient dynamics, and optimization landscapes, the framework demonstrates robust performance when applied to a multi-class classification task, successfully validating its correctness, numerical stability, and generalization across varied configurations. The extensible design and clean modularity further position it as a reliable baseline for educational purposes and future research exploration.

AI.tldr: A neural network framework built entirely from scratch (no auto-diff or deep learning libraries) for educational purposes, demonstrating all core components and achieving robust performance on multi-class classification.
AI.motivation: The widespread use of high-level deep learning libraries has abstracted away neural network internals, creating a gap between practical usage and fundamental understanding.
AI.method: A self-contained neural network framework implemented from scratch without automatic differentiation or pre-built modules, covering multi-layer architectures, activation functions, regularization, and optimizers.
AI.result: The framework demonstrates robust performance on multi-class classification, validating correctness, numerical stability, and generalization across varied configurations.
AI.conclusion: The extensible, modular design serves as an effective pedagogical tool and reliable baseline for education and future research.

title: Toward Anthropomorphic Dialogue: A Closed-Loop Framework for Human-Like Chat Generation, Evaluation, and Preference Alignment
summary: Human-like private chat requires more than fluent response generation: a system must preserve persona, relationship, memory, bounded knowledge, medium-specific timing, and a coherent multi-turn arc. We present AnthroDial, a closed-loop framework that formulates anthropomorphic dialogue as a joint problem of system architecture, executable evaluation, and diagnostic alignment. It combines (1) a role-conditioned scheduled dialogue runtime with persona and scenario cards, long-term memory, virtual time, and single-draft message decisions; (2) an executable benchmark with an L0 validity gate, five per-turn dimensions, and five dialogue-level dimensions; and (3) a post-training pipeline that filters 16,436 scheduled-decision examples for SFT and applies GRPO with a cognitive-diagnostic, ZPD-aware reward. The reward maintains Kalman-filtered capability estimates for each behavioral dimension, upweights dimensions with larger capability deficits, and uses rollout scores as task-level ZPD matches to focus optimization on learnable weak skills. On a benchmark with 55 personas, 50 scenarios, 50 persona-scenario bindings, and 100 role-conditioned cases per model, we evaluate 16 systems spanning frontier baselines, open models, thinking/no-think variants, and SFT/RL ablations. The strongest non-trained baseline reaches 32.00% strict ACC, while Qwen3.6-27B-SFT+RL reaches 39.00% strict ACC and a 98.5 overall score. In the 9B no-think setting, SFT and RL improve strict ACC from 0.00% to 13.00% and 18.37%. These results show that anthropomorphic dialogue benefits when generation, evaluation, and reward shaping share the same behavioral dimensions.

AI.tldr: AnthroDial is a closed-loop framework for anthropomorphic dialogue that integrates a role-conditioned runtime, an executable benchmark with multi-level evaluation dimensions, and a post-training pipeline (SFT + GRPO with ZPD-aware Kalman-filtered rewards). It achieves 39.00% strict ACC (Qwen3.6-27B-SFT+RL) vs. 32.00% for the best non-trained baseline, demonstrating that aligning generation, evaluation, and reward shaping across shared behavioral dimensions improves anthropomorphic dialogue quality.
AI.motivation: Human-like private chat requires preserving persona, relationship, memory, bounded knowledge, timing, and multi-turn coherence—capabilities beyond fluent response generation that existing systems lack.
AI.method: AnthroDial combines: (1) a role-conditioned scheduled dialogue runtime with persona/scenario cards, long-term memory, virtual time, and single-draft decisions; (2) an executable L0-gated benchmark with 5 per-turn + 5 dialogue-level evaluation dimensions; (3) post-training via SFT on 16,436 filtered examples + GRPO using a ZPD-aware, Kalman-filtered cognitive-diagnostic reward that upweights dimensions with larger capability deficits.
AI.result: Evaluated on 55 personas, 50 scenarios, 100 role-conditioned cases per model across 16 systems. Best baseline: 32.00% strict ACC; Qwen3.6-27B-SFT+RL: 39.00% strict ACC, 98.5 overall score. In 9B no-think, SFT→13.00%, RL→18.37% strict ACC from 0.00%.
AI.conclusion: Anthropomorphic dialogue improves significantly when generation, evaluation, and reward shaping are unified under the same behavioral dimensions, as demonstrated by the closed-loop AnthroDial framework.

title: Digital measurement of droplet flame diameter in microgravity combustion images using Segment Anything Model 2 with automatic prompt selection
summary:
Flame diameter is a key measurable parameter in microgravity droplet combustion, but its extraction from self-illuminated frames remains difficult because soot tails, blurred luminous boundaries, chamber reflections, and droplet drift introduce substantial measurement bias and operator dependence. This work presents an AI-enabled digital measurement workflow for automated flame diameter from combustion images. The workflow integrates automatic prompt-point generation into Segment Anything Model 2, employing Random Sample Consensus (RANSAC)-based circle fitting. The automatic prompt strategy removes subjective manual point selection, while the video memory mechanism maintains temporal consistency for drifting droplets, and the RANSAC fitting rejects soot-tail pixels as geometric outliers.
  The method is validated by 19,537 flame images of n-heptane, n-decane, and n-octane droplets with varying initial diameters. Compared with manual-reference measurements, the proposed workflow achieves a mean relative agreement of 96.9%, a mean absolute percentage error of 3.1%, and substantially outperforms conventional Hough circle detection, which performed worse under the same evaluation conditions. The results also show that the measurement accuracy improves with increasing droplet size. The proposed workflow has a combined standard uncertainty of 8.54% and achieves approximately a 229-fold improvement in efficiency over manual measurement.
  These results demonstrate that the proposed SAM2-based workflow provides a reproducible, fully automated, and metrologically characterized digital measurement system for extracting flame diameter from challenging combustion images. The approach supports high-throughput combustion diagnostics and illustrates that AI-based segmentation can be integrated into quantitative measurement workflows for digitalized image-based metrology.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an AI-enabled digital measurement workflow using SAM2, automatic prompt-point generation, RANSAC-based circle fitting, and a video memory mechanism to extract flame diameter from microgravity droplet combustion images. Validated on 19,537 flame images, it achieves 96.9% mean relative agreement, 3.1% MAPE, 8.54% combined standard uncertainty, and ~229× efficiency improvement over manual measurement, outperforming conventional Hough circle detection.
AI.motivation: Flame diameter is a key measurable parameter in microgravity droplet combustion, but its extraction from self-illuminated frames is difficult due to soot tails, blurred luminous boundaries, chamber reflections, and droplet drift, which introduce measurement bias and operator dependence.
AI.method: The workflow integrates automatic prompt-point generation into Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2), employs Random Sample Consensus (RANSAC)-based circle fitting, uses an automatic prompt strategy to remove subjective manual point selection, incorporates a video memory mechanism for temporal consistency of drifting droplets, and uses RANSAC fitting to reject soot-tail pixels as geometric outliers.
AI.result: Validated on 19,537 flame images (n-heptane, n-decane, n-octane), achieves 96.9% mean relative agreement, 3.1% MAPE, 8.54% combined standard uncertainty, ~229× efficiency improvement over manual measurement, and substantially outperforms conventional Hough circle detection. Accuracy improves with increasing droplet size.
AI.conclusion: The SAM2-based workflow provides a reproducible, fully automated, metrologically characterized digital measurement system for extracting flame diameter from challenging combustion images. It supports high-throughput combustion diagnostics and demonstrates that AI-based segmentation can be integrated into quantitative measurement workflows for digitalized image-based metrology.

title: Effects of width-dependent model hyperparameters and $\ell_2$-regularization on the loss landscape of two-layer ReLU networks
comment: ICML2026 4th Workshop on High-dimensional Learning Dynamics (HiLD)
summary: Understanding deep neural networks remains a central challenge in machine learning. In particular, the theoretical properties of even two-layer ReLU networks, especially in the presence of weight decay, remain poorly understood. To this end, we derive a sufficient condition on the hyperparameter settings under which the global minima collapse to the zero solution. Interestingly, our experiments reveal that using AdamW as an optimizer prevents the collapse of the learned parameters, whereas using SGD does not, which may help explain the success of AdamW in deep learning training. In addition, when restricting the input dimension to one, we derive an analytical solution for the globally optimal parameter sets of two-layer ReLU networks and show that $\ell_2$-regularization has a width-invariant effect on connectivity, but its dimensionality-reducing effect becomes stronger as the network width increases. These results provide insight into how width-dependent hyperparameters influence the geometry of regularized loss landscapes.

AI.tldr: This paper studies two-layer ReLU networks with weight decay, finding conditions for global minima collapse to zero, showing AdamW prevents collapse while SGD does not, and deriving analytical solutions for 1D inputs revealing width-dependent effects of ℓ2-regularization on connectivity and dimensionality.
AI.motivation: Understanding deep neural networks remains a central challenge in machine learning, and the theoretical properties of even two-layer ReLU networks, especially with weight decay, remain poorly understood.
AI.method: Derives sufficient conditions for hyperparameter settings leading to zero collapse; performs experiments comparing AdamW and SGD; derives analytical solutions for globally optimal parameters of two-layer ReLU networks in the 1D input setting.
AI.result: Global minima can collapse to zero under certain hyperparameter conditions; AdamW prevents collapse while SGD does not; ℓ2-regularization has a width-invariant effect on connectivity but a width-increasing dimensionality-reducing effect.
AI.conclusion: Width-dependent hyperparameters influence the geometry of regularized loss landscapes, and the findings help explain the empirical success of AdamW over SGD in deep learning training.

title: PAVXploreRL: Physical-Action-Visual World Model Reinforcement Learning with Action Exploration
summary: Action-conditioned world models are a key component of embodied AI, serving as scalable policy evaluators that reduce reliance on expensive real-world rollouts. To accurately capture diverse action-induced dynamics, such models should satisfy three key objectives-Physical Plausibility (P), Action Adherence (A), and Visual Fidelity (V), collectively referred to as PAV-while remaining robust to both in-distribution (ID) expert demonstrations and out-of-distribution (OOD) actions. However, existing methods primarily rely on ID action-video pairs and pixel-level reconstruction losses, which do not explicitly optimize PAV objectives and generalize poorly beyond expert data. To address this, we propose PAVXploreRL, a reinforcement learning framework built on a pretrained latent world model that explicitly optimizes PAV objectives through reward-driven training. To improve action generalization, our method jointly leverages ID trajectories and noise-driven OOD action exploration, without paired video supervision. Experiments show that PAVXploreRL consistently outperforms pretrained baselines, achieving a 5.6% average gain across benchmarks and producing higher-quality PAV properties. As a policy evaluator, it also yields more reliable performance estimates and reduces the overestimation bias of prior expert-only world models such as Ctrl-World. Code: https://github.com/Social-AI-Studio/PAVXploreRL

AI.tldr: PAVXploreRL is a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes Physical Plausibility, Action Adherence, and Visual Fidelity in world models through reward-driven training and OOD action exploration, outperforming pretrained baselines by 5.6% on average.
AI.motivation: Existing world models rely on ID action-video pairs and pixel-level reconstruction losses, which fail to explicitly optimize PAV objectives (Physical Plausibility, Action Adherence, Visual Fidelity) and generalize poorly to OOD actions beyond expert demonstrations.
AI.method: PAVXploreRL uses a reinforcement learning framework built on a pretrained latent world model that explicitly optimizes PAV objectives via reward-driven training, jointly leveraging ID trajectories and noise-driven OOD action exploration without requiring paired video supervision.
AI.result: PAVXploreRL achieves a 5.6% average gain across benchmarks, produces higher-quality PAV properties, and as a policy evaluator, yields more reliable performance estimates while reducing overestimation bias compared to prior expert-only world models like Ctrl-World.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly optimizing PAV objectives via RL with OOD exploration significantly improves world model generalization and evaluation reliability, addressing key limitations of reconstruction-based pretrained world models.

title: Half the Experts, All the Code: One-Shot Domain Pruning of Mixture-of-Experts LLMs for Coding
comment: 15 pages, 3 figures. Code and pruned checkpoints: github.com/anik-jha/moep
summary: The strongest open-weight coding models are mixture-of-experts (MoE) networks: most of their size comes from large pools of "expert" subnetworks, of which only a few act on any token. That pool is why these models do not fit on the machines most developers own, yet for a user who only wants coding help, most experts encode abilities that will never be invoked. We ask how many experts can be removed, and which, by pruning two recent open-weight MoE models from different families (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B) under five selection strategies, judged the way a user would: by whether the model still writes correct code. Half the experts can be removed from either model with no statistically detectable loss on the primary code benchmark, and the damage lands almost entirely on abilities outside coding, the intended trade. But the winning strategy flips between the two models, so a recipe validated on one family cannot be assumed to work on another. We further show that perplexity, the metric much of the pruning literature leans on, can rate a broken model above an intact one; that a lightweight fine-tune recovers about half of what aggressive pruning loses; and that against quantizing the full model to the same memory, pruning wins only where quantization would have to drop below 3 bits per weight. Five attempts to overturn that crossover, with failure criteria fixed in advance (better calibration, guarded selection, causal expert importance, failure attribution, and an agentic evaluation letting each model repair its failures from execution feedback), all leave it standing; the last shows single-shot benchmarks overstate compression penalties broadly, as one repair turn erases the 2-bit quantization penalty entirely. Expert pruning works, but it demands per-model validation on the task the model will actually serve.

AI.tldr: Half the experts can be removed from MoE coding models with no loss in code quality, but the optimal pruning strategy varies per model; perplexity is unreliable for evaluation; pruning beats quantization only below 3 bits/weight; single-shot benchmarks overstate penalties as iterative repair recovers losses.
AI.motivation: Open-weight MoE coding models are too large for most developers' hardware, yet most expert subnetworks encode abilities irrelevant to coding tasks. The authors investigate whether selective expert pruning can reduce model size without degrading code generation performance.
AI.method: Pruned two MoE models (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B) using five expert selection strategies, evaluated by code correctness benchmarks, perplexity, and fine-tuning recovery; compared pruning against quantization; tested with agentic repair loops.
AI.result: Removing half the experts caused no statistically detectable loss on code benchmarks; the best pruning strategy differed between model families; perplexity was unreliable; fine-tuning recovered ~50% of losses; pruning only outperformed quantization below 3 bits/weight; single-turn benchmarks exaggerated compression penalties.
AI.conclusion: Expert pruning effectively reduces model size for coding tasks but requires per-model validation on the target task; single-shot benchmarks systematically overstate compression penalties.

title: Constrained Path Reasoning: Measuring When Committed Stages Earn Their Cost
summary: When does a committed intermediate stage in an LLM reasoning pipeline earn its cost? Constrained Path Reasoning (CPR) pairs a source-aware path hypothesis with stage-level accounting. Search generates provisional states; trusted or validated invariants can constrain hard, while other proposals remain soft and revisable. CPR predicts that task-compatible commitments can factor transitions, concentrate candidate mass, induce regularity, and expose feedback when their gains exceed propagated error and execution cost. The formalism covers discrete commitments and continuous flows and measures effective branching, endpoint concentration, and cost per usable output. Across 1,180 generated QCQPs and 40 engineered degenerate polynomial instances (2,140 endpoints), residual triage recovers 63.0% of repair-all's additional feasible yield with 17.7% of its attempts. Fixed-LLM accounting (270 unique calls shared across nested arms) finds usable yield of 41.1% direct, 90.0% after formalization and deterministic execution, 20.0% after one-shot convexification, and 21.1% for the full path. In 120 paired-condition calls, a two-action rollback rule reaches 90% usable yield versus 36.7% for the feedback-conditioned selector. Two endpoint probes separate source from validation: a 72-output cross-trajectory transplant reduces entropy and acceptable mass; a 24-output same-call self-proposal pilot gives unchanged two-repeat collision entropy, 25.0% versus 8.3% usable yield, and 1/8 deterministically confirmed endpoint checks. Model-generated states supply hypotheses; trusted execution earns constraint strength.

AI.tldr: CPR pairs source-aware path hypotheses with stage-level accounting, showing that task-compatible commitments can factor transitions and concentrate candidate mass when gains exceed error and execution cost. Across QCQPs and degenerate polynomials, residual triage recovers 63% of repair-all's yield with 17.7% of attempts; fixed-LLM accounting yields 41.1% direct, 90% after formalization, and two-action rollback achieves 90% usable yield vs 36.7% for a feedback-conditioned selector.
AI.motivation: To determine when a committed intermediate stage in an LLM reasoning pipeline justifies its cost by characterizing conditions under which constraints improve search efficiency, reduce branching, and concentrate candidate mass rather than introducing error.
AI.method: CPR formalism covers discrete commitments and continuous flows, measuring effective branching, endpoint concentration, and cost per usable output. Empirical evaluation uses 1,180 generated QCQPs and 40 engineered degenerate polynomial instances (2,140 endpoints), comparing residual triage, fixed-LLM accounting, rollback rules, and endpoint probes (cross-trajectory transplant and same-call self-proposal).
AI.result: Residual triage: 63.0% of repair-all's feasible yield with 17.7% of attempts. Fixed-LLM: 41.1% direct yield, 90.0% after formalization+deterministic execution, 20.0% after one-shot convexification, 21.1% full path. Two-action rollback: 90% usable yield vs 36.7% feedback-conditioned selector. Cross-trajectory transplant reduces entropy/acceptable mass; self-proposal pilot gives unchanged collision entropy, 25.0% vs 8.3% usable yield, 1/8 confirmed endpoints.
AI.conclusion: Model-generated states serve as hypotheses; trusted execution earns constraint strength. Committed intermediate stages are justified when their gains (factor transitions, concentrate candidate mass, expose feedback) exceed propagated error and execution cost, as demonstrated across multiple accounting regimes and probe experiments.

title: Can Multimodal Large Language Models Understand OCT?
summary: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) imaging is essential for the diagnosis and treatment of retinal diseases. Although multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have demonstrated considerable potential in medical image analysis, existing benchmarks largely reduce OCT understanding to coarse-grained disease classification or isolated visual question answering, leaving the complete cognitive process from visual perception to clinical reasoning insufficiently evaluated. To address this limitation, we introduce OCT-Bench, a comprehensive benchmark dedicated to OCT image understanding. OCT-Bench comprises 10,076 high-quality multiple-choice questions constructed from 4,137 OCT images across seven public datasets. Following the real-world clinical interpretation workflow, we establish a hierarchical capability taxonomy consisting of 20 fine-grained tasks across three dimensions: Perception, Cognition, and Reasoning. These tasks cover a broad range of capabilities, including imaging attributes, retinal anatomy, lesion characteristics, spatial relationships, disease assessment, therapeutic decision-making, and prognostic management. We systematically evaluate 20 representative MLLMs, including proprietary models, open-source general-purpose models, and medical-domain models. Experimental results demonstrate that current models remain substantially short of reliable OCT understanding. Moreover, neither medical-domain adaptation nor increased model scale consistently improves performance across capability levels. OCT-Bench enables comprehensive and fine-grained evaluation of MLLMs, providing a foundation for identifying capability bottlenecks and advancing clinically grounded OCT understanding.

AI.tldr: OCT-Bench is a comprehensive benchmark with 10,076 multiple-choice questions from 4,137 OCT images across 7 datasets, evaluating MLLMs across 20 fine-grained tasks spanning Perception, Cognition, and Reasoning. Evaluation of 20 models shows current MLLMs are far from reliable OCT understanding, with neither medical adaptation nor larger scale consistently improving performance.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks reduce OCT understanding to coarse disease classification or isolated VQA, failing to evaluate the complete cognitive process from visual perception to clinical reasoning.
AI.method: Constructed 10,076 MCQs from 4,137 OCT images across 7 public datasets; established a hierarchical taxonomy of 20 fine-grained tasks across Perception, Cognition, and Reasoning dimensions; evaluated 20 representative MLLMs including proprietary, open-source general-purpose, and medical-domain models.
AI.result: Current MLLMs remain substantially short of reliable OCT understanding; neither medical-domain adaptation nor increased model scale consistently improves performance across capability levels.
AI.conclusion: OCT-Bench enables comprehensive fine-grained evaluation of MLLMs, identifies capability bottlenecks, and advances clinically grounded OCT understanding.

title: Graph-Embedded Intuitionistic Fuzzy Broad Learning System: A Multi-view Framework
summary: The Broad Learning System (BLS) has been widely used for data classification and is based on a layer-by-layer feed-forward structure. However, it gives the same importance to all data points, which reduces its effectiveness on real-world datasets with noise and outliers. In addition, it does not consider the geometric structure of the data and has limitations in handling data from multiple sources. To address these challenges, we propose a Multi-View Graph-Embedded Intuitionistic Fuzzy Broad Learning System (MVGIFBLS) that integrates multi-view learning, graph embedding, and intuitionistic fuzzy theory into the BLS framework. This design enables the model to combine information from multiple sources and learn more discriminative representations. Graph embedding captures the geometric relationships among samples and improves class separation through intrinsic and penalty subspaces based on local Fisher discriminant analysis. Intuitionistic fuzzy theory enhances robustness to noise, while kernel-based neighborhood analysis captures local data structures. We evaluate the proposed framework on several UCI, KEEL, and AwA benchmark datasets using comparative evaluation, Gaussian feature noise analysis, ablation studies, and statistical analysis. The results demonstrate that each component contributes positively to the overall framework and that the proposed MVGIFBLS consistently achieves higher Area Under the Curve (AUC) scores and maintains robust performance under Gaussian feature noise.

AI.tldr: MVGIFBLS integrates multi-view learning, graph embedding, and intuitionistic fuzzy theory into BLS to improve robustness, capture geometric data structures, and handle multi-source data, achieving higher AUC and noise robustness on benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: Standard BLS treats all data points equally, ignoring noise/outliers, geometric structure, and multi-source data, limiting its real-world effectiveness.
AI.method: Proposes MVGIFBLS combining multi-view learning, graph embedding (local Fisher discriminant analysis with intrinsic and penalty subspaces), intuitionistic fuzzy theory, and kernel-based neighborhood analysis within the BLS framework.
AI.result: Evaluated on UCI, KEEL, and AwA datasets with comparative evaluation, Gaussian feature noise analysis, ablation studies, and statistical analysis; achieves higher AUC and robust performance under noise.
AI.conclusion: Each component positively contributes; MVGIFBLS consistently outperforms baselines in AUC and robustness to Gaussian feature noise.

title: LenGuard-GPC: Length Guarding with Guided-Prompt Consistency for Spatial Reasoning Reinforce Learning
summary: Multi-view spatial reasoning requires vision-language models to compare visual evidence across images, align object correspondences, and infer spatial relations over long visual contexts, a setting where chain-of-thought reasoning tends to grow verbose without becoming more accurate. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is a natural fit for this task, but standard GRPO reward relies on sparse outcome-level feedback and gives no signal about where a reasoning trajectory goes wrong, nor any control over its length. We propose LenGuard-GPC, a dense reward framework that addresses both problems together. For each sampled trajectory, it compares the token-wise predictive distributions under a standard prompt and a guided prompt, and uses the resulting token-sum KL divergence as a dense reward signal. Since this KL penalty accumulates over tokens and would otherwise reward shorter responses regardless of their quality, we introduce a staged length bonus that keeps reasoning length within a controlled range without simply encouraging brevity. On six multi-view spatial reasoning benchmarks, LenGuard-GPC improves accuracy over vanilla GRPO while reducing average response length.

AI.tldr: LenGuard-GPC is a dense reward framework for reinforcement learning that uses token-wise KL divergence between standard and guided prompts to provide fine-grained feedback, plus a staged length bonus to control reasoning length. It improves accuracy and reduces response length on multi-view spatial reasoning tasks compared to vanilla GRPO.
AI.motivation: Standard GRPO uses sparse outcome-level rewards that fail to identify where reasoning goes wrong or control trajectory length, while chain-of-thought reasoning on multi-view spatial reasoning tasks grows verbose without improving accuracy.
AI.method: LenGuard-GPC computes token-wise KL divergence between predictive distributions under a standard prompt and a guided prompt as a dense reward signal, and adds a staged length bonus to keep reasoning within a controlled range without simply encouraging brevity.
AI.result: On six multi-view spatial reasoning benchmarks, LenGuard-GPC improves accuracy over vanilla GRPO while reducing average response length.
AI.conclusion: Dense token-level rewards with controlled length bonuses are more effective than sparse outcome-level rewards for multi-view spatial reasoning, simultaneously improving accuracy and efficiency.

title: SPARE-GS: Structural Parsimony and Resource Efficiency for 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) achieves high-fidelity novel view synthesis in real-time; however its training efficiency and representation compactness are hindered by excessive primitive proliferation. To address this challenge, we formulate the structural evolution of 3DGS as a global budget-constrained optimization problem and derive an optimality condition, which requires the marginal utility of structural resources to be balanced across spatial regions under a finite primitive budget. Based on this formulation, we propose SPARE-GS, a general plug-and-play framework that dynamically aligns the distribution of 3D Gaussian primitives with regional representational demand. SPARE-GS estimates capacity-normalized regional demand, assigns adaptive target quotas, and uses regional budget deviations to coordinate densification, pruning and adaptive termination toward a more balanced structural allocation. Extensive experiments across standard, accelerated, and structure-enhanced 3DGS pipelines demonstrate that SPARE-GS reduces the Gaussian count and training time by an average of 30.38% and 23.81%, respectively, while improving the average PSNR. Moreover, the resulting compact representations reduce downstream processing time and improve the rate-distortion performance of diverse compression and pruning methods, demonstrating the broad applicability of global structural budget regulation.

AI.tldr: SPARE-GS is a plug-and-play framework that formulates 3DGS structural evolution as a global budget-constrained optimization problem, dynamically balancing primitive allocation across spatial regions, reducing Gaussian count by 30.38% and training time by 23.81% while improving PSNR across multiple 3DGS pipelines.
AI.motivation: 3DGS achieves high-fidelity real-time novel view synthesis but suffers from excessive primitive proliferation, hindering both training efficiency and representation compactness.
AI.method: Formulates structural evolution as a global budget-constrained optimization with an optimality condition requiring balanced marginal utility across regions. SPARE-GS estimates capacity-normalized regional demand, assigns adaptive target quotas, and uses regional budget deviations to coordinate densification, pruning, and adaptive termination.
AI.result: Reduces Gaussian count by 30.38% and training time by 23.81% on average while improving PSNR across standard, accelerated, and structure-enhanced 3DGS pipelines. Compact representations also improve downstream compression and pruning rate-distortion performance.
AI.conclusion: Global structural budget regulation via SPARE-GS is broadly applicable and effective for improving efficiency and compactness of 3DGS without sacrificing quality.
