Comprehensive experiments across U-Net models and DiT models on both natural and adversarial datasets demonstrate substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods, including SLD, UCE, Safree, etc. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Aries-iai/UniNDM.

AI.tldr: UniNDM is a unified noise-driven framework that leverages noise dynamics in diffusion models to detect and mitigate implicit sexual content. It uses early-stage predicted noise separability for lightweight detection and noise-enhanced adaptive negative guidance for mitigation, outperforming existing methods on both U-Net and DiT architectures.
AI.motivation: Text-to-image diffusion models are vulnerable to implicit sexual prompts that bypass existing safety mechanisms. Current detection methods fail to capture implicit malicious intent, and mitigation approaches rely on static negative prompts insufficient for diverse scenarios.
AI.method: UniNDM leverages early-stage predicted noise separability between normal and explicit content (theoretically shown to have quadratically increasing semantic concentration with timestep). It includes: (1) a lightweight noise-based detector, (2) noise-enhanced adaptive negative guidance using LLM-generated context-specific negative prompts, and (3) optimization of initial noise by suppressing attention concentration on explicit tokens. Extended to Diffusion Transformers via region-constrained semantic guidance.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments on both U-Net and DiT models across natural and adversarial datasets show substantial improvements over state-of-the-art methods (SLD, UCE, Safree).
AI.conclusion: UniNDM provides an effective unified framework for implicit sexual content safety in diffusion models by exploiting noise dynamics, achieving superior detection and mitigation with minimal computational overhead.

title: Investigation of Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) Diagnosis Using Machine Learning Approaches
comment: Published in 2023 5th International Conference on Sustainable Technologies for Industry 5.0 (STI), December 2023, Dhaka, Bangladesh
summary: Polycystic Ovarian Syndrome (PCOS) is a widespread hormone problem for women of childbearing age. Women with PCOS may not ovulate; they might have high levels of androgens and have many small cysts on the ovaries. It can cause missed or irregular menstrual periods, excess hair growth, acne, infertility, and weight gain. Machine Learning (ML) can effectively diagnose this disease at an earlier stage as tons of medical data are available now. Traditional approaches to detect PCOS encompass a combination of clinical evaluation, medical history assessment, physical examination, and laboratory tests. These approaches aim to identify the characteristic symptoms and hormonal imbalances associated with PCOS. Physical examination requires good resources and costs time and money. In recent times, data-driven techniques have substantially advanced disease prediction within the medical field. We aim to utilize ML approaches, incorporating unique feature selection algorithms, to predict PCOS. This paper introduces a data-driven approach to PCOS diagnosis, combining Feature Engineering and ML. Several feature selection approaches have been considered to select sets of features for training the ML model, including CatBoost, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LGBM), AdaBoost, Random Forest (RF). Results demonstrate that AdaBoost, with ten features selected by RF Feature Importance and Highest Correlation (HC), provides the highest test accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a data-driven approach using ML and feature selection (CatBoost, XGBoost, LGBM, AdaBoost, RF) to diagnose PCOS. AdaBoost with 10 features selected by RF Feature Importance and Highest Correlation achieves the highest test accuracy.
AI.motivation: PCOS is a widespread hormone problem for women of childbearing age causing irregular periods, infertility, and weight gain. Traditional diagnosis is costly and time-consuming. The authors aim to utilize ML with feature selection to enable earlier, more efficient PCOS detection.
AI.method: The authors combine Feature Engineering and ML using feature selection algorithms (CatBoost, XGBoost, LGBM, AdaBoost, RF) to select feature subsets for training ML models for PCOS prediction.
AI.result: AdaBoost, using ten features selected by RF Feature Importance and Highest Correlation (HC), provides the highest test accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Data-driven ML approaches with effective feature selection can improve PCOS diagnosis compared to traditional resource-intensive clinical methods.

title: Reinforcement Learning: From Algorithms To Foundation Models
summary:
Reinforcement learning (RL) provides a framework for sequential decision making under explicit objectives. In its classical form, RL studies how an agent should act to maximise long-term reward in a dynamic environment. In richer settings, the problem extends beyond a single agent and fixed environment: intelligent behavior may require strategic interaction, adaptation to uncertainty, and reasoning over high-dimensional worlds. This thesis studies RL from two perspectives: algorithms in games and RL in the era of foundation models.
  The first part focuses on multi-agent RL in games. It examines how incentives, policies, and equilibrium concepts interact in competitive and general-sum environments, spanning two-player zero-sum games, large-scale video games, and multi-player settings with general structure. These works investigate learning in multi-agent systems and the behavior of RL methods in interactive environments. The second part studies RL with generative and foundation models, motivated by the idea that prior knowledge can enrich sequential decision making. Pretrained generative models and learned world models serve as representation tools and structured priors for planning, control, and policy optimization. The thesis develops diffusion-based world models, investigates RL for efficient video generation, explores generative models as policy classes, and studies interactive video world models in which actions shape future observations. It also addresses long-horizon modeling through architectures with memory. Together, these contributions present a unified view of RL as objective-driven adaptation in complex sequential domains. From strategic games to generative world models, the thesis highlights how RL connects decision making, environment modeling, and emerging foundation-model capabilities, offering a broader perspective on the principles underlying intelligent behavior.

AI.tldr: This thesis studies reinforcement learning from two perspectives: multi-agent RL in games (competitive and general-sum environments) and RL with generative/foundation models (diffusion-based world models, policy optimization, video generation, and long-horizon modeling).
AI.motivation: To extend RL beyond single-agent fixed environments toward richer settings involving strategic interaction, uncertainty, and high-dimensional worlds, leveraging both game-theoretic multi-agent learning and foundation-model capabilities.
AI.method: Two-part approach: (1) Multi-agent RL analyzing incentives, policies, and equilibrium in zero-sum, general-sum, and large-scale game settings. (2) RL with generative models using diffusion-based world models, generative models as policy classes, interactive video world models, and memory architectures for long-horizon modeling.
AI.result: Developed diffusion-based world models, investigated RL for efficient video generation, explored generative models as policy classes, and studied interactive video world models where actions shape future observations, alongside multi-agent learning dynamics in games.
AI.conclusion: RL provides a unified framework for objective-driven adaptation across complex sequential domains, connecting decision making, environment modeling, and foundation-model capabilities to offer broader principles underlying intelligent behavior.

title: Robust PnP on a Neuromorphic Processor for Object Pose Estimation
summary: Neuromorphic computing is gaining attention in robotic perception due to its higher energy efficiency. While neural network-based methods can more readily exploit the distributed and parallelized structure of neuromorphic computers, crafting neuromorphic solutions for non-learning tasks is less straightforward. This hampers the usage of neuromorphic computing for perception pipelines that depend on both learning and non-learning components, such as object pose estimation (OPE) where state-of-the-art methods use a deep network to predict 2D landmarks and nonlinear optimization to solve perspective-n-point (PnP). In this paper, we propose a novel neuromorphic-deployable formulation for robust PnP, where given outlier-prone 2D-3D correspondences, the object pose with the largest number of inliers is determined. Underpinning our method is a distributed algorithm for robust least squares estimation of rigid body pose that can be executed on a neuromorphic processor. We also design a spiking neural network (SNN) to predict 2D landmarks from event data, where the main layers of the SNN were designed according to the principles of spiking neurons. Overall, our work enables neuromorphic treatment of the major stages of an OPE pipeline, from event sensing and learned landmark prediction, to geometric optimization for robust PnP. Results on neuromophic hardware (Intel Loihi 2) indicate the higher energy efficiency our neuromorphic robust PnP, while achieving competitive accuracy.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a fully neuromorphic-deployable object pose estimation (OPE) pipeline, including a spiking neural network (SNN) for 2D landmark prediction from event data and a distributed algorithm for robust Perspective-n-Point (PnP) solving on neuromorphic hardware (Intel Loihi 2), achieving higher energy efficiency with competitive accuracy.
AI.motivation: Neuromorphic computing's application in perception is hindered because non-learning components (e.g., geometric optimization for PnP) are not easily deployable on neuromorphic processors, limiting end-to-end energy efficiency gains for tasks like object pose estimation that combine learning and non-learning stages.
AI.method: 1) A distributed algorithm for robust least squares estimation of rigid body pose, designed for neuromorphic execution to solve PnP with outlier-prone 2D-3D correspondences. 2) A spiking neural network (SNN) with main layers designed according to spiking neuron principles to predict 2D landmarks from event data.
AI.result: On Intel Loihi 2, the proposed neuromorphic robust PnP achieves higher energy efficiency while maintaining competitive accuracy compared to conventional methods.
AI.conclusion: The work enables a fully neuromorphic object pose estimation pipeline covering event sensing, learned landmark prediction, and geometric optimization for robust PnP, demonstrating energy efficiency gains on neuromorphic hardware without sacrificing accuracy.

title: CADENCE: Closing the Reasoning Gap via Coverage-Adaptive On-Policy Distillation
summary:
On-policy knowledge distillation transfers reasoning from large teachers to compact students, but existing approaches suffer three compounding failure modes: (i) cold-start collapse, where a fresh student assigns near-zero mass to teacher-preferred tokens; (ii) state-agnostic divergence scheduling, where time-only forward/reverse-KL interpolation ignores the student's coverage state; and (iii) binary reward sparsity, where pass/fail signals discard information from partially correct traces.
  We present CADENCE, a unified framework with a targeted fix for each. Its DRIFT mechanism schedules a per-token convex mixture of forward-KL and reverse-KL surrogate objectives on student-sampled trajectories (per-token surrogates, not sequence-level KL gradient estimators). Six components extend it: (A) COVA, a coverage-adaptive $β$ schedule accelerating the forward-to-reverse transition; (B) FTB, a forking-token boost concentrating gradient at high-entropy positions via a globally-normalized entropy reference; (C) CCD, a dense reward adding numerical-proximity partial credit for incorrect-but-close traces; (D) LAP, brevity-preferential correct-rollout reinforcement; (E) EMR, an entropy-matching calibration regularizer; (F) BSD, a bootstrapped self-distillation phase.
  On GSM8K and MATH-500 (corrected 512-token protocol, 5 seeds, reported std), CADENCE distills a 0.5B student from a 1.5B teacher to 69.8 $\pm$ 0.5% GSM8K pass@1 (from 48.7% pretrained; 63.2% of the teacher gap closed) and to 72.1 $\pm$ 0.4% with a 3B teacher (76.2% closed), beating the strongest matched-compute label-using baseline (DRIFT+binary reward) by +4.4 $\pm$ 0.7 points. All experiments run on a single Apple Mac Studio (M-series, 64GB unified memory), showing principled distillation reaches strong reasoning quality without datacenter-scale hardware.

AI.tldr: CADENCE is a unified on-policy knowledge distillation framework that addresses three failure modes (cold-start collapse, state-agnostic divergence scheduling, binary reward sparsity) via six components including DRIFT (per-token forward/reverse-KL mixture), achieving 69.8% GSM8K pass@1 on a 0.5B student distilled from a 1.5B teacher, closing 63.2% of the teacher gap, all on a single Apple Mac Studio.
AI.motivation: Existing on-policy knowledge distillation suffers from three compounding failure modes: (i) cold-start collapse where fresh students assign near-zero mass to teacher-preferred tokens; (ii) state-agnostic divergence scheduling where time-only interpolation ignores the student's coverage state; (iii) binary reward sparsity where pass/fail signals discard information from partially correct traces.
AI.method: CADENCE proposes a unified framework with six components: (A) COVA: coverage-adaptive β schedule for forward-to-reverse KL transition; (B) FTB: forking-token boost concentrating gradient at high-entropy positions; (C) CCD: dense reward with numerical-proximity partial credit; (D) LAP: brevity-preferential correct-rollout reinforcement; (E) EMR: entropy-matching calibration regularizer; (F) BSD: bootstrapped self-distillation phase. Central to the method is DRIFT, a per-token convex mixture of forward-KL and reverse-KL surrogate objectives on student-sampled trajectories.
AI.result: On GSM8K and MATH-500, CADENCE distills a 0.5B student from a 1.5B teacher to 69.8±0.5% GSM8K pass@1 (from 48.7% pretrained; 63.2% of the teacher gap closed) and 72.1±0.4% with a 3B teacher (76.2% closed), beating DRIFT+binary reward baseline by +4.4±0.7 points. All experiments run on a single Apple Mac Studio (M-series, 64GB unified memory).
AI.conclusion: Principled distillation can reach strong reasoning quality without datacenter-scale hardware, demonstrating that targeted fixes for each identified failure mode enable compact students to effectively learn from larger teachers on reasoning tasks.

title: ZifaMem: Structured Memory for Persona, Preference, and Emotional Continuity in AI Companions
summary: AI companions are judged not only by single-turn fluency but by whether they sustain emotional continuity: remembering who the companion is, what the user prefers, and how the relationship has felt. We present ZifaMem, a structured memory system that organizes dialogue into session summaries, episodic memories, and a consolidated user model. Against a deployment-honest comparator that supplies the full raw dialogue history, and under a fixed LLM-as-a-judge protocol with route audits, structured memory raises pooled four-backbone emotional-intelligence scores by 11.4% (95% CI 6.3% to 17.1%), and persona grounding improves on all four backbones (Claude +42% relative). Multi-turn affect context wins a +39% net preference over a single-turn snapshot (exploratory), whereas an additional emotion state machine yields no measurable gain on any of five endpoints. Under an identical preregistered protocol, three memory systems (ZifaMem, Mem0, and filtered verbatim retrieval) each improve significantly over raw-history deployment, and ZifaMem and Mem0 are statistically equivalent within +/-5 points on the preregistered primary preference endpoint. The ZifaMem SDK, CLI, and portable Agent Skills are open-sourced at https://github.com/zifacorp/zifamem.

AI.tldr: ZifaMem is a structured memory system for AI companions that organizes dialogue into sessions, episodic memories, and user models. It improves emotional-intelligence scores by 11.4% over raw dialogue history across four LLM backbones, with persona grounding boosting Claude by +42%. Three memory systems (ZifaMem, Mem0, filtered retrieval) all outperform raw-history deployment; ZifaMem and Mem0 are statistically equivalent. An emotion state machine yields no gain.
AI.motivation: AI companions need sustained emotional continuity (remembering user identity, preferences, and relationship history), which single-turn fluency alone cannot achieve. Existing systems using raw full dialogue history are inefficient and lack structured memory organization.
AI.method: ZifaMem organizes dialogue into three components: session summaries, episodic memories, and a consolidated user model. It was evaluated with a fixed LLM-as-a-judge protocol with route audits, comparing against raw-history deployment, Mem0, and filtered verbatim retrieval across four LLM backbones. An emotion state machine variant was also tested.
AI.result: Structured memory raised pooled four-backbone emotional-intelligence scores by 11.4% (95% CI 6.3%-17.1%). Persona grounding improved all four backbones (Claude +42% relative). Multi-turn affect context won +39% net preference over single-turn. Emotion state machine showed no measurable gain on any endpoint. ZifaMem and Mem0 are statistically equivalent within +/-5 points on the primary preference endpoint.
AI.conclusion: Structured memory systems significantly outperform raw-history deployment for AI companion emotional continuity. An emotion state machine adds no value, suggesting that well-structured episodic/persona memory is sufficient. ZifaMem is open-sourced (SDK, CLI, Agent Skills) for community adoption.

title: SurvCF(t): Counterfactual Explanations for Survival Analysis in Predictive Maintenance Multivariate Time Series Data
summary: Predictive maintenance relies on accurate Remaining Useful Life estimation, often formulated using survival analysis over multivariate time-series data. While modern deep survival models achieve strong predictive performance, their black-box nature limits their use in safety-critical settings where actionable insight is required. In this work, we introduce \textit{SurvCF(t)}, the first framework for generating counterfactual explanations for survival models operating on time-series data. \textit{SurvCF(t)} identifies minimal, plausible, and temporally consistent changes to an asset's operational history that increase its predicted life time, framing explanation as a constrained optimization problem combining validity, proximity, sparsity, and plausibility. We evaluate the method on multiple benchmarks, including C-MAPSS, N-CMAPSS, and a real-world case study of the Scania Component\_X dataset, demonstrating its ability to produce actionable and interpretable interventions. Our results show that \textit{SurvCF(t)} bridges the gap between survival prediction and prescriptive maintenance, enabling explainable and decision-oriented AI for maintenance strategies.

AI.tldr: SurvCF(t) is a framework that generates counterfactual explanations for survival models on time-series data, identifying minimal changes to operational history that increase predicted lifetime, bridging survival prediction and prescriptive maintenance.
AI.motivation: Modern deep survival models achieve strong predictive performance for Remaining Useful Life estimation but are black-box, limiting their use in safety-critical settings where actionable insight is required.
AI.method: SurvCF(t) formulates counterfactual explanation as a constrained optimization problem combining validity, proximity, sparsity, and plausibility, identifying minimal, plausible, and temporally consistent changes to an asset's operational history that increase its predicted lifetime.
AI.result: Evaluated on C-MAPSS, N-CMAPSS, and the real-world Scania Component_X dataset, demonstrating ability to produce actionable and interpretable interventions.
AI.conclusion: SurvCF(t) bridges the gap between survival prediction and prescriptive maintenance, enabling explainable and decision-oriented AI for maintenance strategies.

title: A Dual-Hypothesis Reasoning Framework for LLM Guardrails
summary: We propose ARBITER, a novel LLM guardrail framework that introduces two key ideas: (i) dual-hypothesis reasoning, a reasoning method for LLM guardrails that explicitly considers both safe and unsafe interpretations of a prompt before making a safety decision, and (ii) multi-component supervised fine-tuning (MC-SFT), a structured training loss for reasoning-based guardrails that decomposes LLM outputs into logical components and weights them according to their importance. Existing reasoning-based guardrails often rely on expensive procedures, such as generating reasoning traces using larger or closed-source teacher models and applying full-parameter fine-tuning. In contrast, ARBITER uses a cost-effective self-generation strategy for reasoning traces and LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning while still achieving better performance than these expensive approaches. Additionally, ARBITER provides faithful evidence-phrase explanations for unsafe decisions, enabling a more transparent and interpretable guardrail method. Experiments on three safety moderation benchmarks show that ARBITER outperforms existing reasoning-based and non-reasoning guardrail baselines, with clear gains in out-of-domain evaluations.

AI.tldr: ARBITER is a novel LLM guardrail framework using dual-hypothesis reasoning (considering both safe and unsafe interpretations) and multi-component supervised fine-tuning (MC-SFT) to achieve better safety moderation than existing methods, while being cost-effective with self-generated reasoning traces and LoRA fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing reasoning-based guardrails rely on expensive procedures (e.g., generating reasoning traces using larger/closed-source teacher models and full-parameter fine-tuning). The authors aim to develop a more cost-effective yet higher-performing guardrail framework that also provides interpretable evidence-phrase explanations.
AI.method: ARBITER introduces two key ideas: (1) dual-hypothesis reasoning — explicitly reasoning over both safe and unsafe interpretations of a prompt before making a safety decision; (2) multi-component supervised fine-tuning (MC-SFT) — a structured training loss that decomposes LLM outputs into logical components and weights them by importance. It uses self-generated reasoning traces and LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
AI.result: On three safety moderation benchmarks, ARBITER outperforms both existing reasoning-based and non-reasoning guardrail baselines, with clear gains in out-of-domain evaluations. It achieves better performance than expensive approaches that use teacher models and full-parameter fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: ARBITER demonstrates that cost-effective self-generation strategies and LoRA fine-tuning can surpass expensive training procedures for LLM guardrails, while additionally providing faithful evidence-phrase explanations for safer and more interpretable decisions.

title: TurboVec: A Case Study in Cost-Efficient Private Retrieval for Enterprise RAG via Codebook-Oblivious Quantization
summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems increasingly power enterprise LLM applications, yet the vector retrieval layer introduces two underexplored challenges: (1) trained codebook quantizers may expose corpus statistics during index construction, creating a leakage channel in multi-tenant deployments, and (2) post-hoc filtering for tenant isolation degrades recall on selective queries. We study TurboVec, an open-source vector index built on TurboQuant - a codebook-oblivious scalar quantizer requiring no corpus-dependent training. On the DBpedia OpenAI embeddings benchmark (d=1536, 100K-999K vectors), TurboQuant 4-bit outperforms trained FAISS Product Quantization at the same memory budget by 8.5-8.9 percentage points in Recall@5 across all scales. Compared to HNSW (R@5=0.991) and IVF-PQ (R@5=0.840), TurboQuant occupies a distinct design point: higher recall than IVF-PQ without training, at 4-8x less memory than HNSW. Deployed on Snowpark Container Services, TurboVec achieves 11ms median query latency at 100K vectors versus 707ms for warehouse brute-force scan. Kernel-level allowlist filtering maintains 0.86-0.93 Recall@10 across 10-1000 tenant workloads versus 0.09-0.19 for post-filter baselines. Codebook-oblivious design reduces membership inference accuracy to near-random (50.0%) versus 57.3% for PQ codebooks. Limitations include single dataset evaluation, uncompressed HNSW comparison, and privacy evaluation on synthetic data only.

AI.tldr: TurboVec is an open-source vector index using TurboQuant, a codebook-oblivious scalar quantizer that eliminates training-based privacy leakage in multi-tenant RAG systems. It achieves 8.5-8.9% higher Recall@5 than FAISS PQ at same memory, 11ms median latency (vs 707ms brute-force), and near-random membership inference (50% vs 57.3% for PQ).
AI.motivation: RAG systems face two underexplored challenges: (1) trained codebook quantizers leak corpus statistics during index construction in multi-tenant deployments, and (2) post-hoc filtering for tenant isolation degrades recall on selective queries.
AI.method: TurboQuant, a codebook-oblivious scalar quantizer requiring no corpus-dependent training, deployed as TurboVec on Snowpark Container Services with kernel-level allowlist filtering for tenant isolation.
AI.result: TurboQuant 4-bit outperforms FAISS PQ by 8.5-8.9 ppt in R@5 across scales; 11ms median latency at 100K vs 707ms brute-force; 0.86-0.93 R@10 for kernel filtering vs 0.09-0.19 post-filter baselines; membership inference 50% (near-random) vs 57.3% for PQ.
AI.conclusion: Codebook-oblivious quantization provides a privacy-preserving alternative to trained quantization for RAG vector retrieval, with competitive recall and significant latency improvements, though limited by single dataset evaluation and synthetic privacy tests.

title: Dataset Distillation by Influence Matching
summary: We revisit dataset distillation from an outcome-centric perspective. Rather than aligning process surrogates (per-step gradients or training trajectories), Influence Matching (Inf-Match) aligns the final outcome of training: it learns a compact synthetic set whose effect on the converged parameters matches that of the full dataset. Concretely, we introduce a fully differentiable, sample-level influence estimator that quantifies parameter shifts from adding or removing data, without time-consuming inverse-Hessian products or convexity assumptions. The estimator runs in linear time by unrolling the optimization dynamics and applying a first-order Taylor approximation. We then learn the synthetic set by minimizing the mismatch between its influence and that of the real dataset, yielding outcome alignment rather than heuristic process imitation. Inf-Match delivers the best accuracy across standard classification benchmarks. For instance, on Tiny-ImageNet (IPC=10), Inf-Match attains 31.5\%, a +4.7\% improvement over NCFM. Beyond classification, Inf-Match scales to vision-language distillation on Flickr30K, outperforming strong process-matching baselines. For instance, with 200 to 1000 synthetic samples, our method achieved a leading impressive average on image/text retrieval tasks, higher than NCFM by 2.5\%. The code will be released via https://github.com/hrtan/infmatch.

AI.tldr: Inf-Match performs dataset distillation by aligning the final outcome (parameter influence) of synthetic vs. real data, using a linear-time differentiable influence estimator, achieving state-of-the-art results on classification (e.g., +4.7% on Tiny-ImageNet) and vision-language retrieval tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing dataset distillation methods rely on aligning process surrogates (e.g., per-step gradients or training trajectories), which are heuristic and may not capture the true effect of data on the final model. The authors aim to directly align the outcome—how synthetic data influences the converged parameters—for more principled and effective distillation.
AI.method: Introduces Influence Matching (Inf-Match) with a differentiable, sample-level influence estimator that quantifies parameter shifts from adding/removing data. It avoids costly inverse-Hessian products by unrolling optimization dynamics and applying a first-order Taylor approximation, running in linear time. The synthetic set is learned by minimizing the mismatch between its influence and that of the real dataset.
AI.result: Inf-Match achieves best accuracy on standard classification benchmarks: on Tiny-ImageNet (IPC=10), it attains 31.5% (+4.7% over NCFM). On vision-language distillation (Flickr30K), it outperforms strong process-matching baselines, e.g., with 200-1000 synthetic samples, it beats NCFM by 2.5% average on image/text retrieval.
AI.conclusion: Outcome-centric influence matching is more effective than process-matching for dataset distillation, achieving SOTA across both classification and vision-language tasks, and scales well to larger-scale multimodal settings.

title: Periodic Bootstrap Thompson Sampling For Periodically Non-Stationary Bandit Problems
comment: 9 pages, 10 figures, Accepted to 2025 3rd International Conference on Data Science, Advanced Algorithms, and Intelligent Computing
summary: This paper introduces Periodic Bootstrap Thompson Sampling (PBTS), an innovative extension of the classic Thompson Sampling (TS) algorithm tailored for bandit problems with periodic non-stationarity. Conventional TS accumulates all past observations, leading to biased posteriors when reward distributions cycle over time. PBTS overcomes this by synchronizing belief resets with known or inferred period intervals and embedding structured bootstrap exploration phases, effectively purging obsolete data while preserving uncertainty estimates. PBTS is tested in artificially constructed environments, which include skewed and balanced reward distributions, along with different bootstrap proportions and misaligned periodic intervals. Results indicate that PBTS generally achieves statistically significant reductions in cumulative regret against traditional TS in periodic non-stationary environments. Subsequent discussion further articulates the potential of PBTS's real-world deployment. The study mentions limitations like extreme periodic misalignment and proposes future research such as self-adjusting cycle-recognition. With memory reset and bootstrap phase, PBTS introduces a novel approach to optimizing bandit algorithms in periodic reward contexts.

AI.tldr: Periodic Bootstrap Thompson Sampling (PBTS) extends Thompson Sampling for periodic non-stationary bandits by synchronizing belief resets with known/inferred periods and using bootstrap exploration phases, achieving significant regret reduction over traditional TS.
AI.motivation: Classic Thompson Sampling accumulates all past observations, causing biased posteriors when reward distributions cycle periodically over time. This paper aims to address periodic non-stationarity in bandit problems.
AI.method: PBTS synchronizes belief resets with known or inferred periodic intervals and embeds structured bootstrap exploration phases to purge obsolete data while preserving uncertainty estimates.
AI.result: PBTS achieves statistically significant reductions in cumulative regret compared to traditional TS in periodic non-stationary environments, tested across skewed and balanced reward distributions with varying bootstrap proportions and misaligned intervals.
AI.conclusion: PBTS offers a novel approach for optimizing bandit algorithms in periodic reward contexts. Limitations include extreme periodic misalignment; future work includes self-adjusting cycle-recognition.

title: Mechanistic Attention Guidance for Agent Memory Refinement
summary: Existing self-evolving memory systems mainly improve agent memory based on textual outputs, such as task trajectories and reflections. However, this text-based paradigm rarely incorporates internal mechanistic signals, leaving how retrieved memory is actually utilized during task execution underexplored. This limitation can lead to unreliable error attribution and hallucinated memory modifications. In this work, we show that retrieval-head attention provides a mechanistic signal for revealing segment-level memory utilization. By aggregating attention over memory segments and decision steps, we construct a context utilization matrix that exposes recurring memory-use patterns and indicates corresponding refinement strategies. Building on this observation, we propose Attention-Guided Memory Refinement (AGMR), a framework that uses utilization patterns revealed by attention to guide targeted segment-level memory updates. AGMR corrects or enhances memory for failed executions, simplifies memory for successful executions, and verifies each update through re-execution. Experiments on interactive decision-making benchmarks show that AGMR improves both task performance and memory efficiency over text-only memory refinement baselines. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/AGMR_code-3262/

AI.tldr: AGMR uses retrieval-head attention signals to guide segment-level memory refinement, outperforming text-only baselines on interactive decision-making tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing self-evolving memory systems rely on textual outputs (task trajectories, reflections) and ignore internal mechanistic signals, leading to unreliable error attribution and hallucinated memory modifications.
AI.method: AGMR constructs a context utilization matrix by aggregating retrieval-head attention over memory segments and decision steps to expose usage patterns, then applies targeted segment-level updates: correct/enhance for failed executions, simplify for successful executions, and verify via re-execution.
AI.result: AGMR improves both task performance and memory efficiency over text-only memory refinement baselines on interactive decision-making benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Leveraging internal attention signals for memory refinement yields more reliable and efficient self-evolving memory systems than text-only approaches.

title: InLiER: Learning-Free Heterogeneous LiDAR Place Recognition via Intermediate Mixed-Radix Structural Keypoint Tokenization
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L). 8 pages, 8 figures
summary: LiDAR place recognition supports loop closure, relocalization, and multi-agent map management. As robotic platforms increasingly combine LiDARs with different fields of view, resolutions, and scanning patterns, existing descriptors degrade because they are tightly coupled to sensor-specific characteristics. We present InLiER, a learning-free pipeline based on an intermediate tokenization step. Height-sliced keypoints from structural elements receive mixed-radix token IDs encoding height, radial distance, local shape, and azimuth from local 3D geometry, in a compact sub-2KB representation. The same vocabulary is reorganized across three retrieval stages: height-ceiling histogram intersection for fast rotation-invariant shortlisting, binary bitmask alignment for yaw estimation and reranking, and token-guided geometric verification for 6-DoF pose estimation. InLiER achieves state-of-the-art performance on the HeLiPR dataset and in real-world field experiments, among modern handcrafted methods and outperforms the learning-based baseline on most cross-sensor configurations.

AI.tldr: InLiER is a learning-free LiDAR place recognition pipeline using intermediate tokenization (height-sliced keypoints with mixed-radix token IDs) for cross-sensor matching across different LiDAR configurations, achieving state-of-the-art performance via three-stage retrieval.
AI.motivation: Existing LiDAR place recognition methods degrade across different sensor configurations (varying FOV, resolution, scanning patterns) because they are tightly coupled to sensor-specific characteristics.
AI.method: A learning-free pipeline with three stages: (1) height-ceiling histogram intersection for fast rotation-invariant shortlisting, (2) binary bitmask alignment for yaw estimation and reranking, (3) token-guided geometric verification for 6-DoF pose estimation. Uses mixed-radix token IDs encoding height, radial distance, local shape, and azimuth from local 3D geometry in a sub-2KB representation.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance on HeLiPR dataset and real-world field experiments, outperforming learning-based baselines on most cross-sensor configurations.
AI.conclusion: InLiER demonstrates that a learning-free, tokenization-based approach can achieve superior cross-sensor LiDAR place recognition without being coupled to specific sensor characteristics.

title: Counterfactual Shapley Credit Assignment
summary: The Credit Assignment Problem (CAP) is fundamental to developing efficient and explainable Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents. Existing frameworks, whether relying on temporal contiguity or hindsight-conditioned reward reweighting, frequently fail to attribute properly between an agent's policy (skill) and environmental stochasticity (luck). A principled approach to CAP must isolate the true causal drivers of observed outcomes from spurious correlations and environmental randomness. We introduce Counterfactual Shapley Credit Assignment, a novel framework grounded in causal theory that attributes credit and blame via the Counterfactual Shapley Value ($φ$-value). By redistributing environmental rewards, $φ$-values enhance temporal credit assignment across three critical dimensions: sparse causality, high stochasticity, and delayed rewards, all while preserving the optimal policy. We derive a consistent estimator that computes $φ$-values efficiently, enabling a new class of policy gradient methods, $φ$-PPO, combined with Prioritized Trajectory Replay (PTR). Empirical results demonstrate that $φ$-values align precisely to the ground truth causes of task rewards with superior sample efficiency in challenging environments where prior state-of-the-art methods fail to converge.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Counterfactual Shapley Credit Assignment (φ-value), a causal theory-based framework for Reinforcement Learning that isolates true causal drivers from luck. It enables φ-PPO with Prioritized Trajectory Replay, achieving superior sample efficiency and convergence in environments with sparse causality, high stochasticity, and delayed rewards.
AI.motivation: Existing credit assignment methods in RL fail to properly distinguish between an agent's skill and environmental stochasticity (luck), leading to spurious causal attributions and inefficient learning.
AI.method: The authors propose Counterfactual Shapley Credit Assignment, which uses the Counterfactual Shapley Value (φ-value) to redistribute rewards based on causal theory. They derive a consistent estimator for φ-values and combine it with Prioritized Trajectory Replay (PTR) to create a new policy gradient method called φ-PPO.
AI.result: φ-values align precisely with ground truth causes of task rewards, and φ-PPO achieves superior sample efficiency in challenging environments with sparse causality, high stochasticity, and delayed rewards, outperforming prior state-of-the-art methods that fail to converge.
AI.conclusion: Counterfactual Shapley Value-based credit assignment provides a principled, causally grounded solution to the Credit Assignment Problem, enabling more efficient and explainable RL agents, while preserving the optimal policy.

title: InfoDense: Density-Aware Regional Decisive Replay for Memory-Efficient Incremental Face Forgery Detection
summary: The rapid evolution of face forgery techniques has introduced an increasing variety of manipulations. Incremental Face Forgery Detection (IFFD), which incrementally adds new forgery data to fine-tune previously trained models, has emerged as a promising approach to handle evolving forgery threats. However, conventional replay-based IFFD methods suffer from catastrophic forgetting. Storing full historical images under limited memory often either fails to preserve subtle forgery cues or introduces domain bias, reducing the model's ability to learn intrinsic and transferable manipulation characteristics. In this paper, we propose a Density-Aware Regional Decisive replay strategy, termed InfoDense, to address these challenges. InfoDense prioritizes artifact-dense and forgery-critical regions, significantly reducing storage requirements while maintaining high-fidelity forgery evidence. We first introduce InfoDense Cut to localize decisive patches using CLIP-based embeddings. Then, InfoDense Select ranks candidate segments by combining latent-space representativeness and decisive patch counts, ensuring both diversity and information density in the replay buffer. Finally, InfoDense Fuse reconstructs unbiased training inputs by adaptively merging stored segments with current-task samples, enhancing knowledge retention and generalization. Extensive experiments on challenging incremental deepfake benchmarks demonstrate that InfoDense effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting while improving cross-domain generalization.

AI.tldr: InfoDense is a Density-Aware Regional Decisive replay strategy for Incremental Face Forgery Detection that mitigates catastrophic forgetting by prioritizing artifact-dense regions, using CLIP-based patch selection, latent-space ranking, and adaptive fusion to reduce storage while improving cross-domain generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing replay-based IFFD methods suffer from catastrophic forgetting due to limited memory; storing full images either fails to preserve subtle forgery cues or introduces domain bias, reducing the model's ability to learn intrinsic and transferable manipulation characteristics.
AI.method: InfoDense consists of three components: (1) InfoDense Cut — localizes decisive (artifact-dense) patches using CLIP-based embeddings; (2) InfoDense Select — ranks candidate segments by latent-space representativeness and decisive patch counts for diversity and information density; (3) InfoDense Fuse — reconstructs unbiased training inputs by adaptively merging stored segments with current-task samples.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on challenging incremental deepfake benchmarks show that InfoDense effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting and improves cross-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: The proposed density-aware regional decisive replay strategy significantly reduces storage requirements while maintaining high-fidelity forgery evidence, outperforming conventional replay-based IFFD methods.

title: Scalable Causal Imitation Learning
summary: Imitation learning enables learning a policy in an unknown environment with a latent reward signal using expert demonstrations, but it struggles when the imitator's and expert's observations are mismatched and unobserved confounders are present in expert demonstrations. By identifying appropriate adjustment sets via the sequential $π$-backdoor criterion, causal imitation learning (CIL) provides a framework for approximating the expert's policy from confounded data. However, existing CIL methods, Causal Behavioral Cloning (Causal BC) and Causal Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning (Causal GAIL), are designed for short-horizon, low-dimensional settings. When applied to continuous control tasks with long horizons and high-dimensional state-action spaces, these methods exhibit poor performance: Causal BC suffers from compounding errors, Causal GAIL is unstable and sample-inefficient, and sequential $π$-backdoor adjustment becomes impractical. We introduce Causal Soft Q Imitation Learning (SQIL) and Causal Inverse soft-Q Learning (IQ-Learn), two off-policy causal imitation learning algorithms that combine the causal adjustment framework with state-of-the-art inverse reinforcement learning objectives. Both algorithms operate on causally-adjusted state representations produced by an efficient approximation of the sequential $π$-backdoor criterion, exploiting the causal structure of continuous control environments to reduce the full-horizon adjustment to a fixed-size sliding window. We evaluate all methods in a suite of confounded environments and find that Causal SQIL and Causal IQ-Learn substantially outperform prior CIL algorithms on long-horizon tasks, sometimes surpassing the expert, whereas all causally unaware imitation methods fail to learn meaningful behavior.

AI.tldr: Introduces Causal SQIL and Causal IQ-Learn, two off-policy causal imitation learning algorithms that combine sequential π-backdoor adjustment with state-of-the-art inverse RL objectives, outperforming prior CIL methods in long-horizon, high-dimensional continuous control tasks with confounded data.
AI.motivation: Existing causal imitation learning methods (Causal BC, Causal GAIL) perform poorly in continuous control tasks with long horizons, high-dimensional state-action spaces, and confounded expert demonstrations; they suffer from compounding errors, instability, sample inefficiency, and impractical adjustment procedures.
AI.method: Proposes Causal SQIL and Causal IQ-Learn, which combine causal adjustment (sequential π-backdoor criterion approximated via a fixed-size sliding window) with off-policy inverse RL objectives (soft Q-imitation learning and inverse soft-Q learning) to produce causally adjusted state representations for policy learning.
AI.result: Causal SQIL and Causal IQ-Learn substantially outperform prior CIL algorithms (Causal BC, Causal GAIL) on long-horizon confounded continuous control tasks, sometimes surpassing the expert, while causally unaware methods fail entirely.
AI.conclusion: Off-policy causal imitation learning with efficient adjustment of confounded observations is effective for high-dimensional, long-horizon continuous control, enabling robust policy learning from expert demonstrations under observational mismatch and unobserved confounders.

title: FlowBlock: Wavefront-Parallel Decoding for Self-Correcting Diffusion Language Models
summary: Block-wise diffusion large language models (dLLMs) decode sequentially at the block level, enabling effective KV-cache reuse across blocks but making inter-block decoding strictly serial. Prior work has attempted to unlock inter-block parallelism through post-training methods, but achieves only modest speedups and often degrades accuracy. We observe that self-correcting dLLMs offer a training-free alternative: token-to-token (T2T) editing can repair tokens drafted with a slightly stale upstream context, so a downstream block requires only an informative draft rather than a finalized predecessor. This turns block finality from a hard dependency into a scheduling resource. We propose \textbf{\flowblock{}}, a training-free parallel decoding framework built on two mechanisms. (i) \emph{Gated Wavefront Decoding} admits blocks into a bounded wavefront only when a readiness gate is satisfied, jointly refines active blocks via T2T editing, and commits blocks in order under a windowed block-causal mask that preserves exact frozen-prefix KV caches reuse. (ii) \emph{Heterogeneous Wavefront Packing} assigns each request an independent wavefront while packing asynchronous windows into dense, shape-stable batched forwards. Across different benchmarks, \flowblock{} improves tokens per second (TPS) over LLaDA-2.1 and LLaDA-2.0, two serial block-wise dLLMs, by up to 2.95$\times$ and 4.01$\times$, while reducing latency by up to 53.6\% and 77.1\%, respectively. It also improves average accuracy by 1.3 points. Compared with D2F, a training-based inter-block-parallel baseline, \flowblock{} achieves higher accuracy and up to 16$\times$ higher batched serving throughput.

AI.tldr: FlowBlock is a training-free parallel decoding framework for block-wise diffusion LLMs that uses Gated Wavefront Decoding and Heterogeneous Wavefront Packing to achieve inter-block parallelism, improving throughput by up to 4.01× and reducing latency by up to 77.1% while maintaining or improving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Block-wise diffusion LLMs decode sequentially at the block level, making inter-block decoding strictly serial. Prior post-training methods for inter-block parallelism achieve only modest speedups with accuracy degradation. The authors observe that self-correcting dLLMs enable token-to-token editing, turning block finality from a hard dependency into a scheduling resource.
AI.method: Proposes FlowBlock with two mechanisms: (i) Gated Wavefront Decoding, which admits blocks into a bounded wavefront based on a readiness gate, jointly refines active blocks via T2T editing, and commits blocks in order under a windowed block-causal mask preserving exact frozen-prefix KV cache reuse; (ii) Heterogeneous Wavefront Packing, which assigns each request an independent wavefront while packing asynchronous windows into dense, shape-stable batched forwards.
AI.result: FlowBlock improves TPS over LLaDA-2.1 and LLaDA-2.0 by up to 2.95× and 4.01×, reduces latency by up to 53.6% and 77.1%, improves average accuracy by 1.3 points. Compared to D2F (training-based baseline), achieves higher accuracy and up to 16× higher batched serving throughput.
AI.conclusion: Training-free parallel decoding via scheduling-aware wavefront methods is effective for block-wise dLLMs, achieving substantial speedups and throughput improvements without sacrificing accuracy, outperforming both serial baselines and training-based parallel approaches.

title: Transferable Low-Rank Convolutional Bases for Onboarding Unseen Medical Imaging Modalities
summary: Deploying a medical imaging model that must later accommodate a modality it has never seen is a recurring practical problem: retraining the shared representation is expensive and destroys performance on the modalities already in service. We study this \emph{onboarding} problem under a strict leave-one-domain-out protocol, in which a convolutional backbone is pre-trained on source modalities (Kidney CT and Brain MRI), frozen permanently, and then required to accommodate an unseen modality (Chest X-ray). Under this protocol we establish three findings. First, decision-layer parameter-efficient fine-tuning is insufficient when the backbone has never observed the target modality: a linear probe and fully-connected LoRA both fall well short, whereas convolutional LoRA recovers most of the achievable accuracy, showing that adaptation must reach the convolutional features. Second, and centrally, the low-rank convolutional \emph{basis} learned on the source modalities \emph{transfers}: freezing that basis and training only its up-projections onboards the unseen modality using just $0.78\%$ of full fine-tuning's parameters, at an accuracy $6.11$ percentage points above a random basis of identical size, while an equivalent decision-layer basis exhibits no reliable transfer. Third, adapter-based onboarding leaves source-modality accuracy exactly unchanged ($Δ= 0.00$ pp), whereas full fine-tuning reaches the highest target accuracy only by catastrophically degrading the source modalities. A Mahalanobis score on frozen backbone features detects the unseen modality with high sensitivity at a strict source-retention threshold, providing a practical trigger for when onboarding is required. All results are reported over three seeds with paired bootstrap confidence intervals.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the problem of onboarding a medical imaging model to an unseen modality without retraining the shared representation. Using a strict leave-one-domain-out protocol, they find that convolutional low-rank adaptation (LoRA) transfers effectively from source modalities (Kidney CT, Brain MRI) to an unseen modality (Chest X-ray), achieving high accuracy with only 0.78% of full fine-tuning's parameters while leaving source modality accuracy unchanged. A Mahalanobis score on frozen backbone features can detect when onboarding is needed.
AI.motivation: Deploying medical imaging models that must later accommodate unseen modalities is a practical problem; retraining the shared representation is expensive and degrades performance on existing modalities. The paper aims to study this "onboarding" problem under a strict protocol where the backbone is frozen after pre-training on source modalities.
AI.method: A strict leave-one-domain-out protocol is used: a convolutional backbone is pre-trained on source modalities (Kidney CT and Brain MRI), frozen permanently, and required to accommodate an unseen modality (Chest X-ray). Various parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (linear probe, fully-connected LoRA, convolutional LoRA) are compared. The key method involves transferring a low-rank convolutional basis learned on source modalities, freezing that basis and training only its up-projections. A Mahalanobis score on frozen backbone features is used to detect unseen modalities.
AI.result: Decision-layer fine-tuning (linear probe, fully-connected LoRA) is insufficient when the backbone has never seen the target modality. Convolutional LoRA recovers most achievable accuracy. The low-rank convolutional basis learned on source modalities transfers: freezing the basis and training only up-projections onboards the unseen modality using 0.78% of full fine-tuning's parameters, with accuracy 6.11 percentage points above a random basis. Adapter-based onboarding leaves source modality accuracy unchanged (Δ=0.00 pp), while full fine-tuning catastrophically degrades source modalities. A Mahalanobis score detects the unseen modality with high sensitivity at a strict source-retention threshold.
AI.conclusion: Convolutional low-rank adaptation enables effective onboarding of unseen medical imaging modalities without retraining the shared representation, preserving source modality performance. The transferred convolutional basis is more effective than decision-layer adaptation. A Mahalanobis-based trigger can detect when onboarding is required.

title: Regularize or Localize: When Training-Time KV-Cache Geometry Pays Under Quantization
summary: We study whether \sigreg -- LeJEPA's anti-collapse objective -- can reshape representations during standard autoregressive language-model pretraining, and when the resulting geometry helps \kv-cache quantization. We train 110M-parameter models on 10B FineWeb tokens and report three findings. \textbf{(1)} At $λ{=}0.01$, \sigreg reduces hidden-state pairwise-cosine anisotropy by $38\%$ across three paired seeds. Perplexity increases by less than $0.35\%$ in every pair, with no consistent zero-shot loss. \textbf{(2)} This change does not propagate from hidden states to the \kv cache. Applying \sigreg directly to K and V during continued training, however, reduces mean cache anisotropy by $94\%$ across four checkpoints. A matched continuation without the \kv term leaves cache geometry nearly unchanged, and the frozen-trunk retrofits we tested do not reproduce the effect. \textbf{(3)} Under untransformed symmetric group-free quantization, direct \kv regularization is the only training condition that prefers per-channel scaling in all three seeds, and under that same 3-bit per-channel scheme the baseline incurs $4.3$--$7.9\times$ the directly regularized model's \dnll. Under the full simulated KIVI-style configuration (mixed arrangement, zero-points, grouped scales), however, all models reach near-parity, including when storage overhead is approximately matched. In this 110M regime, the training intervention helps when quantizer scales are coarse; the advantage vanishes under the tested combination of token-local grouping, mixed \kv scaling, and zero-points. To our knowledge this is the first training-time \emph{distributional} regularization of standard \kv-cache geometry evaluated against post-hoc cache quantization.

AI.tldr: SigReg (LeJEPA's anti-collapse objective) applied during autoregressive LM pretraining reduces hidden-state anisotropy by 38% with negligible perplexity loss. Directly regularizing K/V cache geometry reduces cache anisotropy by 94%, which improves 3-bit per-channel quantization (baseline incurs 4.3–7.9× the regularized model's DNLL), but parity is reached under more sophisticated KIVI-style quantization with grouping, mixed scaling, and zero-points.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether SigReg can reshape representations during standard autoregressive LM pretraining and whether the resulting geometric changes help KV-cache quantization, a practical post-hoc compression challenge.
AI.method: Trained 110M-parameter models on 10B FineWeb tokens with SigReg applied to hidden states (λ=0.01) and/or directly to K/V cache during continued training. Evaluated anisotropy reduction, perplexity impact, and downstream quantization performance under symmetric group-free and KIVI-style schemes.
AI.result: (1) SigReg reduces hidden-state pairwise-cosine anisotropy by 38% with <0.35% perplexity increase. (2) This effect does not propagate to KV cache; direct KV regularization reduces cache anisotropy by 94%. (3) Under 3-bit per-channel quantization, directly regularized model drastically outperforms baseline (4.3–7.9× lower DNLL), but all models reach near-parity under full KIVI-style quantization.
AI.conclusion: Training-time distributional regularization of KV-cache geometry helps when quantizer scales are coarse (e.g., per-channel), but the advantage vanishes under sufficiently expressive quantization schemes (grouped, mixed scaling, zero-points). This is the first training-time distributional regularization of KV-cache geometry evaluated against post-hoc cache quantization.

title: Cross-Branch Conflict as a Shield: Safeguarding Facial Identities in Unified Multimodal Image Editing
summary: Unified multimodal models (UMMs) have recently demonstrated powerful instruction-based image editing capabilities, but they also raise serious concerns about unauthorized manipulation of personal portraits. Existing adversarial protection methods are mainly designed for either visual understanding or image generation models and often become ineffective when transferred to UMMs, which process an image through multiple complementary visual pathways. In this work, we first conduct a feature-level analysis of unified image editing. We observe that the ViT-based understanding branch and the VAE-based generation branch exhibit non-trivial structural agreement for the same input image. Although perturbing an individual branch can reduce this agreement and induce intermediate hidden-state deviations, such effects are asymmetric and gradually attenuated during multimodal fusion and generation. These observations reveal that single-branch feature distortion is insufficient for consistently disrupting unified image editing. Motivated by this finding, we propose CCS, a unified adversarial protection framework that jointly drives the ViT and VAE representations away from their clean counterparts while explicitly disrupting their cross-branch compatibility through linear CKA. By simultaneously removing stable information from both visual pathways and creating incompatible visual contexts, CCS prevents the UMM from recovering reliable identity information during editing. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CCS consistently outperforms existing protection methods in suppressing identity-preserving edits.

AI.tldr: CCS is a unified adversarial protection framework that disrupts both ViT and VAE branches to prevent unauthorized image editing by unified multimodal models.
AI.motivation: Existing adversarial protection methods fail against unified multimodal models (UMMs) that process images through multiple complementary visual pathways, leaving personal portraits vulnerable to unauthorized manipulation.
AI.method: CCS jointly disrupts ViT (understanding) and VAE (generation) representations while explicitly breaking cross-branch compatibility using linear CKA, removing stable information from both visual pathways.
AI.result: CCS consistently outperforms existing protection methods in suppressing identity-preserving edits across extensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: Single-branch feature distortion is insufficient against UMMs; cross-branch disruption is necessary for robust adversarial protection against unified image editing.

title: Interpretable Machine Learning for Air Pollution and Respiratory Health Prediction: A Socioeconomic Subgroup Analysis
summary: Air pollution and climate-related stressors are increasingly important concerns for respiratory health, especially in settings with unequal environmental exposure and healthcare capacity. This study evaluates an interpretable machine learning framework for predicting respiratory disease rates and air-quality status using structured country-level weekly data. Two supervised learning tasks were considered: regression of respiratory disease rate per 100,000 population and binary classification of air-quality status. Nine regression models and nine classification models were compared using nested cross-validation. Model interpretation was conducted using SHAP values, and subgroup analysis was performed across income levels and geographic regions. The results showed that PM2.5 concentration was the dominant predictor of respiratory disease rate, with linear and regularized linear models achieving the strongest regression performance. For air-quality classification, models achieved high balanced accuracy when PM2.5 was included, but performance decreased substantially when PM2.5 was removed, indicating strong dependence on pollutant-related information. SHAP analysis showed that, without PM2.5, socioeconomic and meteorological variables such as GDP per capita, precipitation, and healthcare access became more influential. Subgroup analysis showed similar aggregate regression error across income groups, but PM2.5 contributed more strongly to predictions in lower-middle-income countries. These results show that model accuracy alone is not sufficient for climate-health prediction. Interpretable models can help identify dominant pollution-related signals, test whether results depend on key pollutant variables, and show whether prediction patterns differ across socioeconomic groups.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates interpretable machine learning models for predicting respiratory disease rates and air-quality status using country-level weekly data. PM2.5 concentration was the dominant predictor, and linear models performed best. Without PM2.5, socioeconomic and meteorological variables gained importance. Subgroup analysis revealed PM2.5 contributed more strongly in lower-middle-income countries.
AI.motivation: Air pollution and climate-related stressors increasingly threaten respiratory health, especially in contexts with unequal environmental exposure and healthcare capacity, motivating the need for interpretable prediction frameworks.
AI.method: Two supervised learning tasks: regression (respiratory disease rate per 100,000 population) and binary classification (air-quality status). Nine regression and nine classification models compared via nested cross-validation. SHAP values used for interpretation, with subgroup analysis across income levels and geographic regions.
AI.result: PM2.5 was the dominant predictor for respiratory disease rates; linear/regularized linear models achieved best regression performance. Air-quality classification depended heavily on PM2.5; without it, performance dropped substantially, and socioeconomic/meteorological variables (GDP per capita, precipitation, healthcare access) became more influential. Subgroup analysis showed similar aggregate error across income groups but stronger PM2.5 contribution in lower-middle-income countries.
AI.conclusion: Model accuracy alone is insufficient for climate-health prediction. Interpretable models help identify dominant pollution signals, test dependence on key pollutants, and reveal differential prediction patterns across socioeconomic groups.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Understanding and Managing Transportation Behavior in Sustainable Smart Cities
summary: Urban transportation systems generate heterogeneous data, yet these data do not automatically become actionable management intelligence. This chapter adopts a behavior-centered perspective on artificial intelligence (AI), treating mobility records and passenger-generated text as behavioral evidence rather than behavioral truth. It examines four directions: bus arrival prediction for service reliability, taxi mobility pattern discovery for demand analysis and planning, abnormal behavior detection for accountable regulatory support, and passenger-perceived risk mining for service improvement. These directions are integrated through a closed-loop framework linking data input, behavior representation, AI inference, decision support, public value, and governance feedback. The chapter identifies data quality, privacy, fairness, interpretability, uncertainty, transferability, and human accountability as essential conditions for deployment. It thereby establishes a unified pathway from behavioral evidence to operational, planning, regulatory, and passenger-service decisions.

AI.tldr: This chapter proposes a behavior-centered AI framework for urban transportation that treats mobility data as behavioral evidence (not truth), integrating bus arrival prediction, taxi pattern discovery, anomaly detection, and passenger risk mining into a closed-loop system from data to governance feedback, while identifying key deployment conditions like privacy, fairness, and interpretability.
AI.motivation: Urban transportation generates heterogeneous data but lacks actionable management intelligence. The chapter addresses the gap between raw data and decision-making by adopting a behavior-centered AI perspective that treats mobility records as behavioral evidence rather than behavioral truth.
AI.method: A closed-loop framework linking data input, behavior representation, AI inference, decision support, public value, and governance feedback. Examines four specific AI application directions: bus arrival prediction, taxi mobility pattern discovery, abnormal behavior detection, and passenger-perceived risk mining.
AI.result: Identifies a unified pathway from behavioral evidence to operational, planning, regulatory, and passenger-service decisions. Establishes essential deployment conditions: data quality, privacy, fairness, interpretability, uncertainty, transferability, and human accountability.
AI.conclusion: A behavior-centered AI approach with a closed-loop governance framework can transform heterogeneous urban transportation data into actionable intelligence across multiple decision domains, provided key conditions (privacy, fairness, interpretability, etc.) are met for responsible deployment.

title: Pedestrian Archetypes Extension -- More Pedestrian Models for Autonomous Vehicle Safety Testing
comment: Extended version of Pedestrian Archetypes paper (published in IEEE IV 2025)
summary: In our prior work, Pedestrian Archetypes, we defined pedestrian archetypes as collections of behaviors that uniquely identify a specific type of pedestrian. The first paper proposed 12 pedestrian archetypes, including the Wanderer, Drunk, Distracted, Flash, Indecisive, Blind, Flock, Jaywalker, Elderly, Kid, Eventful, and Parked Pedestrian. These archetypes were introduced to move beyond single behavior labels and provide a more natural way to describe how dangerous pedestrians actually behave progressively in real-world traffic scenarios. However, upon further annotation of YouTube dash-cam videos, we identified 7 additional pedestrian archetypes with observable and significant behavioral differences from the previously proposed ones. These new archetypes capture pedestrian behavior patterns that could not be fully explained by the original taxonomy. In this pre-print, we introduce each new archetype, define its essential and optional behaviors, explain how it differs from previously proposed archetypes, and provide video-frame evidence showing the archetype in action.

AI.tldr: This paper extends the Pedestrian Archetypes taxonomy from 12 to 19 archetypes by identifying 7 new pedestrian behavior patterns observed in YouTube dash-cam videos that were not covered by the original framework.
AI.motivation: The original 12 pedestrian archetypes were insufficient to fully describe all observable pedestrian behavior patterns in real-world traffic scenarios, as additional annotation of YouTube dash-cam videos revealed 7 distinct archetypes with significant behavioral differences.
AI.method: The authors annotated YouTube dash-cam videos and identified 7 new pedestrian archetypes with observable behavioral patterns. For each new archetype, they define essential and optional behaviors, compare them against previously proposed archetypes, and provide video-frame evidence.
AI.result: 7 additional pedestrian archetypes were identified that capture behavior patterns not explainable by the original 12-archetype taxonomy, bringing the total to 19 archetypes.
AI.conclusion: The pedestrian archetype taxonomy is expanded to better model the progressive and nuanced behavioral patterns of pedestrians in real-world traffic, enabling more natural descriptions of dangerous pedestrian behaviors.

title: ChemFusion: A Multimodal Cross-Attention Network for Reaction Yield Prediction
summary: Forecasting the outcomes of transition-metal-catalyzed reactions is notoriously complex due to the interplay of diverse physical and chemical variables. A persistent computational bottleneck has been effectively merging broad electronic descriptors with the localized, three-dimensional geometry of the reactive site. To bridge this representation gap, we present ChemFusion, a hybrid neural network that fuses conventional electronic features with explicit 3D atomic coordinates. Using a cross-attention mechanism, the model enables global electronic states to dynamically attend to specific spatial constraints within un-pooled molecular point clouds. When benchmarked against a diverse library of cross-couplings, this approach delivers exceptional predictive performance, decisively surpassing traditional single-modality frameworks. Importantly, extracting the attention matrices reveals that the architecture autonomously learns to identify and penalize restrictive steric hindrances. This provides a physically grounded interpretability, demonstrating that spatially aware networks can navigate complex reaction sterics that standard statistical models typically miss.

AI.tldr: ChemFusion is a hybrid neural network that fuses global electronic features with explicit 3D atomic coordinates via cross-attention, outperforming single-modality models in predicting transition-metal-catalyzed reaction outcomes and autonomously learning to identify steric hindrances.
AI.motivation: Forecasting outcomes of transition-metal-catalyzed reactions is complex due to interplay of diverse physical/chemical variables, and there is a persistent bottleneck in merging broad electronic descriptors with localized 3D geometry of the reactive site.
AI.method: ChemFusion uses a hybrid neural network with cross-attention mechanism to fuse conventional electronic features with explicit 3D atomic coordinates within un-pooled molecular point clouds, enabling global electronic states to dynamically attend to specific spatial constraints.
AI.result: Exceptional predictive performance on diverse cross-coupling library, decisively surpassing traditional single-modality frameworks. Attention matrices reveal the architecture autonomously learns to identify and penalize restrictive steric hindrances.
AI.conclusion: Spatially aware networks can navigate complex reaction sterics that standard statistical models typically miss, providing physically grounded interpretability.

title: ProEvent: An Event-centric Benchmark for Proactive Agents
summary:
Proactive agents are expected to anticipate user needs and provide autonomous assistance by perceiving environmental context without explicit instructions. A fundamental capability of such agents is to identify and track users' upcoming events, enabling continuous and event-specific assistance. For example, by recording the time and location of a planned hike, an agent can deliver weather reminders in advance or provide navigation support before departure. However, existing works on proactive agents largely overlook event-centric assistance, and the open-ended nature of proactive assistance poses challenges for reliable evaluation.
  To bridge these gaps, we introduce ProEvent, the first event-centric benchmark designed to assess an agent's ability to proactively maintain a user's timetable based on ongoing instant messaging chats. ProEvent provides synthesized yet realistic chats that consider the dynamic interaction among users, concurrent chat threads, and noise in the real world, and evaluates proactive agents on response timing, single-step response correctness, and multi-step response correctness. Experiments on eight LLMs and pipelines reveal that current agents frequently overact and struggle with event cancellation. Notably, even GPT-5.1 only reacts correctly in 26.7% of scenarios. Further qualitative analysis reveals fundamental limitations of current LLMs as proactive agents, particularly in detecting implicit events and reasoning from the user's first-person perspective.

AI.tldr: ProEvent is the first event-centric benchmark for evaluating proactive agents' ability to track user timetables from chats. Experiments on 8 LLMs show current agents overact and struggle with event cancellation, with GPT-5.1 achieving only 26.7% correct reactions.
AI.motivation: Existing works on proactive agents overlook event-centric assistance, and the open-ended nature of proactive assistance poses challenges for reliable evaluation.
AI.method: The authors introduce ProEvent, an event-centric benchmark providing synthesized yet realistic chat data considering dynamic user interaction, concurrent threads, and real-world noise. It evaluates agents on response timing, single-step correctness, and multi-step correctness.
AI.result: Current agents frequently overact and struggle with event cancellation; GPT-5.1 only reacts correctly in 26.7% of scenarios. Qualitative analysis reveals limitations in detecting implicit events and reasoning from the user's first-person perspective.
AI.conclusion: Current LLMs have fundamental limitations as proactive agents, particularly in implicit event detection and first-person perspective reasoning, indicating significant room for improvement.

title: Splat-based 3D Scene Reconstruction with Extreme Motion-blur
summary: We propose a splat-based 3D scene reconstruction method from RGB-D input that effectively handles extreme motion blur, a frequent challenge in low-light environments. Under dim illumination, RGB frames often suffer from severe motion blur due to extended exposure times, causing traditional camera pose estimation methods, such as COLMAP, to fail. This results in inaccurate camera pose and blurry color input, compromising the quality of 3D reconstructions. Although recent 3D reconstruction techniques like Neural Radiance Fields and Gaussian Splatting have demonstrated impressive results, they rely on accurate camera trajectory estimation, which becomes challenging under fast motion or poor lighting conditions. Furthermore, rapid camera movement and the limited field of view of depth sensors reduce point cloud overlap, limiting the effectiveness of pose estimation with the ICP algorithm. To address these issues, we introduce a method that combines camera pose estimation and image deblurring using a Gaussian Splatting framework, leveraging both 3D Gaussian splats and depth inputs for enhanced scene representation. Our method first aligns consecutive RGB-D frames through optical flow and ICP, then refines camera poses and 3D geometry by adjusting Gaussian positions for optimal depth alignment. To handle motion blur, we model camera movement during exposure and deblur images by comparing the input with a series of sharp, rendered frames. Experiments on a new RGB-D dataset with extreme motion blur show that our method outperforms existing approaches, enabling high-quality reconstructions even in challenging conditions. This approach has broad implications for 3D mapping applications in robotics, autonomous navigation, and augmented reality. Both code and dataset are publicly available on https://github.com/KAIST-VCLAB/gs-extreme-motion-blur.

AI.tldr: A splat-based 3D reconstruction method from RGB-D input that handles extreme motion blur by combining camera pose estimation, image deblurring, and Gaussian Splatting, outperforming existing approaches on a new benchmark dataset.
AI.motivation: Extreme motion blur in low-light environments causes traditional pose estimation (e.g., COLMAP, ICP) and modern 3D methods (NeRF, Gaussian Splatting) to fail due to inaccurate camera trajectories, limited point cloud overlap, and blurry color input.
AI.method: Aligns consecutive RGB-D frames via optical flow and ICP, refines camera poses and 3D geometry by adjusting Gaussian splat positions for depth alignment, and handles motion blur by modeling camera movement during exposure and comparing input with sharp rendered frames.
AI.result: Outperforms existing approaches on a new RGB-D dataset with extreme motion blur, enabling high-quality 3D reconstructions under challenging conditions.
AI.conclusion: The method enables high-quality 3D reconstructions under extreme motion blur, with broad implications for robotics, autonomous navigation, and augmented reality; code and dataset are publicly available.

title: Apeliotes: A Diffusion-Based Modeling Framework for km-scale Multi-Level Atmospheric Fields
summary: High-resolution atmospheric data are required to resolve mesoscale and localized meteorological structures, however such datasets remain limited in many regions of the world. Existing high-resolution weather products are typically produced through dynamical downscaling, which is computationally expensive and difficult to scale across locations, variables, and forecast scenarios. These limitations motivate machine-learning-based downscaling systems that can generate multiple weather variables stochastically while producing new high-resolution fields directly. In this paper we present Apeliotes, a framework for high-resolution weather forecasting. Built on the global re-analysis atmospheric data, a pre-trained global weather foundation model, and a regionally trained generative diffusion model, Apeliotes not only provides accurate kilometer-scale weather variables, but also multi-level atmospheric fields which are not directly available in the existing global atmospheric data. Our comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that Apeliotes achieves highly competitive performance.
