title: When Drift Detectors cry Wolf: False Alarm Rates in continuous ML Monitoring
summary: Drift detection is a core component of production machine learning monitoring systems, where detectors are used to compare incoming data with a reference distribution and trigger alerts when changes occur. However, these detectors are often evaluated in research settings that emphasize detection accuracy under synthetic shifts, while overlooking false alarms under continuous monitoring. In production environments, models are monitored repeatedly over time and across many features, and even small false positive rates can accumulate into frequent alerts, leading to alarm fatigue. We empirically analyze false positive behavior across five commonly used drift detectors: PSI, KS, MMD, LSDD, and adversarial validation. Consistent with existing literature, PSI exhibits strong sensitivity to batch size, producing frequent false alarms at small sample sizes; however, we further observe that its behavior stabilizes and improves substantially once batch sizes exceed approximately 200 samples. In contrast, KS, MMD, and LSDD display persistent fluctuations across batch sizes, while remaining comparatively more reliable than PSI in low-data regimes. Applying a Bonferroni correction reduces false positive rates, but often at the cost of reduced true positive sensitivity, reinforcing the well-known stability - sensitivity trade-off in drift detection. This work provides a systematic comparison of false positive behavior across multiple drift detectors under continuous monitoring conditions. We identify tradeoffs across detector families and provide practical guidelines for selecting and calibrating drift detectors in production ML systems.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates false positive rates of five common drift detectors (PSI, KS, MMD, LSDD, adversarial validation) under continuous monitoring conditions in production ML, revealing that PSI stabilizes with larger batch sizes (>200 samples), while KS, MMD, LSDD show persistent fluctuations but better reliability in low-data regimes, and Bonferroni correction reduces false positives at the cost of sensitivity.
AI.motivation: Drift detectors are typically evaluated on detection accuracy under synthetic shifts in research settings, but their false positive behavior under continuous monitoring in production environments is overlooked. Small false positive rates can accumulate into frequent alerts, causing alarm fatigue. This work aims to fill this gap.
AI.method: Empirical analysis of five drift detectors (PSI, KS, MMD, LSDD, adversarial validation) under continuous monitoring conditions, examining false positive behavior across different batch sizes and applying Bonferroni correction.
AI.result: PSI is highly sensitive to batch size with frequent false alarms at small sample sizes but stabilizes beyond ~200 samples. KS, MMD, and LSDD show persistent fluctuations but are more reliable than PSI in low-data regimes. Bonferroni correction reduces false positives but decreases true positive sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: The work identifies trade-offs across detector families and provides practical guidelines for selecting and calibrating drift detectors in production ML systems, highlighting the stability-sensitivity trade-off.

title: PAMD: Structured Adaptive Distances for Bisimulation Representations in Visual Reinforcement Learning
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures, plus appendix. Accepted to the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary:
Many visual reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms learn representations by matching latent distances to a behavioral distance induced by reward and transition similarity. In practice, the choice of the latent distance can strongly affect performance: using a fixed, pre-specified global norms (e.g., $\ell_p$ norms or other hand-designed metrics) may be overly restrictive to capture the behavioral distance. In contrast, unconstrained pairwise distances may admit degenerate solutions that drive the metric loss down without improving the representation. To address this gap, we introduce **PAMD: Pairwise Adaptive Mahalanobis Distance**, which parameterizes a positive-definite, pair-conditioned metric for measuring latent state similarity.
  PAMD is a simple plug-in for existing bisimulation-based methods, offering a more expressive yet structured alternative to fixed, pre-specified latent distances. We empirically validate our method on visual MuJoCo continuous-control tasks, where final performance of several recent bisimulation-based RL algorithms is substantially improved when equipped with the distance we propose.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PAMD, a Pairwise Adaptive Mahalanobis Distance that parameterizes a learnable, structured metric for measuring latent state similarity in visual RL, replacing fixed norms used in bisimulation-based methods and improving performance on MuJoCo tasks.
AI.motivation: Fixed pre-specified latent distances (e.g., ℓp norms) are overly restrictive for capturing behavioral distance induced by reward and transition similarity, while unconstrained pairwise distances admit degenerate solutions. A more expressive yet structured alternative is needed.
AI.method: PAMD parameterizes a positive-definite, pair-conditioned metric (Mahalanobis distance) for measuring latent state similarity. It serves as a plug-in module for existing bisimulation-based RL algorithms.
AI.result: On visual MuJoCo continuous-control tasks, several recent bisimulation-based RL algorithms equipped with PAMD show substantially improved final performance compared to using fixed, pre-specified latent distances.
AI.conclusion: PAMD offers a structured, learnable distance metric that balances expressiveness and regularization, effectively bridging the gap between overly restrictive fixed norms and degenerate unconstrained distances in bisimulation-based visual RL.

title: BanClickThumb: A Multimodal Dataset and Transformer Fusion Benchmarks for Clickbait Detection in Bengali YouTube Videos
summary: Clickbait, where video titles and thumbnails exaggerate or misrepresent content, reduces user trust, wastes attention, and promotes misinformation on video-sharing platforms. Detecting Bengali clickbait remains challenging because publicly available multimodal datasets are limited. To address this gap, we introduce BanClickThumb, a curated dataset of 7,147 Bengali YouTube thumbnail-title pairs from five content domains, annotated by ten annotators with high agreement (Cohen's Kappa: 0.83-0.93). Using this dataset, we benchmark text-only, image-only, and multimodal approaches. Among unimodal models, BanClickTextFormer (XLM-RoBERTa) achieves 0.82 accuracy, while BanClickImageFormer (SwiftFormer) reaches 0.68. Our proposed multimodal model, BanClickFusionFormer, combines ViT and XLM-RoBERTa through intermediate fusion and achieves the best accuracy of 0.84. Error analysis shows that dense thumbnail text, figurative language, and culturally specific slang remain challenging. Our findings demonstrate the effectiveness of multimodal fusion for Bengali clickbait detection and provide a publicly available benchmark to support future research on low-resource multimodal content analysis.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces BanClickThumb, a manually annotated dataset of 7,147 Bengali YouTube thumbnail-title pairs, and proposes BanClickFusionFormer, a multimodal model combining ViT and XLM-RoBERTa with intermediate fusion, achieving 0.84 accuracy for clickbait detection, outperforming unimodal baselines.
AI.motivation: Clickbait in Bengali video content remains underexplored due to the lack of publicly available multimodal datasets, despite the prevalence of misleading titles and thumbnails on video-sharing platforms.
AI.method: The authors curate BanClickThumb (7,147 Bengali YouTube thumbnail-title pairs from five domains, annotated by 10 annotators with high agreement 0.83-0.93 Cohen's Kappa) and benchmark text-only (XLM-RoBERTa: BanClickTextFormer), image-only (SwiftFormer: BanClickImageFormer), and multimodal approaches. Their proposed model, BanClickFusionFormer, uses ViT and XLM-RoBERTa with intermediate fusion.
AI.result: BanClickTextFormer achieves 0.82 accuracy, BanClickImageFormer 0.68, and BanClickFusionFormer achieves the best 0.84 accuracy. Error analysis reveals challenges from dense thumbnail text, figurative language, and culturally specific slang.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal fusion is effective for Bengali clickbait detection; the dataset and benchmark are publicly released to support low-resource multimodal content analysis research.

title: A multiverse-consensus pipeline for reproducible feature selection in untargeted LC-MS metabolomics
summary: Background: Untargeted LC-MS metabolomics requires a long chain of preprocessing decisions, each with several equally defensible options. Analysts typically commit to one pipeline and report the resulting feature shortlist. How strongly that shortlist depends on choices that were never varied stays invisible. Results: We adapt multiverse analysis to untargeted metabolomics feature selection. We present an auditable, configuration-driven pipeline that (i) applies a ten-stage quality-control filter cascade in which every feature's fate is logged, and (ii) runs the downstream analysis as a multiverse over four contrasting preprocessing philosophies, each combined with four feature-ranking methods under bootstrap stability selection and label-permutation testing. Only features recurring across paths enter a tiered consensus. On a demonstration dataset of five breast-cancer cell lines (30,370 detected features), the four single pipelines individually returned shortlists of 4-20 features whose pairwise agreement was as low as Jaccard = 0.05. The multiverse consensus retained 15 features (>=2/4 paths), of which one recurred across all four, although two paths (sharing normalization and drift-correction methods) dominate the consensus. A pipeline-wide label-permutation test found no false discoveries in 50 null permutations. Conclusions: Reporting only preprocessing-robust features, with a complete kept/dropped audit trail, converts hidden analytical degrees of freedom into an explicit, inspectable output. We discuss scope and limitations, including single-batch design and the need for independent validation.

AI.tldr: The paper adapts multiverse analysis to untargeted LC-MS metabolomics, running multiple preprocessing pipelines (4 philosophies × 4 ranking methods) with a tiered consensus approach. On a breast-cancer cell-line dataset, single pipelines showed poor agreement (Jaccard = 0.05), while the multiverse consensus retained 15 robust features (one across all four paths), and label-permutation testing found zero false discoveries.
AI.motivation: Untargeted LC-MS metabolomics involves many preprocessing decisions with equally defensible options, but analysts typically commit to one pipeline. The impact of these hidden analytical choices on reported feature shortlists remains invisible and unquantified.
AI.method: A configuration-driven pipeline with (i) a ten-stage quality-control filter cascade logging each feature's fate, and (ii) a multiverse over four preprocessing philosophies × four feature-ranking methods with bootstrap stability selection and label-permutation testing. Only features recurring across paths enter a tiered consensus.
AI.result: On five breast-cancer cell lines (30,370 features), single pipelines returned 4-20 features with pairwise agreement as low as Jaccard = 0.05. Multiverse consensus retained 15 features (≥2/4 paths), one across all four paths. Two paths sharing normalization and drift-correction dominated the consensus. A pipeline-wide label-permutation test found zero false discoveries in 50 null permutations.
AI.conclusion: Reporting only preprocessing-robust features with a complete kept/dropped audit trail converts hidden analytical degrees of freedom into explicit, inspectable output. Limitations include single-batch design and the need for independent validation.

title: Rethinking Heterogeneous LLM Merging: A Weighted Model Averaging Perspective
summary: Can large language models with substantially different parameter spaces be merged by direct weighted averaging, without training or semantic alignment? Existing heterogeneous fusion methods typically introduce distillation, adapters, learned latent spaces, routing, or feature alignment, leaving open whether a simpler recipe can work for genuinely different billion-parameter checkpoints. We revisit this counterintuitive question through training-free dimensional adaptation followed by ratio-controlled interpolation. In union-style merging, we expand the smaller model into the larger parameter space; in intersection-style merging, we truncate the larger model into the smaller parameter space. Across Qwen-family model pairs and benchmarks covering mathematical reasoning, code generation, language understanding, commonsense reasoning, knowledge, and instruction following, deterministic expansion largely preserves the source model function, and small-ratio interpolation can improve over strong source checkpoints by transferring complementary capabilities. However, near-balanced interpolation often collapses, and task-level results reveal a seesaw effect in which gains on some capabilities coexist with regressions on others. These results show that simple parameter averaging, when paired with lightweight dimensional adaptation and carefully controlled ratios, is a surprisingly strong baseline for heterogeneous LLM merging, suggesting that the limits of direct weighted fusion may also bound what more complex heterogeneous merging methods can achieve at scale.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether large language models with different parameter spaces can be merged via simple direct weighted averaging without training or semantic alignment, using only dimensional adaptation and ratio-controlled interpolation. Results show that deterministic expansion preserves source model function, small-ratio interpolation can improve performance by transferring complementary capabilities, but balanced interpolation often collapses and reveals a seesaw effect across tasks.
AI.motivation: To determine whether simple, training-free weighted averaging can merge heterogeneous LLMs with different parameter spaces, challenging the prevailing assumption that complex methods (distillation, adapters, latent spaces, routing, feature alignment) are necessary.
AI.method: Training-free dimensional adaptation (expansion or truncation) followed by ratio-controlled interpolation between model checkpoints. Union-style merging expands the smaller model into the larger parameter space; intersection-style merging truncates the larger model into the smaller parameter space.
AI.result: Deterministic expansion largely preserves source model function; small-ratio interpolation can improve over strong source checkpoints via complementary capability transfer; near-balanced interpolation often collapses; task-level results exhibit a seesaw effect with gains on some capabilities and regressions on others.
AI.conclusion: Simple parameter averaging with lightweight dimensional adaptation and carefully controlled ratios is a surprisingly strong baseline for heterogeneous LLM merging, suggesting that the limits of direct weighted fusion may bound what more complex methods can achieve at scale.

title: Cross-Coordinate Correspondence Pruning for Image-to-Point Cloud Registration
summary: Recent detection-free approaches have shown significant efficacy in image-to-point cloud (I2P) registration by employing a coarse-to-fine matching pipeline. In the coarse stage, down-sampled image features and voxelized point cloud features are typically fused to establish initial coarse correspondences for subsequent refinement. However, existing methods largely overlook the critical role of point cloud density, which fundamentally dictates the quality of coarse correspondences and the final registration results. Specifically, excessively sparse point clouds lead to an insufficient number of inliers, while overly dense ones often introduce a high outlier ratio. Consequently, this creates an inherent density trade-off, thereby significantly limiting the registration accuracy of current approaches. For mitigating this trade-off, we propose a novel Cross-Coordinate Correspondences Pruning (CCP) strategy to acquire sufficient inliers while ensuring a low outlier ratio. To minimize interference from inter-modal coordinate discrepancies, we first project cross-coordinate coarse correspondences to the 2D image coordinate system for spatial unification. Subsequently, a lightweight pruning network is responsible for predicting the inlier confidences, which are used to filter coarse outliers, from coordinate geometric and modal feature dimensions. To maximize inlier recall, we further design a Multi-Density Point Ensemble (MDPE) strategy that consolidates and deduplicates pruned coarse correspondences across varying point cloud densities. Our method achieves a significant performance improvement, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods by at least 8.6% in Registration Recall across various benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Cross-Coordinate Correspondences Pruning (CCP) strategy and Multi-Density Point Ensemble (MDPE) to address the point cloud density trade-off in detection-free image-to-point cloud registration, achieving >8.6% improvement in Registration Recall over SOTA.
AI.motivation: Existing detection-free I2P registration methods overlook the critical role of point cloud density, which creates an inherent trade-off: sparse point clouds yield insufficient inliers while dense ones introduce high outlier ratios, limiting registration accuracy.
AI.method: (1) Cross-Coordinate Correspondences Pruning (CCP): project cross-coordinate coarse correspondences to 2D image coordinate system for spatial unification, then use a lightweight pruning network to predict inlier confidences from coordinate geometric and modal feature dimensions. (2) Multi-Density Point Ensemble (MDPE): consolidate and deduplicate pruned coarse correspondences across varying point cloud densities to maximize inlier recall.
AI.result: Surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods by at least 8.6% in Registration Recall across various benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Mitigating the point cloud density trade-off via CCP and MDPE significantly improves I2P registration accuracy, demonstrating the importance of addressing density issues in cross-modal matching.

title: Chebyshev Manifold Adaptation
summary: The paper presents a new parameter-efficient adaptation method called ChebyMA (Chebyshev Manifold Adaptation). ChebyMA adopts weight matrices through a multi-surface superposition of Chebyshev polynomial bases evaluated on learnable coordinates and combined via trainable coefficient matrices, replacing standard linear projections with highly expressive continuous function approximation. Theoretically, we establish an Approximation Expressivity Theorem, proving from the perspective of function approximation theory that single-manifold ChebyMA guarantees convergence in Frobenius norm error of reconstruction. Besides, drawing on Kolmogorov $n$-width intuition, we demonstrate the expressive advantages of multi-manifold superposition ($S > 1$) in decoupling high-dimensional complex features. Experimental results on Computer Vision CIFAR datasets(CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100)\cite{CIFAR} and Natural Language Processing (AG News, SST-2) datasets demonstrate that ChebyMA consistently achieves a superior parameter-accuracy Pareto front compared to standard full-parameter fine-tuning, LoRA\cite{LoRA}, TLoRA\cite{TLoRA}, and StelLA\cite{StelLA}. ChebyMA significantly outperforms other tested methods in tested datasets, validating its solid theoretical foundation for generality with purely vectorized computations.

AI.tldr: ChebyMA is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method using Chebyshev polynomial bases and multi-surface superposition to replace standard linear projections, with theoretical guarantees on expressivity and superior performance on CV and NLP benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To design a parameter-efficient adaptation method that surpasses existing methods (LoRA, TLoRA, StelLA) in the accuracy-parameter trade-off, grounded in function approximation theory and Kolmogorov n-width principles.
AI.method: ChebyMA learns weight matrices via multi-surface superposition of Chebyshev polynomial bases evaluated on learnable coordinates, combined via trainable coefficient matrices, enabling continuous function approximation instead of standard linear projections.
AI.result: On CIFAR-10/100 and AG News/SST-2, ChebyMA achieves superior parameter-accuracy Pareto front compared to full fine-tuning, LoRA, TLoRA, and StelLA, consistently outperforming all tested baselines.
AI.conclusion: ChebyMA provides a theoretically grounded, purely vectorized parameter-efficient adaptation method with strong empirical generalization, validated on both CV and NLP tasks.

title: AdaHome: An Adaptive Smart Home Assistant using Local Small Language Models
summary: Smart home assistants interpret a wide range of user commands, from explicit device control to underspecified and preference dependent requests. While recent systems based on Large Language Models (LLMs) improve this capability, they often rely on heavyweight reasoning pipelines and cloud-based deployment, limiting their efficiency and suitability for resource-constrained environments, and raising privacy concerns. In addition, existing approaches provide limited support for stable long-term personalization. To address these issues, we present AdaHome, an adaptive smart home assistant designed for locally deployed small language models in smart home environments. Rather than applying complex reasoning uniformly, AdaHome introduces an intent-aware planning framework that dynamically routes commands either to straightforward prompt-based or lightweight reasoning-based components. For commands requiring interpretation, we adopt a Chain-of-Draft strategy to enable efficient and stable decision-making. To support personalization, we further propose a preference adaptation mechanism that learns from user feedback over time without requiring prompt augmentation or model retraining. We evaluate AdaHome against representative LLM-based baselines under a unified small model setting. AdaHome achieves substantially higher accuracy on direct commands (86.7%) while reducing latency by up to 3$\times$. Furthermore, it maintains competitive performance on ambiguous inputs with lower computational cost. In multi-turn scenarios, AdaHome achieves 88% preference consistency, compared to 52.5% for a prompt augmentation baseline.

AI.tldr: AdaHome is a locally-deployed smart home assistant using small language models with an intent-aware planning framework that dynamically routes commands to appropriate processing components, achieving higher accuracy (86.7%) on direct commands, 3× latency reduction, and 88% preference consistency in multi-turn scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based smart home assistants rely on heavyweight reasoning pipelines and cloud deployment, which are inefficient for resource-constrained environments, raise privacy concerns, and provide limited support for stable long-term personalization.
AI.method: AdaHome introduces an intent-aware planning framework that dynamically routes commands to either simple prompt-based or lightweight reasoning-based components, employs Chain-of-Draft for efficient decision-making, and uses a preference adaptation mechanism that learns from user feedback over time without prompt augmentation or model retraining.
AI.result: AdaHome achieves 86.7% accuracy on direct commands with 3× latency reduction, maintains competitive performance on ambiguous inputs with lower computational cost, and achieves 88% preference consistency in multi-turn scenarios versus 52.5% for prompt augmentation baselines.
AI.conclusion: AdaHome demonstrates that locally deployed small language models with efficient routing and adaptive personalization can outperform cloud-based LLM approaches in smart home environments, particularly for direct commands and long-term preference consistency.

title: Induce to Empower: Improving Lightweight Baselines via Foundation Model Induction for Generalized Polyp Segmentation
summary: Automated polyp segmentation in colonoscopy continues to pose challenges due to substantial appearance variations and indistinct polyp boundaries. Although emerging foundation models (FMs) such as DINOv2, SAM, and OneFormer, demonstrate remarkable generalization capabilities, their direct transfer to the polyp segmentation task and deployment in real-time clinical settings are difficult due to lack of large-scale labeled data and high computational demands. In addition, adopting multiple FMs together raises concerns, even though they encode complementary semantic and structural information. While lightweight models, including U-Net, PraNet and U-Net++, are computationally efficient, they often struggle to generalize across datasets due to limited representational capacity. To address this gap, we propose Lite-Polyp Inductor (Lite-Pi), a novel foundation model induction framework that significantly enhances lightweight polyp segmentation baselines. Our proposed framework generates FM-specific prototype representations and aligns them semantically with the corresponding foundation model priors through reconstruction-based supervision. Subsequently, transformer-based fusion is introduced to highlight the polyp relevant representations, including salient boundary information, while preserving complementary semantic cues. Extensive experiments across five polyp segmentation benchmark datasets demonstrate that Lite-π significantly improves lightweight baselines, achieving superior generalization performance with minimal computational overhead and thereby, offering a practical solution for generalized polyp segmentation. Our code is available at GitHub. https://github.com/lostinrepo/Lite-Pi

AI.tldr: Lite-Pi is a foundation model induction framework that enhances lightweight polyp segmentation models by generating and aligning FM-specific prototype representations with foundation model priors, using transformer-based fusion to boost generalization and boundary detection with minimal computational overhead.
AI.motivation: Foundation models (DINOv2, SAM, OneFormer) offer strong generalization but are impractical for real-time polyp segmentation due to high compute and data demands, while lightweight models (U-Net, PraNet) are efficient but lack generalization across datasets. The gap motivates a framework that transfers FM knowledge to lightweight baselines efficiently.
AI.method: Lite-Pi generates FM-specific prototype representations and aligns them semantically with foundation model priors via reconstruction-based supervision, then applies transformer-based fusion to emphasize polyp-relevant features (including boundary information) while preserving complementary semantic cues.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on five polyp segmentation benchmarks show Lite-Pi significantly improves lightweight baselines' generalization performance with minimal computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: Lite-Pi offers a practical, efficient solution for generalized polyp segmentation by inducting foundation model knowledge into lightweight models, balancing accuracy and computational cost.

title: CoEvoP&R: Co-Evolving Placement Objectives with Routing Feedback via Large Language Models
comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Corresponding author: Weihua Xiao
summary: Analytical placers rely on differentiable objective functions to guide placement, typically combining intermediate surrogate metrics such as half-perimeter wirelength (HPWL) and cell-density penalties. However, these placement-stage surrogates remain misaligned with downstream routed and timing quality. Prior work reduces this gap with human-designed terms or learned black-box surrogates, but the former requires expert retuning and the latter is difficult to explain, debug, or deploy in analytical placement flows. CoEvoP&R addresses these limitations with a large language model (LLM)-based framework that automatically evolves analytical placement objectives. At each generation, the prompt combines the restricted objective interface, baseline context, and archived prior candidates with routing-related feedback from placement, timing proxy, and routing tools. The LLM proposes readable differentiable objectives, which are embedded and validated in DREAMPlace, evaluated through a timing proxy and an actual router, and stored with their feedback to guide later generations. Across eight ChiP-Bench Nangate45 designs and three seeds, CoEvoP&R reduces post-route routed wirelength and congestion by 16.9% and 36.7%, with gains of 0.70 ns in worst negative slack and a 912 ns reduction in total negative slack magnitude over native DREAMPlace. Across eight ICCAD 2015 Superblue designs, it reduces post-route routed wirelength and congestion by 5.4% and 23.2%. Code is available at https://github.com/FCHXWH823/CoEvoP-R.git.

AI.tldr: CoEvoP&R is an LLM-based framework that automatically evolves analytical placement objectives by combining LLM proposals with routing-related feedback, reducing post-route wirelength (16.9%), congestion (36.7%), and improving timing (0.70 ns WNS) over native DREAMPlace across multiple design benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Traditional analytical placers use surrogate objectives (HPWL, cell-density) that are misaligned with downstream routed and timing quality. Prior solutions either require expert retuning (human-designed terms) or are difficult to explain/deploy (black-box surrogates). The authors aim to bridge this gap automatically.
AI.method: An LLM-based evolutionary framework where at each generation, a prompt combining restricted objective interface, baseline context, and archived prior candidates with routing-related feedback is fed to an LLM. The LLM proposes readable differentiable objectives, which are validated in DREAMPlace, evaluated through timing proxy and actual router, and stored with feedback to guide later generations.
AI.result: On eight ChiP-Bench Nangate45 designs: 16.9% reduction in routed wirelength, 36.7% reduction in congestion, 0.70 ns improvement in WNS, 912 ns reduction in TNS magnitude. On eight ICCAD 2015 Superblue designs: 5.4% wirelength reduction and 23.2% congestion reduction over native DREAMPlace.
AI.conclusion: CoEvoP&R demonstrates that LLM-guided evolution of differentiable placement objectives can effectively bridge the gap between surrogate metrics and actual routing/timing quality, outperforming native DREAMPlace without requiring manual re-tuning or opaque black-box surrogates.

title: The Shared Discovery Paradox: How a One-Answer Rule Turns Better Information into Worse Search
comment: 29 pages, 4 figures. Code, data, and an interactive guide: https://github.com/yoheinakajima/shared-discovery-paradox
summary: Organizations often pool dispersed information into one ranking and then allow many agents to act on that shared view. In a discovery problem, this can improve beliefs while reducing coverage. We develop an exactly solvable benchmark with sixteen boxes, one target, eight searchers, and noisy private clues. Pooling raises the accuracy of the best single recommendation from 0.20 to 0.3835, but repeating that recommendation lowers group discovery from 0.8322 under decentralized clue-following to 0.3835. A coordinated eight-action portfolio using the same pooled reports reaches 0.8594, and seven coordinated actions recover the decentralized benchmark. The paradox is a protocol failure, not an information failure: a one-answer rule compresses a portfolio of available actions into one repeated choice. We then replace the planner with self-interested searchers who split a prize. The equal-split game is a potential game. Its anonymous symmetric equilibrium obeys a water-filling rule. In the canonical instance it achieves 0.5991: strictly above consensus, but below both private search and the planner. The exact mixed price of anarchy is 2 - 1/N. A sole-rescue reward, which pays only an agent who covers the target alone, makes every pure Nash equilibrium first-best. Finally, a latent common-cue model shows how correlated reports collapse effective discovery channels. The centralized planner gain rises strictly with copying, and in the canonical environment the symmetric market overtakes decentralized report-following at copying probability c = 0.788462. In a proportional large-market limit the five-protocol ordering survives exactly: consensus discovery vanishes while blind, market, private, and portfolio search converge to 0.500, 0.547, 0.847, and 0.874. The contribution is a compact benchmark that separates information, allocation, incentives, and dependence into exact, reusable quantities.

AI.tldr: The paper develops an exactly solvable benchmark model of discovery with 16 boxes, one target, eight searchers, and noisy private clues. It shows that pooling information into a single ranking improves belief accuracy but reduces group discovery due to repeated use of the same recommendation — a protocol failure. Coordinated portfolios recover performance. Self-interested searchers under equal splitting achieve intermediate outcomes (price of anarchy = 2 - 1/N). A sole-rescue reward restores first-best efficiency. A latent common-cue model shows correlated reports degrade discovery. Five protocols (consensus, market, private, portfolio, blind) are compared, and ordering survives in a large-market limit.
AI.motivation: To understand how pooling dispersed information into a single ranking affects group discovery, and to disentangle information failure from protocol failure in organizations where many agents act on a shared view.
AI.method: Exactly solvable benchmark model with 16 boxes, 1 target, 8 searchers, and noisy private clues. Game-theoretic analysis (potential game, water-filling equilibrium, price of anarchy). Large-market proportional limit analysis.
AI.result: Pooling raises single recommendation accuracy from 0.20 to 0.3835 but repeated consensus lowers discovery from 0.8322 (decentralized) to 0.3835. Coordinated portfolio reaches 0.8594. Equal-split game yields 0.5991. Price of anarchy = 2 - 1/N. Sole-rescue reward achieves first-best. At copying probability c=0.788462 market overtakes decentralized. In large-market limit: consensus→0, blind→0.500, market→0.547, private→0.847, portfolio→0.874.
AI.conclusion: The paradox is a protocol failure (one-answer rule compressing a portfolio into repeated choice), not an information failure. Incentive design (sole-rescue) can restore efficiency. The five-protocol ordering is robust in large markets.

title: CORAL: Learning Amyloid Fibril Ligand Docking with Cooperative Binding Rewards
summary: A hallmark of neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's and Parkinson's is the aberrant aggregation of proteins into amyloid fibrils, and small molecules that selectively bind to these fibrils hold promise as diagnostics, imaging probes, and therapeutics. Predicting how such ligands bind to fibril targets, however, presents two fundamental challenges. First, resolved co-crystal structures of amyloid-ligand complexes are exceptionally scarce; even with recent advances in cryo-EM only a handful have been structurally characterized, making supervised training of docking models impractical for this target class. Second, amyloid fibrils present a binding mode fundamentally different from globular proteins: ligands intercalate into longitudinal cross-$β$ grooves and stack cooperatively along the fibril axis, a geometry that existing docking models are not designed to capture. To address these challenges, we present CORAL (COopeRative Amyloid Ligand docking), a reinforcement learning framework that trains a generative docking model to produce ligand pose distributions tailored to the cross-$β$ groove geometry. Our reward explicitly incorporates cooperative ligand-ligand stacking energy alongside protein-ligand docking affinity, directly capturing the distinctive binding geometry of amyloid fibrils. We further introduce a curated evaluation set of amyloid-ligand complexes constructed from model-generated poses validated by domain experts. Experiments on both experimentally resolved structures and this evaluation set demonstrate improved pose quality and binding affinity correlation over existing docking baselines.

AI.tldr: CORAL is a reinforcement learning framework for docking ligands onto amyloid fibrils, addressing the scarcity of co-crystal structures and the unique cross-β groove binding geometry by incorporating cooperative ligand-ligand stacking into the reward function.
AI.motivation: Amyloid fibril-ligand docking is challenging due to (1) extreme scarcity of resolved co-crystal structures preventing supervised training, and (2) the unique binding mode where ligands intercalate into longitudinal cross-β grooves and stack cooperatively, which traditional docking models cannot capture.
AI.method: A reinforcement learning framework (CORAL) that trains a generative docking model to produce ligand pose distributions for amyloid fibrils. The reward function combines protein-ligand docking affinity with cooperative ligand-ligand stacking energy. A curated evaluation set was constructed from model-generated poses validated by domain experts.
AI.result: CORAL demonstrates improved pose quality and binding affinity correlation over existing docking baselines on both experimentally resolved structures and the curated evaluation set.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning with a reward that explicitly models cooperative stacking along the fibril axis enables effective amyloid-ligand docking without requiring supervised training on scarce co-crystal structures.

title: WorldCupArena: Fine-Grained Evaluation of Language Models and Deep-Research Agents on Football Forecasting
summary: Predicting a football match before kickoff requires more than knowing past results: a model must use changing information and make a clear prediction before the answer is available. We present WorldCupArena, a dynamic benchmark for language models and deep-research agents. The 2026 FIFA World Cup is its first evaluation, and the same process can be reused for future leagues and cups. Before each match, a model either receives a common evidence package or searches for information itself. It predicts the result and score, likely players and events, match statistics, and the outcome of the competition. After the match, these predictions are compared with the recorded result. We report result accuracy, exact-score accuracy, and a scoreline score that gives some credit when a predicted score is close but not exact, together with scores for the other prediction tasks. Across 104 matches and 13 systems, models with similar result accuracy differ more clearly on detailed predictions. Compared with betting-market and human-fan baselines, the best system shows only small gains in result and exact-score accuracy, but a clearer gain in Scoreline. New schedules can be added as they begin, allowing the benchmark to evaluate future models without using outcomes that are already known. Code, prompts, predictions, and evaluation scripts are open sourced at https://github.com/wzk1015/WorldCupArena.

AI.tldr: WorldCupArena is a dynamic benchmark for evaluating language models and deep-research agents on football match prediction, using the 2026 FIFA World Cup (and extendable to future events). It tests models on result accuracy, exact-score accuracy, scoreline closeness, and detailed predictions (players, events, statistics) across 104 matches and 13 systems, showing that scoreline scores better differentiate model performance than result accuracy alone.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation methods for language models often rely on static datasets where answers are already known, failing to test a model's ability to use changing, real-time information and make predictions before outcomes are available. The authors aim to create a dynamic, reproducible benchmark that assesses predictive reasoning under realistic temporal constraints.
AI.method: The benchmark operates on a per-match basis: before each match, a model either receives a shared evidence package or conducts its own information search. The model must predict the match result, exact score, likely players and events, match statistics, and competition outcome. After the match, predictions are compared to recorded results using metrics: result accuracy, exact-score accuracy, a scoreline score (rewarding near-exact predictions), and scores for other prediction tasks. The benchmark was tested on 104 matches across 13 systems.
AI.result: Models with similar result accuracy showed more pronounced differences on detailed predictions (e.g., scoreline score). Compared to betting-market and human-fan baselines, the best system achieved only small gains in result and exact-score accuracy but a clearer improvement in scoreline score. The benchmark supports adding new schedules dynamically to avoid data leakage from already-known outcomes.
AI.conclusion: WorldCupArena provides a reusable, dynamic evaluation framework for assessing predictive capabilities of language models in real-world, time-sensitive settings. The scoreline metric offers finer-grained differentiation than traditional accuracy measures. The benchmark is open-sourced and extendable to future leagues and cups.

title: VecFontLLM: Anchor-Guided Direct Synthesis of Chinese Vector Fonts
summary: Direct generation of Chinese vector fonts is a challenging and ongoing problem. A Chinese vector glyph contains complex component structure, anchor layout, and Bézier curve details, which work at different scales, but a standard vector sequence writes them together in one long sequence, making the task of vector font synthesis challenging. Existing direct vector generators often fail on complex characters, while raster-domain methods must vectorize the synthesized glyph images afterward. To address the above-mentioned problem, this paper proposes VecFontLLM, an anchor-guided multimodal large language model for direct few-shot synthesis of Chinese vector fonts. Our key idea is to generate vector glyphs through anchors rather than a standard vector sequence. Specifically, the proposed VecFontLLM first predicts and refines an anchor scaffold that fixes the coarse layout of components and contours, and then completes Bézier control points to recover local curvature and style. At test time, a confidence-guided generation chain samples multiple component candidates and continues synthesis from the highest-confidence one, improving stability for complex glyphs. This work demonstrates, for the first time, high-quality few-shot synthesis of complex Chinese vector glyphs directly in the vector domain, without raster generation or vectorization. Experiments on several Chinese font datasets show substantial improvements over existing vector font synthesis methods, competitive glyph rendering quality against raster-domain baselines, and vector command distributions close to real fonts.

AI.tldr: VecFontLLM is an anchor-guided multimodal LLM for direct few-shot synthesis of Chinese vector fonts, which first predicts an anchor scaffold for coarse layout and then completes Bézier control points, using a confidence-guided generation chain for stability, achieving high-quality results without rasterization/vectorization.
AI.motivation: Direct generation of Chinese vector fonts is challenging due to complex component structure, anchor layout, and Bézier curve details working at different scales, while standard vector sequences write them together in one long sequence. Existing vector generators often fail on complex characters, and raster-domain methods require post-vectorization.
AI.method: VecFontLLM first predicts and refines an anchor scaffold to fix coarse layout of components and contours, then completes Bézier control points for local curvature and style. A confidence-guided generation chain samples multiple component candidates and continues from the highest-confidence one, improving stability for complex glyphs.
AI.result: Substantial improvements over existing vector font synthesis methods, competitive glyph rendering quality against raster-domain baselines, and vector command distributions close to real fonts.
AI.conclusion: This work demonstrates, for the first time, high-quality few-shot synthesis of complex Chinese vector glyphs directly in the vector domain, without raster generation or vectorization.

title: Grounded verification of chemical and materials reasoning: detection is the bottleneck
summary: Large language models confabulate chemical objects (molecular formulas, space groups, formation energies) in fluent reasoning traces, concentrated on long-tail entities where confidence is least trustworthy. Deterministic, database-grounded verification can catch and repair such errors without the coverage cost of blanket retrieval; the binding constraint, we find, is detection, not repair. Our tiered verifier extracts each checkable claim, checks it against authoritative databases and physics, and feeds the reference into a gated correction loop. Across four models and 528 condition-pinned prompts, gated correction cuts committed-formula error from 22% to 4% at $3.2\times$ fewer retrievals than blanket augmentation, beating a conversational oracle. Repair succeeds wherever a flag fires (80--97%); the bottleneck is in-loop detection recall. Grounding improves the final answer only when the verifier's scope reaches the deliverable (83% to 90%), and the lift appears only where extractable long-tail error exists: absent on near-ceiling physical constants, large on isotope half-lives (11% to 0%).

AI.tldr: LLMs generate incorrect chemical information in reasoning traces, especially for rare entities. A tiered verifier that extracts claims, checks them against databases/physics, and applies gated correction reduces formula errors from 22% to 4% with 3.2× fewer retrievals than blanket augmentation. Repair is highly effective (80–97%) when detection succeeds, but detection recall is the bottleneck. Grounding improves answers only when the verifier's scope matches the deliverable, with gains concentrated on long-tail entities.
AI.motivation: LLMs confabulate chemical objects (molecular formulas, space groups, formation energies) in fluent reasoning traces, especially on long-tail entities where confidence is low. Existing blanket retrieval approaches have high coverage cost. The authors aim to determine whether deterministic, database-grounded verification can catch and repair such errors more efficiently.
AI.method: A tiered verifier that extracts each checkable claim from LLM outputs, verifies them against authoritative databases and physics laws, and feeds reference information into a gated correction loop. The approach was tested across four models and 528 condition-pinned prompts, comparing against blanket augmentation and a conversational oracle.
AI.result: Gated correction reduced committed-formula error from 22% to 4% with 3.2× fewer retrievals than blanket augmentation, beating a conversational oracle. Repair succeeds 80–97% when a flag fires, but the bottleneck is in-loop detection recall. Grounding improves the final answer only when the verifier's scope reaches the deliverable (83% to 90%), with gains concentrated on long-tail entities: absent on near-ceiling physical constants, large on isotope half-lives (11% to 0%).
AI.conclusion: Deterministic, database-grounded verification can efficiently catch and repair LLM confabulations in chemistry, with detection being the binding constraint rather than repair. The approach offers significant efficiency gains over blanket retrieval augmentation, though its benefits are most pronounced for long-tail, less confident entities.

title: Judge-dependent safety gains and model-specific helpfulness costs of evidence-sufficiency prompting in clinical LLMs
summary:
Background: LLM judges increasingly score whether clinical language models give overconfident answers under incomplete evidence, yet whether a measured "safety gain" reflects real behavior change or the judge's calibration is unresolved. Using a structured evidence-sufficiency prompt as a test case, we asked whether it reduces unsafe overconfident answers, how far that effect depends on the scoring judge, and what it costs in helpfulness.
  Methods: In a retrospective public-data benchmark (Real-POCQi, HealthBench, MedRBench), four models (GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.8, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Grok 4.3) answered a fully paired common panel (1,200 cells) with a standard prompt and the wrapper. The pre-specified endpoint was the paired reduction in unsafe overconfidence scored by the primary judge (GPT-5.4-nano); secondary analyses added a different-family judge (Claude Sonnet 5), a correctness judge, matched scaffold controls, and a blinded three-clinician review.
  Results: Unsafe overconfidence fell from 49.3% to 24.7%, a paired reduction of 24.7 points (95% CI 21.8-27.7; p<0.001), robust in direction across models and paraphrases. Magnitude was judge-dependent: Sonnet agreed on direction but nearly halved the effect (+13.1 points), with one-directional disagreement. Blinded clinicians characterized the primary judge as a high-sensitivity (1.00), low-specificity (0.55) screen, not a calibrated rate. The gain carried a model-specific helpfulness cost (correct diagnosis 80.3% to 50.3%): near-free for GPT-5.5, near-total for Gemini (-58 points). Matched scaffold controls showed genuine behavior change, not judge circularity.
  Conclusions: LLM-judged clinical safety effects should be reported as directional and relative, anchored to human review and evaluated jointly with helpfulness, not as calibrated absolute rates. This does not establish clinical deployment readiness.

AI.tldr: LLM-judged safety gains from evidence-sufficiency prompts are directionally robust but magnitude depends heavily on the scoring judge; the effect reflects genuine behavior change but carries model-specific helpfulness costs, and should be reported as directional/relative rather than calibrated absolute rates.
AI.motivation: To resolve whether measured "safety gains" from LLM judges reflect real behavior change or scoring judge calibration, using a structured evidence-sufficiency prompt as a test case.
AI.method: Retrospective benchmark on three datasets (Real-POCQi, HealthBench, MedRBench) with four models and 1,200 paired cells; primary endpoint was unsafe overconfidence reduction scored by GPT-5.4-nano, with secondary judges (Claude Sonnet 5), correctness judge, scaffold controls, and blinded clinician review.
AI.result: Unsafe overconfidence dropped 24.7 points (49.3%→24.7%, p<0.001), but magnitude was judge-dependent (Sonnet halved the effect to +13.1 points). Clinicians rated the primary judge as high-sensitivity (1.00), low-specificity (0.55). Helpfulness cost varied drastically (0 to -58 points across models). Scaffold controls confirmed genuine behavior change.
AI.conclusion: LLM-judged clinical safety effects should be reported as directional and relative, anchored to human review and evaluated jointly with helpfulness, not as calibrated absolute rates. Findings do not establish clinical deployment readiness.

title: PACE: Polar Axis-Conditioned Estimation for PairUAV Relative Localization
summary: PairUAV relative localization maps two UAV images to a polar navigation command. Although heading and range share the same pairwise pose context, treating them as homogeneous coordinates forces both outputs to use the same decoder evidence and optimization state. Controlled readout probes reveal a different structure: the two axes favor different decoder-depth combinations, their best checkpoints disagree on 80.8% of a validation trajectory, and range errors exhibit a distinct high-error tail. We introduce method, Polar Axis-Conditioned Estimation, which retains a shared Reloc3r-style pair representation while assigning axis-specific readout interfaces. Heading uses mid/late relational evidence, whereas range remains attached to a direct late metric path. On the official hidden test, the strongest released raw predictor scores 0.002460; the complementary PAAER predictor scores 0.002514 with a slightly lower angle error. Deterministic challenge packaging, reported separately from learned estimation, yields the final score of 0.001874. Code, checkpoints, predictions, and reconstruction tools are available at https://github.com/zerong7777-boop/PairUAV-PACE.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Polar Axis-Conditioned Estimation (PACE) for PairUAV relative localization, showing that heading and range estimation benefit from different decoder depths despite sharing a common pair representation, leading to improved performance on hidden test data.
AI.motivation: Existing methods treat heading and range as homogeneous coordinates in pairwise UAV relative localization, forcing both outputs to use the same decoder evidence and optimization, whereas controlled probes reveal that the two axes favor different decoder-depth combinations and exhibit different error structures.
AI.method: Polar Axis-Conditioned Estimation (PACE) retains a shared Reloc3r-style pair representation but assigns axis-specific readout interfaces: heading uses mid/late relational evidence, while range remains attached to a direct late metric path.
AI.result: The strongest raw predictor scores 0.002460 on the official hidden test; the complementary PAAER predictor scores 0.002514 with lower angle error; deterministic challenge packaging yields a final score of 0.001874. Best checkpoints disagree on 80.8% of a validation trajectory.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling axis-specific readout from a shared representation improves pairwise UAV relative localization, and the approach achieves strong results on the official benchmark.

title: Kernelized Linear Attention: Breaking the Capacity Wall with Symmetric Cones
summary: Linear attention promises constant-time recurrent inference but degrades sharply on associative recall. We formulate attention recall as a spherical-packing problem and introduce Kernelized Linear Attention Activations (KATA), a framework whose feature maps are derived from first principles by certifying nonnegative attention weights through a self-dual homogeneous cone. Building on this observation, we show that rank-one positive semi-definite (PSD) features offer a favorable capacity--interference tradeoff. KATA recovers a parameter-free convex output gate and characterizes associative capacity through the Welch interference floor. For tolerances above this floor, KATA enlarges the state without adding parameters and admits spherical codes with exponentially many keys in the projection dimension. We implement KATA as fused Triton kernels at two operating points: a flash-attention-style forward up to ${\sim}1.6\times$ FlashAttention-2 throughput, and an exact $O(T)$ chunked-state form that reaches ${\sim}11\times$ FlashAttention-2 forward throughput at $131$k tokens. An associative scan of the first-order feature lowers the inter-chunk recurrence depth to $O(\log(T/C))$ for chunk size $C$ and averages ${\sim}2.4\times$ the throughput of a matched sequential linear-attention baseline. On long-range MQAR and repeated-key overwrite, several KATA variants outperform Gated DeltaNet, with parameter counts and state sizes reported alongside accuracy. Induction preserves near-perfect recall, while kernel benchmarks show that the maps can be implemented efficiently. KATA retains $0.985$ MQAR at a $16\times$ out-of-distribution length, approaching the softmax with roughly one quarter of the KV-cache entries. Experiments on 340M-parameter LLMs reveal a feature-dependent fluency trade-off and clarify how positional embeddings, delta rules, and decay gates interact with feature geometry.

AI.tldr: KATA introduces kernelized linear attention with rank-one PSD features that achieve near-softmax associative recall while enabling up to 11× FlashAttention-2 throughput at 131k tokens, with strong long-range MQAR performance and exponential key capacity.
AI.motivation: Linear attention suffers from poor associative recall despite efficient recurrent inference. The paper aims to bridge this gap by deriving feature maps from first principles that certify nonnegative attention weights through self-dual homogeneous cones.
AI.method: Formulates attention recall as a spherical-packing problem; introduces rank-one PSD features with a convex output gate; characterizes associative capacity via Welch interference floor; implements fused Triton kernels with flash-attention-style forward and exact O(T) chunked-state form with O(log(T/C)) recurrence depth.
AI.result: Up to ~1.6× FlashAttention-2 throughput (flash mode), ~11× at 131k tokens (chunked mode); ~2.4× sequential linear-attention baseline; 0.985 MQAR at 16× out-of-distribution length; outperforms Gated DeltaNet on long-range MQAR and repeated-key overwrite.
AI.conclusion: KATA demonstrates that linear attention can approach softmax-level associative recall with significant throughput gains, revealing feature-dependent fluency trade-offs and interaction between positional embeddings, delta rules, and decay gates with feature geometry.

title: Can We Break LLMs Out of Self-Loops? Fine-Grained Reasoning Control with Activation Steering
summary: Extended reasoning has become standard for frontier Large Language Models (LLMs), yet the trajectories these models produce remain largely uncontrollable. Existing methods for shaping how a model reasons are prompt based approaches and operate at the input level, offering no fine-grained control over the reasoning process itself. Related work analyzes and discovers latent transition dynamics in the reasoning traces from Large Language Models. Building on this, we statistically characterize these states, and show that failure trajectories get stuck in self-loops, exhausting the token budget without progress toward the final answer. To intervene on these failures, We propose SOPHIA: Steering Of reasoning Processes via Hidden-state Intervention and Activations. We treat each reasoning trace as a sequence of latent states rather than an unstructured texts, and investigate whether inference time interventions can provide fine-grained control over the self-looping reasoning process. We classify every prefix to a latent state, record step level transitions, and use them to construct a bank of steering vectors indexed by state pairs. At inference time, a controller infers the current state and, given a target state, retrieves the corresponding vector and can also detect self-loops online from the transition structure to prevent the model from sinking into a reasoning black hole. Through extensive experiments, our method reliably intervenes on self-loop failures, with steering vectors that generalize to different state pairs. End task accuracy and token efficiency indicate that fine-grained controllability results in better reasoning quality.

AI.tldr: SOPHIA provides fine-grained control over LLM reasoning by detecting self-loop failure states via latent state analysis and applying inference-time steering interventions to prevent token waste and improve reasoning quality.
AI.motivation: Existing methods for shaping LLM reasoning are prompt-based, operating only at the input level with no fine-grained control over the reasoning process itself. Failure trajectories (e.g., self-loops) exhaust token budgets without progress, and there is no mechanism to intervene on such failures during inference.
AI.method: Treats reasoning traces as sequences of latent states. Classifies every prefix to a latent state, records step-level transitions, and builds a bank of steering vectors indexed by state pairs. At inference, a controller infers the current state, retrieves the appropriate steering vector for a target state, and detects self-loops online to trigger intervention.
AI.result: SOPHIA reliably intervenes on self-loop failures; steering vectors generalize across different state pairs. End-task accuracy and token efficiency improve, demonstrating that fine-grained controllability enhances reasoning quality.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained, inference-time control over reasoning processes is feasible and beneficial, offering a path to mitigate reasoning failures like self-loops that degrade LLM performance.

title: MIS-HCC: Hierarchical Channel Clustering for Efficient Medical Image Segmentation
summary: Medical image segmentation models require both high accuracy and lightweight design to accommodate real-world medical applications. The deployment of these models on resource-limited medical platforms remains a significant challenge due to their high computational and parameter requirements. Existing pruning methods for model compression mostly overlook the intrinsic connections and similarity between the internal structures of complex deep neural networks. As a result, compressed models may not effectively retain the basic features of the pretrained network. To solve this problem, we propose a hierarchical clustering compression method for medical image segmentation models (MIS-HCC). This approach employs hierarchical clustering to partition channels and fuse their parameters efficiently. Specifically, it leverages the Wasserstein distance to represent similarity of channels within layers of pre-trained network, forming a similarity matrix that guides the clustering process. Channels within each cluster are then fused to produce a compressed network. Experimental results on three medical image datasets application demonstrate that MIS-HCC outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and compression efficiency, offering an effective solution for deploying medical image segmentation models on resource-limited medical platforms.

AI.tldr: Proposes MIS-HCC, a hierarchical clustering compression method for medical image segmentation models that uses Wasserstein distance to measure channel similarity and fuses similar channels to produce lightweight, accurate models suitable for resource-limited platforms.
AI.motivation: Medical image segmentation models need both high accuracy and lightweight design for deployment on resource-limited platforms. Existing pruning methods overlook intrinsic connections and similarity between internal structures of deep neural networks, causing compressed models to fail in retaining basic pretrained features.
AI.method: MIS-HCC employs hierarchical clustering to partition channels within layers using Wasserstein distance as a similarity metric, constructing a similarity matrix to guide clustering, then fuses channels within each cluster to produce a compressed network.
AI.result: Outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both accuracy and compression efficiency on three medical image datasets.
AI.conclusion: MIS-HCC offers an effective solution for deploying medical image segmentation models on resource-limited medical platforms by balancing compression and accuracy through hierarchical clustering-based channel fusion.

title: Decoder-Preserving Sparse Autoencoders: Which Readouts Survive Sparse Compression?
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) compress model activations into sparse codes, but equal reconstruction error and sparsity can preserve different linearly decodable signals. We formalize this ambiguity as a matrix-valued distortion between optimal ridge-prediction operators and train decoder-preserving SAEs by combining this distortion with reconstruction loss. In a rank relaxation, an isotropic task prior saturates per-mode omission costs without changing PCA's ordering, whereas a structured prior can change which modes are retained. A controlled sparse experiment shows that a declared prior protects held-out combinations from its task subspace. On GPT-2 small block 8, DPSAE reduces held-out decoder distortion by 10.6--11.4% across three paired runs while matching reconstruction NMSE. The same checkpoints pass an average natural-text output-KL noninferiority test, but one matched Pythia pair shows no improvement in probes restricted to a few sparse features. These results show that reconstruction quality does not determine which refitted linear readouts survive sparse compression, and that readout preservation is distinct from learning cleaner benchmark concepts or preserving every frozen-model behavior.

AI.tldr: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can yield different sparse codes with identical reconstruction error and sparsity, preserving different linearly decodable signals. The paper proposes DPSAE, which adds a matrix-valued distortion between optimal ridge-prediction operators to training loss. DPSAE reduces held-out decoder distortion by 10.6–11.4% on GPT-2 small while matching reconstruction NMSE, showing reconstruction quality does not determine which linear readouts survive sparse compression.
AI.motivation: SAEs can achieve equal reconstruction error and sparsity while preserving different linearly decodable signals, creating an ambiguity that needs formalization and control.
AI.method: Formalize the ambiguity as matrix-valued distortion between optimal ridge-prediction operators; train decoder-preserving SAEs (DPSAE) by combining this distortion with reconstruction loss, using rank relaxation and isotropic/structured task priors.
AI.result: On GPT-2 small block 8, DPSAE reduces held-out decoder distortion by 10.6–11.4% across three paired runs while matching reconstruction NMSE; passes natural-text output-KL noninferiority test; one Pythia pair shows no improvement in probes restricted to few sparse features.
AI.conclusion: Reconstruction quality does not determine which refitted linear readouts survive sparse compression; readout preservation is distinct from learning cleaner benchmark concepts or preserving every frozen-model behavior.

title: Orthogonal Knowledge Refreshing for Domain-Incremental Object Detection
summary: Domain-incremental object detection (DIOD) requires models to continually adapt to new domains while preserving prior knowledge. Recently, parameter-efficient fine-tuning offers a promising avenue, wherein a pre-trained model is frozen and a small number of learnable parameters are injected for downstream tasks. However, these methods risk overwriting critical past knowledge, triggering inter-domain interference and performance degradation. To address this challenge, we propose Orthogonal Knowledge Refreshing (OKR), a simple yet effective framework for DIOD. OKR incrementally constructs independent domain-specific subspaces via dedicated low-rank branches for each domain, which are seamlessly fused for a holistic decision, enabling conflict-free capacity expansion without domain selection during inference. To minimize knowledge interference during fusion, we present a gradient-based orthogonal refreshing strategy that projects gradient updates of new domains onto the orthogonal complement of the fused historical subspace, supporting continual adaptation without forgetting. Moreover, to mitigate semantic fragmentation across domains, we enforce topology-aware consistency, aligning the semantic structures of old and new domains. Extensive experiments validate the superiority of OKR, outperforming the best exemplar-free method by significant margins of +5.6% and +6.5% mAP on the Pascal VOC and BDD100K series, respectively.

AI.tldr: OKR proposes orthogonal low-rank branches with gradient projection and topology-aware consistency for exemplar-free domain-incremental object detection, achieving +5.6% and +6.5% mAP gains over SOTA on VOC and BDD100K.
AI.motivation: Existing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods for DIOD risk overwriting critical past knowledge, causing inter-domain interference and catastrophic forgetting.
AI.method: (1) Incrementally constructs independent domain-specific subspaces via dedicated low-rank branches fused for holistic decisions. (2) Gradient-based orthogonal refreshing projects new domain updates onto the orthogonal complement of the fused historical subspace. (3) Topology-aware consistency aligns semantic structures across old and new domains.
AI.result: Outperforms best exemplar-free method by +5.6% mAP on Pascal VOC and +6.5% mAP on BDD100K series.
AI.conclusion: OKR is a simple, effective, exemplar-free framework that resolves inter-domain interference and semantic fragmentation for DIOD.

title: Abliteration Is Not a Scalpel: Off-Target Effects of Refusal Removal on Decision Disposition Across Model Families
comment: 11 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Preregistered. Data and code: https://github.com/oleczek/paper-abliteration-not-a-scalpel ; dataset DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21314839
summary: Abliteration - deleting a model's refusal direction from its weights - is the standard recipe behind popular "uncensored" open-weight models. We show the surgery is not clean. As a disposition probe we use 21,600 decisions under uncertainty - weekly up/down calls on 60 Warsaw Stock Exchange equities over 18 weeks, replayed through a frozen pipeline so the decision-layer model is the only variable. The task elicits no refusals at all, so any between-arm delta is pure side effect. Holding provenance constant (official BF16 checkpoints, a single abliteration author, an identical serving stack, one byte-identical frozen prompt), we compare base and abliterated arms of two Mixture-of-Experts families, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. Three effects replicate across both families (weeks-clustered bootstrap CIs excluding zero): abliterated models are systematically more optimistic (+12.2 pp Gemma, +7.4 pp Qwen; the confirmed preregistered endpoint), justify themselves at greater length, and use fewer explicit uncertainty words in forced self-critiques (both exploratory). A fourth effect reverses sign: the same operation makes Gemma-abliterated less confident and Qwen-abliterated more (family CIs non-overlapping) - one weight surgery, opposite shifts in expressed confidence. Capability covariates rule out instruction-following degradation as the driver, and no arm shows economic skill: the apparent edge of abliterated arms is regime beta, not alpha. Our provenance audit also caught two independent contamination channels - a mismatched-quantizer pilot pair and a stale community chat template that silently mangled the rendered prompt - suggesting toolchain artifacts are the rule in studies of community-modified checkpoints. Whoever deploys an "uncensored" model as an agent is deploying a measurably different decision-maker, not the base model minus refusals.

AI.tldr: Abliteration (removing refusal direction from model weights) produces measurable decision-making side effects beyond just removing refusals, including increased optimism, longer justifications, fewer uncertainty words in self-critiques, and inconsistent confidence shifts across model families, with no economic skill improvement.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether "uncensored" models produced by abliteration (removing refusal direction from weights) are functionally equivalent to base models minus refusals, or whether the surgery introduces unintended behavioral side effects.
AI.method: Used 21,600 uncertainty decisions (weekly equity up/down calls on 60 Warsaw Stock Exchange stocks over 18 weeks) via a frozen pipeline where only the decision-layer model varies. Compared base vs. abliterated versions of Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 under strict provenance control (same checkpoints, author, stack, prompt). Used weeks-clustered bootstrap CIs for statistical testing.
AI.result: Three effects replicated across both families: abliterated models are more optimistic (+12.2 pp Gemma, +7.4 pp Qwen), write longer justifications, and use fewer explicit uncertainty words in forced self-critiques. A fourth effect (expressed confidence) reversed sign between families. No abliterated arm showed economic skill; apparent edge was regime beta, not alpha. Two contamination channels (mismatched quantizer, stale chat template) were also discovered.
AI.conclusion: Abliteration produces a measurably different decision-maker, not simply the base model minus refusals. Side effects are systematic, model-family-dependent in some dimensions, and toolchain artifacts are common in studies of community-modified checkpoints.

title: Logical Judgments Under Pressure: Diagnosing Syllogistic Stability with Learned Soft Prefixes
summary: To test how correct logical judgments respond to learned context, we prepend a soft prefix to an exactly labeled syllogistic reasoning benchmark while keeping the model fixed. Soft prefixes are opaque continuous vectors, so we characterize them through the behavior they induce across controlled variations in logical form and interface. By studying which prefixes succeed and how their effects generalize, we characterize how learned contextual pressure can override correct judgments and expose limits in a model's logical stability. Across Qwen3.6-35B-A3B MoE, Qwen3-8B, and Gemma 4 31B, learned prefixes redirect many correct answers and remain effective across unseen forms and interface changes. In repeated tests with Qwen3.6 MoE and Gemma, they outperform paired random controls in all 16 model--direction--split comparisons by 37 to 99 percentage points. Qwen3.6 MoE flip rates remain between 72% and 90% across wording and prompt changes, while Gemma validity prefixes retain 54% to 56% flip compared with less than 1% for matched random prefixes. Diagnostic tests show that the dominant effect is a broad preference for one answer meaning rather than fixed-symbol forcing or a logical operation that transfers reliably between tasks. The form of this bias differs across models. In both Qwen models, simple score models often predict which judgments will flip but not how far their margins will move, whereas Gemma's overall response is more closely approximated by the same models. These results show that the dominant behavioral effect of successful soft prefixes is a broad answer preference, while the remaining response reveals substantial model-specific differences in logical stability.

AI.tldr: Soft prefixes (learned continuous vectors) prepended to syllogistic reasoning benchmarks can override correct logical judgments in LLMs, inducing broad answer preferences rather than specific logical operations. Effectiveness varies across models: Qwen models show predictable flip decisions but unpredictable margin changes, while Gemma's responses are more uniformly approximated by simple score models.
AI.motivation: To investigate how learned contextual pressure (via soft prefixes) can override correct logical judgments in LLMs, and to characterize the limits of models' logical stability under such perturbations.
AI.method: Prepend soft prefixes (opaque continuous vectors) to a labeled syllogistic reasoning benchmark with fixed model weights. Study prefix success and generalization across controlled variations in logical form and interface. Conduct diagnostic tests to distinguish between broad answer preference, fixed-symbol forcing, and logical operation transfer.
AI.result: Learned prefixes redirect many correct answers and generalize across unseen forms and interface changes. Outperform random controls by 37–99 percentage points across 16 model–direction–split comparisons. Qwen3.6 MoE flip rates: 72%–90% across wording/prompt changes; Gemma validity prefixes: 54%–56% flip vs. <1% for random prefixes. Dominant effect is broad answer preference, not fixed-symbol forcing or transferable logical operations. Bias form differs across models.
AI.conclusion: Soft prefixes induce a broad answer preference as the dominant behavioral effect, revealing substantial model-specific differences in logical stability. Qwen models' flip decisions are predictable but margin shifts are not; Gemma's responses are more closely approximated by simple score models.

title: Understanding From Human Perspective: A Multi-agent System for Interactive Egocentric Medical Image Segmentation
summary: Interactive egocentric medical image segmentation (IEMIS) plays an important role in smart-glasses-assisted medical image review, segmenting the medical targets a clinician refers to from their egocentric view. Once it succeeds, the object-level visual evidence it provides strengthens the review and underpins fine-grained analysis and clinical decision-making. However, the instruction and the video both come from the user's egocentric perspective, which poses two challenges. (1) Semantic ambiguity leaves the model unable to confirm the user-intended target. (2) Visual variability makes the segmentation jump from frame to frame. In this paper, we propose EgoMed-Agent, a multi-agent system that understands the target from the human perspective through two workflows. (1) The \textit{Target Confirmation Workflow} grounds the instruction against candidate targets with a reliability score, confirming the target when the grounding is reliable and asking the user to clarify when it is not, thereby confirming the segmentation target. (2) The \textit{Localization-Guided Propagation Workflow} couples mask propagation with per-frame target localization, using the localized target to correct the propagated mask whenever the two diverge, so the segmentation stays on the target across the egocentric video. Extensive experiments show that EgoMed-Agent reaches 71.34\% average Dice, far above the best text-prompted baseline (11.70\%). Our code is available at \href{https://github.com/wdyyyyyy/EgoMed-Agent}{our project page}.

AI.tldr: EgoMed-Agent is a multi-agent system for interactive egocentric medical image segmentation that handles semantic ambiguity by confirming targets with reliability scoring and manages visual variability through localization-guided mask propagation, achieving 71.34% average Dice vs. 11.70% for baselines.
AI.motivation: Interactive egocentric medical image segmentation (IEMIS) is crucial for smart-glasses-assisted medical review, but faces challenges from semantic ambiguity (unclear user-intended target) and visual variability (frame-to-frame segmentation jitter) inherent in egocentric perspectives.
AI.method: EgoMed-Agent is a multi-agent system with two workflows: (1) Target Confirmation Workflow grounds instruction against candidate targets with a reliability score, confirming when reliable and asking for clarification otherwise; (2) Localization-Guided Propagation Workflow couples mask propagation with per-frame target localization, correcting propagated masks when divergence occurs.
AI.result: EgoMed-Agent achieves 71.34% average Dice, significantly outperforming the best text-prompted baseline at 11.70%.
AI.conclusion: The proposed multi-agent approach effectively addresses semantic ambiguity and visual variability in egocentric medical segmentation, demonstrating substantial improvement over existing methods.

title: Calibrated Alzheimer's Conversion Risk in Mild Cognitive Impairment: Persistent Homology of Clinical Trajectories with Conformal Guarantees
comment: 17 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). Code available upon reasonable request
summary: Background.
