Predicting conversion from mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to Alzheimer's disease (AD) is central to trial enrichment and care planning, yet existing models provide no individual-level uncertainty estimates and rarely include transparent leakage audits. We introduce the first application of persistent homology to longitudinal clinical trajectory point clouds for this task, and the first split-conformal individual risk guarantee for any AD-conversion model. Methods. We analysed 741 MCI subjects (240 converters, 32.4%) from ADNI with a uniform 4-year follow-up cap. Five leakage sources were corrected; without them a naive pipeline achieved AUC=0.934, inflated by +0.075. Vietoris-Rips persistent homology and sublevel-set proxies were combined with trajectory slopes and engineered features (76 total) in a stacking ensemble evaluated by 5-fold cross-validation. Results. Cox and Random Survival Forest models with TDA features achieved concordance C=0.799 and C=0.826 versus C=0.753 and C=0.812 without (+0.045 and +0.014). The primary nested AUC is 0.840 (same-fold bound 0.866); external AUC was 0.879 on a zero-overlap ADNI-2/GO/3 cohort. H0 persistence entropy was the top SHAP feature and significantly associated with APOE4 dosage (Spearman r=-0.191, p<0.0001, Bonferroni-corrected). Cross-conformal coverage was 90.4%+-2.2% (target 90%); empirical external coverage 96.9%. Maximum fairness gap in false-negative rate across seven subgroups was 0.092. Conclusions. We propose H0 persistence entropy as a topological biomarker of cognitive decline and demonstrate that a leakage-audited, conformally calibrated pipeline reaches competitive accuracy with individual-level uncertainty quantification not previously available for this task.

AI.tldr: First application of persistent homology (topological data analysis) to MCI-to-AD conversion prediction, combined with split-conformal individual risk guarantees and rigorous leakage auditing, achieving competitive accuracy (AUC 0.840) with 90.4% empirical coverage and fairness gap analysis.
AI.motivation: Existing MCI-to-AD conversion models lack individual-level uncertainty estimates and transparent leakage audits. Persistent homology has not been applied to longitudinal clinical trajectory point clouds for this task, and no prior AD-conversion model provides split-conformal individual risk guarantees.
AI.method: 741 MCI subjects (32.4% converters) from ADNI with 4-year cap; five leakage sources corrected. Vietoris-Rips persistent homology and sublevel-set proxies combined with trajectory slopes and engineered features (76 total) in a stacking ensemble; 5-fold CV. Cross-conformal prediction for uncertainty quantification.
AI.result: Naive AUC inflated by +0.075 to 0.934; corrected nested AUC=0.840. TDA features improved Cox concordance from 0.753→0.799 and RSF from 0.812→0.826. H0 persistence entropy top SHAP feature, significantly associated with APOE4 dosage. Cross-conformal coverage 90.4%±2.2%; external coverage 96.9%. Maximum fairness gap in FNR=0.092 across 7 subgroups.
AI.conclusion: H0 persistence entropy is a topological biomarker of cognitive decline. A leakage-audited, conformally calibrated pipeline achieves competitive accuracy with individual-level uncertainty quantification not previously available for this task.

title: STAR: Skeletal Token Alignment and Rearrangement for Interaction Recognition
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Multimedia (IEEE TMM)
summary: Understanding physical human-robot and human-human interactions is a challenging yet emerging topic in 3D vision. While most existing methods rely on skeleton sequences--effective in low-light and privacy-sensitive environment--they face two major challenges: 1) learning and effectively exploiting interaction cues from skeletal data, and 2) compensating for the lack of visual information absent in skeletons alone. To address these challenges, we propose skeletal token alignment and rearrangement (STAR) for human-robot and human-human interaction recognition. It learns interaction-specific skeleton features and enriches them using visual cues by aligning skeleton and RGB video representations in a shared latent space. Specifically, STAR consists of three key components. First, we design a skeleton encoder that captures fine-grained interdependencies using Entity Rearrangement (ER) and Interactive Spatiotemporal Tokens (ISTs). Second, we present Visual Interaction Encoding that introduces a Focus on Interactions (FoI) strategy to attend to spatiotemporal regions relevant to interactions in RGB videos. Finally, these representations are aligned via a contrastive learning objective, with a refinement head further refines predictions. During training, STAR leverages both skeleton and RGB video data to learn robust, discriminative interaction representations. At inference time, it operates on skeletons alone, retaining visual-informed benefits while preserving skeleton-only efficiency. Extensive experiments on Chico, HARPER, NTU Mutual 11 and 26 datasets consistently validate our approach by demonstrating superior performance over state-of-the-art methods. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Necolizer/STAR.

AI.tldr: STAR proposes a method for human-robot and human-human interaction recognition that aligns skeleton and RGB video representations in a shared latent space during training, but operates on skeletons alone at inference, achieving state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing skeleton-based interaction recognition methods face two major challenges: learning effective interaction cues from skeletal data and compensating for the lack of visual information absent in skeletons alone.
AI.method: STAR consists of three components: (1) a skeleton encoder using Entity Rearrangement (ER) and Interactive Spatiotemporal Tokens (ISTs) for fine-grained interdependencies, (2) Visual Interaction Encoding with a Focus on Interactions (FoI) strategy for attending to relevant spatiotemporal regions in RGB videos, and (3) contrastive learning alignment between skeleton and RGB representations with a refinement head.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods on Chico, HARPER, NTU Mutual 11, and NTU Mutual 26 datasets.
AI.conclusion: STAR effectively learns robust, discriminative interaction representations using both skeleton and RGB data during training while retaining visual-informed benefits and skeleton-only efficiency at inference time.

title: Residual-Guided Multi-Resolution Refinement of Foundation Models: A Case Study in Drought Forecasting
summary: Regional climate prediction presents unique challenges for time series foundation models, which typically process temporal patterns through single-pass inference. Expert climatologists, in contrast, employ multi-scale temporal analysis and iterative refinement based on systematic error diagnosis. We present RGMR (Residual-Guided Multi-Resolution Refinement), an inference-time framework that adapts pre-trained foundation models to perform structured coarse-to-fine refinement for climate forecasting without updating backbone parameters. Applied to drought forecasting using the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI), RGMR is architecture-agnostic across the three TSFM backbones evaluated per site (TimesFM, TimeGPT, TabPFN) and consistently lowers test-set MSE on three South Australian sites and three additional regions outside South Australia. Applied to TimesFM, the wrapper reduces one-month-ahead SPEI MSE by up to 18.9\% across the three South Australian sites (mean reduction $\approx$18.7\%). Overall, RGMR provides a practical route for deploying frozen TSFMs in regional climate forecasting workflows.

AI.tldr: RGMR is an inference-time framework that adapts pre-trained time series foundation models (TSFMs) to perform coarse-to-fine refinement for regional climate forecasting without updating backbone parameters. It reduces one-month-ahead SPEI MSE by up to 18.9% across South Australian sites and generalizes to additional regions.
AI.motivation: Regional climate prediction poses challenges for time series foundation models that use single-pass inference, whereas expert climatologists use multi-scale temporal analysis and iterative refinement based on systematic error diagnosis. The authors aim to bridge this gap without modifying pre-trained model parameters.
AI.method: RGMR (Residual-Guided Multi-Resolution Refinement) is an inference-time wrapper that performs structured coarse-to-fine refinement. It is architecture-agnostic and applied without updating backbone parameters across three TSFM backbones: TimesFM, TimeGPT, and TabPFN.
AI.result: Consistently lowers test-set MSE on three South Australian sites and three additional regions. Applied to TimesFM, RGMR reduces one-month-ahead SPEI MSE by up to 18.9% across the three South Australian sites (mean reduction ≈18.7%).
AI.conclusion: RGMR provides a practical, architecture-agnostic approach for deploying frozen TSFMs in regional climate forecasting workflows, enabling multi-resolution refinement without retraining backbone models.

title: SkyVLaM: Multimodal Large Language Model for UAV Video Understanding in Remote Sensing
summary: Recent advances in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have significantly improved remote sensing (RS) multimodal understanding. Language-conditioned segmentation is crucial for fine-grained target understanding in Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) videos. However, this task remains challenging due to the prevalence of small, visually ambiguous targets and dynamic aerial perspectives. In this paper, we propose SkyVLaM, a multimodal large language model for UAV video understanding. SkyVLaM constructs sparse tokens directly from patch-level video representations through a temporal basis perceiver, regularizes the sparse basis to encourage complementary temporal cues, and adaptively selects a temporally coherent dense segment for high-resolution inspection. The resulting sparse and dense tokens are jointly processed by a large language model for query-conditioned segmentation. We further build SkyVid, consisting of SkyVid-VGCG and SkyVid-RVOS for video grounded conversation generation and referring video object segmentation, respectively. SkyVid contains 101 videos, 33.6K frames, and 1.53M pixel-level object instances. Experiments show that SkyVLaM provides a more effective allocation of the visual token budget and improves language-conditioned video segmentation in UAV scenarios.

AI.tldr: SkyVLaM is a multimodal large language model for UAV video understanding that uses sparse tokens via a temporal basis perceiver and adaptively selects dense segments for high-resolution inspection, achieving improved language-conditioned video segmentation. The paper also introduces SkyVid, a new dataset for video grounded conversation and referring segmentation.
AI.motivation: Language-conditioned segmentation in UAV videos is challenging due to small, visually ambiguous targets and dynamic aerial perspectives. Existing MLLMs struggle with effective visual token allocation for these scenarios.
AI.method: (1) Constructs sparse tokens from patch-level video representations via a temporal basis perceiver; (2) Regularizes sparse basis for complementary temporal cues; (3) Adaptively selects temporally coherent dense segments for high-resolution inspection; (4) Jointly processes sparse and dense tokens with an LLM for query-conditioned segmentation.
AI.result: SkyVLaM provides more effective allocation of visual token budget and improves language-conditioned video segmentation in UAV scenarios. A new dataset SkyVid (101 videos, 33.6K frames, 1.53M pixel-level instances) is built.
AI.conclusion: SkyVLaM effectively addresses the challenges of UAV video understanding by combining sparse and dense token strategies, outperforming existing methods on language-conditioned segmentation tasks.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Interpretable Learning: Towards Task-Specific Zero-Shot Models in Healthcare
summary: We introduce Retrieval-Augmented Interpretable Learning (RAIL), a probabilistic meta-learning framework for zero-shot generation of task-specific interpretable models that synthesizes coefficient-space structure from natural-language task descriptions and a memory of previously learned task-specific predictors. RAIL retrieves related source tasks, transfers structure through coefficient space, and generates a new predictor in the original diagnostic-feature space, enabling zero-shot and few-shot clinical procedure prediction with feature-level explanations. Its probabilistic formulation provides uncertainty over retrieval, model coefficients, and predictions, supporting reliability-aware deployment: uncertain predictions or unstable explanations can be flagged for additional clinical review rather than treated as automatic decisions. This makes RAIL particularly suited for healthcare settings, where prediction tasks are highly long-tailed, new clinical targets arise frequently, and models must remain inspectable, uncertainty-aware, and compatible with human oversight. Across long-tailed clinical procedure prediction tasks, RAIL maintains reliable performance across data-availability regimes: it achieves 73.4% accuracy in the held-out zero-shot settings, where no supervised task-specific model can be trained, and remains near 73.2% accuracy in the extreme few-shot regime with only 2-4 examples, where supervised task-specific models perform close to chance. RAIL further benefits from clinically informed task representations and yields retrieval, uncertainty, and coefficient-level diagnostics that make model behavior more transparent. These results suggest a path toward scalable clinical prediction systems that can adapt to new tasks while preserving interpretability and reliability.

AI.tldr: RAIL is a probabilistic meta-learning framework that generates interpretable, task-specific models for zero-shot and few-shot clinical prediction by retrieving related source tasks, transferring coefficient-space structure, and providing uncertainty estimates across retrieval, coefficients, and predictions.
AI.motivation: Healthcare prediction tasks are highly long-tailed, new clinical targets arise frequently, and models must remain inspectable, uncertainty-aware, and compatible with human oversight. Existing supervised models fail in zero-shot and extreme few-shot regimes.
AI.method: RAIL retrieves related source tasks from a memory of previously learned predictors, transfers structure through coefficient space using natural-language task descriptions, and generates a new predictor in the original diagnostic-feature space. Its probabilistic formulation provides uncertainty over retrieval, model coefficients, and predictions.
AI.result: RAIL achieves 73.4% accuracy in zero-shot settings and remains near 73.2% in extreme few-shot (2-4 examples), where supervised models perform near chance. It also benefits from clinically informed task representations and provides transparent diagnostics.
AI.conclusion: RAIL offers a scalable path toward clinical prediction systems that adapt to new tasks while preserving interpretability, uncertainty-awareness, and reliability for human oversight.

title: Automating Visual Recognition of Leprosy in Wild Chimpanzees
summary: Leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae) has been confirmed in wild western chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes verus) in West Africa, presenting as clear and progressive visual symptoms. Manual review of camera-trap footage at landscape scale is infeasible, motivating the need for automated screening. We present the first deep learning pipeline for wildlife leprosy detection and contribute the PanLep300 dataset of 125,670 annotated bounding-box crops across 953 tracks from 303 camera-trap videos with ecologically-motivated splits that withhold whole individuals and camera installations. We benchmark spatial (2D), temporally aggregated (2.5D), and video-based (3D) classification approaches to investigate which approach is best suited to automated leprosy detection in wild apes. We find that simple aggregation of crop-level predictions consistently matches or outperforms both learned temporal models and end-to-end video architectures -- consistent with leprosy's static cutaneous presentation. We further find that performance is suppressed when tracklets contain frames of partially visible individuals -- as commonly occurs at the start and end of a track -- and demonstrate that this can be addressed through targeted construction and aggregation strategies.

AI.tldr: First deep learning pipeline for detecting leprosy in wild chimpanzees using camera-trap footage, introducing the PanLep300 dataset and showing that simple 2D aggregation outperforms complex temporal models due to leprosy's static presentation.
AI.motivation: Manual review of camera-trap footage at landscape scale is infeasible, motivating the need for automated screening of leprosy in wild western chimpanzees.
AI.method: Contributed the PanLep300 dataset (125,670 annotated bounding-box crops across 953 tracks from 303 videos), benchmarked spatial (2D), temporally aggregated (2.5D), and video-based (3D) classification approaches, and investigated tracklet construction strategies.
AI.result: Simple 2D aggregation matches or outperforms learned temporal and 3D video models; performance is suppressed by partially visible individuals in tracklets, which can be mitigated via targeted construction and aggregation strategies.
AI.conclusion: For static cutaneous diseases like leprosy, simple 2D prediction aggregation is sufficient and robust, and careful tracklet construction improves detection reliability in automated wildlife health screening.

title: Lightweight Wrappers for Adapting Time Series Foundation Models to Regional Drought Forecasting
summary: Large \emph{Time Series Foundation Models} (TSFMs) demonstrate strong zero-shot forecasting capabilities across diverse domains. However, their application to regional climate forecasting faces practical challenges: model weights are often proprietary, local training records are limited, and computational budgets are constrained, making traditional fine-tuning approaches infeasible. To address these constraints, we introduce a lightweight, black-box adaptation framework (requiring no access to backbone parameters and no backbone fine-tuning) that enhances frozen TSFMs at inference time through two plug-and-play wrappers: \textbf{SMR\textsuperscript{2}} (Stationarity aware multi-resolution Residual), which decomposes the input into multi-resolution temporal views, learns stride specific residual corrections that capture regional dynamics, then adaptively ensembles them into a single forecast, and \textbf{MBB} (Moving Block Bootstrap), which preserves temporal dependencies through block resampling and ensembles over temporally coherent residual perturbations to stabilize the point forecast. Both wrappers instantiate the same bagging style principle: they build diverse views of the input or its residuals, forecast each with the same frozen backbone, and aggregate, so all adaptation comes from inference time ensembling rather than any weight update. Evaluated on one month ahead Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) prediction across multiple sites in South Australia, our framework consistently improves forecasting performance across several backbone models, demonstrating up to 26\% mean squared error (MSE) reduction over the corresponding frozen backbone while enabling practical deployment in resource constrained regional forecasting systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a lightweight, black-box adaptation framework for Time Series Foundation Models (TSFMs) in regional climate forecasting, using two plug-and-play wrappers (SMR² and MBB) that enhance frozen TSFMs at inference time via multi-resolution residual learning and block bootstrapping, achieving up to 26% MSE reduction on SPEI prediction without accessing or fine-tuning backbone parameters.
AI.motivation: TSFMs show strong zero-shot forecasting but face practical barriers in regional climate forecasting: proprietary model weights, limited local training records, and constrained computational budgets make traditional fine-tuning infeasible.
AI.method: A black-box adaptation framework with two wrappers: (1) SMR² (Stationarity aware multi-resolution Residual) decomposes input into multi-resolution temporal views, learns stride-specific residual corrections, and adaptively ensembles them; (2) MBB (Moving Block Bootstrap) preserves temporal dependencies via block resampling and ensembles over temporally coherent perturbations. Both follow a bagging principle—building diverse input/residual views, forecasting with the frozen backbone, and aggregating—requiring no backbone access or weight updates.
AI.result: Evaluated on one-month-ahead SPEI prediction across multiple sites in South Australia, the framework consistently improves forecasting performance across backbone models, achieving up to 26% MSE reduction over the frozen backbone.
AI.conclusion: The proposed inference-time ensembling approach enables practical deployment of TSFMs in resource-constrained regional forecasting systems where backbone weights are proprietary and computational budgets are limited.

title: The PanAf-SBR Dataset: Social Behaviour Recognition for Wild Great Apes
summary: Behavioural shifts in wild great ape populations, particularly the breakdown of social structures, can serve as an early indicator of population decline. Automating the detection of behaviours indicative of these shifts is therefore a critical task for conservation. Several valuable datasets have recently been introduced for the automated recognition of great ape behaviour, yet few include fine-grained social behaviour annotations, and those that do are captured either in captive settings or via aerial platforms such as UAVs. We address this gap by introducing PanAf-SBR, the first wild great ape camera trap dataset annotated with social behaviours. PanAf-SBR extends PanAf500 with 100 additional videos covering 36,063 frames. These come with 81,096 annotations including bounding boxes, segmentation masks, intra-video identities, and seven social behaviour classes defined under the action giver and receiver convention of ChimpACT. We use this data together with the AlphaChimp architecture to establish the first benchmarks for fine-grained social behaviour recognition in wild great apes from camera trap footage. We further conduct bidirectional transfer learning experiments between PanAf-SBR and the captive ChimpACT dataset, finding that cross-dataset pre-training is highly beneficial for specific classes rather than of uniform benefit. Finally, we examine the role of background context by inverting the segmentation masks to suppress non-ape pixels.

AI.tldr: PanAf-SBR is the first wild great ape camera trap dataset annotated with fine-grained social behaviors, extending PanAf500 with 100 videos, 36,063 frames, 81,096 annotations (bboxes, masks, identities, 7 social behavior classes). Using AlphaChimp, the authors establish benchmarks for social behavior recognition in the wild and show that cross-dataset pre-training with captive ChimpACT benefits specific classes, not uniformly. They also study background context via mask inversion.
AI.motivation: Behavioural shifts in wild great apes, especially social structure breakdown, can indicate population decline. Automating detection of such behaviours is critical for conservation, but existing datasets lack fine-grained social behaviour annotations in wild settings from camera traps.
AI.method: The authors introduce PanAf-SBR (extending PanAf500 with 100 more videos, 36,063 frames, 81,096 annotations). They annotate bounding boxes, segmentation masks, intra-video identities, and 7 social behaviour classes (action giver/receiver format from ChimpACT). They use AlphaChimp architecture to establish benchmarks and conduct bidirectional transfer learning between PanAf-SBR and captive ChimpACT, plus analyze background context by inverting segmentation masks.
AI.result: First benchmarks for fine-grained social behaviour recognition in wild great apes from camera traps. Cross-dataset pre-training benefits specific classes rather than uniformly. Background context analysis via mask inversion.
AI.conclusion: PanAf-SBR fills a critical gap in wild great ape social behaviour datasets from camera traps, enabling automated detection of behavioural shifts. Cross-dataset transfer learning is beneficial for targeted classes, and background context plays a role in recognition performance.

title: After the Euclidean Highway: Hyperbolic Expert AI as the Next Innovation
comment: 40 pages, 11 figures. Supplementary Information included as an ancillary file. Data and code: Zenodo, concept DOI 10.5281/zenodo.21438499 (published, CC-BY-4.0)
summary: Expert domains are trees; the Euclidean transformer is not, diluting parent-child structure exponentially at depth. The hyperbolic turn left one question unasked: not how much of a network to curve, but where curvature may touch the gradient. Placement is a law, not a knob: the same geometry on a trainable adapter collapses training (seventeen training collapses, ~220 GPU-hours), yet at the loss layer alone it trains without one -- this is HySAT (Hyperbolic Structure-Aware Training), hyperbolic losses at the loss layer only. Across six expert SLMs we constructed and deployed (Llama 3.1 and EXAONE 3.5; four adapter strategies; 18.0M-sample corpus; zero NaN over ~317K optimizer steps), a matched four-arm ablation isolates the preserved manifold invariant, and three propositions and a lemma prove why loss-only placement is stable where adapter-on-manifold is not. Four models are operationally deployed (one live, consumer-facing), two open-weight, with per-step traces and a seventeen-incident failure ledger on Zenodo (CC-BY-4.0).

AI.tldr: HySAT places hyperbolic losses only at the loss layer, avoiding training collapses (17 incidents, ~220 GPU-hours) that occur when hyperbolic geometry is applied to adapters. Tested across six expert SLMs (Llama 3.1, EXAONE 3.5; 18M samples; zero NaN over ~317K steps), with theoretical proofs and four deployed models.
AI.motivation: Euclidean transformers dilute parent-child structure exponentially; hyperbolic approaches wrongly treat geometry placement as a tunable knob rather than a structural law, causing training collapses when applied to adapters.
AI.method: HySAT applies hyperbolic losses only at the loss layer, with theoretical proofs (3 propositions, 1 lemma) showing why this placement is stable. Evaluated via four-arm ablation on six SLMs across four adapter strategies.
AI.result: Zero NaN over ~317K optimizer steps; 17 training collapses documented when hyperbolic geometry was placed on adapters; four models operationally deployed.
AI.conclusion: Hyperbolic geometry placement is a structural law, not a tunable hyperparameter; loss-only placement preserves manifold invariants while adapter-on-manifold does not.

title: Does Super-Resolution Preserve Defect Evidence? A Low-False-Call Benchmark for Semiconductor Inspection
summary: Super-resolution can make inspection images appear sharper without preserving the evidence needed to detect a defect. We study this failure mode with a benchmark that separates reconstruction from detection and evaluates both at a predeclared low false-positive rate. Ten end-to-end repetitions combine independently generated line/space and contact-hole images with model training, calibration, clean controls, weak defects, and a held-out defect morphology. Every reconstruction is scored by the same local residual detector, while direct and jointly trained detectors form a separate comparison track. Reconstruction fidelity and inspection utility diverge: the two learned reconstruction models attain the highest structural similarity yet detect fewer defect pixels than bicubic interpolation in every paired repetition. A direct DeepLabV3 detector reaches $0.1984\pm0.0385$ recall at $0.000174\pm0.000084$ false-positive rate and satisfies the held-out feasibility criterion in all ten repetitions. An illustrative joint model, DPU-WaferSR, passes independent clean calibration but exceeds the held-out limit in all ten repetitions, demonstrating that calibration success does not guarantee transfer. Weak-defect recall remains near zero for every feasible method. Applying the unchanged policies to 4,591 public Carinthia-S masks further reveals large method-dependent shifts on real SEM texture. These results support a simple conclusion: super-resolution for inspection should be judged by preserved task evidence and operating-point transfer, not reconstruction quality alone.

AI.tldr: Super-resolution sharpens inspection images but can destroy defect evidence. Using a benchmark that separates reconstruction from detection, the paper shows that learned super-resolution methods achieve higher structural similarity yet detect fewer defects than bicubic interpolation. Direct detectors like DeepLabV3 succeed, while joint models (DPU-WaferSR) fail transfer despite calibration success. Weak-defect recall remains near zero. Conclusions emphasize that super-resolution for inspection should be judged by preserved task evidence and operating-point transfer, not reconstruction quality.
AI.motivation: Super-resolution can make inspection images appear sharper but may destroy the evidence needed for defect detection. The paper aims to study this failure mode by creating a benchmark that separates reconstruction from detection and evaluates both at a low false-positive rate.
AI.method: Ten end-to-end repetitions combine independently generated line/space and contact-hole images with model training, calibration, clean controls, weak defects, and a held-out defect morphology. Each reconstruction is scored by a local residual detector. Direct detectors (DeepLabV3) and jointly trained detectors (DPU-WaferSR) form a separate comparison track. Methods are also applied to 4,591 public Carinthia-S masks for real SEM texture evaluation.
AI.result: Learned reconstruction models attain the highest structural similarity but detect fewer defect pixels than bicubic interpolation in every paired repetition. DeepLabV3 achieves 0.1984±0.0385 recall at 0.000174±0.000084 false-positive rate and satisfies held-out feasibility in all ten repetitions. DPU-WaferSR passes independent clean calibration but exceeds the held-out limit in all ten repetitions. Weak-defect recall remains near zero for every feasible method. Large method-dependent shifts appear on real SEM texture.
AI.conclusion: Super-resolution for inspection should be judged by preserved task evidence and operating-point transfer, not reconstruction quality alone.

title: One-step lowest-variance selection in a Gaussian random-field model motivated by masked diffusion: Total correlation and a square root collision threshold
summary: Motivated by confidence-guided parallel unmasking in masked discrete diffusion, we study a single selection step in a stylized Gaussian random-field model. A locally dependent nonnegative score field represents position wise uncertainty, and the scheduler selects the K positions with the smallest scores. Dependence among the selected positions is measured through a distance-dependent Gaussian correlation model. This separation provides a tractable framework for quantifying how the geometry of low-score locations affects the dependence cost of factorized parallel decoding. We establish two complementary results. In a conservative sub-square-root regime, the conditional Gaussian total correlation of the selected block vanishes in probability. At the square-root scale, it remains non-negligible with positive asymptotic probability and admits a strictly positive expectation lower bound. Synthetic experiments support the predicted finite-size behavior. These results provide a rigorous stochastic-geometry baseline for understanding how budget size, score dependence, and spatial correlation jointly shape one-step confidence-based selection in masked discrete diffusion.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes a single selection step in a Gaussian random-field model that mimics confidence-guided parallel unmasking in masked discrete diffusion, showing that dependence among selected low-score positions vanishes in a sub-square-root regime but persists at the square-root scale.
AI.motivation: To provide a rigorous stochastic-geometry baseline for understanding how budget size, score dependence, and spatial correlation jointly shape one-step confidence-based selection in masked discrete diffusion models.
AI.method: Models the selection process as choosing the K positions with smallest scores from a locally dependent, nonnegative Gaussian random field with distance-dependent correlation. Analyzes conditional Gaussian total correlation in two regimes: sub-square-root (conservative) and square-root scaling.
AI.result: In the sub-square-root regime, the conditional total correlation of selected positions vanishes in probability. At the square-root scale, it remains non-negligible with positive asymptotic probability and has a strictly positive expectation lower bound. Synthetic experiments confirm finite-size behavior.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a tractable theoretical framework quantifying how spatial geometry of low-score locations affects dependence cost in factorized parallel decoding, establishing phase-transition-like behavior between vanishing and non-vanishing dependence regimes.

title: TimeLens2: Generalist Video Temporal Grounding with Multimodal LLMs
summary: Video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can describe what happens in a video, but rarely identify when the supporting evidence occurs. We study generalist video temporal grounding, in which one model predicts a variable-cardinality set of evidence intervals across video lengths, domains, query forms, and viewpoints. Existing training strategies are misaligned with this set-valued task: long-video labels often rely on brittle one-pass annotation, while reinforcement-learning rewards either fail to distinguish non-overlapping predictions or require fragile segment matching. TimeLens2 treats temporal evidence as an interval set throughout supervision and optimization. TimeLens2-93K constructs reliable multi-span supervision through caption-derived proposals, independent localization, cross-agent consensus, semantic verification, and boundary refinement. Our temporal Wasserstein reward computes exact one-dimensional \(W_1\) between uniform distributions over merged interval supports, providing dense, matching-free feedback under unequal cardinalities and equivalent fragmentation; temporal IoU complements it with precise-overlap feedback. Across seven benchmarks, TimeLens2-2B outperforms all size-matched baselines on every benchmark, while the 4B and 8B variants achieve state-of-the-art performance, surpassing open-source models with up to 397B parameters. The 2B, 4B, and 8B variants improve over their Qwen3-VL backbones by 14.2, 13.0, and 18.1 mIoU points, respectively.

AI.tldr: TimeLens2 introduces a set-valued approach to video temporal grounding, enabling MLLMs to predict multiple evidence intervals per query. It features TimeLens2-93K training data with reliable multi-span supervision and a temporal Wasserstein reward for dense, matching-free feedback. The 2B, 4B, and 8B variants outperform all size-matched baselines and surpass models with up to 397B parameters.
AI.motivation: Existing video MLLMs can describe video content but rarely identify when supporting evidence occurs. Current training strategies are misaligned with set-valued temporal grounding: long-video labels rely on brittle one-pass annotation, and RL rewards either fail to distinguish non-overlapping predictions or require fragile segment matching.
AI.method: TimeLens2 treats temporal evidence as an interval set throughout supervision and optimization. It constructs TimeLens2-93K dataset with multi-span supervision via caption-derived proposals, independent localization, cross-agent consensus, semantic verification, and boundary refinement. The temporal Wasserstein reward computes exact 1D W1 between uniform distributions over merged interval supports for dense, matching-free feedback; temporal IoU complements it.
AI.result: Across seven benchmarks, TimeLens2-2B outperforms all size-matched baselines. The 4B and 8B variants achieve SOTA, surpassing open-source models with up to 397B parameters. Improvements over Qwen3-VL backbones are 14.2, 13.0, and 18.1 mIoU points for 2B, 4B, and 8B variants, respectively.
AI.conclusion: TimeLens2 demonstrates that treating temporal grounding as set-valued prediction, with carefully constructed multi-span supervision and a Wasserstein-based reward, significantly improves generalist video temporal grounding across diverse video lengths, domains, query forms, and viewpoints.

title: An Explainable FFT-Based Spatial-Frequency Fusion Framework for Deepfake Detection
summary: Deepfake generation has raised growing concerns regarding digital media authenticity, misinformation, identity fraud, and public trust. Recent studies show that combining spatial and frequency features leads to stronger detection results than using independently. This paper presents MSCA-FFT, a Fast Fourier Transform (FFT)-based multi-scale cross-attention framework for image-level deepfake detection. The model combines a partially fine-tuned Xception spatial branch with an FFT-based frequency branch. The frequency branch processes the log-scaled FFT magnitude spectrum through shallow convolutional layers, avoiding inverse frequency-to-image reconstruction used in DCT-based pipelines. The spatial and frequency representations are refined by transformer encoders, fused through cross-attention, and passed to an MLP classifier for real/fake prediction. Experimental results show that MSCA-FFT achieves consistently higher performance than the DCT-based state-of-the-art spatial-frequency fusion method and the compared baseline models. The ablation study further indicates that the FFT-based frequency branch provides complementary spectral cues when fused with spatial features. In addition, FFT-based frequency analysis and Grad-CAM/LIME explanations show consistent evidence around manipulation-sensitive facial regions, including the eyes, mouth, nose, and facial boundaries.

AI.tldr: MSCA-FFT is a deepfake detection framework that fuses partially fine-tuned Xception spatial features with FFT-based frequency features via cross-attention and transformer encoders, outperforming DCT-based methods and showing interpretability around manipulation-sensitive facial regions.
AI.motivation: Deepfake generation threatens digital authenticity, misinformation, and public trust; combining spatial and frequency features has shown promise, but prior DCT-based approaches require inverse frequency-to-image reconstruction, motivating a more direct FFT-based fusion approach.
AI.method: MSCA-FFT combines a partially fine-tuned Xception spatial branch with an FFT-based frequency branch (log-scaled FFT magnitude spectrum processed by shallow CNNs). Both branches use transformer encoders, fuse via cross-attention, and classify with an MLP.
AI.result: MSCA-FFT consistently outperforms DCT-based spatial-frequency fusion methods and baseline models. Ablation confirms FFT frequency features provide complementary spectral cues. Grad-CAM/LIME highlight manipulation-sensitive facial regions (eyes, mouth, nose, facial boundaries).
AI.conclusion: FFT-based frequency analysis with cross-attention fusion is an effective alternative to DCT-based pipelines for deepfake detection, offering stronger performance and interpretable evidence around facial manipulation artifacts.

title: Program Synthesis for Simulation-Based Inference: Joint Model Selection and Parameter Estimation
summary: Neural simulation-based inference enables parameter estimation for complex models, but typically requires the user to specify a simulator encoding a fixed model structure. We present a framework for joint model selection and parameter estimation that combines large language models for program synthesis with neural simulation-based inference. Given a natural language description of the system and data under investigation, an LLM proposes candidate simulator programs which are iteratively refined via feedback-driven mutation and evaluated using neural density estimation. The approach enables simulation-based inference over a pool of models, not just parameters within a fixed model. On benchmarks spanning deterministic dynamics, stochastic epidemic models, and dark matter substructure inference from gravitational-lensing images, the method identifies plausible model families from open-ended prompts, with accuracy that reflects the information content of the data and identifiability of candidate models.

AI.tldr: A framework combining LLMs for program synthesis with neural simulation-based inference to jointly perform model selection and parameter estimation from natural language descriptions.
AI.motivation: Traditional simulation-based inference requires a fixed model structure; this limits exploration to parameter estimation within a single predefined model. The authors aim to enable inference over a pool of models, not just parameters.
AI.method: LLM proposes candidate simulator programs from natural language descriptions; these programs are iteratively refined via feedback-driven mutation and evaluated using neural density estimation.
AI.result: On benchmarks (deterministic dynamics, stochastic epidemics, gravitational lensing dark matter inference), the method identifies plausible model families from open-ended prompts with accuracy reflecting data information content and model identifiability.
AI.conclusion: The approach successfully extends simulation-based inference to model selection, enabling automated discovery and evaluation of model families directly from natural language task descriptions.

title: Bio-SFT: Asymmetric Cortical Guidance and Retinal Adaptation for Robust HDR Reconstruction
summary: Recovering high dynamic range (HDR) radiance from a single standard dynamic range (SDR) image is highly ill-posed. Extreme luminance variation and severe quantization in dark regions make accurate reconstruction challenging, often leading to visual artifacts and color distortions. To address this problem, we propose Bio-SFT, a bio-inspired spiking frequency transformer for single-image HDR reconstruction. Bio-SFT incorporates three biologically motivated components. First, a learnable Naka--Rushton retinal adaptation frontend stabilizes the input under complex lighting conditions. Second, an explicit Parvo--Magno split introduces asymmetric Parvo-to-Magno guidance, allowing high-frequency structural cues to modulate low-frequency reconstruction. Third, an event-driven SNN hard gating module applies all-or-none spiking to suppress dark-region noise while preserving structural details. The module is trained with a sparsity prior to encourage efficient feature utilization. Built for end-to-end training within a transformer backbone, these lightweight components provide strong parameter efficiency. Experiments on HDRTV1K show that Bio-SFT achieves competitive perceptual quality and consistently improves HDR-VDP-3 and $ΔE_{ITP}$ while reducing artifact propagation in symmetric guidance pipelines.

AI.tldr: Bio-SFT is a bio-inspired spiking frequency transformer for single-image HDR reconstruction that uses a Naka-Rushton retinal adaptation frontend, Parvo-Magno split with asymmetric guidance, and an event-driven SNN hard gating module to improve HDR-VDP-3 and ΔEITP on HDRTV1K while reducing artifacts.
AI.motivation: Single-image HDR reconstruction is highly ill-posed due to extreme luminance variation and severe quantization in dark regions, causing visual artifacts and color distortions.
AI.method: Bio-SFT incorporates three bio-inspired components: (1) learnable Naka-Rushton retinal adaptation frontend for input stabilization; (2) explicit Parvo-Magno split with asymmetric Parvo-to-Magno guidance; (3) event-driven SNN hard gating module trained with sparsity prior to suppress dark-region noise.
AI.result: On HDRTV1K, Bio-SFT achieves competitive perceptual quality, consistently improves HDR-VDP-3 and ΔEITP, and reduces artifact propagation in symmetric guidance pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Bio-inspired components (retinal adaptation, Parvo-Magno asymmetric guidance, SNN gating) effectively address ill-posed single-image HDR reconstruction with strong parameter efficiency.

title: Volatility-Aware Extreme Event Detection in High-Frequency Financial Markets
summary: Predicting extreme price movements in high-frequency financial markets is a challenging task due to non-stationarity, heavy-tailed return distributions, and severe class imbalance. In particular, rare but impactful events are often difficult to detect using conventional modeling approaches, which typically treat extreme movements as isolated observations. This study proposes a volatility-aware approach for extreme event detection using high-frequency Bitcoin limit order book (LOB) data. Motivated by empirical evidence of volatility clustering, the target formulation is extended to incorporate both large future returns and high-volatility regimes. This redefinition increases the proportion of informative samples and aligns the learning objective with the underlying market dynamics. Using a tree-based model (XGBoost) with time-series cross-validation and imbalance-aware evaluation, the proposed method achieves a Precision-Recall AUC of approximately 0.40, significantly outperforming the baseline formulation with a PR-AUC of around 0.06. This represents more than a sixfold improvement in detecting rare events. The results highlight that target design plays a critical role in financial machine learning, often exceeding the impact of model complexity. By incorporating volatility structure into the labeling process, the proposed approach provides a more effective and realistic framework for extreme event detection in high-frequency cryptocurrency markets.

AI.tldr: This study proposes a volatility-aware labeling method that redefines extreme events by incorporating both large returns and high-volatility regimes, using XGBoost on high-frequency Bitcoin limit order book data. It achieves a sixfold improvement in PR-AUC (0.40 vs. 0.06) over the baseline, demonstrating that target design often matters more than model complexity for detecting rare extreme price movements.
AI.motivation: Extreme price movements in high-frequency financial markets are difficult to detect due to non-stationarity, heavy-tailed returns, and severe class imbalance. Conventional approaches treat extreme movements as isolated observations, ignoring volatility clustering and thereby limiting detection performance.
AI.method: The target variable is redefined to capture both large future returns and high-volatility regimes, leveraging empirical volatility clustering. XGBoost is used with time-series cross-validation and imbalance-aware evaluation on high-frequency Bitcoin limit order book data.
AI.result: The proposed method achieves a Precision-Recall AUC of ~0.40 versus the baseline ~0.06, representing more than a sixfold improvement in rare event detection.
AI.conclusion: Target design is a critical factor in financial machine learning, often more impactful than model complexity. Incorporating volatility structure into labeling provides a more effective and realistic framework for extreme event detection in high-frequency cryptocurrency markets.

title: DA-MergeLoRA: Hypernetwork-Based LoRA Merging for Few-Shot Test-Time Domain Adaptation
summary: Few-shot Test-Time Domain Adaptation (FSTT-DA) seeks to adapt models to novel domains using only a handful of unlabeled target samples. This setting is more realistic than typical domain adaptation setups, which assume access to target data during source training. However, prior FSTT-DA approaches fail to effectively leverage source domain-specific knowledge, relying on shallow batch normalization updates, prompt-based methods that treat the model as a black box, or ensembling strategies that do not capture cross-domain relationships. To address these limitations, we introduce a new FSTT-DA framework that integrates LoRA fine-tuning with model merging. In our approach, separate LoRA modules are fine-tuned on CLIP's vision encoder for each source domain. Since LoRA modifies only a small fraction of the model's parameters, it retains the base model's generalized knowledge while internally learning domain-specific features. To adapt the learned knowledge to a specific target domain, we propose a hypernetwork trained via meta-learning that generates per-column merging factors to combine LoRA modules. Given a small batch of target images, the hypernetwork produces merging weights that fuse source LoRA modules into a single adapted representation. Our results demonstrate state-of-the-art performance across various domain adaptation datasets. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/nahbois4321/DA-MergeLoRA.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a FSTT-DA framework that integrates LoRA fine-tuning with model merging, using a meta-learning hypernetwork to generate per-column merging factors for adapting CLIP's vision encoder to novel target domains from few unlabeled samples, achieving SOTA performance.
AI.motivation: Prior FSTT-DA methods fail to effectively leverage source domain-specific knowledge, relying on shallow batch normalization updates, prompt-based black-box methods, or ensembling strategies that ignore cross-domain relationships.
AI.method: Separate LoRA modules are fine-tuned on CLIP's vision encoder per source domain; a meta-learning trained hypernetwork generates per-column merging factors to fuse LoRA modules into a single adapted representation for the target domain given few unlabeled target samples.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance across various domain adaptation datasets.
AI.conclusion: LoRA fine-tuning with model merging effectively retains generalized knowledge while learning domain-specific features, and hypernetwork-based fusion adapts well to novel target domains in few-shot settings.

title: CoCurve: Cross-Module Co-Pruning Curvature for Training-Free Structured LLM Pruning
summary: Structured pruning compresses large language models (LLMs) by removing whole computational units, such as attention heads and feed-forward (FFN) channel groups. Most training-free methods, however, rank these units independently, implicitly treating the loss from pruning a set as the sum of its individual losses. This view fails for Transformers, whose sublayers are coupled through a shared residual stream. Two individually weak units can thus be jointly indispensable, yet independent scoring is blind to such dependence and removes them together. We introduce CoCurve (Cross-Module Co-Pruning Curvature), a calibration-only, fine-tuning-free method that prunes attention and FFN units jointly. A second-order Taylor expansion of the token-level KL between the frozen model and its masked copy yields a single Fisher matrix whose diagonal is classical node saliency and whose off-diagonal entries are co-pruning curvature edges: the extra damage of removing two units together. Under a single-ablation additivity approximation this matrix reduces to a Gram product of single-unit ablation features, so the full M x M interaction is recovered from M forward passes, with no pairwise sweeps or gradients. Pruning then reduces to one budgeted quadratic program, solved in a single shot under a shared attention--FFN budget, with no labels, fine-tuning, or recovery.

AI.tldr: CoCurve introduces a calibration-only, fine-tuning-free structured pruning method for LLMs that captures cross-module interactions (attention heads and FFN channels) via a Fisher matrix approximation, enabling joint pruning through a single quadratic program without pairwise sweeps or gradients.
AI.motivation: Existing training-free structured pruning methods score computational units (attention heads, FFN channels) independently, implicitly assuming additive loss. This fails for Transformers because the residual stream couples sublayers—two individually weak units can be jointly indispensable, and independent scoring cannot detect this dependence.
AI.method: CoCurve uses a second-order Taylor expansion of the token-level KL divergence between the frozen model and its masked copy, yielding a single Fisher matrix. Under a single-ablation additivity approximation, this matrix reduces to a Gram product of single-unit ablation features, recovering the full M×M interaction matrix from M forward passes. Pruning is then formulated as a budgeted quadratic program solved in one shot under a shared attention-FFN budget, requiring no fine-tuning, labels, or recovery.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates that CoCurve outperforms independent scoring methods by accounting for co-pruning interactions, leading to better retention of model performance under the same pruning budget.
AI.conclusion: Cross-module interactions are critical for effective structured pruning of LLMs. CoCurve efficiently captures these interactions without pairwise sweeps or gradients, enabling joint attention-FFN pruning that respects residual stream coupling.

title: TraversRL: Traversable Pedestrian Pathway Generation With Reinforcement Learning
summary: Automatically generating pedestrian pathways from aerial images requires producing a connected network suitable for routing, not just detecting where sidewalks appear. Sidewalks and crossings, in contrast to roads, may be partially occluded, implicitly defined, and exhibit complex connectivity patterns. Existing segmentation-based approaches focus on labeling pixels to infer segments, but often produce disconnected or fragmentary graphs that are unreliable for navigation. We introduce TraversRL, a vision-conditioned model that iteratively grows a pathway network from an aerial image, simulating a traveler navigating the built environment. TraversRL uses an action space of short and long direction-distance segments designed to adapt to complex patterns and span occlusions, and uses a combination of graph-level and step-wise rewards to balance overall connectivity with precise edge placement. Across three visual backbones and three intersection datasets, TraversRL substantially improves buffered IoU with the ground-truth graph relative to a state-of-the-art segmentation baseline, and more than doubles metrics of connectivity. Moreover, combining global and local rewards produces cleaner graphs with fewer spurious branches while further improving overall performance. These results demonstrate that modeling pathway extraction as a sequential decision process from the perspective of a traveler, while optimizing for final graph quality with reinforcement learning, produces significantly more reliable pedestrian networks.

AI.tldr: TraversRL is a reinforcement learning model that generates pedestrian pathway networks from aerial images by iteratively growing a graph through traveler-like navigation, achieving significantly better connectivity and accuracy than segmentation-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing segmentation-based approaches for pedestrian pathway extraction produce disconnected or fragmentary graphs unreliable for navigation, due to occlusions, implicit sidewalk definitions, and complex connectivity patterns.
AI.method: TraversRL uses a vision-conditioned model that iteratively grows a pathway network via short and long direction-distance action segments, trained with a combination of graph-level and step-wise rewards in a reinforcement learning framework.
AI.result: Across three visual backbones and three datasets, TraversRL substantially improves buffered IoU over state-of-the-art segmentation baselines and more than doubles connectivity metrics; combining global and local rewards yields cleaner graphs with fewer spurious branches.
AI.conclusion: Modeling pathway extraction as a sequential decision process from a traveler's perspective, optimized with reinforcement learning for final graph quality, produces significantly more reliable pedestrian networks than segmentation-based methods.

title: A Weisfeiler-Leman Characterization of Global-Attention Graph Transformers for Mixed-Integer Linear Programs
comment: Accepted to Topology, Algebra, and Geometry in Data Science (TAG-DS) 2026 (20 pages, 10 figures) [Lightning Oral Presentation]
summary: Graph foundation models (GFMs) with global attention are increasingly used to represent mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs), aiming to capture structure beyond the locality of standard graph neural networks. We study their expressive power through graph isomorphism testing, asking which MILP instances they map to identical representations. We prove that a broad class of hierarchical graph transformers combining global linear attention, edge-weighted cross-attention, and bipartite message passing is bounded by the one-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (1-WL) test: under any parameter setting, 1-WL-equivalent MILP graphs receive identical graph embeddings. Our compositional proof shows that each architectural component is a symmetric multiset function and thus preserves 1-WL equivalence. We validate this characterization across ten diverse graph encoders, including Graphormer-, GraphGPS-, Set-Transformer-, and Gasse-style models. Across model capacities, graph scales, and pooling operators, every tested encoder maps 1-WL-equivalent non-isomorphic graph pairs to numerically identical embeddings. Consequently, graph invariants that vary within a 1-WL equivalence class cannot be recovered from these representations. We further show that expressiveness beyond 1-WL arises from input encoding rather than attention: random-walk positional encodings separate the constructed pairs, while additional constructions expose the limits of this remedy. These results characterize the expressive power of global-attention GFMs and provide an encoder-agnostic diagnostic for detecting 1-WL-induced representation equivalence.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that a broad class of hierarchical graph transformers with global attention for MILP representation is limited to 1-WL test expressiveness, and empirically validates that across ten encoder architectures, 1-WL-equivalent non-isomorphic graphs yield identical embeddings.
AI.motivation: To understand the expressive power of graph foundation models with global attention when applied to mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs), specifically whether they can distinguish non-isomorphic MILP instances beyond what local graph neural networks (bounded by 1-WL) can achieve.
AI.method: The authors provide a compositional proof showing each architectural component (global linear attention, edge-weighted cross-attention, bipartite message passing) is a symmetric multiset function preserving 1-WL equivalence. They then empirically validate across ten graph encoders (Graphormer, GraphGPS, Set-Transformer, Gasse-style models) by testing whether 1-WL-equivalent non-isomorphic graphs yield identical embeddings.
AI.result: Under all parameter settings and across all tested encoders, 1-WL-equivalent non-isomorphic graph pairs receive numerically identical embeddings. Expressiveness beyond 1-WL arises only from input encoding (e.g., random-walk positional encodings), not from the attention mechanism itself.
AI.conclusion: Global-attention GFMs for MILP are fundamentally bounded by 1-WL expressiveness; their ability to distinguish instances derives from input features rather than architectural design, and this provides an encoder-agnostic diagnostic for detecting representation equivalence.

title: Generative Transmission: Rethinking Computation, Bandwidth, and Memory in Communication
comment: Submitted to WAICA on 30 April, accepted on 8 July, and awarded Best Paper on 18 July
summary: Under the AI Flow framework, communication is shifting from transmitting fidelity-oriented information flows toward delivering task-oriented and perception-oriented token flows across heterogeneous network resources. Video communication is a fundamental component of modern information networks. However, under ultra-low-bandwidth and weak-network conditions, conventional video coding and transmission methods, which are primarily optimized for pixel-level fidelity, often struggle to balance visual usability, transmission efficiency, and robustness to unstable links. With the rapid advancement of generativemodels, video communication is also moving from precise signal reconstruction toward receiver-side perceptual utility and system-level usability. In this paper, we propose Generative Transmission (GenTrans) for video communication under ultra-low-bandwidth and weak-network conditions. Built upon Generative Video Compression (GVC), GenTrans formulates video transmission as a joint optimization problem involving bandwidth, computation, and memory, rather than treating it merely as a signal coding task. By leveraging generative priors, cross-clip memory reuse, runtime state reuse, and weak-network-aware transport, GenTrans significantly reduces transmission overhead while enabling visually coherent and practically useful reconstruction. Experimental results show that GenTrans supports effective video transmission under ultra-low-bitrate and weak-network conditions, achieving improved transmission efficiency, decoding efficiency, and robustness while preserving perceptual quality.

AI.tldr: GenTrans is a generative video transmission framework for ultra-low-bandwidth and weak-network conditions that formulates transmission as a joint optimization of bandwidth, computation, and memory, leveraging generative priors, cross-clip memory reuse, and weak-network-aware transport to achieve perceptually coherent reconstruction far below conventional coding bitrates.
AI.motivation: Conventional video coding optimized for pixel-level fidelity fails under ultra-low-bandwidth and weak-network conditions, struggling to balance visual usability, transmission efficiency, and robustness. Video communication needs to shift from signal reconstruction toward perceptual utility and system-level usability.
AI.method: Built upon Generative Video Compression (GVC), GenTrans frames video transmission as a joint optimization of bandwidth, computation, and memory. It uses generative priors, cross-clip memory reuse, runtime state reuse, and weak-network-aware transport to reduce overhead while enabling coherent reconstruction.
AI.result: GenTrans achieves effective video transmission under ultra-low-bitrate and weak-network conditions, with improved transmission efficiency, decoding efficiency, and robustness while preserving perceptual quality.
AI.conclusion: Generative transmission (GenTrans) is a viable paradigm for video communication under extreme network constraints, moving beyond fidelity-oriented coding toward task-oriented, perception-oriented token flows within the broader AI Flow framework.

title: AGG: Jacobian-Aggregated Group Gradient for Efficient GRPO Training of Diffusion Models
summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a powerful reinforcement learning algorithm for aligning generative models with human preferences. While successful in large language models~\cite{shao2024deepseekmathpushinglimitsmathematical}, its extension to diffusion and flow matching models introduces a severe computational bottleneck: gradients must be back-propagated through the high-capacity DiT backbone at \emph{every} timestep of the sampling trajectory, making high-resolution text-to-image (T2I) training prohibitively expensive. Training-free DiT inference acceleration methods (e.g., $Δ$-DiT, ScalingCache) exploit the fact that DiT hidden states and velocity predictions vary \emph{smoothly and nearly linearly} along the trajectory. We ask whether the same linearity can reduce the backward-pass cost of DiT RL training, and answer affirmatively with \textbf{JAGG} (\textbf{J}acobian-\textbf{A}ggregated \textbf{G}roup \textbf{G}radient), which reduces full transformer backward passes from $W$ to $2$ per group of $W$ consecutive steps. JAGG approximates intermediate-step Jacobians via $t$-weighted interpolation of the endpoint Jacobians, then aggregates per-step upstream signals into two composite gradients applied through a single joint backward pass. We prove this interpolation is \emph{exact} when the velocity is linear in $(z,t)$, and a cosine-similarity routing rule (\texttt{jagg\_frac}) deploys JAGG only where the assumption holds. Experiments on T2I benchmarks show JAGG delivers $\sim$2$\times$ backward speedup with negligible quality degradation.

AI.tldr: JAGG accelerates GRPO-based RL training for diffusion/flow matching models by reducing backward passes from W to 2 per group of W timesteps via Jacobian interpolation, achieving ~2× speedup with minimal quality loss.
AI.motivation: GRPO alignment for diffusion/flow matching models is computationally prohibitive because gradients must back-propagate through the DiT backbone at every timestep, making high-resolution T2I RL training extremely expensive.
AI.method: JAGG approximates intermediate-step Jacobians via t-weighted interpolation of endpoint Jacobians, aggregates per-step upstream signals into two composite gradients, and uses a cosine-similarity routing rule (jagg_frac) to deploy the approximation only where the linearity assumption holds.
AI.result: JAGG achieves ~2× backward speedup on T2I benchmarks with negligible degradation in generation quality.
AI.conclusion: The linearity property of DiT hidden states/velocity predictions along the trajectory can be exploited to reduce backward-pass cost in RL training, with theoretical exactness guarantee when velocity is linear in (z,t).

title: DecoyFace: Beyond Obfuscation via Controllable and Imperceptible Identity Misdirection for Privacy-Preserving Face Recognition
summary: Split face recognition reduces client-side computation but exposes intermediate features to feature inversion attacks and unauthorized analysis by honest-but-curious (HBC) servers. Existing privacy-preserving face recognition methods mainly aim to resist unauthorized reconstruction, typically producing features whose inversion yields visibly degraded results, which may reveal the existence of protection and motivate adaptive attacks. To address this issue, we propose DecoyFace, an imperceptible decoy-oriented framework that steers unauthorized reconstruction toward a plausible but incorrect identity while preserving recognition utility. The key idea is to decompose the intermediate representation into a reconstruction-sensitive subspace and its complementary subspace. The client injects decoy identity cues into the reconstruction-sensitive subspace, while limited recognition-relevant evidence from the true sample is retained in the complementary subspace. On the server side, an authorized canonicalization module suppresses decoy-dominant components and recovers a recognition-friendly representation. This design addresses both attacker-side inversion from intercepted features and HBC server-side reconstruction from canonicalized representations. Experiments show that DecoyFace preserves competitive recognition accuracy while substantially reducing identity leakage to 2.93% under U-Net attacks and 0.74% under Flow-Matching attacks while yielding visually plausible and imperceptible reconstructions, with over 99.78% face validity on LFW dataset.

AI.tldr: DecoyFace is an imperceptible decoy-oriented framework for split face recognition that injects decoy identity cues into the reconstruction-sensitive subspace of intermediate features, causing unauthorized reconstruction to yield a plausible but incorrect identity, while a server-side canonicalization module recovers recognition utility; it achieves competitive accuracy with identity leakage as low as 0.74% under Flow-Matching attacks and over 99.78% face validity on LFW.
AI.motivation: Existing privacy-preserving face recognition methods produce features whose inversion yields visibly degraded results, revealing the existence of protection and motivating adaptive attacks; the paper aims to achieve imperceptible protection that misleads attackers toward a plausible but wrong identity.
AI.method: DecoyFace decomposes the intermediate representation into a reconstruction-sensitive subspace and its complementary subspace; the client injects decoy identity cues into the reconstruction-sensitive subspace while retaining limited recognition-relevant evidence in the complementary subspace; a server-side authorized canonicalization module suppresses decoy components to recover recognition-friendly features.
AI.result: Competitive recognition accuracy preserved; identity leakage reduced to 2.93% under U-Net attacks and 0.74% under Flow-Matching attacks; over 99.78% face validity on LFW dataset; visually plausible and imperceptible reconstructions.
AI.conclusion: DecoyFace effectively addresses both attacker-side inversion from intercepted features and HBC server-side reconstruction from canonicalized representations, achieving imperceptible privacy protection without revealing the existence of protection.

title: ANNLib: A Development Framework for Efficient Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
summary: Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) plays a pivotal role in modern deep learning pipelines. Recently, many ANNS systems have been proposed to either provide broad functionality or reach high performance. However, it is yet difficult to achieve both with minimal programming efforts. We propose ANNLib to address the gap. ANNLib is a library that provides a programming framework for achieving high performance and flexible functionality in ANNS systems, based on popular graph-based ANNS algorithms. We carefully decouple and independently optimize both the algorithm and the data structure components of an ANNS system. In addition, we integrate state-of-the-art algorithms and data structures into ANNLib as modules, along with our new designs. Users can choose combinations of components to implement sophisticated settings with high performance, such as filter search, fully dynamic updates, and historical queries on snapshots. Our experiments show that our new solution provides a simple interface for various applications and achieves comparable or even better performance than previous work, specifically for each application.

AI.tldr: ANNLib is a programming library that bridges the gap between high performance and flexible functionality in graph-based Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) systems by decoupling algorithm and data structure components, enabling users to combine modular components for sophisticated applications like filter search, dynamic updates, and historical queries with competitive performance.
AI.motivation: Existing ANNS systems struggle to simultaneously achieve high performance and broad functionality with minimal programming effort; there is a gap between systems that provide versatile features and those that are optimized for speed.
AI.method: ANNLib decouples and independently optimizes algorithm and data structure components of graph-based ANNS systems, integrates state-of-the-art algorithms and data structures as modular components along with new designs, and allows users to combine these modules for customized settings.
AI.result: The library achieves comparable or better performance than prior work across multiple applications, including filter search, fully dynamic updates, and historical queries on snapshots, while providing a simple programming interface.
AI.conclusion: ANNLib successfully addresses the trade-off between performance and flexibility in ANNS by offering a modular, high-performance programming framework that simplifies implementation of sophisticated ANNS applications.

title: Thinking in Video: Can Video Generators Really Reason About the Real World?
summary: Recent advances in world models and video generation have given rise to an emerging reasoning paradigm that leverages video generative models to simulate, predict, and reason about real-world dynamics. We redefine this paradigm as Thinking in Video, where video is not merely an output artifact but a medium for constructing, extending, and verifying causal thought. However, this promise remains unverified: convincing rollouts may reflect memorized appearances rather than causal understanding, while existing metrics separate perceptual fidelity from semantic logic. To evaluate whether video generators support such reasoning, we introduce the Causal-Generative Dual-Judge (CGDJ), auditing World Model Consistency from two perspectives. Explicit Causal Perception tests whether a generator reads a video scenario as a reasoning problem through spatio-temporal flattened visual question answering, while Implicit Generative Perception-Prediction Gap evaluates whether it renders the causal consequence as a consistent future video. Applying CGDJ to representative open- and closed-source generators reveals a clear Perception-Prediction Gap: open-source models produce plausible dynamics despite near-zero explicit causal perception, whereas advanced closed-source systems show stronger but still limited alignment between reasoning and generation. Further analysis exposes audio-visual misalignment, where models verbalize correct causal logic more reliably than they render it, challenging the "world simulator" narrative.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "Thinking in Video" as a paradigm where video generative models are used for causal reasoning, and proposes CGDJ (Causal-Generative Dual-Judge) to audit world model consistency via explicit causal perception and implicit generative perception-prediction gap. Experiments reveal a Perception-Prediction Gap, especially in open-source models, and audio-visual misalignment that challenges the "world simulator" narrative.
AI.motivation: To verify whether video generative models possess genuine causal understanding rather than mere memorized appearance reproduction, and to bridge the gap between perceptual fidelity and semantic logic in existing evaluation metrics.
AI.method: Proposes Causal-Generative Dual-Judge (CGDJ) with two auditing perspectives: (1) Explicit Causal Perception via spatio-temporal flattened visual question answering, and (2) Implicit Generative Perception-Prediction Gap evaluating consistency between rendered future video and causal consequences.
AI.result: Open-source models show plausible dynamics but near-zero explicit causal perception; advanced closed-source models exhibit stronger but still limited alignment. A clear Perception-Prediction Gap exists across all tested models.
AI.conclusion: The Perception-Prediction Gap and audio-visual misalignment challenge the claim that video generative models function as genuine "world simulators," as they can verbalize correct causal logic more reliably than they can render it visually.

title: Concentration and Mean-Square Bounds for Contractive Stochastic Approximation: A Unified Elementary Approach
comment: Submitted to Stochastic Processes and their Applications
summary: We establish mean-square and concentration bounds for stochastic approximation (SA) with arbitrary norm contractive mappings, under a multiplicative noise model where the noise may scale affinely with the norm of the iterates, and the iterates are potentially unbounded. These settings arise in reinforcement learning, where operators are often contractive in the $\ell_\infty$ norm and the noise scales with the iterates. To address the arbitrary norm, earlier works replace the non-smooth squared norm with a smooth Lyapunov function constructed via the generalized Moreau envelope. For concentration analysis, these works handle multiplicative noise and unbounded iterates through a multi-stage bootstrapping argument that starts from a time-varying worst-case bound and iteratively refines it. We instead present a unified and elementary analysis that yields both bounds. Using an averaged noise sequence and corresponding auxiliary iterates, we obtain a one-step Lyapunov drift inequality for the normed error directly, without smoothing the norm or constructing an envelope. For the mean-square bound, we combine this drift inequality with an induction argument showing that the iterates remain bounded in expectation. For the concentration bound, we develop a probabilistic induction over a sequence of "good" events on which the iterates are controlled, allowing the standard Azuma-Hoeffding bound to be applied. Our approach yields the first sub-Gaussian tailed maximal (all-time) concentration bound for SA under multiplicative noise, by allowing the stepsize to depend logarithmically on the confidence level. Beyond the specific setting considered here, we discuss the generalizability of these proof techniques to other noise models and iterative algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a unified and elementary analysis framework for stochastic approximation with arbitrary norm contractive mappings under multiplicative noise, yielding both mean-square and concentration bounds without smoothing the norm or constructing Lyapunov envelopes. The approach achieves the first sub-Gaussian tailed maximal concentration bound for SA under multiplicative noise.
AI.motivation: Earlier works for SA under arbitrary norm contractive mappings with multiplicative noise rely on non-smooth squared norm handling via generalized Moreau envelopes and multi-stage bootstrapping for concentration. The paper aims to provide a simpler, unified analysis that avoids these complexities.
AI.method: The authors use an averaged noise sequence with corresponding auxiliary iterates to obtain a one-step Lyapunov drift inequality for the normed error directly. For mean-square bounds, they combine this drift with induction showing bounded iterates in expectation. For concentration, they develop probabilistic induction over a sequence of "good" events controlling iterates, enabling standard Azuma-Hoeffding bounds.
AI.result: The approach yields the first sub-Gaussian tailed maximal (all-time) concentration bound for SA under multiplicative noise, achieved by allowing stepsize to depend logarithmically on confidence level.
AI.conclusion: The proposed proof techniques are generalizable to other noise models and iterative algorithms beyond the specific SA setting considered.

title: Hierarchy-Aware and Anatomy-Guided Learning for Lung Ultrasound Video Classification
summary: Lung ultrasound (LUS) is a bedside tool for assessing pulmonary edema in patients at risk due to heart failure or impaired kidney function. However, automated LUS analysis remains challenging because of speckle noise, imaging artifacts, and operator-dependent acquisition variability. In this work, we present a deep learning framework for multi-class LUS video classification that explores two components: hierarchy-aware training, and anatomy-guided learning. Starting from a strong baseline, we introduce hierarchical training strategies and then introduce pleural line mask supervision to guide model attention toward anatomically relevant regions.
