We study four clinically relevant classes--healthy, B-lines, consolidations, and mixed B-lines with consolidations--using an open-access dataset of 1,886 videos from 219 patients, evaluated with patient-level five-fold cross-validation. Results show that hierarchy-aware training improves pathological separation relative to flat classification, while mask-guided attention supervision achieves the highest mean macro-F1 of 65.7\% and produces more localized attention patterns. Transfer experiments on the external COVID-BLUeS dataset further show competitive and parameter-efficient adaptation while preserving pleural-focused attention behavior. These findings suggest that combining clinically structured objectives with anatomy-guided supervision is a practical approach to robust, interpretable LUS video analysis. Code and model implementations are available at https://github.com/Alya-Almsouti/LUS-video-classification.

AI.tldr: A deep learning framework for multi-class lung ultrasound video classification using hierarchy-aware training and anatomy-guided (pleural line mask) supervision, achieving 65.7% macro-F1 on 1,886 videos across 4 clinical classes, with improved interpretability and parameter-efficient transfer learning.
AI.motivation: Lung ultrasound is useful for bedside pulmonary edema assessment but automated analysis is challenging due to speckle noise, artifacts, and operator-dependent variability; existing methods lack structured clinical knowledge integration.
AI.method: Proposes a deep learning framework with (1) hierarchy-aware training strategies for structured clinical classification and (2) pleural line mask supervision to guide attention toward anatomically relevant regions. Evaluated on 1,886 videos (219 patients) with patient-level 5-fold CV across 4 classes: healthy, B-lines, consolidations, mixed.
AI.result: Hierarchy-aware training outperforms flat classification; mask-guided attention achieves 65.7% mean macro-F1 with more localized attention. External COVID-BLUeS transfer experiments show competitive, parameter-efficient adaptation with preserved pleural-focused attention.
AI.conclusion: Combining clinically structured objectives with anatomy-guided supervision is a practical approach for robust, interpretable LUS video analysis.

title: Trustworthy Protein-Ligand Binding Affinity Prediction via Reliability-Aware Multi-Engine Fusion
summary: Accurate protein-ligand binding affinity prediction is central to computational drug discovery, yet modern docking engines frequently disagree without indicating which prediction to trust. Consensus scoring and ensemble methods improve mean accuracy but treat all predictions identically without interpretable confidence measures or uncertainty decomposition, ignoring the chemical context of each protein-ligand pair. To address this limitation, we introduce RELIABLE-BA (RELIABiLity-aware Evidential fusion for Binding Affinity), an evidential framework for multi-engine binding affinity prediction. Our model comprises three steps: (1) modeling each engine as an evidential expert via Normal-Inverse-Gamma distributions, (2) scaling epistemic uncertainty through learned reliability from molecular context while preserving each expert's predictive mean, and (3) fusing experts through closed-form aggregation that captures both individual uncertainty and inter-engine disagreement. Experiments on the PDBBind and BDB2020+ benchmarks demonstrate competitive point prediction with substantially improved uncertainty calibration, and additional validation on the SARS-CoV-2 Mpro dataset and 5HT2A receptor demonstrates applicability to clinically relevant drug targets. Crucially, these uncertainty estimates enable reliable filtering of protein-ligand pairs, reducing prediction error by up to 25% when retaining only high-confidence pairs. To our knowledge, RELIABLE-BA is the first multi-engine binding affinity prediction framework to combine evidential fusion with context-dependent reliability, offering a principled path toward trustworthy AI-guided drug discovery. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/yongchand/RELIABLE-BA.

AI.tldr: RELIABLE-BA introduces an evidential fusion framework for protein-ligand binding affinity prediction that models each docking engine as an evidential expert, scales uncertainty via learned reliability from molecular context, and aggregates experts through closed-form fusion. It achieves competitive accuracy with superior uncertainty calibration, enabling up to 25% error reduction through high-confidence filtering, validated on PDBBind, BDB2020+, SARS-CoV-2 Mpro, and 5HT2A datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-engine docking methods improve mean accuracy via consensus scoring and ensemble approaches but lack interpretable confidence measures, uncertainty decomposition, and context-awareness; they treat all predictions identically without considering the chemical context of each protein-ligand pair.
AI.method: Three-step evidential framework: (1) model each engine as an evidential expert using Normal-Inverse-Gamma distributions, (2) scale epistemic uncertainty via learned reliability from molecular context while preserving predictive means, (3) fuse experts via closed-form aggregation capturing individual uncertainty and inter-engine disagreement.
AI.result: Competitive point prediction with substantially improved uncertainty calibration on PDBBind and BDB2020+; validated on SARS-CoV-2 Mpro and 5HT2A targets; uncertainty-based filtering reduces prediction error by up to 25% when retaining only high-confidence pairs.
AI.conclusion: RELIABLE-BA is the first multi-engine binding affinity prediction framework combining evidential fusion with context-dependent reliability, offering a principled approach toward trustworthy AI-guided drug discovery.

title: FlexiGrad: Adaptive Gradient Modulation for Hierarchical Fine-Grained Classification
summary: Many fine-grained recognition tasks contain hierarchical labels such as order, family and species. Although this supervision should be beneficial, jointly optimising all levels often leads to unstable training because coarse and fine classifiers impose inconsistent gradients on the shared backbone. This hierarchical gradient conflict prevents the model from learning a coherent coarse-to-fine representation. In this paper, we propose FlexiGrad, a simple and parameter-free method that regulates gradient interactions during backpropagation. FlexiGrad removes only the harmful conflicting component when tasks disagree and reinforces the shared direction when they partially agree through a smooth hierarchy-aware weighting function. This produces stable optimisation and preserves both global structure and fine-grained discriminative cues. FlexiGrad integrates into existing architectures without modification while improves multi-granularity accuracy on CUB-200-2011, FGVC-Aircraft and Stanford Cars. The code will be available at PRIS-CV/FlexiGrad.

AI.tldr: FlexiGrad is a parameter-free method that resolves hierarchical gradient conflicts in fine-grained recognition by removing harmful conflicting components and reinforcing shared gradient directions, enabling stable training of coarse-to-fine representations without architectural changes.
AI.motivation: Jointly optimizing hierarchical labels (e.g., order, family, species) in fine-grained recognition is unstable due to conflicting gradients between coarse and fine classifiers on the shared backbone, preventing coherent multi-granularity representation learning.
AI.method: FlexiGrad regulates gradient backpropagation by detecting inter-level gradient conflicts, removing the harmful conflicting component when tasks disagree, and reinforcing the shared direction when they partially agree using a smooth hierarchy-aware weighting function. It is parameter-free and requires no architectural modifications.
AI.result: Improves multi-granularity accuracy on CUB-200-2011, FGVC-Aircraft, and Stanford Cars benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: FlexiGrad provides stable optimization for hierarchical fine-grained recognition by resolving gradient conflicts, producing representations that preserve both global structure and fine-grained discriminative cues, and can be integrated into existing architectures without modification.

title: Optimizing the Preconditioner: A Black-box Online-to-Nonconvex Conversion with Static Regret Minimization Oracles
summary:
We study whether stochastic nonconvex optimization can be reduced to ordinary static regret minimization in online convex optimization in a black-box manner. For smooth nonconvex objectives, our reduction maintains a predictable gradient tracker, while a black-box online learner selects a preconditioner that determines how this tracker is transformed into the update direction. The learner receives linear convex losses and is evaluated against a single fixed comparator over one undiscounted online game. For a $β$-smooth objective with range bounded by $M$ and an unbiased stochastic-gradient oracle with variance bounded by \(σ^2\), we establish $$\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^T
  \mathbb E\!\left[\|\nabla f(x_t)\|_2^2\right]
  \lesssim
  \frac{σ\sqrt{Mβ}}{\sqrt T}
  +
  \frac{\sqrt{Mβ}\,
  \mathscr R_T(\mathcal A,I_d)}{T}
  +
  \frac{Mβ}{T}.$$ Consequently, any black-box OCO algorithm with $\mathscr R_T(\mathcal A,I_d)=O(\sqrt T)$ recovers the classical $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}})$ convergence rate.
  We further show that the same black-box framework extends beyond the smooth setting to Lipschitz nonconvex objectives without Lipschitz continuous gradients. Importantly, this extension continues to rely only on an ordinary static-regret guarantee and requires no stronger notion of online regret. When the OCO oracle admits square-root static regret, the resulting conversion achieves the optimal $O(T^{-2/7})$ convergence rate for the corresponding Goldstein stationary point. These results resolve the open problem posed by Chen and Hazan (2024). More broadly, our framework separates optimizer design into gradient prediction and online preconditioner selection, providing a principled perspective on how adaptive optimization methods such as AdaGrad and Shampoo may be understood through static regret and applied in nonconvex optimization.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a black-box reduction from stochastic nonconvex optimization to static regret minimization in online convex optimization. For smooth nonconvex objectives, it achieves O(1/√T) convergence using any OCO algorithm with √T static regret. It extends to Lipschitz nonconvex objectives without gradient smoothness, achieving optimal O(T^{-2/7}) rate for Goldstein stationary points. The framework separates gradient prediction from online preconditioner selection, unifying adaptive methods like AdaGrad and Shampoo.
AI.motivation: To resolve the open problem posed by Chen and Hazan (2024) regarding whether stochastic nonconvex optimization can be reduced to ordinary static regret minimization in online convex optimization in a black-box manner, and to provide a principled framework for understanding adaptive optimization methods in nonconvex settings.
AI.method: A black-box reduction that maintains a predictable gradient tracker while a black-box online learner selects a preconditioner. The learner receives linear convex losses and is evaluated against a single fixed comparator over one undiscounted online game. For smooth objectives, the method uses an OCO algorithm with static regret guarantee. For Lipschitz nonconvex objectives without gradient smoothness, the same framework extends using only ordinary static-regret guarantees.
AI.result: For β-smooth objectives: convergence rate O(σ√(Mβ)/√T + √(Mβ) R_T(A,I_d)/T + Mβ/T). Any OCO algorithm with R_T(A,I_d)=O(√T) recovers classical O(1/√T) rate. For Lipschitz nonconvex objectives: achieves optimal O(T^{-2/7}) convergence rate for Goldstein stationary points when the OCO oracle admits square-root static regret.
AI.conclusion: The framework successfully reduces stochastic nonconvex optimization to static regret minimization in OCO, resolving the open problem by Chen and Hazan (2024). It separates optimizer design into gradient prediction and online preconditioner selection, providing a principled perspective on understanding adaptive methods like AdaGrad and Shampoo through static regret in nonconvex optimization.

title: Scalable Model-Assisted Multi-Target Estimation in Large Image Collections
comment: Accepted at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI 2026)
summary: Computer vision models are increasingly used as measurement tools to estimate population-level quantities from large image collections, but prediction errors introduce bias and the resulting estimates lack statistical guarantees required in scientific applications. Prior work uses a Monte Carlo framework to combine model predictions with ground-truth annotations by sampling some images for humans to label and is able to provide unbiased estimates with controllable accuracy, but primarily addresses single-scalar estimation. We study the more general problem of multi-target estimation, where many quantities (e.g., class counts or proportions) must be estimated simultaneously, and adapt sampling and estimation strategies from survey sampling to this setting. Evaluations on five detection and segmentation datasets with 7-80 classes show that importance sampling excels with moderate annotation budgets or fewer targets, whereas uniform sampling with control variates is superior when estimating many targets or operating with minimal labels. Additionally, a subset-based ratio estimator remains highly competitive across all regimes. Ultimately, our framework effectively combines biased model predictions and limited human labels into rigorous scientific measurements.

AI.tldr: This paper extends Monte Carlo frameworks for unbiased multi-target estimation (e.g., class counts/proportions) from computer vision models by adapting survey sampling techniques, finding that importance sampling works best with moderate budgets/few targets, uniform sampling with control variates excels for many targets or minimal labels, and a subset-based ratio estimator is consistently competitive.
AI.motivation: Computer vision models used as measurement tools for population-level estimation suffer from prediction bias and lack statistical guarantees. Prior Monte Carlo methods provide unbiased estimates with controllable accuracy but primarily handle single-scalar estimation, leaving the more practical multi-target estimation problem unsolved.
AI.method: The authors adapt survey sampling strategies (importance sampling, uniform sampling with control variates, and a subset-based ratio estimator) to multi-target estimation, combining biased model predictions with limited human annotations within a Monte Carlo framework. Evaluations are conducted on five detection and segmentation datasets with 7-80 classes.
AI.result: Importance sampling performs best with moderate annotation budgets or few targets; uniform sampling with control variates is superior for many targets or minimal labels; the subset-based ratio estimator remains highly competitive across all regimes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework effectively combines biased model predictions with limited human labels to produce rigorous, statistically grounded scientific measurements for multi-target estimation tasks.

title: PoLoRA: A Preconditioned Orthogonalized LoRA Optimizer
summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) makes finetuning large language models cheaper by adding to each weight matrix a trainable low-rank update parameterized as the product of two matrices. These matrices are usually trained with Adam, which treats them as a single flat vector of parameters and ignores both the matrix and product structure of LoRA. Applying a matrix-aware optimizer such as Muon to each factor does not consistently improve over Adam, and neither do the product-aware Muon variants proposed in concurrent works. To realize consistent gains, we introduce PoLoRA, a Preconditioned Orthogonalized LoRA optimizer built from three ingredients: a product-aware spectral update direction, curvature preconditioning derived from controlling the per-sample loss change, and a magnitude rule that controls the sizes of both the factor and merged updates. We evaluate PoLoRA on instruction-tuning datasets for code and math across models from 1B to 8B parameters, and find that it reaches the final held-out loss achieved by tuned Adam in 1.2-1.7 times fewer steps, while adding at most 3% per-step overhead. Compared to Adam, PoLoRA is also less sensitive to the learning rate, and its optimal learning rate is stable across ranks.

AI.tldr: PoLoRA is a new optimizer for LoRA fine-tuning that integrates product-aware spectral updates, curvature preconditioning, and a magnitude rule, achieving faster convergence (1.2-1.7x fewer steps) than Adam with minimal overhead and reduced sensitivity to learning rate.
AI.motivation: Standard optimizers like Adam treat LoRA's matrix factors as flat vectors, ignoring both the matrix structure and the product structure of LoRA. Existing matrix-aware (Muon) and product-aware optimizers do not consistently outperform Adam.
AI.method: PoLoRA combines three components: (1) a product-aware spectral update direction leveraging the matrix product structure, (2) curvature preconditioning derived from controlling per-sample loss change, and (3) a magnitude rule that controls the sizes of both factor and merged updates.
AI.result: On instruction-tuning datasets for code and math across 1B-8B models, PoLoRA reaches the final held-out loss of tuned Adam in 1.2-1.7x fewer steps, with at most 3% per-step overhead. It is also less sensitive to learning rate and has stable optimal LR across ranks.
AI.conclusion: PoLoRA consistently outperforms Adam, Muon, and existing product-aware optimizers for LoRA fine-tuning, offering faster convergence, robustness to hyperparameters, and practical efficiency.

title: Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers
summary: Latent diffusion models (LDMs) enable efficient high-resolution image synthesis by denoising in a VAE-compressed latent space. However, fixed visual tokenizers can discard fine textures and structural details, while separate representation and diffusion training creates a mismatch between reconstruction and generation objectives. These limitations have renewed interest in pixel-space diffusion, which models raw pixels directly, removes the VAE bottleneck, and supports end-to-end optimization. This formulation better matches the demands of high-fidelity generation but introduces challenges in high-dimensional modeling, including noise scheduling, loss weighting, token efficiency, and scalable architecture design. Pixel-space modeling also offers a promising basis for unified multimodal systems: raw pixels, text, and task conditions can be represented in a shared token space and jointly processed by a single Transformer, narrowing the gap between visual understanding and generation. This paper reviews Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers (pDiTs) from the perspectives of model architecture, continuous generative mechanisms, and unified multimodal modeling. We summarize representative methods, identify key technical challenges, and discuss future directions toward high-fidelity, end-to-end vision foundation models that integrate generation and understanding.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers (pDiTs), which replace the VAE-compressed latent space of LDMs with direct pixel-space denoising, enabling end-to-end optimization, unified multimodal modeling, and higher-fidelity generation while addressing challenges in high-dimensional modeling.
AI.motivation: Fixed VAE tokenizers in LDMs discard fine textures and structural details, and the separate training of representation and diffusion creates a mismatch between reconstruction and generation objectives, motivating a shift back to pixel-space diffusion.
AI.method: The paper surveys Pixel-Space Diffusion Transformers (pDiTs) from three perspectives: model architecture design, continuous generative mechanisms, and unified multimodal modeling where raw pixels, text, and task conditions share a common token space processed by a single Transformer.
AI.result: Summarizes representative pDiT methods and identifies key technical challenges including noise scheduling, loss weighting, token efficiency, and scalable architecture design for high-dimensional pixel-space modeling.
AI.conclusion: Pixel-space diffusion offers a promising path toward high-fidelity, end-to-end vision foundation models that integrate generation and understanding, with future directions focused on overcoming high-dimensional modeling challenges.

title: Can Transformers Really Do It All? On the Compatibility of Inductive Biases Across Tasks
comment: Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026. https://github.com/idiap/lm-afs
summary:
Transformers are remarkably versatile and their design is largely consistent across a variety of applications. But are they optimal for any given task or dataset? The answer may be key for pushing AI beyond merely scaling current designs.
  *Method.* We present a method to optimize a transformer architecture for a given dataset, which we use as a tool to study optimal task-specific inductive biases. This method replaces the most important non-linearities (GeLUs,;softmax) with functions learned on held-out data. We then train the resulting architectures on other datasets, as a way to evaluate the compatibility between pairs of tasks.
  Findings. On algorithmic toy tasks, we identify new architectures with dramatic improvements in learning speed, in- and out-of-distribution generalization, and stability across seeds. The new designs prove very task-specific however, and indicate that these tasks require inductive biases very different from those of standard transformers. On code and language modeling datasets, we also find architectures with consistent, yet smaller improvements. These designs transfer much better across datasets and domains (English & computer code).
  Implications. Our results show that standard transformers are rarely a local optimum in the space of architectures. Simple alternatives can perform much better but sacrifice universality. This suggests that there may be room for improved architectures that better support multiple capabilities simultaneously, such as fluency and robust reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a method to optimize transformer architectures for specific datasets by learning key nonlinear functions (GeLUs, softmax) on held-out data. Results show dramatic improvements on algorithmic tasks but with high task-specificity, while code/language tasks show smaller but more transferable gains. The authors conclude that standard transformers are rarely locally optimal, and better architectures may exist that balance multiple capabilities.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether standard transformer architectures are optimal for specific tasks/datasets, and to develop a method for discovering task-specific inductive biases that could push AI beyond merely scaling existing designs.
AI.method: The method replaces key nonlinearities (GeLUs, softmax) in transformers with functions learned on held-out data, then evaluates the resulting architectures on other datasets to measure cross-task compatibility.
AI.result: On algorithmic toy tasks: dramatic improvements in learning speed, in-distribution and out-of-distribution generalization, and stability across seeds, but with high task-specificity. On code and language modeling: consistent but smaller improvements, with better transferability across datasets and domains (English & computer code).
AI.conclusion: Standard transformers are rarely local optima in architecture space; simple alternatives can outperform them but sacrifice universality, suggesting potential for improved architectures that better support multiple capabilities simultaneously (e.g., fluency and robust reasoning).

title: Miles: Metric Learning with Expandable Subspace for Pre-Trained Model-Based Class-Incremental Learning
comment: This work has been accepted by IEEE Transactions on Image Processing
summary: Class Incremental Learning (CIL) aims to learn new concepts consistently from a data stream without forgetting. Unlike typical CIL methods which need to learn a model from scratch, pre-trained model (PTM) can easily adapt to a new task with fine-tuning. However, existing PTM-based CIL methods fail to achieve a trade-off between performance and computational expenditure, i.e., they either adopt the same parameter space so that leading catastrophic forgetting, or expand a new branch for each task but adding more computational cost. To this end, we propose MetrIc Learning with Expandable Subspace (Miles) to harness the prior information within pre-trained knowledge, thereby orchestrating an efficient expansion of the parameter space through guided optimization. Specifically, it decouples the learnable modules with the pre-trained model, exploiting prior information from intermediate features of the backbone network to enable more flexible parameter expansion. Then, a central loss is adopted to guide the new category to cluster towards the corresponding prototype in the new task subspace while incorporating an auxiliary distance regularization term to maintain metric equilibrium across tasks. Extensive experiments on six benchmark datasets demonstrate that Miles achieves state-of-the-art performance in various CIL settings.

AI.tldr: Miles is a new Class Incremental Learning method that uses pre-trained models with expandable subspaces and metric learning to achieve effective continual learning without catastrophic forgetting or excessive computational cost.
AI.motivation: Existing PTM-based CIL methods struggle to balance performance and computational cost—they either suffer catastrophic forgetting by using the same parameter space, or expand branches per task at high computational expense.
AI.method: Miles decouples learnable modules from the pre-trained model, exploits prior information from intermediate backbone features for flexible parameter expansion, uses a central loss to cluster new categories toward prototypes in new task subspaces, and incorporates an auxiliary distance regularization term to maintain metric equilibrium across tasks.
AI.result: State-of-the-art performance across six benchmark datasets in various CIL settings.
AI.conclusion: Miles achieves an effective trade-off between performance and computational expenditure for PTM-based class incremental learning through guided parameter expansion and metric learning.

title: TypiCore: A Hybrid Active Query Strategy for Class-Incremental Learning on Time Series
summary: Time series data play a pivotal role across numerous domains, including healthcare and manufacturing. In real-world environments, models must cope with distribution shifts over time, a challenge commonly addressed through Continual Learning (CL) techniques. However, existing CL methods face a critical limitation: real-world data streams are rarely fully labeled, making annotation cost a major practical constraint. This paper investigates Active Class-Incremental Learning (ACIL) for multivariate time series, where a model must sequentially learn new classes while selectively querying labels under a fixed annotation budget. We present a systematic evaluation of a wide range of query strategies combined with multiple rehearsal-based approaches, assessing their impact on plasticity, stability, and label efficiency across four benchmark datasets. Our analysis reveals the limitations of uncertainty-based and distribution-aware methods in achieving strong performance under constrained labeling budgets. To address these shortcomings, we propose TypiCore, a novel hybrid query strategy that alternates between typicality-based and diversity-based sample selection across active learning cycles, enabling the construction of memory buffers that are both representative and diverse. Evaluated on the TSCIL benchmark, TypiCore delivers statistically significant improvements over all baselines and matches or surpasses fully supervised continual learning performance on multiple datasets while requiring a fraction of the available labels.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates Active Class-Incremental Learning (ACIL) for multivariate time series, proposes TypiCore—a hybrid query strategy alternating typicality and diversity sampling—and shows it matches fully supervised CL performance using far fewer labels.
AI.motivation: Real-world time series data streams are rarely fully labeled due to high annotation costs, yet existing Continual Learning methods assume full label availability, creating a gap between CL research and practical deployment constraints.
AI.method: The authors systematically evaluate query strategies combined with rehearsal-based CL methods, then propose TypiCore—a hybrid query strategy that alternates between typicality-based (selecting representative samples) and diversity-based sample selection across active learning cycles to build memory buffers that are both representative and diverse.
AI.result: TypiCore delivers statistically significant improvements over all baselines and matches or surpasses fully supervised continual learning performance on multiple datasets while requiring only a fraction of the available labels.
AI.conclusion: Uncertainty-based and distribution-aware methods struggle under constrained labeling budgets for time series CL, whereas the proposed hybrid typicality-diversity approach (TypiCore) effectively balances plasticity and stability with high label efficiency.

title: ConsiSpace: Learning Geometric Consistency Matters for Video Spatial Reasoning
summary: Video spatial reasoning is essential for navigation-oriented perception and long-video question answering, where models must infer spatial relations across long horizons under changing viewpoints. However, existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) remain largely semantic-centric, and often fail to reliably aggregate consistent spatial evidence from redundant video observations, leading to inefficient or unstable reasoning. To address these issues, we propose ConsiSpace, a geometry-consistency-aware framework for geometry-sensitive video spatial reasoning that turns spatial consistency into both an evidence organization principle and an explicit post-SFT learning signal. We build a geometry-consistent memory (GCM) including implicit evidence tokens and explicit geometric cues, and leverage efficient organization strategies to compactly preserve task-related spatial evidence. Furthermore, we utilize unified consistency self-supervised reinforcement learning (UC-SSRL) after supervised fine-tuning to improve cross-view stability, with answer-, metric-, and topology-consistency rewards. Extensive experiments on three spatial-reasoning benchmarks, VSI-Bench, OSI-Bench, and MMSI-Video-Bench, show consistent gains, improving the average score by 12.6 points over the strongest baselines.

AI.tldr: ConsiSpace is a geometry-consistency-aware framework for video spatial reasoning that uses a Geometry-Consistent Memory (GCM) and Unified Consistency Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning (UC-SSRL) to improve spatial evidence aggregation across changing viewpoints, achieving 12.6-point average gains over baselines on three benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing MLLMs are semantic-centric and fail to reliably aggregate consistent spatial evidence from redundant video observations under changing viewpoints, leading to inefficient or unstable reasoning in navigation-oriented perception and long-video QA.
AI.method: Proposes ConsiSpace with (1) Geometry-Consistent Memory (GCM) combining implicit evidence tokens and explicit geometric cues with efficient organization strategies, and (2) Unified Consistency Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning (UC-SSRL) after SFT, using answer-, metric-, and topology-consistency rewards to improve cross-view stability.
AI.result: Consistent gains on VSI-Bench, OSI-Bench, and MMSI-Video-Bench, improving average score by 12.6 points over strongest baselines.
AI.conclusion: Turning spatial consistency into an evidence organization principle and an explicit post-SFT learning signal effectively enhances geometry-sensitive video spatial reasoning in MLLMs.

title: Selectivity Matters: Source Node Influence Pruning for Unsupervised Graph Domain Adaptation
summary: Unsupervised Graph Domain Adaptation (UGDA) aims to facilitate knowledge transfer from a labeled source graph to an unlabeled target graph by mitigating cross-domain distribution shifts. Existing methods primarily focus on node-level feature alignment in latent spaces, relying on the implicit assumption that all source nodes contribute positively to the alignment. However, this assumption often fails because a node's semantic information is intrinsically coupled with its topological graph structure. Due to structural shifts, source nodes with severe structural deviations (e.g., structural outliers) lack semantic counterparts in the target graph, and forcing alignment on them introduces severe noise and causes negative transfer. To bridge this gap, we argue that selective source node utilization is superior to full-graph training, thereby shifting the research paradigm from feature-level alignment to data-level refinement. To this end, we propose Source Node Influence Pruning (SNIP), a novel model-agnostic, data-centric refinement framework. Specifically, SNIP quantifies the structural discrepancy between individual source nodes and the target domain by integrating multiple centrality measures, assigning each source node an influence score. A rank-based normalization mechanism is further employed to eliminate scale variations across different measures, allowing SNIP to effectively identify and filter out structurally incompatible nodes with low influence scores. As a plug-and-play method, SNIP constructs a refined "sub-source" graph that is inherently more beneficial for subsequent alignment. Comprehensive experiments across eight transfer scenarios on five real-world datasets demonstrate that SNIP consistently outperforms competitive baselines and significantly enhances adaptation performance, validating the superiority of selective node utilization over full-graph training.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes SNIP, a model-agnostic data-centric refinement framework for Unsupervised Graph Domain Adaptation that selectively prunes structurally incompatible source nodes (e.g., structural outliers) before alignment, shifting the paradigm from feature-level alignment to data-level refinement and demonstrating superior performance over full-graph training across multiple transfer scenarios.
AI.motivation: Existing UGDA methods assume all source nodes contribute positively to alignment, but this fails because semantic information is coupled with topological structure. Source nodes with structural deviations lack semantic counterparts in the target graph, and forcing alignment introduces noise and causes negative transfer.
AI.method: SNIP quantifies structural discrepancy between individual source nodes and the target domain by integrating multiple centrality measures, assigns each source node an influence score, uses rank-based normalization to eliminate scale variations across measures, and filters out structurally incompatible nodes with low influence scores to construct a refined "sub-source" graph for subsequent alignment.
AI.result: Comprehensive experiments across eight transfer scenarios on five real-world datasets show SNIP consistently outperforms competitive baselines and significantly enhances adaptation performance, validating the superiority of selective node utilization over full-graph training.
AI.conclusion: The paper shifts the UGDA research paradigm from feature-level alignment to data-level refinement, demonstrating that selective source node utilization (via influence-based pruning) is superior to full-graph training for domain adaptation.

title: Semantic Color Naturalness Breaker: Preventing Illegitimate Colorization via Content-Aware Color Priors
summary: Automatic image colorization enables large-scale and low-cost reuse of grayscale media (e.g., manga panels and archival photographs), facilitating unauthorized reuse and redistribution. Once released online, grayscale content can be readily turned into unauthorized colorized derivatives using off-the-shelf models, creating a practical need for proactive, content-side protection at publication time. Building on Uncolorable Examples (UE), which add imperceptible perturbations to released grayscale images to degrade unauthorized colorization, we propose Semantic Color Naturalness Breaker (SCNB) -- a semantic-level UE framework that drives colorization outputs toward content-inconsistent colors while preserving the visual fidelity of the released grayscale media. We further introduce Content-aware Color Distributional Distance (CaCDD), a ground-truth-free, content-aware measure of color plausibility derived from semantic color priors, used both as the optimization objective of SCNB and as an evaluation metric. Experiments on ImageNet show that our method remains effective under small perturbation budgets and common post-processing, supporting practical deployment in real-world content-sharing pipelines.

AI.tldr: SCNB is a semantic-level protection framework that adds imperceptible perturbations to grayscale images to prevent unauthorized AI colorization by forcing outputs toward content-inconsistent colors, using a new metric (CaCDD) for optimization and evaluation.
AI.motivation: Automatic image colorization enables unauthorized reuse and redistribution of grayscale media (e.g., manga, archival photos), creating a need for proactive content-side protection at publication time.
AI.method: Proposes Semantic Color Naturalness Breaker (SCNB), a semantic-level Uncolorable Examples (UE) framework that adds imperceptible perturbations to grayscale images to drive colorization outputs toward content-inconsistent colors. Introduces Content-aware Color Distributional Distance (CaCDD), a ground-truth-free metric derived from semantic color priors, used as both optimization objective and evaluation metric.
AI.result: On ImageNet, SCNB remains effective under small perturbation budgets and common post-processing, supporting practical deployment in real-world content-sharing pipelines.
AI.conclusion: SCNB provides a practical, semantic-level defense against unauthorized AI colorization of grayscale content, with demonstrated robustness and deployment feasibility.

title: GeneSpeak-FP: Target and Compound Retrieval from Observed Cell-Level Perturbation Signatures
summary: Large-scale single-cell perturbation atlases make it possible to ask an inverse question: given an observed transcriptional response, which annotated targets and compounds in a fixed library are most consistent with that response? We present \model, a Transformer retrieval model for this closed-library setting. Each input is a cell-level perturbation signature formed by contrasting one treated cell with a cell-line-specific mean DMSO reference. The encoder maps the signature to a target-retrieval vector and a molecular-embedding vector, trained jointly with supervised target losses and structure--transcriptome alignment. We evaluate on Tahoe-100M conditions with mapped target annotations using a within-compound stratified 90/10 condition-pair split of 10,505 training and 1,168 validation drug--cell-line pairs. Because compounds and cell lines can occur in both partitions, the experiment measures held-out condition-pair retrieval rather than generalization to unseen compounds or cellular contexts. In a Monte Carlo evaluation over 38,400 sampled validation cells, \model\ achieved target Recall@10 of 0.408 and Recall@20 of 0.544, together with compound Hit@1 of 0.129, Hit@10 of 0.343, and mean reciprocal rank of 0.205 over a 379-compound bank. A separate diagnostic evaluation produced nearly identical values for the main model and large gains over a random-vector control and post-hoc bag-of-genes controls. These results demonstrate that a single multi-task model can recover both mapped target annotations and recorded compound identities from observed cell-level responses in the evaluated Tahoe-100M closed-library setting. Generalization to unseen compounds and cellular contexts remains to be established.

AI.tldr: A Transformer-based retrieval model (PertEval) is presented that, given a single-cell perturbation transcriptional signature, retrieves the most consistent annotated targets and compounds from a fixed library. Evaluated on Tahoe-100M with a closed-library setup, it achieves target Recall@10 of 0.408 and compound Hit@1 of 0.129 over 379 compounds, showing feasibility of multi-task retrieval from cell-level responses.
AI.motivation: To address the inverse question in large-scale single-cell perturbation atlases: given an observed transcriptional response, which annotated targets and compounds in a fixed library are most consistent with that response.
AI.method: A Transformer retrieval model (PertEval) that takes cell-level perturbation signatures (treated cell vs. DMSO reference) as input. The encoder produces a target-retrieval vector and a molecular-embedding vector, jointly trained with supervised target losses and structure–transcriptome alignment. Evaluation uses a within-compound stratified 90/10 condition-pair split on Tahoe-100M with 10,505 training and 1,168 validation drug–cell-line pairs.
AI.result: Target Recall@10=0.408, Recall@20=0.544; compound Hit@1=0.129, Hit@10=0.343, MRR=0.205 over 379 compounds across 38,400 sampled validation cells. Nearly identical values for the main model and large gains over random-vector and bag-of-genes controls.
AI.conclusion: A single multi-task Transformer model can recover both mapped target annotations and recorded compound identities from observed cell-level responses in the closed-library setting. Generalization to unseen compounds and cellular contexts remains to be established.

title: Coarse-to-fine Framework for Generative MEF via Implicit Neural Representation
summary: Multi-exposure fusion (MEF) expands the luminance range beyond what a single exposure can capture. Combining images taken at different exposure levels requires handling geometric differences while naturally merging their complementary brightness information. It often demands generative completion where details are missing. Diffusion-based generative methods address these challenges, however, they are computationally expensive and struggle to preserve fine structures in saturated regions. We propose LIIFusion, a coarse-to-fine framework that balances fusion quality and efficiency in generative MEF. The coarse stage performs low resolution generative fusion, enhanced by an adaptive exposure correction that recovers structure lost in saturated over-exposed areas. The fine stage adapts a local implicit image function into a multi-exposure fusion function: conditioned on the HR OE/UE sources and the coarse output, it queries arbitrary target coordinates and fuses source evidence regardless of the HR input resolution. LIIFusion achieves up to 3.5$\times$ speed-up over existing generative methods while maintaining or improving structural fidelity and perceptual quality. We believe this framework provides an effective pathway toward making generative MEF more practical in real-world applications.

AI.tldr: LIIFusion is a coarse-to-fine framework for generative multi-exposure fusion that achieves up to 3.5× speed-up over existing methods while maintaining quality, using low-resolution generative fusion with adaptive exposure correction and a local implicit image function for high-resolution fusion.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based generative MEF methods are computationally expensive and struggle to preserve fine structures in saturated regions, limiting practical real-world applicability.
AI.method: A two-stage coarse-to-fine framework: (1) coarse stage performs low-resolution generative fusion with adaptive exposure correction to recover structure in saturated areas; (2) fine stage adapts a local implicit image function into a multi-exposure fusion function that queries arbitrary target coordinates and fuses source evidence regardless of HR input resolution.
AI.result: Achieves up to 3.5× speed-up over existing generative methods while maintaining or improving structural fidelity and perceptual quality.
AI.conclusion: This framework provides an effective pathway toward making generative MEF more practical in real-world applications by balancing fusion quality and computational efficiency.

title: Beyond Objective Expressivity: Geometry Preservation in Multimodal Contrastive Learning
summary: Contrastive learning is increasingly moving toward settings with three or more modalities instead of image-text pairs. Yet, extending models from pairwise to higher-order multimodal alignment can introduce optimization and representation challenges. We identify encoder Jacobian conditioning as a key factor in trimodal contrastive learning: poorly conditioned encoders exhibit collapsing or amplified singular-value spectra, leading to exploding Jacobian condition numbers and degraded multimodal alignment. We introduce geometry-preserving encoders (GPEs) by directly conditioning the Jacobian through regularization and demonstrating that simple modifications like LeakyReLU activations and residual paths recover these geometric benefits. Across a synthetic benchmark and four real-world datasets including missing modalities, improving Jacobian conditioning boosts retrieval and linear probe performance across multiple contrastive objectives, whereas expressive objectives yield little benefit in linear probes. More broadly, our results show that multimodal contrastive learning depends not only on objective expressivity, but also on the geometric and optimization properties of the underlying encoders.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies encoder Jacobian conditioning as a critical factor in multimodal contrastive learning beyond image-text pairs. Poorly conditioned encoders degrade alignment; geometry-preserving encoders (GPEs) with Jacobian regularization, LeakyReLU, and residual paths improve conditioning and boost retrieval and linear probe performance across multiple objectives and datasets.
AI.motivation: Extending contrastive learning from pairwise (image-text) to three or more modalities introduces optimization and representation challenges that are not well understood.
AI.method: Identifies encoder Jacobian conditioning as a key factor; introduces geometry-preserving encoders (GPEs) via Jacobian regularization combined with simple architectural modifications (LeakyReLU activations, residual paths) to improve conditioning.
AI.result: Improving Jacobian conditioning boosts retrieval and linear probe performance across multiple contrastive objectives on synthetic benchmarks and four real-world datasets, including scenarios with missing modalities.
AI.conclusion: Multimodal contrastive learning depends not only on objective expressivity but also on the geometric and optimization properties of encoders.

title: Rarity-Aware Discrete Diffusion with Spatially Consistent Decoding for Photo-Realistic Image Super-Resolution
summary: Continuous diffusion models have become the dominant paradigm for photo-realistic image Super-Resolution (SR), but they typically formulate reconstruction as continuous signal-level denoising and incorporate semantic priors through external conditioning modules. This makes it less direct to exploit the unified token-based scaling paradigm of modern multimodal models. Autoregressive models provide a more native semantic representation by modeling images as discrete visual tokens, yet their causal decoding is inefficient for high-resolution reconstruction. Discrete diffusion offers a promising middle ground by enabling non-causal, parallel prediction over visual tokens. However, directly adapting discrete diffusion to SR remains non-trivial due to two task-specific challenges: (1) the long-tailed distribution of visual tokens, which under-represents rare but perceptually critical textures; and (2) spatially inconsistent parallel decoding, which may introduce isolated artifacts. To address these issues, we propose DiMOO-SR, a rarity-aware multimodal discrete diffusion framework for photo-realistic image SR. During training, Inverse Frequency Sampling (IFS) prioritizes under-represented but information-rich tokens. During inference, Spatial Consistency Ranking (SCR) refines token confidence using local neighborhood agreement to improve structural coherence. Extensive experiments on widely used real-world SR benchmarks demonstrate that DiMOO-SR achieves competitive perceptual quality with only a few parallel decoding steps, highlighting the potential of discrete diffusion for generative image super-resolution. The code will be released upon publication.

AI.tldr: DiMOO-SR is a rarity-aware multimodal discrete diffusion framework for image super-resolution that addresses long-tailed token distribution via Inverse Frequency Sampling and spatial inconsistencies via Spatial Consistency Ranking, achieving competitive perceptual quality with few parallel decoding steps.
AI.motivation: Continuous diffusion models for SR are less direct for exploiting unified token-based scaling paradigms; autoregressive models are inefficient for high-resolution reconstruction; discrete diffusion is promising but faces challenges: (1) long-tailed distribution of visual tokens under-representing rare but perceptually critical textures, and (2) spatially inconsistent parallel decoding introducing isolated artifacts.
AI.method: DiMOO-SR, a rarity-aware multimodal discrete diffusion framework for photo-realistic image SR. During training, Inverse Frequency Sampling (IFS) prioritizes under-represented but information-rich tokens. During inference, Spatial Consistency Ranking (SCR) refines token confidence using local neighborhood agreement to improve structural coherence.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on widely used real-world SR benchmarks demonstrate competitive perceptual quality with only a few parallel decoding steps.
AI.conclusion: DiMOO-SR achieves competitive perceptual quality with only a few parallel decoding steps, highlighting the potential of discrete diffusion for generative image super-resolution.

title: Uncovering Latent Reasoning Strategies in Language Models
summary: A language model $p_θ(y \mid x)$ trained on reasoning tasks learns to solve problems via multiple distinct strategies, yet these strategies are implicit and entangled within the model's response distribution. We study the problem of decomposing the response distribution of a given pretrained language model into a structured, strategy-conditioned representation. Specifically, we learn a latent-variable factorization $p_θ(y \mid x) \leadsto (r_φ(z \mid x), g_φ(y \mid x,z))$, where a router $r$ maps each input to a distribution over latent strategies $z$ and a generator $g$ produces the response conditioned on that strategy. A key challenge is that the generator, initialized from the base model, already represents $p_θ(y \mid x)$ without using $z$. Standard variational inference therefore gives the model no incentive to route information through $z$ and can yield a severe form of posterior collapse. To address this, we propose a variational objective that measures fractional information gain relative to the base model's response loss and concentrates reconstruction pressure on tokens with high base model surprisal, encouraging $z$ to encode strategy-relevant response variation. We introduce a benchmark of multi-strategy algorithmic tasks and show that this objective recovers latent codes aligned with distinct reference strategies while preserving the base model's response distribution.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a method to decompose a language model's response distribution into structured, strategy-conditioned representations via a latent-variable factorization, using a novel variational objective based on fractional information gain to prevent posterior collapse. The method recovers interpretable latent strategies on multi-strategy algorithmic tasks while preserving the original response distribution.
AI.motivation: Language models trained on reasoning tasks learn multiple implicit strategies to solve problems, but these strategies are entangled within the model's response distribution. The authors aim to decompose this distribution into structured, strategy-conditioned representations to make the strategies explicit and interpretable.
AI.method: The authors learn a latent-variable factorization (router r_φ and generator g_φ) from a pretrained base model. They propose a variational objective that measures fractional information gain relative to the base model's response loss and concentrates reconstruction pressure on tokens with high base model surprisal, addressing the posterior collapse problem inherent in standard variational inference.
AI.result: The method recovers latent codes aligned with distinct reference strategies on a benchmark of multi-strategy algorithmic tasks, while preserving the base model's response distribution.
AI.conclusion: The proposed variational objective successfully enables strategy decomposition in pretrained language models, making multiple reasoning strategies explicit without degrading the original model's performance.

title: Brain-Aligned Multi-Stream Video Transformers with Sparse Self-Selection
summary: Modern video transformers typically ignore principles from primate vision and are rarely evaluated against neural data, limiting their biological interpretability. We introduce a sparse winner-takes-all token selection module that replaces dense self-attention to improve efficiency and approximate competitive routing observed in biological visual circuits. We further propose a neuro-inspired split-and-fuse video transformer which uses two complementary pathways: a high-resolution, low-frame-rate "what" stream and a low-resolution, high-frame-rate "where" stream, fused before classification. On Kinetics-400 and Something-Something V2, our best variant operates on the Pareto frontier of accuracy versus inference time among models of comparable scale and pretraining, and showing improved robustness to spatial perturbations. Using representational similarity analysis between model embeddings and time-resolved EEG recordings for the same video stimuli, our model attains a peak brain-model correlation of 0.18 (about 78% of the noise ceiling) and consistently outperforms strong video transformer baselines, suggesting that pathway specialization and sparse competition are useful inductive biases for efficient, brain-aligned video understanding.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a neuro-inspired split-and-fuse video transformer with sparse winner-takes-all token selection, achieving efficient video understanding with improved brain alignment and competitive accuracy-speed trade-offs on Kinetics-400 and Something-Something V2.
AI.motivation: Modern video transformers ignore principles from primate vision and are rarely evaluated against neural data, limiting their biological interpretability.
AI.method: Proposes (1) a sparse winner-takes-all token selection module replacing dense self-attention, and (2) a split-and-fuse architecture with two complementary pathways: a high-resolution, low-frame-rate "what" stream and a low-resolution, high-frame-rate "where" stream, fused before classification.
AI.result: Achieves Pareto-optimal accuracy vs. inference time on Kinetics-400 and Something-Something V2, improved robustness to spatial perturbations, and a peak brain-model correlation of 0.18 (~78% of noise ceiling) against time-resolved EEG recordings, outperforming strong video transformer baselines.
AI.conclusion: Pathway specialization and sparse competition are useful inductive biases for efficient, brain-aligned video understanding.

title: Planning with Transformers: Chain of Computation and Structured Context Windows
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have had a remarkable impact across many areas of machine learning. However, recent studies have shown that they struggle to reliably solve planning problems. At the same time, theoretical results have shown that transformers, the core architecture underlying modern LLMs, are Turing-complete. In this work, we investigate this apparent gap between the theoretical computational power of LLMs and their empirical planning performance. We propose Chain of Computation (COC), a computational architecture that places a transformer-based LM inside an iterative loop, leveraging its strength as a pattern-matching system. The COC uses a Structured Context Window (SCW) which provides a constant-sized context window with support for choosing which window is used at each planning step. Within this architecture, the LM is able to learn a planning policy, predicts the world model, and performs the arithmetic operations required during planning. We show that, when given an append-only SCW (resembling a Turing Machine tape), even relatively small LMs trained from scratch can learn planning policies and generalize from a small number of training instances within each planning domain, achieving success rates above 99.89\% on BlocksWorld and the Pancake puzzle. Our analysis of failure cases in Tower of Hanoi (TOH) reveals that they arise from arithmetic operations or from encountering previously unseen tokens. We show that COC can solve TOH problem instances with up to 20 disks, requiring over 1 million actions, while requiring substantially less training data by either (1) planning with symbolical support for arithmetic or by (2) using a deterministic pushdown automaton (PDA) formulation for the SCW.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Chain of Computation (COC), a computational architecture combining a transformer-based LM with an iterative loop and Structured Context Window (SCW), enabling small LMs trained from scratch to achieve over 99.89% success on planning problems like BlocksWorld and Pancake puzzle, and solve Tower of Hanoi with up to 20 disks (over 1 million actions) using symbolic arithmetic or PDA-based context windows.
AI.motivation: There is an apparent gap between the theoretical Turing-completeness of transformers and their empirical poor performance on planning problems. The paper aims to bridge this gap by designing an architecture that leverages LLMs' pattern-matching strengths within a structured computational loop for reliable planning.
AI.method: Chain of Computation (COC) places a transformer-based LM in an iterative loop with a Structured Context Window (SCW) of constant size but with a selection mechanism. The LM learns a planning policy, predicts the world model, and performs arithmetic operations. Two variants address Tower of Hanoi limitations: (1) symbolic arithmetic support, (2) deterministic pushdown automaton (PDA) formulation for the SCW.
AI.result: Small LMs trained from scratch achieve >99.89% success on BlocksWorld and Pancake puzzle, generalizing from few training instances. COC solves Tower of Hanoi with up to 20 disks (1M+ actions). Failure cases in TOH stem from arithmetic errors or unseen tokens, mitigated by symbolic arithmetic or PDA-based SCW.
AI.conclusion: The apparent gap between transformer computational power and planning performance can be bridged by appropriate architectural design (COC + SCW). Small LMs can learn effective planning policies with minimal data when given structured context and iterative computation loops.

title: MixDiffusion: Mixing Diffusion-based Uni-condition Text-to-Image Generation Models for Multi-condition Image Synthesis
summary: Recent advances in text-to-image (T2I) generation have enabled controllable image synthesis by incorporating conditions beyond text. However, most existing diffusion-based methods are limited to a single type of control condition (e.g., bounding boxes or keypoints), which restricts their flexibility. To address this limitation, we propose MixDiffusion, a training-free diffusion framework for multi-condition T2I generation. MixDiffusion theoretically supports an arbitrary number of control conditions, including bounding boxes, keypoints, sketches, depth maps, reference images, and text, by collaboratively integrating multiple pre-trained uni-condition diffusion models. The key insight of the proposed approach is to derive the predicted noise distribution in each denoising step of the diffusion-based multi-condition image generation model from the predicted noise distributions of multiple diffusion-based uni-condition models with a derived integration formula, which is supported by rigorous theory proof. Owing to its training-free nature, MixDiffusion is easy to deploy and readily extensible to new control modalities.

AI.tldr: MixDiffusion is a training-free diffusion framework that integrates multiple pre-trained uni-condition diffusion models to enable multi-condition text-to-image generation with arbitrary numbers and types of control conditions (bounding boxes, keypoints, sketches, depth maps, reference images, text).
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based T2I methods are limited to a single type of control condition (e.g., bounding boxes or keypoints), which restricts their flexibility for multi-condition synthesis.
AI.method: MixDiffusion derives the predicted noise distribution at each denoising step for multi-condition generation by integrating predicted noise distributions from multiple pre-trained uni-condition diffusion models via a theoretically proven integration formula, requiring no additional training.
AI.result: The framework theoretically supports arbitrary numbers of control conditions (bounding boxes, keypoints, sketches, depth maps, reference images, text) and is easy to deploy due to its training-free nature.
AI.conclusion: MixDiffusion is readily extensible to new control modalities, offering a flexible and practical solution for multi-condition T2I generation without requiring retraining.

title: MXSens: Sensitivity-Aware Mixed-Precision Quantization for Efficient LLM Inference
summary: 4-bit quantization enables efficient LLM inference, but suffers from significant accuracy degradation due to outliers. Prior work addresses this problem via data rotation or mixed-precision integer quantization, but often relies on software-managed scaling and frequent dequantization, incurring substantial overhead. Microscaling formats, such as MXINT, eliminate these inefficiencies by encoding scales in hardware, yet remain incompatible with rotation-based methods. Our analysis reveals that outliers vary in severity, from rare extremes to frequent mild deviations, and that quantization sensitivity is unevenly distributed across layers and columns. These insights motivate a fine-grained, sensitivity-guided approach. We introduce MXSens, a training-free method that assigns mixed mantissa bitwidths (4/6/8) based on column- and layer-wise sensitivity, naturally leveraging the block-wise structure of MXINT. MXSens outperforms state-of-the-art quantization methods across a range of models and tasks. Under the W4A4KV4 setting, MXSens achieves perplexities of 3.77 and 7.63 on LLaMA-2-70B and LLaMA-3-8B, respectively, substantially improving over existing baselines on WikiText-2. Our work establishes a new balance between accuracy and resource efficiency for LLM quantization.

AI.tldr: MXSens introduces a training-free, sensitivity-guided mixed-precision quantization method for LLMs using MXINT microscaling formats, assigning 4/6/8 mantissa bitwidths based on column- and layer-wise sensitivity to outliers, achieving superior perplexity on LLaMA models under W4A4KV4 settings compared to prior work.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM quantization methods suffer from either (1) accuracy degradation due to outliers in 4-bit settings, (2) overhead from software-managed scaling and frequent dequantization in rotation-based or mixed-precision integer methods, or (3) incompatibility with rotation-based approaches when using MXINT formats. The authors observe that outlier severity varies and quantization sensitivity is uneven, motivating a fine-grained, sensitivity-guided approach.
AI.method: MXSens assigns mixed mantissa bitwidths (4/6/8) to different columns and layers based on sensitivity metrics, operating within the block-wise structure of MXINT microscaling formats. This is training-free and naturally leverages hardware-encoded scales to avoid dequantization overhead.
AI.result: Under W4A4KV4 quantization, MXSens achieves perplexities of 3.77 on LLaMA-2-70B and 7.63 on LLaMA-3-8B on WikiText-2, outperforming existing state-of-the-art quantization baselines.
AI.conclusion: MXSens establishes a new balance between accuracy and resource efficiency for LLM quantization, demonstrating that sensitivity-guided mixed mantissa allocation within MXINT formats is effective and practical.

title: Reviving Ancient Paintings via Poem: A Colorization Framework for Aligning Cultural Semantics
summary: The irreversible fading of ancient paintings disrupts the "congruence between poems and paintings", a core aesthetic principle where visual imagery harmonizes with literary inscriptions. Although diffusion models provide strong generative priors, restoring historically faithful colors remains difficult: visual restoration is inherently ambiguous, while direct text guidance often causes modern semantic bias, over-saturation, and cross-boundary color leakage. To address this, we propose PoemColor, a poem-guided ancient painting colorization framework. Our method aligns poetic cultural semantics with painting restoration through two key designs. First, the Poetic Painting Projector (P3) converts implicit poetic context into a classical color-aware condition via poem-to-palette pretraining, reducing the ambiguity of poem-to-color mapping. Second, Structure-Aware Semantic Attention (SASA) regulates how poetic color semantics are injected into the diffusion backbone by jointly controlling their propagation direction and regional injection strength. In addition, we construct a hybrid restoration dataset that integrates synthetic degradation with expert-restored artifacts, providing both scalable supervision and real classical color references. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, delivering controllable colorization that revives both historical authenticity and poetic semantics.

AI.tldr: PoemColor is a poem-guided framework for restoring historically authentic colors to faded ancient paintings, using a Poetic Painting Projector (P3) to map poetic semantics to classical color palettes and Structure-Aware Semantic Attention (SASA) to control color injection, achieving state-of-the-art results in reviving both historical fidelity and poetic meaning.
AI.motivation: The fading of ancient paintings breaks the aesthetic principle of "congruence between poems and paintings." Existing diffusion models struggle with visual restoration ambiguity, modern semantic bias, over-saturation, and color leakage when guided by text.
AI.method: PoemColor framework with two key components: (1) Poetic Painting Projector (P3) for poem-to-palette pretraining that converts implicit poetic context into classical color-aware conditions; (2) Structure-Aware Semantic Attention (SASA) that regulates the propagation direction and regional injection strength of poetic color semantics into the diffusion backbone. A hybrid restoration dataset combining synthetic degradation with expert-restored artifacts is also constructed.
AI.result: The framework significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, delivering controllable colorization that revives both historical authenticity and poetic semantics.
AI.conclusion: PoemColor effectively addresses the ambiguity and bias issues in poem-guided ancient painting colorization by aligning poetic cultural semantics with visual restoration through structured semantic projection and attention control.

title: Towards Reliable Zero-Shot Crowd Forecasting: Evaluating Time Series Foundation Models for Special Event Pedestrian Forecasting
comment: 9 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables. Accepted for presentation at IEEE ITSC 2026
summary: Managing massive crowds during infrequent special events requires reliable real-time pedestrian-flow forecasting to ensure public safety and operational efficiency. However, supervised forecasting methods face limitations in these contexts due to scarce historical data, heterogeneous data distributions, and short in-event observation windows. To effectively support operational decision-making, forecasts should provide not only accurate point estimates but also informative predictive uncertainty. Probabilistic uncertainty quantification plays a critical role in this aspect, particularly capturing sudden volatility and tail risks. This paper investigates pretrained time series foundation models as a lightweight approach for zero-shot probabilistic forecasting without extensive local retraining. Using decision-oriented metrics tailored to short events, we conduct a comprehensive assessment of two time series foundation models on crowd forecasting, with the SAIL2025 event as a use case. We then distill practical insights for crowd managers, specifying when zero-shot forecasts remain operationally reliable.

AI.tldr: This paper explores using pretrained time series foundation models for zero-shot probabilistic crowd flow forecasting at special events, evaluating them on the SAIL2025 event to provide decision-oriented uncertainty quantification and practical guidelines for crowd managers.
AI.motivation: Supervised forecasting methods struggle with infrequent special events due to scarce historical data, heterogeneous distributions, and short observation windows. Reliable real-time pedestrian flow forecasting with probabilistic uncertainty quantification is needed for public safety and operational decision-making.
AI.method: The authors employ pretrained time series foundation models as a lightweight zero-shot approach for probabilistic forecasting, requiring no extensive local retraining. They conduct a comprehensive assessment using decision-oriented metrics on crowd forecasting data from the SAIL2025 event.
AI.result: The study evaluates two time series foundation models on crowd forecasting for a short special event, providing insights into when zero-shot forecasts remain operationally reliable based on decision-oriented metrics.
AI.conclusion: The paper distills practical guidelines for crowd managers, specifying operational conditions under which zero-shot probabilistic forecasts from pretrained models can be trusted for managing massive crowds during infrequent events.

title: Direct Clinical Joint Angle Extraction from Parametric Body Model Rotation Matrices
summary: Quantitative joint angles are rarely available in routine care because the tools are slow, costly, or confined to a laboratory. We show that clinical joint angles can be read directly from the per-segment rotation matrices a parametric body model already produces, with no inverse-kinematics or musculoskeletal-model fitting step. On the OpenCap LabValidation cohort, using the GEM-X body-model estimator on single-smartphone video, our pooled mean absolute error is 4.50 degrees over the fifteen joint angles that match the OpenCap Monocular reference set, the same accuracy range as OpenCap Monocular's 4.8 degrees on the same cohort and reference standard, from a much simpler pipeline. The step that connects a body model to clinical angles is a small calibration table rather than an optimisation, so the same procedure transfers unchanged to other body models: repeating it on SAM 3D Body, changing only the table, gives 4.66 degrees, statistically indistinguishable from GEM-X, and runs in real time from a live single-camera stream. The method needs no per-recording inputs beyond the video itself: no participant height, no camera-intrinsics database, no per-subject model scaling. This broadens where movement analysis is practical, from in-clinic and at-home recording to telerehabilitation and large-scale decentralised studies.

AI.tldr: Clinical joint angles can be directly extracted from body model rotation matrices using a simple calibration table (no inverse kinematics needed), achieving ~4.5° mean absolute error from single-smartphone video, matching OpenCap Monocular accuracy with a much simpler pipeline.
AI.motivation: Quantitative joint angles are rarely available in routine care because existing tools are slow, costly, or confined to laboratory settings; the authors aim to make movement analysis practical for in-clinic, at-home, telerehabilitation, and large-scale studies.
AI.method: Joint angles are read directly from per-segment rotation matrices produced by a parametric body model (e.g., GEM-X, SAM 3D Body) using a small calibration table instead of inverse-kinematics or musculoskeletal-model fitting. The method requires no per-recording inputs beyond video (no height, camera-intrinsics, or per-subject scaling).
AI.result: Pooled mean absolute error of 4.50° over 15 joint angles on OpenCap LabValidation with GEM-X (vs. OpenCap Monocular's 4.8°). SAM 3D Body achieves 4.66°, statistically indistinguishable from GEM-X, and runs in real time from live single-camera stream.
AI.conclusion: The calibration-table approach decouples body model from clinical angle conversion, transfers unchanged across models, and eliminates per-recording setup. This broadens movement analysis to in-clinic, at-home, telerehabilitation, and decentralized studies.

title: Generalize and Guide: Decomposing Rewards for Few-Shot Inverse Reinforcement Learning
summary: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) provides a powerful framework for learning from demonstrations. However, real-world tasks often exhibit substantial natural variations (e.g., picking up mugs with varying shapes), making it impractical to collect demonstrations that fully specify a new task under every possible scenario. In practice, while demonstrations for the target task are limited, it is often easier to obtain datasets of heterogeneous but related behaviors. This motivates the problem of few-shot IRL with multi-task demonstrations (FM-IRL), where an agent must learn a new task with substantial variations from only a limited number of target-task demonstrations, together with sufficient demonstrations of related tasks and online agent experience. To do so, we must both recover the expert distribution of the new task and provide guidance when the agent deviates from it. We introduce Multitask discriminator Proximity-Guided IRL (MPG), which learns two complementary reward components: (1) a generalizable discriminator that transfers shared structure across related tasks to identify expert behavior in a new task, and (2) a proximity function that measures how far a state deviates from expert behavior and provides corrective guidance during exploration. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method on multiple challenging navigation and manipulation tasks under significant variations (e.g., object configurations, table layouts, and initial robot poses), achieving an average success rate of 81.2%, outperforming the strongest per-task baseline by an average of 24.7 percentage points.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces MPG, a few-shot inverse reinforcement learning method that uses a generalizable discriminator and proximity function to learn new tasks from limited demonstrations by transferring knowledge from related tasks, achieving 81.2% success rate across navigation and manipulation tasks.
AI.motivation: Real-world tasks exhibit substantial natural variations, making it impractical to collect exhaustive demonstrations for every scenario. While target-task demonstrations are limited, datasets of heterogeneous but related behaviors are often easier to obtain, motivating the need for few-shot IRL with multi-task demonstrations.
AI.method: MPG (Multitask discriminator Proximity-Guided IRL) learns two complementary reward components: (1) a generalizable discriminator that transfers shared structure across related tasks to identify expert behavior in a new task, and (2) a proximity function that measures deviation from expert behavior and provides corrective guidance during exploration.
AI.result: Achieved 81.2% average success rate on challenging navigation and manipulation tasks with significant variations (object configurations, table layouts, initial robot poses), outperforming the strongest per-task baseline by 24.7 percentage points on average.
AI.conclusion: MPG effectively addresses few-shot IRL with multi-task demonstrations by combining transferable discriminator learning with proximity-guided exploration, enabling robust task learning under substantial variations from limited demonstrations.

title: FIFA World Cup 2026 as a Contamination-Free Benchmark for LLM Forecasting Agents: Four Models, a Bookmaker, and 104 Matches
summary: We introduce WC2026-Agents, a benchmark and dataset for evaluating large language models (LLMs) as autonomous forecasting agents on real, future events. For every one of the 104 matches of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, four frontier models -- Claude Opus 4.8, ChatGPT (GPT-5.5, high reasoning), Gemini 3.1 Pro, and Grok (Expert Mode) -- ran an identical search-act-reflect loop: gather evidence with a web tool, commit to a 1X2 (team-A win / draw / team-B win) distribution and a virtual 100-USD bet, and, after the match, reflect given only the final score. Because every match kicked off after the models' training cutoffs, the benchmark is contamination-free by construction. Crucially, we pair the four agents with a fifth competitor drawn from the same information environment -- the pre-match betting market -- collected as per-match 1X2 odds, giving an economically grounded baseline and letting us score not just what an agent predicts but what it does with money. The release contains 416 forecasts and 414 reflections with verbatim reasoning, ground truth (including penalty shootouts), odds, and a reproducible evaluation suite. A reference evaluation surfaces findings that raw accuracy hides: the four agents issue an identical top pick in 92% of matches and none beats the market's Brier score; indeed, a naive flat stake on the market favorite out-earns all four agents. Yet the agents diverge sharply as decision-makers: betting return-on-investment ranges from -18% to +10%, fading the market is unprofitable for all four, the share of forecasts that cite the market ranges from 12% to 100%, and self-reported error rates on wrong picks range from 36% to 86%. The benchmark thus measures calibration, decision quality, and self-knowledge -- axes on which frontier models differ even when their predictions do not. Data and code: https://github.com/graphuofm/FIFA2026LLM

AI.tldr: WC2026-Agents is a benchmark evaluating four frontier LLMs (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok) as autonomous forecasting agents on 104 FIFA 2026 World Cup matches.
