Despite 92% agreement on top picks and none beating market Brier scores, agents diverge sharply in ROI (-18% to +10%), market citation rates (12%-100%), and self-reported error rates (36%-86%), revealing that calibration, decision quality, and self-knowledge vary significantly even when predictions align.
AI.motivation: To evaluate LLMs as autonomous forecasting agents on real future events in a contamination-free setting, using economically grounded baselines (betting markets) to measure not just prediction accuracy but decision quality and self-knowledge.
AI.method: Four frontier LLMs (Claude Opus 4.8, ChatGPT GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, Grok Expert Mode) ran an identical search-act-reflect loop on all 104 FIFA 2026 matches: web evidence gathering → 1X2 probability distribution + $100 bet → post-match reflection from final score only. Compared against pre-match betting market odds. Dataset: 416 forecasts, 414 reflections, ground truth, odds.
AI.result: Agents agreed on top pick in 92% of matches; none beat market Brier score; naive flat stake on market favorite outperformed all agents. However, ROI ranged -18% to +10%, market citation 12%-100%, self-reported error 36%-86%. Fading the market was unprofitable for all.
AI.conclusion: Raw accuracy is insufficient for evaluating forecasting agents; calibration, decision quality, and self-knowledge are critical axes where frontier models differ even when predictions are similar. The benchmark reveals these divergences.

title: BMFA: Boundary-Minority Free-Energy Adaptive Screening
comment: 14 pages. Experiments include synthetic analysis, COCO, LVIS, closed-loop DeiT-Tiny evaluation, and ImageNet-1K classification
summary: Vision Transformers process spatially redundant tokens efficiently only when coarse token summaries preserve the evidence required by exponential attention aggregation. We identify a boundary-minority underestimation failure in which a spatially small, high-response region contributes dominant Gibbs mass while remaining nearly invisible to a block mean. We formalize the failure through the discrepancy between normalized log-mean-exp free energy and mean summarization, prove that minority Gibbs mass can remain non-vanishing as its spatial support and mean contribution vanish, and characterize the limitations of finite-order moment corrections. Building on the resulting analysis, we introduce Boundary-Minority Free-Energy Adaptive Screening (BMFA), which constructs a hierarchical piecewise-constant approximation and recursively refines blocks according to a computable lower-bound increment of local free energy. Controlled synthetic tests, COCO and LVIS diagnostic probes, closed-loop DeiT-Tiny evaluations, and ImageNet-1K experiments establish a consistent evidence chain. BMFA reduces the mean synthetic underestimate from 2.582 to 0.261 at a 5.794% leaf ratio, lowers the COCO image-edge mean gap from 2.254 to 0.526, and preserves 71.520% ImageNet Top-1 accuracy at a 55.861% leaf ratio. The current prototype evaluates selection quality after full QK computation; the reported leaf ratio therefore characterizes representation granularity rather than verified sparse-kernel speedup.

AI.tldr: Vision Transformers can fail to capture small but high-response regions when using coarse token summaries. The authors formalize this "boundary-minority underestimation" failure, prove it persists despite finite-order moment corrections, and introduce BMFA—a hierarchical screening method that recursively refines blocks based on free-energy lower bounds. BMFA reduces estimation errors substantially across synthetic tests, COCO/LVIS, DeiT-Tiny, and ImageNet-1K benchmarks while preserving accuracy at moderate leaf ratios.
AI.motivation: Vision Transformers rely on coarse token summaries for efficiency, but these summaries can miss spatially small regions with high response (Gibbs mass) that dominate the attention output. The paper aims to identify, formalize, and address this failure mode.
AI.method: The authors formalize the failure via the discrepancy between normalized log-mean-exp free energy and mean summarization, prove that minority Gibbs mass can persist as its spatial support vanishes, and characterize limitations of finite-order moment corrections. They propose Boundary-Minority Free-Energy Adaptive Screening (BMFA), which builds a hierarchical piecewise-constant approximation and recursively refines blocks based on a computable lower-bound increment of local free energy.
AI.result: BMFA reduces mean synthetic underestimate from 2.582 to 0.261 at 5.794% leaf ratio, lowers COCO image-edge mean gap from 2.254 to 0.526, and retains 71.520% ImageNet Top-1 accuracy at 55.861% leaf ratio.
AI.conclusion: BMFA effectively corrects boundary-minority underestimation in Vision Transformers while maintaining competitive accuracy at reduced token granularity. The prototype evaluates selection quality after full QK computation, so the reported leaf ratio reflects representation granularity rather than verified sparse-kernel speedup.

title: Feature Attribution-Based Explainability Analysis of Deep Learning Models in Predictive Process Monitoring
summary: Predictive process monitoring supports the optimization and control of operational business processes by forecasting the future state or outcome of ongoing cases. While deep neural networks have achieved strong performance for these tasks by modeling sequential dependencies in event logs, their black-box nature limits trust and practical adoption. Feature attribution methods are often used to address this, but applying them directly poses a dilemma: event-level attributions impose high computational complexity for long traces, while explanations based on aggregated trace representations often fail to capture the underlying control-flow dynamics. To address this issue, we propose a local post-hoc explainability method for deep neural networks in outcome prediction. The method relies on a control-flow-aware segmentation algorithm that partitions a trace into meaningful segments and supports the computation of segment-level SHAP explanations. This makes it possible to identify which parts of a trace influence a prediction and which change points steer the case toward the predicted outcome. We assess the proposed segmentation method on a synthetic dataset with known process logic, where meaningful change points can be explicitly verified, and we demonstrate its usefulness on real-world event logs from a loan application process and an administrative process of a Dutch municipality.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a local post-hoc explainability method for deep neural networks in predictive process monitoring. It uses control-flow-aware segmentation to partition traces into meaningful segments and computes segment-level SHAP explanations, addressing the trade-off between computational complexity and explanatory power of existing feature attribution methods.
AI.motivation: Deep neural networks achieve strong performance in predictive process monitoring but are black-box, limiting trust and adoption. Existing feature attribution methods face a dilemma: event-level attributions are computationally expensive for long traces, while aggregated trace-level explanations fail to capture control-flow dynamics.
AI.method: A local post-hoc explainability method that uses a control-flow-aware segmentation algorithm to partition a trace into meaningful segments, enabling segment-level SHAP explanations to identify influential parts of a trace and change points steering the prediction outcome.
AI.result: The segmentation method is evaluated on a synthetic dataset with known process logic to verify meaningful change points, and demonstrated on real-world event logs from a loan application process and an administrative process of a Dutch municipality.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method effectively identifies which parts of a trace influence a prediction and which change points steer the case toward the predicted outcome, balancing computational feasibility and explanation quality.

title: RayOcc: Occlusion-Aware Ray Occupancy Estimation via Gaussian Mixture Intensity
summary: Camera-only 3D semantic occupancy prediction aims to infer voxel-wise scene semantics from multi-view images, yet remains fundamentally challenging due to depth ambiguity and occlusion. Along a single camera ray, multiple spatially separated surfaces may coexist, making occupancy inherently a multi-label existence problem rather than a single-depth estimation task. However, most existing approaches favor a single dominant depth hypothesis per ray, limiting their ability to model volumetric scenes under complex occlusion. To address this limitation, we introduce RayOcc, an occlusion-aware ray occupancy framework that reformulates ray modeling as multi-label existence prediction. Instead of predicting a categorical depth distribution, RayOcc estimates a non-normalized Gaussian mixture intensity along each ray and converts it into interval-wise occupancy probabilities via a Poisson event formulation, allowing multiple occupied hypotheses to coexist without enforcing mutual competition across depth. The predicted mixture components are interpreted as occupancy hypotheses to initialize sparse 3D Gaussian primitives, which are refined and rasterized for semantic occupancy prediction. Experiments on the nuScenes benchmark show that RayOcc achieves state-of-the-art overall IoU and mIoU among the compared Gaussian-based occupancy methods.

AI.tldr: RayOcc reformulates camera-only 3D semantic occupancy prediction as multi-label existence prediction along camera rays using a non-normalized Gaussian mixture intensity with Poisson event formulation, enabling multiple depth hypotheses per ray. It then initializes sparse 3D Gaussian primitives from these hypotheses for semantic occupancy prediction, achieving SOTA among Gaussian-based methods on nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Existing camera-only occupancy methods assume a single dominant depth hypothesis per ray, which fails to model volumetric scenes under complex occlusion where multiple spatially separated surfaces coexist along a single ray.
AI.method: RayOcc models each ray as multi-label existence prediction by estimating a non-normalized Gaussian mixture intensity, converting it into interval-wise occupancy probabilities via a Poisson event formulation, then interpreting mixture components as occupancy hypotheses to initialize sparse 3D Gaussian primitives refined and rasterized for semantic occupancy prediction.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art overall IoU and mIoU among compared Gaussian-based occupancy methods on the nuScenes benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Reformulating ray modeling as multi-label existence prediction with non-normalized Gaussian mixture intensity and Poisson event formulation effectively addresses depth ambiguity and occlusion in camera-only 3D semantic occupancy prediction.

title: The Concept of Representation in ML: Beyond Plato and Aristotle
comment: 8 pages. Accepted for oral presentation at ICML 2026
summary: Representation is a central concept in modern machine learning, where it usually refers to internal encodings that support learning and generalization. As models scale and their capabilities become increasingly human-level, this representational language sometimes shifts from an engineering context into the more philosophically loaded domain of mental representation. We argue that this is the case for recent claims about the convergence of representational properties across different AI models. In particular, we assess the arguments developed in The Platonic Representation Hypothesis, according to which this convergence is driven by a unified structure of reality. We examine this claim by introducing arguments and ideas from debates about mental representation in the philosophy of mind. We argue that these philosophical resources can clarify what is at stake in such claims, explain why alignment evidence alone is insufficient for strong metaphysical conclusions, and suggest directions for future research.

AI.tldr: This paper critically examines the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, arguing that claims about convergence of AI representations toward a unified structure of reality lack sufficient evidence and would benefit from philosophical perspectives on mental representation.
AI.motivation: To evaluate whether recent claims about representational convergence across AI models (particularly the Platonic Representation Hypothesis) are justified, and to introduce philosophical insights from debates about mental representation to clarify what these claims entail.
AI.method: Conceptual analysis drawing on philosophy of mind literature on mental representation, applied to machine learning claims about representational convergence.
AI.result: Alignment evidence alone is insufficient to support strong metaphysical conclusions about a unified structure of reality driving representational convergence.
AI.conclusion: Philosophical resources from debates on mental representation help clarify stakes, expose evidential gaps in the Platonic Representation Hypothesis, and point toward more rigorous future research directions.

title: Early Yield Prediction for Sugar Beet Fields using Satellite Data -- Learnings from Specialized Vision Transformers
summary: Remote sensing has become an increasingly valuable tool for agricultural monitoring, particularly through the use of publicly available satellite imagery. However, effectively integrating domain knowledge into machine learning methods remains challenging. This study presents a real-world example of early sugar beet harvest yield forecasting from purely optical Sentinel-2 imagery, demonstrating how a tight integration of domain knowledge and machine learning can lead to synergistic gains. We empirically find that using very small vision transformer patch sizes and all available Sentinel-2 spectral bands improves our model despite being uncommon design choices in the domain. As a practical contribution, we were able to identify a large fraction of low-yield fields in a different year early on in the growth cycle through a modified training setup and a ranking-based detection of underperforming fields.

AI.tldr: This study demonstrates how tightly integrating domain knowledge with machine learning, using very small ViT patch sizes and all Sentinel-2 spectral bands, improves early sugar beet yield forecasting from optical satellite imagery, enabling early detection of low-yield fields.
AI.motivation: Effectively integrating domain knowledge into machine learning methods for agricultural monitoring from satellite imagery remains challenging.
AI.method: Uses a vision transformer with very small patch sizes and all available Sentinel-2 spectral bands; employs a modified training setup with ranking-based detection to identify underperforming fields early in the growth cycle.
AI.result: The uncommon design choices (small ViT patches, full spectral bands) improved model performance; the approach successfully identified a large fraction of low-yield fields in a different year early in the growth cycle.
AI.conclusion: Tight integration of domain knowledge and machine learning yields synergistic gains, with practical utility for early forecasting and detection of low-yield fields.

title: Phasor Attention: Mean Root Square Normalization for Phase Manifold Preservation
summary:
While Root Mean Square Normalization has become the de facto standard for accelerating modern sequence models, its reliance on the quadratic accumulation of independent scalars ($\sum x^2$) inherently triggers outlier-induced numerical instability, gradient starvation, and anisotropic phase distortion. We introduce Mean Root Square Normalization (MRSNorm). By structurally pairing channels into 2D phasors, MRSNorm mathematically inverts the traditional scaling paradigm: it computes the localized $L_2$ magnitudes (Root Square) before aggregating them via a global $L_1$ average (Mean).
  This operational inversion strictly constrains activations to a phasor manifold, preserving conformal invariance. By sharing a single affine weight across phasor components, MRSNorm halves the total number of learnable parameters, proving that unconstrained spatial scaling in standard norms is a harmful redundancy. We analytically demonstrate that this geometric constraint yields a built-in, trigonometric gradient clipper governed by the Pythagorean identity, unconditionally equalizing the local gradient norm to ensure Gradient Homogeneity.
  Empirical evaluations on a ResNet with CIFAR-100 show that despite halved parameters, MRSNorm provides critical structural stability under rigorous stress tests. Under extreme hyperparameter settings where standard normalizations suffer from gradient divergence, MRSNorm successfully prevents numerical explosion and secures stable optimization trajectories. Our findings propose a fundamental paradigm shift toward phasor-based deep representation learning. The implementation of MRSNorm is available at Appendix C.

AI.tldr: MRSNorm replaces RMSNorm by pairing channels into 2D phasors, computing local L2 magnitudes then global L1 average, halving parameters while providing built-in gradient clipping and numerical stability through geometric constraints.
AI.motivation: RMSNorm's reliance on quadratic scalar accumulation ($\sum x^2$) causes outlier-induced numerical instability, gradient starvation, and anisotropic phase distortion. The authors aim to eliminate these issues through a geometrically constrained normalization paradigm.
AI.method: MRSNorm structurally pairs channels into 2D phasors, computes localized L2 magnitudes (Root Square), then aggregates via global L1 average (Mean). This inverts the traditional RMSNorm pipeline. A single affine weight is shared across phasor components, halving parameters. The phasor manifold preserves conformal invariance and yields a built-in trigonometric gradient clipper via the Pythagorean identity, ensuring Gradient Homogeneity.
AI.result: On ResNet with CIFAR-100, MRSNorm (with half the parameters) provides critical structural stability under extreme hyperparameter settings where standard normalizations suffer gradient divergence, preventing numerical explosion and securing stable optimization trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Unconstrained spatial scaling in standard norms is harmful redundancy. The work proposes a paradigm shift toward phasor-based deep representation learning, proving that geometric constraints improve stability and efficiency simultaneously.

title: Attention from Above: A Multimodal Model for Drone-Based Object Localization
comment: Preprint. Accepted for publication in the International Journal of Interactive Mobile Technologies
summary: Drone-based object detection technology has advanced rapidly, becoming increasingly sophisticated and efficient. Recently, research trends have expanded beyond the detection of predefined objects toward the identification of specified target objects. For example, desired targets can be specified through textual prompts, enabling accurate detection of objects of interest. To address this demand, this paper proposes an efficient multimodal-based object detection model aimed at improving small object detection performance. The proposed method is built upon the YOLO-World framework and replaces the C2f layers used in the YOLOv8 backbone with attention-based A2C2f layers. This modification enables more precise representation of local features, particularly for small objects or objects with well-defined boundaries. In addition, the incorporation of attention mechanisms and parallel processing structures significantly enhances the model's computational accuracy. Comparative experiments conducted on the VisDrone dataset demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms the original YOLO-World model. Specifically, precision increases from 43.0% to 45.1%, recall from 32.8% to 35.0%, the F1 score from 37.2% to 39.4%, mAP@0.5 from 32.5% to 35.2%, and mAP@0.5-0.95 from 18.5% to 19.9%, confirming a substantial improvement in detection accuracy. These results verify that the proposed approach provides an effective and highly accurate solution for object detection in drone-based image and video application environments.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an efficient multimodal object detection model for drone-based applications by integrating attention-based A2C2f layers into the YOLO-World framework. The method improves small object detection performance and achieves significant accuracy gains on the VisDrone dataset (e.g., mAP@0.5 from 32.5% to 35.2%).
AI.motivation: Research trends have shifted from detecting predefined objects to identifying specified target objects via textual prompts. However, existing models struggle with small object detection in drone-based environments.
AI.method: The method builds upon the YOLO-World framework by replacing C2f layers in the YOLOv8 backbone with attention-based A2C2f layers, enabling better local feature representation for small objects. Attention mechanisms and parallel processing structures are also incorporated to enhance computational accuracy.
AI.result: On the VisDrone dataset, the proposed model outperforms the original YOLO-World: precision (+2.1%), recall (+2.2%), F1 (+2.2%), mAP@0.5 (+2.7%), and mAP@0.5-0.95 (+1.4%).
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach provides an effective and highly accurate solution for object detection in drone-based image and video applications.

title: Theoretical Foundations of $\max$@$k$ Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement Learning is a cornerstone technique for modern large reasoning models. Usually, for difficult tasks such as code generation and theorem proving, the agent is evaluated by generating $K$ responses rather than sampling a single response, and performance is then measured using a retry-aware metric such as $\max$@$k$. Despite their practical importance, the theoretical foundations of learning under such criteria remain limited. In this work, we provide a theoretical study of the $\max$@$k$ learning problem in finite-horizon reinforcement learning. We show that optimizing the $\max$@$k$ objectives is fundamentally different from standard expected-return maximization. In particular, we prove that Markovian policies are in general insufficient, identify a compact state augmentation that restores optimality, and explicitly characterize the performance gap that can arise between history-dependent and non-history-dependent policies. Moreover, we show that learning $\max$@$k$-optimal policies is statistically harder than standard reinforcement learning and provide an efficient algorithm that achieves the optimal sample complexity rate.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically studies the max@k learning problem in finite-horizon RL, showing it fundamentally differs from standard expected-return maximization: Markovian policies are insufficient, a state augmentation restores optimality, a performance gap exists between history-dependent and non-history-dependent policies, and learning max@k-optimal policies is statistically harder with an efficient algorithm achieving optimal sample complexity.
AI.motivation: Despite the practical importance of retry-aware metrics like max@k in code generation and theorem proving, their theoretical foundations in RL remain limited.
AI.method: The authors provide a theoretical study of the max@k learning problem in finite-horizon RL, analyzing Markovian policy insufficiency, compact state augmentation for optimality, performance gaps between policy classes, and sample complexity bounds.
AI.result: Markovian policies are insufficient for max@k optimality; a compact state augmentation restores optimality; there is an explicit performance gap between history-dependent and non-history-dependent policies; learning max@k-optimal policies is statistically harder than standard RL; an efficient algorithm achieves optimal sample complexity.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing max@k objectives is fundamentally different from standard expected-return maximization, with unique challenges in policy representation, statistical hardness, and algorithmic design.

title: ShotPlan: Cinematic Video Generation with Learnable Planning Token
summary: Current video generation models achieve impressive results in single-shot generation, yet remain limited in cinematic video generation, where coherent narratives and effective multi-shot composition require explicit shot planning. To address this challenge, we propose ShotPlan, a framework for explicit multi-shot cinematic video generation built upon a video diffusion foundation model. Our method introduces learnable planning tokens that capture shot-level transition cues and can be seamlessly integrated with the original video generation tokens to control transition timestamps. Unlike standard video generation tokens, the proposed planning tokens are equipped with Fractional Temporal Rotary Position Embedding (FRoPE), enabling shot transitions to be modeled at the frame level. Experiments demonstrate that ShotPlan significantly outperforms existing cinematic video generation methods, offering more flexible shot management and stronger inter-shot consistency.

AI.tldr: ShotPlan introduces learnable planning tokens with FRoPE positional encoding to enable explicit multi-shot control in cinematic video generation, achieving flexible shot transitions and inter-shot consistency beyond existing methods.
AI.motivation: Current video generation models excel at single-shot generation but lack capabilities for cinematic video generation requiring coherent narratives and multi-shot composition with explicit shot planning.
AI.method: A framework built upon a video diffusion foundation model, introducing learnable planning tokens that capture shot-level transition cues and integrate with original video generation tokens to control transition timestamps. Planning tokens use Fractional Temporal Rotary Position Embedding (FRoPE) for frame-level shot transition modeling.
AI.result: ShotPlan significantly outperforms existing cinematic video generation methods, offering more flexible shot management and stronger inter-shot consistency.
AI.conclusion: Explicit shot planning via learnable planning tokens with FRoPE is an effective approach for multi-shot cinematic video generation.

title: Mobius Learning: Cyclic Depth Folding in Transformers
summary: Transformer-based language models organize computation along an ordered depth axis, where shallow and deep blocks often develop distinct representational roles. We challenge the conventional view that these roles must remain tied to a block's position in the ordered sequence. We introduce Mobius Learning, a training architecture based on cyclic depth folding, in which different data streams follow cyclically shifted block orders. The same block group is therefore applied early in the block sequence for some data streams and late for others, so it is optimized in both shallow and deep roles, a phenomenon we call depth-role superposition. Surprisingly, in four-worker experiments with a modded GPT-2 small (124M) model trained on 2.5B FineWeb tokens using Muon, Mobius Learning achieves lower validation loss than a fixed-order looped Transformer at larger numbers of Transformer block-sequence passes. This counterintuitive result shows that a block group need not remain confined to one fixed shallow or deep role within the block sequence and opens a new design space based on cyclic depth folding. Crucially, this structure makes Mobius Learning particularly well suited to memory-constrained distributed training: raw training data remain local, while each worker stores one block group rather than the complete Transformer block stack.

AI.tldr: Mobius Learning introduces cyclic depth folding where different data streams follow cyclically shifted block orders, enabling depth-role superposition. This achieves lower validation loss than fixed-order looped Transformers in distributed training with 4 workers, while allowing each worker to store only one block group instead of the full stack.
AI.motivation: Challenge the conventional view that representational roles of Transformer blocks must remain tied to their position in the ordered sequence, and explore whether block groups can be optimized for both shallow and deep roles simultaneously.
AI.method: Cyclic depth folding: different data streams follow cyclically shifted block orders, causing the same block group to appear at different positions (shallow vs. deep) for different streams. Trained a modded GPT-2 small (124M) on 2.5B FineWeb tokens with Muon optimizer across 4 workers.
AI.result: Mobius Learning achieves lower validation loss than fixed-order looped Transformers at larger numbers of block-sequence passes, showing blocks need not remain confined to shallow or deep roles.
AI.conclusion: Opens a new design space based on cyclic depth folding, particularly beneficial for memory-constrained distributed training where each worker stores only one block group while raw data remain local.

title: Memory-Supported Synergistic Adaptation for Training-Free Test-Time Medical Image Segmentation
summary: Test-time adaptation (TTA) aims to mitigate distribution shifts by adapting models with unlabeled target data at inference time. While TTA with vision-language models (VLMs) has shown promising results in classification, extending it to medical image segmentation remains challenging. In this setting, the adaptation gains from optimizing on VLM-generated predictions are often outweighed by the degradation to the VLM's strong pretrained features caused by noisy, update-driven learning, resulting in limited and unstable improvements. We therefore propose Memory-Supported Synergistic Adaptation (MSSA), a novel training-free TTA framework for medical image segmentation. Without updating model parameters, MSSA dynamically selects reliable image-text predictions to construct an online memory, uses them as text-guided semantic priors, and couples them with cross-image structural alignment for robust adaptation. Specifically, MSSA consists of (i) a noise-aware memory construction module that filters and stabilizes cross-modal predictions, and (ii) a relevance-driven prototype alignment module that aligns the target sample with structurally consistent memory samples and their reliable predictions to improve adaptation. Extensive experiments on multiple medical segmentation benchmarks demonstrate that MSSA consistently improves VLM-based segmentation models and outperforms existing fine-tuning-based TTA methods by a clear margin, with gains of up to 12.2% DSC and 11.7% mIoU. Project page: https://lingrayy.github.io/MSSA/ .

AI.tldr: MSSA is a training-free test-time adaptation framework for medical image segmentation that constructs an online memory of reliable image-text predictions and uses text-guided semantic priors with cross-image structural alignment to adapt vision-language models without updating parameters, outperforming existing fine-tuning-based TTA methods by up to 12.2% DSC and 11.7% mIoU.
AI.motivation: Extending TTA with VLMs to medical image segmentation is challenging because adapting on noisy VLM-generated predictions degrades the VLM's strong pretrained features, leading to limited and unstable improvements.
AI.method: MSSA is a training-free TTA framework with two modules: (i) a noise-aware memory construction module that filters and stabilizes cross-modal predictions to build an online memory, and (ii) a relevance-driven prototype alignment module that aligns target samples with structurally consistent memory samples and their reliable predictions using text-guided semantic priors and cross-image structural alignment.
AI.result: MSSA consistently improves VLM-based segmentation models and outperforms existing fine-tuning-based TTA methods by a clear margin, achieving gains of up to 12.2% DSC and 11.7% mIoU on multiple medical segmentation benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: MSSA demonstrates that training-free TTA via dynamic memory construction and prototype alignment can effectively adapt VLMs for medical image segmentation without the degradation issues caused by parameter updates.

title: Distributional Soft Bellman Operator under the Cramér Geometry
summary: Distributional soft policy iteration (DSPI) provides an important framework for combining distributional reinforcement learning (DRL) with maximum-entropy control, in which the policy evaluation step is governed by a distributional soft Bellman operator acting on entropy-regularised returns. Theoretical analysis of such an evaluation step requires a probability metric under which Bellman updates can be controlled, typically by showing that the operator contracts the distance between any two candidate return-distribution estimates. In this paper, we focus on the Cramér geometry, a cumulative distribution function (CDF)-based metric with an $L^2$ structure, and study whether the fixed-policy distributional soft Bellman operator has this contraction property and hence a unique fixed point under this metric. Working directly on an admissible CDF field domain, we formulate the CDF-level distributional soft Bellman operator, prove that it is a $\sqrtγ$-contraction, and obtain the corresponding unique fixed point together with convergent iterative policy evaluation. The CDF formulation also shows that this finite-Cramér-domain property follows from a uniform first-moment condition on the combined one-step reward entropy shift, rather than from separate uniform boundedness assumptions on the reward and entropy terms. We then transport the same evaluation problem to the spectral domain by conjugation, obtaining an equivalent Hilbert-space representation of the same decision process. Taken together, these results identify the Cramér-geometric Bellman fixed point associated with the policy-evaluation step of DSPI, providing a reference point for studying approximate critics, evaluation error, and critic-loss design in DSPI-style algorithms.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the distributional soft policy iteration (DSPI) framework, proving that the distributional soft Bellman operator is a √γ-contraction in the Cramér geometry (an L2-style CDF-based metric). The authors formulate the operator at the CDF level, derive its unique fixed point under a uniform first-moment condition on the entropy-adjusted reward, and translate the evaluation problem to the spectral domain via conjugation, establishing a Hilbert-space representation of the same decision process.
AI.motivation: To fill a theoretical gap in distributional reinforcement learning with maximum-entropy control: ensuring that the distributional soft Bellman operator has a contraction property and a unique fixed point under the Cramér metric, which is necessary for principled policy evaluation in DSPI-style algorithms.
AI.method: The authors work directly on the CDF field domain to formulate a CDF-level distributional soft Bellman operator. They prove it is a √γ-contraction under the Cramér distance by imposing a uniform first-moment condition on the combined reward-entropy shift. They then transport the problem to the spectral domain via conjugation for an equivalent Hilbert-space representation.
AI.result: The distributional soft Bellman operator is a √γ-contraction in the Cramér geometry, guaranteeing a unique fixed point and convergent iterative policy evaluation. The contraction property stems from a uniform first-moment condition on the one-step reward plus entropy shift, not from separate boundedness assumptions. The CDF and spectral formulations are equivalent representations of the same process.
AI.conclusion: This work identifies the Cramér-geometric Bellman fixed point for DSPI policy evaluation, providing a theoretical foundation for studying approximate critics, evaluation error, and critic-loss design in DSPI-based algorithms.

title: PC-Seg: Progressive Cross-View Consistency for 3D OCT Segmentation from Sparse 2D Annotations
summary: Volumetric segmentation of optical coherence tomography (OCT) images is essential for diagnosing ocular diseases but requires labor-intensive voxel-wise annotations. While semi-supervised learning (SSL) can reduce annotation costs, most existing methods process data slice by slice and fail to exploit the inherent 3D spatial context. We propose PC-Seg, a progressive cross-view consistency framework that learns high-accuracy 3D segmentation models from sparse 2D annotations. Unlike conventional multi-view approaches, PC-Seg uses a single 2D model to learn cross-view consistency from standard B-scans and orthogonal slices, thereby generating reliable volumetric pseudo-labels. These pseudo-labels are then distilled into a 3D model, followed by a co-training stage in which the 2D and 3D models mutually refine each other through ensemble pseudo-labeling. Experiments on the MSHC and Duke DME datasets demonstrate that PC-Seg achieves accuracy comparable to fully supervised learning while using labels for only about 0.7% of the training data, outperforming state-of-the-art semi-supervised and retinal layer segmentation methods. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/gsisaoki/pc-seg-official.

AI.tldr: PC-Seg is a progressive cross-view consistency framework for semi-supervised 3D volumetric segmentation of OCT images, using a single 2D model to learn from sparse 2D annotations and generate pseudo-labels for a 3D model via co-training, achieving fully-supervised-level accuracy with only ~0.7% labeled training data.
AI.motivation: Volumetric segmentation of OCT images requires labor-intensive voxel-wise annotations. Existing semi-supervised methods process data slice-by-slice and fail to leverage inherent 3D spatial context, motivating a need for efficient 3D segmentation from sparse annotations.
AI.method: PC-Seg uses a single 2D model to learn cross-view consistency from B-scans and orthogonal slices, generating reliable volumetric pseudo-labels, which are distilled into a 3D model. A co-training stage then mutually refines both 2D and 3D models through ensemble pseudo-labeling.
AI.result: On MSHC and Duke DME datasets, PC-Seg achieves accuracy comparable to fully supervised learning using labels for only ~0.7% of training data, outperforming state-of-the-art semi-supervised and retinal layer segmentation methods.
AI.conclusion: PC-Seg demonstrates that high-accuracy 3D OCT segmentation is achievable from extremely sparse 2D annotations via progressive cross-view consistency and co-training, effectively reducing annotation burden without sacrificing performance.

title: The Art of Not Forgetting
summary: We introduce CMP (Cognitive Memory Primitive), an architecture that represents inputs as sparse relational codes, stores them in a two-tier competitive memory, and learns entirely through local, gradient-free updates, with no backpropagation anywhere in the network. We use this architecture to test a specific hypothesis: that catastrophic forgetting, usually treated as a training-time defect to be patched with replay or regularization, is instead a structural consequence of how backpropagation assigns credit and that a learning rule that is local and sparse by construction should resist it without a patch. On a controlled domain-incremental protocol across 15 text domains, three-seed replicated, CMP's backward transfer is 15-19x better than a matched-size Transformer trained with online EWC, and the result survives a domain-order control (reported as a range, +0.24 to +0.44, rather than a single figure). We report this alongside a real, substantial accuracy gap versus the Transformer baseline, a null result on a recognized vision benchmark, and a diagnosed, unresolved failure attempting to combine this architecture with a separate mechanism that improves raw accuracy, disclosed because an honest negative result is more useful than an omitted one. The central claim is narrow and falsifiable: local, sparse, non-backpropagation learning measurably resists catastrophic forgetting better than backpropagation with its standard fix, under conditions we state precisely.

AI.tldr: CMP is a non-backpropagation architecture using sparse relational codes and local competitive learning that resists catastrophic forgetting 15-19x better than a Transformer with EWC, with honest reporting of accuracy gaps and negative results.
AI.motivation: To test the hypothesis that catastrophic forgetting is a structural consequence of backpropagation's credit assignment, not merely a training-time defect, and that local, sparse, gradient-free learning can inherently resist it without replay or regularization patches.
AI.method: CMP architecture encodes inputs as sparse relational codes stored in a two-tier competitive memory, learned entirely through local, gradient-free updates with no backpropagation. Evaluated on a domain-incremental protocol across 15 text domains with three-seed replication and domain-order control.
AI.result: CMP's backward transfer is 15-19x better than a matched-size Transformer with online EWC (backward transfer range +0.24 to +0.44 across domain-order control). However, there is a real accuracy gap vs. Transformer, a null result on a vision benchmark, and a disclosed failure when combining with a raw-accuracy-boosting mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Local, sparse, non-backpropagation learning demonstrably resists catastrophic forgetting better than backpropagation with EWC under precisely stated conditions, with honest negative results disclosed.

title: DA-Fusion: Deformable Attention-Based RGB-D Fusion Transformer for Unseen Object Instance Segmentation
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures. Published in the Proceedings of the 2025 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2025)
summary: In logistics automation, precise segmentation of unseen objects is crucial for efficient robotic manipulation in cluttered environments. Tasks such as bin-picking and shelf-picking require robust perception to handle occlusions, varying object shapes, and complex spatial arrangements. Traditional RGB-based methods tend to over-segment objects due to their reliance on texture, while depth-based methods often under-segment by focusing primarily on geometric features. To address these limitations, we propose DA-Fusion, a deformable attention-based RGB-D fusion Transformer designed for unseen object instance segmentation. DA-Fusion effectively combines the strengths of both RGB and depth data, enhancing segmentation accuracy in cluttered and multi-layered object environments. We also introduce the Object Clutter Bin Dataset (OCBD), a benchmark dataset specifically tailored for evaluating bin-picking scenarios in top-down views. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that DA-Fusion outperforms state-of-the-art methods across diverse environments, making it particularly suited for real-world logistics tasks.

AI.tldr: DA-Fusion proposes a deformable attention-based RGB-D fusion Transformer for unseen object instance segmentation in cluttered logistics environments, along with a new benchmark dataset (OCBD), and shows superior performance over existing methods.
AI.motivation: RGB-based methods over-segment due to texture reliance, while depth-based methods under-segment from focusing on geometry alone. Existing approaches fail to handle occlusions, varied shapes, and complex spatial arrangements in logistics automation (e.g., bin-picking, shelf-picking).
AI.method: DA-Fusion employs a deformable attention-based RGB-D fusion Transformer architecture that integrates both RGB and depth modalities, leveraging deformable attention to efficiently fuse multi-modal features for unseen object instance segmentation.
AI.result: DA-Fusion outperforms state-of-the-art methods across diverse environments in extensive evaluations, demonstrating effectiveness in cluttered and multi-layered object scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The proposed fusion approach and the OCBD benchmark enable more precise unseen object instance segmentation for real-world logistics automation tasks like bin-picking.

title: A Geometric Perspective on Stabilizing Value Conflict Resolution
comment: Accepted to ICML Workshop on High-Dimensional Learning Dynamics
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) often struggle to navigate value conflicts when trained with the compressed scalar rewards of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). To address this challenge, we investigate how chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning can help improve performance in this domain. Geometrically, we show that CoT correlates with further smoothing the model's loss landscape in its sharpest direction, helping resolve the optimization instability of traditional scalar rewards. We also demonstrate via relevant downstream benchmarks that value conflict-focused CoT may generalize to different kinds of moral reasoning, demonstrating that this CoT has the potential to be an effective mechanism for better moral reasoning. To capitalize on this potential, we create a new value conflict-focused CoT design that further smooths the sharpest direction of the loss landscape and increases moral reasoning performance. This finding shows that explicitly modifying and improving the design of reasoning dynamics offers a promising avenue for improving model performance on user requests with complex value conflicts, advancing pluralistic alignment in LLMs.

AI.tldr: LLMs struggle with value conflicts under RLHF's scalar rewards. CoT reasoning smooths the loss landscape in its sharpest direction, improving optimization stability. A new value conflict-focused CoT design further enhances moral reasoning and pluralistic alignment.
AI.motivation: RLHF's compressed scalar rewards cause optimization instability and poor handling of value conflicts in LLMs. The paper seeks to address this by leveraging CoT reasoning.
AI.method: The authors geometrically analyze CoT's effect on the loss landscape (smoothing the sharpest direction), demonstrate generalization via moral reasoning benchmarks, and propose a novel value conflict-focused CoT design.
AI.result: CoT smooths the sharpest direction of the loss landscape, resolving optimization instability. The proposed CoT design further smooths this direction and improves moral reasoning performance on downstream benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly designing reasoning dynamics (CoT) is a promising approach for improving LLM performance on complex value conflicts, advancing pluralistic alignment.

title: To Blend In, First Decouple: Rethinking Camouflage Image Generation via Context-Decoupled Representations
summary: Camouflage image generation (CIG) focuses on generating visually concealed objects that seamlessly blend into their backgrounds. Existing methods typically follow either background-guided paradigms that adapt object appearance via style transfer, or foreground-guided strategies that outpaint surrounding regions conditioned on object features. However, they still suffer from appearance discrepancy and background artifacts. We attribute these limitations to cross-context representation leakage, where object and background cues are entangled in a coupled conditional space, resulting in ambiguous control and degraded camouflage fidelity. To tackle this, we propose a new context-decoupled generative paradigm, termed CamoDreamer, which aims to isolate contextual conditional guidance and explicitly decouple latent camouflage features into coordinated object and background control streams. First, a Contrast-aware Contextual Bridge is designed to model cross-context discrepancies and construct contrast-aware dual conditional guidance. Second, Context-Decoupled Assimilation Streams are employed to separate generative interactions conditioned on the dual guidance, while facilitating background rendering with target-aware cues in the latent space. Finally, a Frequency-Adaptive Contextual Blend module integrates complementary high-frequency textures and low-frequency structures from decoupled features to improve holistic coherence. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CamoDreamer consistently outperforms existing methods with a substantial margin, while maintaining a relatively lightweight design.

AI.tldr: CamoDreamer is a context-decoupled generative paradigm for camouflage image generation that isolates object and background conditional guidance to avoid representation leakage, using a Contrast-aware Contextual Bridge, Context-Decoupled Assimilation Streams, and a Frequency-Adaptive Contextual Blend module to produce high-fidelity camouflaged images.
AI.motivation: Existing CIG methods suffer from appearance discrepancy and background artifacts due to cross-context representation leakage, where object and background cues are entangled in a coupled conditional space, leading to ambiguous control and degraded camouflage fidelity.
AI.method: 1) Contrast-aware Contextual Bridge models cross-context discrepancies and constructs contrast-aware dual conditional guidance. 2) Context-Decoupled Assimilation Streams separate generative interactions conditioned on dual guidance, enabling background rendering with target-aware cues. 3) Frequency-Adaptive Contextual Blend integrates complementary high-frequency textures and low-frequency structures from decoupled features for holistic coherence.
AI.result: CamoDreamer consistently outperforms existing methods with a substantial margin while maintaining a relatively lightweight design.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling contextual conditional guidance into coordinated object and background control streams effectively resolves cross-context representation leakage, significantly improving camouflage generation fidelity.

title: Topological Signatures of Context-Level Reliability in TabPFN
summary: TabPFN is a transformer-based foundation model for tabular prediction that performs inference without task-specific training by conditioning on a support set and query inputs. Despite its strong empirical performance, its internal behavior on structurally difficult tabular geometries remains poorly understood. We study this behavior using zigzag persistent homology, treating TabPFN layer representations as evolving point clouds. We construct a controlled benchmark of synthetic tabular tasks with known true probabilities and varied intrinsic topology, including warped circles, tori, spheres, Hopf links, trefoil knots, and Swiss rolls. Across these tasks, we find that the topology of TabPFN's internal representation geometry is strongly associated with dataset-level reliability; for example, the zeroth homology group $H_0$ fragmentation count correlates positively with mean absolute residual across controlled tasks, and this association strengthens in a high-resolution warped circle case study at large sample size. Harder geometries induce a dual topological signature: increased $H_1$ loop activity and increased $H_0$ fragmentation, while the $H_1$ persistence becomes shorter-lived. These descriptors correlate with Bayes error, mean absolute residuals, and overconfidence. Our results suggest that zigzag persistence diagnoses the reliability of the inferred in-context task geometry and provides a context-level view of when TabPFN operates in topologically stressed regimes.

AI.tldr: This paper uses zigzag persistent homology to analyze TabPFN's internal representations, finding that topological features like H0 fragmentation and H1 loop activity correlate with prediction errors and overconfidence on structurally difficult tabular tasks.
AI.motivation: TabPFN's internal behavior on structurally difficult tabular geometries is poorly understood, motivating a topological analysis to diagnose reliability and stress regimes in its in-context learning.
AI.method: The authors construct a controlled benchmark of synthetic tabular tasks with known true probabilities and varied intrinsic topology (warped circles, tori, spheres, Hopf links, trefoil knots, Swiss rolls). They apply zigzag persistent homology to treat TabPFN layer representations as evolving point clouds and compute topological descriptors.
AI.result: H0 fragmentation count positively correlates with mean absolute residual; harder geometries induce a dual topological signature of increased H1 loop activity and increased H0 fragmentation with shorter-lived H1 persistence. These descriptors correlate with Bayes error, mean absolute residuals, and overconfidence.
AI.conclusion: Zigzag persistence diagnoses the reliability of TabPFN's inferred in-context task geometry and provides a context-level view of when the model operates in topologically stressed regimes.

title: Measuring Monosemanticity in Sparse Autoencoders via Latent Activation Coherence
comment: This is a preprint version. A shorter version of this paper has been accepted for presentation and publication in the post-workshop proceedings of the 8th International Workshop on eXplainable Knowledge Discovery in Data Mining (XKDD 2026), co-located with ECML PKDD 2026. The appendix is included only in this preprint and is not part of the peer-reviewed proceedings paper
summary: Within Explainable Artificial Intelligence, mechanistic interpretability uses Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to extract more interpretable features from neural representations. However, assessing their monosemanticity, and thus explanation quality, remains challenging. Existing metrics require external concept labels or depend on pretrained embedding models, making them sensitive to encoder's geometry. We introduce the Tversky Monosemanticity Score (TMS), a label-free metric that operationalizes monosemanticity as activation-set coherence of binarized SAE latents, and does not require external embedding encoders. We evaluate TMS on SAEs trained on features from pretrained vision and vision-language models (DINOv3, CLIP, BLIP2), two common SAE regimes (TopK, BatchTopK), multiple sparsity levels, and expansion factors. Our results show that TMS is less affected by encoder anisotropy than its embedding-based alternative, while remaining aligned with established monosemanticity indicators. TMS also reveals distinct SAE training dynamics across base models. Moreover, under encoder anisotropy, TMS provides a stronger indication of probe-based concept deletion effectiveness, while being competitive otherwise.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces TMS, a label-free metric for measuring monosemanticity in Sparse Autoencoders without requiring external embedding models, showing it is robust to encoder anisotropy while aligning with existing metrics.
AI.motivation: Existing metrics for evaluating monosemanticity in Sparse Autoencoders require external concept labels or pretrained embedding models, which are sensitive to encoder geometry (anisotropy), making assessment unreliable.
AI.method: The authors propose TMS, which operationalizes monosemanticity as activation-set coherence of binarized SAE latents. They evaluate it on SAEs trained on DINOv3, CLIP, and BLIP2 features across TopK and BatchTopK regimes with varying sparsity and expansion factors.
AI.result: TMS is less affected by encoder anisotropy than embedding-based alternatives, aligns with established monosemanticity indicators, reveals distinct training dynamics across base models, and provides stronger indication of probe-based concept deletion effectiveness under anisotropy.
AI.conclusion: TMS is a robust, label-free metric for evaluating SAE monosemanticity that outperforms embedding-based alternatives under anisotropic conditions while remaining competitive otherwise.

title: DiFA: Inference-Time Forward-Process Alignment for Diffusion Models
summary: The prevailing inference framework for diffusion models formulates generation fundamentally as a problem of numerical integration. This perspective casts the model as an exact estimator, neglecting the inherent statistical uncertainty of the denoising process. In this work, we propose Forward-Process Aligned Diffusion prediction (\textbf{DiFA}), a training-free framework that reframes inference-time data prediction refinement as a sequential state estimation problem. Rather than reusing past outputs solely for numerical integration, DiFA treats iterative data predictions along the reverse trajectory as correlated observations to build a forward-aligned temporal consensus. Inspired by Kalman filtering, this consensus aggregates historical predictions according to structural consistency and noise-level compatibility. To counteract the over-smoothing tendency of temporal consensus, we introduce a deviation guidance mechanism to adaptively preserve residual details. Empirically, DiFA yields significant improvements on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet across the evaluated metrics, including FID, IS, and FD-DINOv2, demonstrating that aligning inference with the forward statistical structure substantially improves generative fidelity.

AI.tldr: DiFA is a training-free framework that reframes diffusion model inference from numerical integration to sequential state estimation (inspired by Kalman filtering), aggregating historical predictions for temporal consensus to improve generative fidelity.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion model inference treats generation as numerical integration, neglecting the statistical uncertainty of the denoising process.
AI.method: DiFA reframes inference as sequential state estimation using Kalman filtering-inspired temporal consensus that aggregates historical predictions based on structural consistency and noise-level compatibility, plus a deviation guidance mechanism to prevent over-smoothing.
AI.result: Significant improvements on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet across FID, IS, and FD-DINOv2 metrics.
AI.conclusion: Aligning inference with the forward statistical structure substantially improves generative fidelity.

title: CDIS: Cross-Dimensional Class-Agnostic 3D Instance Segmentation via 2D Mask Tracking and 3D-2D Projection Merging
comment: 6 pages, 5 figures. Published in the proceedings of the 2025 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS)
summary: Class-agnostic 3D instance segmentation is critical for robotic systems operating in unknown environments, enabling perception of previously unseen objects for reliable manipulation and navigation. Existing approaches typically project per-frame 2D instance masks into 3D and merge them, which often breaks object identities across time and yields fragmented 3D instances. We introduce Cross-Dimensional Class-Agnostic 3D Instance Segmentation (CDIS), a zero-shot framework that explicitly tracks 2D instance masks across frames and associates them with 3D superpoints, creating a feedback loop between 2D and 3D. This cross-dimensional reasoning links temporally stable 2D tracks with spatially coherent 3D regions, producing globally consistent 3D instance labels without any 3D-specific training. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate that CDIS achieves higher accuracy and consistency than state-of-the-art zero-shot methods, while remaining efficient and scalable to diverse real-world environments.

AI.tldr: CDIS is a zero-shot framework for class-agnostic 3D instance segmentation that tracks 2D instance masks across frames and associates them with 3D superpoints via a cross-dimensional feedback loop, producing consistent 3D instance labels without 3D-specific training, outperforming existing zero-shot methods.
AI.motivation: Existing class-agnostic 3D instance segmentation methods project per-frame 2D masks into 3D and merge them, which breaks object identities across time and produces fragmented 3D instances, limiting reliability for robotic manipulation and navigation in unknown environments.
AI.method: CDIS introduces a zero-shot framework with cross-dimensional reasoning: it explicitly tracks 2D instance masks across frames and associates them with 3D superpoints, establishing a feedback loop between 2D and 3D that links temporally stable 2D tracks with spatially coherent 3D regions.
AI.result: CDIS achieves higher accuracy and consistency than state-of-the-art zero-shot methods on benchmark datasets, while remaining efficient and scalable to diverse real-world environments.
AI.conclusion: Cross-dimensional reasoning via a feedback loop between temporal 2D tracking and spatial 3D superpoints enables globally consistent zero-shot 3D instance segmentation without 3D-specific training, offering a scalable solution for robotic perception in unknown environments.

title: Harness Engineering for LLM-Driven GPU Kernel Generation
comment: 24 pages, 6 figures. Extended technical report on our submission to the MLSys 2026 FlashInfer AI Kernel Generation Contest. Code: https://github.com/syhya/mlsys26-flashinfer-contest
summary: Large language models (LLMs) can assist GPU kernel generation, but their practical effectiveness depends on whether generated code can be reliably constrained, validated, profiled, and selected. This paper presents a harness-centered system for LLM-driven GPU kernel optimization in the MLSys 2026 FlashInfer AI Kernel Generation Contest on NVIDIA Blackwell B200 GPUs. The system separates an evaluation harness from a profile-backed optimization controller: the harness enforces compilation, correctness, official-aligned timing, and artifact archival, while the controller turns profiler and workload evidence into bounded candidate-generation decisions. Human-authored skills capture operator constraints, references, profiling procedures, and promotion rules, while Codex and Claude Code agents generate candidate kernels inside those constraints. Across five operator definitions, the retained official-aligned artifacts achieved mean-latency speedups over supplied FlashInfer baselines of 1.62x, 18.05x, 29.68x, 1.12x, and 13.70x. The Agent-Assisted kernels outperform the Full-Agent artifacts across the evaluated definitions, indicating that expert-provided optimization directions, high-quality references, and workload context remain critical for reliable AI-driven kernel optimization.

AI.tldr: A harness-centered system for LLM-driven GPU kernel optimization in the MLSys 2026 FlashInfer Contest on NVIDIA Blackwell B200 GPUs separates evaluation from an optimization controller, using human-authored skills and agent-assisted generation to achieve 1.12x–29.68x speedups over baselines.
AI.motivation: LLMs can assist GPU kernel generation, but practical effectiveness depends on whether generated code can be reliably constrained, validated, profiled, and selected.
AI.method: The system separates an evaluation harness from a profile-backed optimization controller: the harness enforces compilation, correctness, official-aligned timing, and artifact archival; the controller uses profiler/workload evidence for bounded candidate-generation decisions. Human-authored skills capture operator constraints, references, profiling procedures, and promotion rules, with Codex and Claude Code agents generating candidate kernels within those constraints.
AI.result: Across five operator definitions, the retained official-aligned artifacts achieved mean-latency speedups over supplied FlashInfer baselines of 1.62x, 18.05x, 29.68x, 1.12x, and 13.70x. Agent-Assisted kernels outperform Full-Agent artifacts across all evaluated definitions.
AI.conclusion: Expert-provided optimization directions, high-quality references, and workload context remain critical for reliable AI-driven kernel optimization, as demonstrated by Agent-Assisted kernels outperforming Full-Agent artifacts.

title: BrainNext: A General-Purpose Self-Supervised Foundation Model for Brain MRI Analysis
summary: Foundation models pretrained using self-supervised learning have transformed computer vision by learning transferable representations from large-scale unlabeled data. However, existing foundation models for neuroimaging remain limited by task-specific training, slice-based learning strategies, or relatively small pretraining datasets, restricting their generalizability across diverse brain MRI applications. In this work, we present BrainNext, a general-purpose self-supervised foundation model for volumetric brain MRI analysis. BrainNext combines masked autoencoder (MAE) pretraining with a native three-dimensional Bi-Directional xLSTM-UNet architecture to learn rich anatomical representations from 60,551 unlabeled brain MRI examinations spanning multiple MRI modalities. The pretrained model is subsequently adapted to downstream tasks through lightweight task-specific fine-tuning. We evaluate BrainNext on the Foundation Models for Medical Imaging (FOMO) 2025 Method Track, encompassing classification, segmentation, and brain-age estimation, where it achieved second place overall and ranked first in the meningioma segmentation task on the official FOMO 2025 challenge leaderboard, demonstrating strong transferability across heterogeneous neuroimaging tasks. These results highlight the potential of large-scale self-supervised pretraining to learn robust and transferable volumetric representations, establishing BrainNext as a scalable foundation model for diverse brain MRI applications.

AI.tldr: BrainNext is a self-supervised foundation model for volumetric brain MRI analysis, combining MAE pretraining with a 3D Bi-Directional xLSTM-UNet architecture trained on 60,551 unlabeled brain MRI exams. It achieved second place overall and first in meningioma segmentation on the FOMO 2025 challenge.
AI.motivation: Existing neuroimaging foundation models are limited by task-specific training, slice-based learning, or small pretraining datasets, restricting generalizability across diverse brain MRI applications.
AI.method: BrainNext combines masked autoencoder (MAE) pretraining with a native 3D Bi-Directional xLSTM-UNet architecture, trained on 60,551 unlabeled brain MRI exams across multiple modalities, then adapted to downstream tasks via lightweight fine-tuning.
AI.result: Second place overall on the FOMO 2025 Method Track (classification, segmentation, brain-age estimation), and ranked first in meningioma segmentation on the official challenge leaderboard.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale self-supervised pretraining can learn robust and transferable volumetric representations, establishing BrainNext as a scalable foundation model for diverse brain MRI applications.

title: Information-Based Exploration via Random Features for Reinforcement Learning
summary: Representation learning has enabled classical exploration strategies to be extended to deep Reinforcement Learning (RL), but often makes algorithms more complex and theoretical guarantees harder to establish. We introduce Random Feature Information Gain (RFIG), grounded in Bayesian kernel methods theory, which uses random Fourier features to approximate information gain and compute exploration bonuses in non-countable spaces. We provide error bounds on information gain approximation and avoid the black-box aspects of neural network-based uncertainty estimation, for optimism-based exploration. We present practical details that make RFIG scalable to deep RL scenarios, enabling smooth integration into standard deep RL algorithms. Experimental evaluation across diverse control and navigation tasks demonstrates that RFIG achieves competitive performance with well-established deep exploration methods while offering superior theoretical interpretation.

AI.tldr: RFIG uses random Fourier features to approximate information gain for exploration in deep RL, providing theoretical guarantees and competitive performance across control and navigation tasks.
AI.motivation: Extending classical exploration strategies to deep RL often adds complexity and weakens theoretical guarantees. The authors aim to design an exploration method that is both scalable to deep RL and theoretically grounded.
AI.method: RFIG leverages random Fourier features within Bayesian kernel methods to approximate information gain, computing exploration bonuses in non-countable spaces. It avoids black-box neural network uncertainty estimation by using theoretically analyzable kernel approximations.
AI.result: RFIG achieves competitive performance with established deep exploration methods across diverse control and navigation tasks, while offering superior theoretical interpretability.
AI.conclusion: RFIG provides a theoretically grounded, scalable exploration approach for deep RL that balances performance with interpretability, avoiding the complexity and opacity of neural network-based uncertainty methods.

title: Medical Imaging Fusing Vision Transformer: Laryngeal Cancer Screening with Explanation
summary: Early and timely screening of laryngeal cancer is crucial for improving clinical outcomes. In recent years, NBI endoscopy has become a standard diagnostic tool for the detection of laryngeal lesions. However, its effective use requires well-trained clinicians and the procedure is time-consuming and subject to interobserver variability. In this context, the application of artificial intelligence (AI) offers a promising solution to support clinical decision-making. In this work, we proposed applying transformer and attention mechanism for analyzing the narrow band imaging and distinguish benign and malignant lesions. Results show it has good classification performance with F1 (82.72%), accuracy(82.33%). In addition, the result of laryngeal cancer screening is explainable for clinicians. The explainability is utilizing the state of art segmentation method (MedSAM) to provide the useful pathological information area for clinicians. The proposed methodology fusing classification and segmentation provides a translating on laryngeal cancer screening.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an AI system using transformer and attention mechanisms to analyze NBI endoscopy images for laryngeal cancer screening, achieving 82.33% accuracy and 82.72% F1 score, with explainability provided by MedSAM segmentation.
AI.motivation: Laryngeal cancer screening via NBI endoscopy is effective but requires well-trained clinicians, is time-consuming, and suffers from interobserver variability. AI is proposed to support clinical decision-making.
AI.method: Applied transformer and attention mechanisms for NBI image analysis to classify benign vs. malignant lesions, integrated with MedSAM segmentation for explainable pathological region identification.
AI.result: F1 score of 82.72% and accuracy of 82.33% for classification; segmentation via MedSAM provides explainable pathological information.
AI.conclusion: The proposed fusion of classification and segmentation offers a translatable approach for AI-assisted laryngeal cancer screening with explainability.

title: fSRD: Fuzzy Spectral Region Decomposition -- Automated Multi Operator Koopman Representations via an Adaptive Spectral Learning Architecture
comment: 66 pages, 30 figures, corresponding author = Charles Bokor
summary: Highly nonlinear chaotic dynamical systems remain difficult to model due to fundamental trade-offs between complexity, expressivity, and data efficiency. Modern machine learning methods achieve strong predictive performance but often rely on a-priori system knowledge or curated data with limited interpretability. Koopman operator theory offers a promising direction via linear representation in an infinite-dimensional observable space. However, many data-driven Koopman methods seek globally valid operators for which useful finite-dimensional spectral embeddings remain difficult to identify under these constraints. To overcome associated limitations, we introduce Fuzzy Spectral Region Decomposition (fSRD), a fully automated learning framework for estimating finite Koopman representation via multiple operators. The proposed method realizes a data-adaptive framework for assembling locally invariant embeddings, termed Invariant Decomposition. fSRD achieves highly accurate linear reconstructions of nonlinear systems while learning finite-dimensional representations of their induced evolution operators, bridging interpretable operator-theoretic models with expressive data-driven sequence learning. These embeddings are adaptively constructed via a global fuzzy tree model, drawing inspiration from fuzzy neural architectures to learn the induced dynamics while prioritizing parsimonious solutions. Empirical results across canonical chaotic systems (e.g., Lorenz and Duffing) and high-dimensional real-world data demonstrate strong predictive accuracy, interpretability, and robust expressivity across data-rich and data-limited regimes, highlighting the method's generality.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Fuzzy Spectral Region Decomposition (fSRD), an automated framework that learns multiple finite Koopman operators via a fuzzy tree architecture to achieve interpretable, data-efficient, and accurate linear representations of highly nonlinear chaotic dynamical systems.
AI.motivation: Highly nonlinear chaotic dynamical systems remain difficult to model due to fundamental trade-offs between complexity, expressivity, and data efficiency. Existing Koopman methods struggle to identify useful finite-dimensional spectral embeddings without a-priori knowledge or curated data.
AI.method: fSRD is a fully automated learning framework that estimates finite Koopman representations via multiple operators. It uses a global fuzzy tree model (inspired by fuzzy neural architectures) to adaptively construct locally invariant embeddings (Invariant Decomposition), enabling data-adaptive assembly of multiple Koopman operators for different regions of the state space.
AI.result: Achieves highly accurate linear reconstructions on canonical chaotic systems (Lorenz, Duffing) and high-dimensional real-world data. Demonstrates strong predictive accuracy, interpretability, and robust expressivity in both data-rich and data-limited regimes.
AI.conclusion: fSRD bridges interpretable operator-theoretic models with expressive data-driven sequence learning, offering a general framework that overcomes limitations of globally valid Koopman operators by learning multiple locally valid linear representations.

title: ReViV: Reconstructing the Viewer and the View in 4D from Monocular Egocentric Video
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. The first two authors contributed equally, and their author order is interchangeable
summary: Egocentric devices, such as wearable front-facing cameras, provide a unique perspective for capturing the continuous interaction between a human viewer and the surrounding environment. A holistic and efficient multimodal model capable of reconstructing this 4D representation is therefore highly desirable. However, existing approaches often rely on auxiliary inputs such as pre-computed camera trajectories, treat scene perception and human ego-motion modeling as separate problems despite their strong interdependency, and suffer from slow inference time. To address these limitations, we present ReViV, the first unified framework for holistic egocentric 4D reconstruction that extracts both viewer and view dynamics from a single monocular RGB video. We formulate the task as learning the full joint probability distribution over multimodal signals, including RGB video, camera trajectory, gaze direction, full-body motion, hand motion, and depth. Powered by a Masked Generative Egocentric Transformer, ReViV operates within a single feed-forward architecture to simultaneously reconstruct the temporally consistent 4D reconstruction across the viewer and the view with fast inference speed. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmarks, including HoloAssist, HOT3D, ARCTIC, Aria Digital Twin, and TACO, demonstrate that ReViV achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency across holistic ego-body, hand, and gaze reconstruction, camera tracking, while maintaining highly competitive egocentric depth estimation without relying on heavy task-specific priors. Code and models are fully open-sourced: https://reviv4d.github.io/.

AI.tldr: ReViV is the first unified framework for holistic egocentric 4D reconstruction from a single monocular RGB video, using a Masked Generative Egocentric Transformer to jointly reconstruct viewer (full-body, hand, gaze, camera trajectory) and view (depth) dynamics with fast inference, achieving state-of-the-art results across multiple benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing egocentric 4D reconstruction approaches rely on auxiliary inputs (e.g., pre-computed camera trajectories), treat scene perception and human ego-motion modeling as separate problems despite their strong interdependency, and suffer from slow inference time. A holistic, efficient, unified multimodal model is needed.
AI.method: The task is formulated as learning the full joint probability distribution over multimodal signals (RGB video, camera trajectory, gaze, full-body motion, hand motion, depth). ReViV uses a Masked Generative Egocentric Transformer within a single feed-forward architecture for simultaneous, temporally consistent 4D reconstruction of both viewer and view dynamics.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and efficiency across holistic ego-body, hand, and gaze reconstruction, camera tracking, and highly competitive egocentric depth estimation on HoloAssist, HOT3D, ARCTIC, Aria Digital Twin, and TACO benchmarks, without relying on heavy task-specific priors.
AI.conclusion: ReViV demonstrates that a unified, feed-forward transformer approach can jointly model viewer and scene dynamics from monocular egocentric video, eliminating the need for auxiliary inputs and separate task-specific models while delivering superior performance and fast inference.

title: MADA-RL: Multi-Agent Debate-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Parameter-Efficient Reasoning in Compact Models
comment: 20 pages, 3 figures, 9 tables, 2 algorithms, under review at TMLR
summary: Large language models achieve strong reasoning performance, but often at prohibitive training cost - a challenge that is especially acute for compact models ($\leq 4 \, \mathrm{B}$ parameters) trained under limited budgets. We introduce MADA-RL, a post-training framework that specializes compact models into generator and critic roles and trains them with a debate-aware learning signal, fine-tuning only a small subset of parameters via LoRA adapters. Our central contribution is a counterfactual critic advantage: a dynamic, role-conditioned baseline that redefines the critic's advantage as its reward minus the generator ensemble's per-instance accuracy. This explicitly optimizes critics to improve over generator consensus rather than to merely reproduce a correct answer, yielding more targeted credit assignment than static mean-reward normalization. At deployment, the specialized agents are composed in a lightweight multi-round protocol. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks, MADA-RL raises the accuracy of the DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B model from $39.9 \, \%$ to $41.9 \, \%$ ($+2.0$ points, $p < 0.001$) using $16$ times fewer trainable parameters than fully fine-tuned baselines, placing it on the accuracy-trainable-parameter Pareto front. It approaches, but does not surpass, the strongest baselines (DeepScaleR, STILL-3), which are trained on substantially larger datasets; we analyse this gap and the associated inference-time cost directly. A controlled study isolates the source of MADA-RL's gains: the counterfactual advantage produces the highest critic improvement rate of any model evaluated, indicating that trained critics learn to correct generator errors rather than to imitate them.
