AI.tldr: MADA-RL is a post-training framework that uses debate-aware learning with a counterfactual critic advantage to specialize compact LLMs (≤4B parameters) into generator and critic roles via LoRA fine-tuning, achieving Pareto-optimal accuracy-trainable-parameter tradeoffs on math reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Large language models achieve strong reasoning but at prohibitive training costs, especially for compact models (≤4B parameters) under limited budgets. Existing methods lack efficient credit assignment for role-specialized agents.
AI.method: MADA-RL fine-tunes compact models into generator and critic roles using LoRA adapters with a counterfactual critic advantage: advantage = reward - generator ensemble's per-instance accuracy, redefining the critic's improvement target relative to generator consensus rather than static mean reward.
AI.result: On five math reasoning benchmarks, MADA-RL improves DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B from 39.9% to 41.9% (+2.0 points, p<0.001) using 16× fewer trainable parameters than full fine-tuning, achieving Pareto-optimal accuracy-efficiency tradeoffs. However, it does not surpass DeepScaleR or STILL-3 trained on larger datasets.
AI.conclusion: Controlled studies confirm the counterfactual advantage drives MADA-RL's gains: trained critics learn to correct generator errors rather than imitate them, achieving the highest critic improvement rate. The gap to stronger baselines and inference costs are analyzed for future work.

title: Toward Optimal Adenovirus Detection Using YOLO26
summary: This study systematically benchmarks different data augmentation setups across YOLO26 model size variants to determine the most effective setup for adenovirus detection in TEM images. The benchmarked setups include NAS, GAS, GMAS and DAS, all evaluated under identical training conditions. The adenovirus dataset, selected from the published TEM virus dataset, was re-annotated by leveraging adenovirus particle positions to generate YOLO-compatible bounding box annotations. The experimental results demonstrated the impact of the benchmarked data augmentation setups on adenovirus detection with YOLO26 and indicated the most effective data augmentation setup.

AI.tldr: Benchmarks data augmentation setups (NAS, GAS, GMAS, DAS) for adenovirus detection in TEM images using YOLOv6 model variants, finding the most effective augmentation strategy.
AI.motivation: To systematically identify the most effective data augmentation setup for improving adenovirus detection accuracy in transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images using YOLOv6.
AI.method: Benchmarked four data augmentation setups (NAS, GAS, GMAS, DAS) across YOLOv6 model size variants under identical training conditions; re-annotated adenovirus particles from a published TEM virus dataset into YOLO-compatible bounding boxes.
AI.result: Demonstrated varying impacts of the four augmentation setups on detection performance and identified the most effective setup for adenovirus detection with YOLOv6.
AI.conclusion: Data augmentation choice significantly affects adenovirus detection in TEM images, and the benchmarked optimal setup provides a guideline for future virus detection tasks using YOLOv6.

title: FlashPDE: A Drop-in Fused Triton Operator Library for Neural PDE Solvers
comment: 9 pages of main text, 4 figures. Code available at https://github.com/factnn/FlashPDE
summary: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) solve PDEs by incorporating physical constraints into neural-network training, but large-scale problems are limited by automatic-differentiation memory overhead and inefficient execution of grid-based PDE operators. We present FlashPDE, a drop-in fused operator library for grid-based scientific machine learning. FlashPDE replaces fragmented PyTorch finite-difference execution with differentiable Triton kernels. Each operator integrates fused stencil evaluation, an analytic discrete-adjoint backward pass, and boundary-gradient correction within a unified torch.autograd.Function interface. The library provides 14 differentiable PDE operators covering 17 configurations across 1D--3D elliptic, parabolic, and Navier--Stokes systems, while remaining independent of neural architectures and training strategies. Experiments on an NVIDIA A100 GPU show that FlashPDE reduces peak memory usage by up to 37.0x compared with coordinate-based automatic differentiation and reduces CUDA kernel launches by up to 3.5x compared with eager PyTorch finite-difference implementations. Across six representative PDE benchmarks, FlashPDE achieves up to 2.30x end-to-end time-to-solution speedup and up to 19.2x kernel-level acceleration while maintaining numerical agreement with PyTorch finite-difference references. FlashPDE provides a hardware-efficient execution layer that bridges differentiable PDE solvers and GPU-optimized numerical computation within the PyTorch ecosystem.

AI.tldr: FlashPDE is a fused operator library for grid-based scientific machine learning that replaces PyTorch finite-difference execution with differentiable Triton kernels, achieving up to 37.0x memory reduction and 2.30x speedup on PDE benchmarks.
AI.motivation: PINNs solving large-scale PDEs are limited by automatic-differentiation memory overhead and inefficient execution of grid-based PDE operators.
AI.method: FlashPDE provides 14 differentiable PDE operators using fused Triton kernels with fused stencil evaluation, analytic discrete-adjoint backward pass, and boundary-gradient correction within a unified torch.autograd.Function interface.
AI.result: On NVIDIA A100: up to 37.0x memory reduction vs. coordinate-based AD, up to 3.5x fewer CUDA kernel launches vs. eager PyTorch, up to 2.30x end-to-end speedup, and up to 19.2x kernel-level acceleration across six PDE benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: FlashPDE bridges differentiable PDE solvers and GPU-optimized numerical computation as a hardware-efficient execution layer within the PyTorch ecosystem.

title: FF-ProCams: Feed-Forward Gaussian Splatting for Projector-Camera System
summary:
Projector-camera (ProCams) systems achieve active scene perception and controllable appearance manipulation via structured illumination, serving as a core infrastructure for spatial augmented reality, projection mapping, and surface reflectance acquisition. Existing inverse-rendering methods for ProCams deliver high-fidelity results but rely on time-consuming per-scene optimization, while mainstream feed-forward 3D reconstruction models produce baked appearance that cannot adapt to spatially varying projector illumination.
  To resolve this accuracy-efficiency trade-off, we propose FF-ProCams, a Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian inverse-rendering framework for ProCams. A hybrid Mamba2-Transformer encoder aggregates cross-view geometric and photometric cues from sparse multi-view observations, and lightweight heads predict a relightable Gaussian representation in a single forward pass. We further design a projector-aware differentiable renderer to synthesize camera observations under arbitrary active illumination and ProCams poses. To enable feed-forward training, we construct a large-scale synthetic ProCams dataset covering diverse object geometries and surface materials. Experiments show FF-ProCams achieves high-fidelity projector-aware rendering, generalizes to unseen patterns, and supports novel projector-camera poses. Using only 8 input views, it outperforms optimization-based baselines with 297 views while reducing test-time reconstruction to 0.13 seconds (a three-to-five-order-of-magnitude speedup). The code and data are available at https://github.com/CPREgroup/FF-ProCams/.

AI.tldr: FF-ProCams is a feed-forward 3D Gaussian inverse-rendering framework for projector-camera systems that achieves high-fidelity relightable scene reconstruction in 0.13 seconds from only 8 input views, outperforming optimization-based baselines that require 297 views, via a hybrid Mamba2-Transformer encoder and projector-aware differentiable rendering.
AI.motivation: Existing ProCams methods rely on time-consuming per-scene optimization (high accuracy but slow), while feed-forward 3D reconstruction models produce baked appearance that cannot adapt to spatially varying projector illumination. The goal is to resolve this accuracy-efficiency trade-off.
AI.method: Proposes FF-ProCams: (1) a hybrid Mamba2-Transformer encoder that aggregates cross-view geometric and photometric cues from sparse multi-view observations; (2) lightweight heads predicting a relightable 3D Gaussian representation in a single forward pass; (3) a projector-aware differentiable renderer for synthesizing camera observations under arbitrary active illumination and ProCams poses; (4) a large-scale synthetic ProCams dataset for training.
AI.result: Achieves high-fidelity projector-aware rendering, generalizes to unseen patterns, and supports novel projector-camera poses. Using only 8 input views, it outperforms optimization-based baselines with 297 views while reducing test-time reconstruction to 0.13 seconds (three-to-five-order-of-magnitude speedup).
AI.conclusion: FF-ProCams effectively resolves the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in ProCams inverse rendering, delivering both high fidelity and dramatic speed improvements over optimization-based methods.

title: L1 Augmented Attention as an Improved Vector Similarity Metric
summary: Scaled dot product attention conflates directional alignment and vector magnitude, limiting its effectiveness as a similarity metric in Transformer models. We introduce L1 augmented attention, a simple and computationally parallelizable modification that subtracts a learned, head specific L1 distance between queries and keys from the dot product score. This hybrid similarity captures complementary geometric information. Dot product rewards directional alignment, while L1 penalizes coordinate deviations. To reduce the cost of L1 computation, we project queries and keys into low dimensional subspaces whose parameters specialize to preserve informative L1 structure. Evaluated on WikiText 2 using a compact transformer, L1 augmented attention achieves up to a 14.5% reduction in perplexity over the original transformer baseline and outperforms an RBF L2 kernel. Analysis of norm variance and learned L1 weights reveals distinct geometric roles across layers and strong head level specialization. These results demonstrate that enriching attention with L1 geometry provides a principled and effective improvement to similarity computation in modern language models, with practical benefits for both accuracy and parallel efficiency.

AI.tldr: L1 augmented attention enhances Transformer similarity computation by combining dot product with learned L1 distance, achieving up to 14.5% perplexity reduction on WikiText-2 through complementary geometric information and efficient subspace projection.
AI.motivation: Scaled dot-product attention conflates directional alignment (captured by dot product) with vector magnitude, limiting its effectiveness as a similarity metric in Transformers.
AI.method: Introduces L1 augmented attention: subtracts a learned head-specific L1 distance between queries and keys from the dot product score. To reduce L1 computation cost, projects queries/keys into low-dimensional subspaces specialized to preserve informative L1 structure.
AI.result: Achieves up to 14.5% perplexity reduction on WikiText-2 over standard Transformer baseline, and outperforms RBF L2 kernel. Analysis shows distinct geometric roles across layers and strong head-level specialization.
AI.conclusion: Enriching attention with L1 geometry provides a principled and effective improvement to similarity computation, with practical benefits for both accuracy and parallel efficiency.

title: Vis2Reg: Visibility-Aware Landmark-Free Geometric 3D--2D Registration for Liver Laparoscopy
summary: Accurate 3D--2D liver registration, which aligns preoperative 3D models to partial, view-dependent intraoperative surface observations, is critical for AR-guided laparoscopic surgery but remains challenging due to severe occlusion, limited visibility, and the lack of 3D ground-truth supervision. Existing landmark-free approaches perform partial-to-complete geometric alignment, yet robust self-supervision under extreme partial visibility remains difficult. We propose Vis2Reg, a visibility-aware registration framework that explicitly constrains deformation using mask-consistent visible regions. We introduce a visibility-aware self-supervision that derives a visible-domain 3D supervision signal from intraoperative masks, enabled by differentiable point rasterization and mask-guided back-projection. This formulation improves robustness under severe occlusion while maintaining fully self-supervised learning. Vis2Reg combines a robust geometric rigid initialization module with an implicit neural deformation field for stable alignment. Vis2Reg achieves a Dice score of 92.6\% and a Chamfer Distance of 1.43 mm on real intraoperative datasets, with 111 ms per-frame inference time, demonstrating both accuracy and practical efficiency.

AI.tldr: Vis2Reg is a visibility-aware, self-supervised 3D-2D liver registration framework for AR-guided laparoscopic surgery that uses mask-consistent visible regions, differentiable point rasterization, and implicit neural deformation to achieve robust partial-to-complete alignment, attaining 92.6% Dice, 1.43 mm Chamfer Distance, and 111 ms per-frame inference on real data.
AI.motivation: Accurate 3D-2D liver registration is critical for AR-guided laparoscopic surgery but remains challenging due to severe occlusion, limited visibility, and lack of 3D ground-truth supervision. Existing landmark-free approaches perform partial-to-complete geometric alignment, yet robust self-supervision under extreme partial visibility remains difficult.
AI.method: Vis2Reg introduces a visibility-aware registration framework that explicitly constrains deformation using mask-consistent visible regions. It employs visibility-aware self-supervision deriving a visible-domain 3D supervision signal from intraoperative masks via differentiable point rasterization and mask-guided back-projection. The framework combines a robust geometric rigid initialization module with an implicit neural deformation field for stable alignment.
AI.result: 92.6% Dice score, 1.43 mm Chamfer Distance, and 111 ms per-frame inference time on real intraoperative datasets.
AI.conclusion: Vis2Reg achieves accurate and efficient partial-to-complete liver registration under severe occlusion with fully self-supervised learning, demonstrating practical clinical feasibility for AR-guided laparoscopic surgery.

title: Adaptive Mamba Neural Operators
summary: Accurately solving partial differential equations (PDEs) on arbitrary geometries and a variety of meshes is an important task in science and engineering applications. In this paper, we propose Adaptive Mamba Neural Operators (AMO), which integrates reproducing kernels for state-space models (SSMs) rather than the kernel integral formulation of SSMs. This is achieved by constructing Takenaka-Malmquist systems for the PDEs. AMO offers new representations that align well with the adaptive Fourier decomposition (AFD) theory and can approximate the solution manifold of PDEs on a wide range of geometries and meshes. In several challenging benchmark PDE problems in the fields of fluid physics, solid physics, and finance on point clouds, structured meshes, regular grids, and irregular domains, AMO consistently outperforms state-of-the-art solvers in terms of relative $L^2$ error. Overall, this work presents a new paradigm for designing explainable neural operator frameworks.

AI.tldr: AMO integrates reproducing kernels for state-space models using Takenaka-Malmquist systems and adaptive Fourier decomposition to solve PDEs on arbitrary geometries, outperforming state-of-the-art solvers across fluid physics, solid physics, and finance benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Accurately solving PDEs on arbitrary geometries and various meshes is important but challenging in science and engineering.
AI.method: AMO constructs Takenaka-Malmquist systems for PDEs, integrating reproducing kernels for SSMs instead of kernel integral formulation, aligned with adaptive Fourier decomposition (AFD) theory.
AI.result: AMO consistently outperforms state-of-the-art solvers in relative L2 error on challenging benchmarks in fluid physics, solid physics, and finance across point clouds, structured meshes, regular grids, and irregular domains.
AI.conclusion: This work presents a new paradigm for designing explainable neural operator frameworks.

title: PRiSM: Prototype Regularization for Few-Shot VLMs
summary: Training-free few-shot adaptation methods have gained significant attention recently in the context of Vision-language Models (VLMs). Yet, current benchmarks rely on strong assumptions about the statistics of the adaptation data, e.g., class balance. We question these simplifying assumptions and introduce a more realistic benchmark that varies both the levels of class balance and the effective number of classes in few-shot tasks via Dirichlet sampling. Surprisingly, under our setting, we observe substantial drops in the performances of state-of-the-art methods, more so when the number of labeled samples increases. To mitigate this, we introduce PRiSM, a class-prototype regularization that can be deployed as a plug and play module on top of any existing baseline method, significantly improving performances. Our method optimizes a novel multi-term loss, which includes a regularizer maximizing inter-class pairwise distances, along with additional terms promoting support-feature alignment and fidelity to the baseline prototypes. Furthermore, we introduce an effective and computationally efficient block Majorize-Minimize optimizer for our objective. More specifically, we derive a valid blockwise Lipschitz constant (i.e., a bound on the Hessian's spectral norm), which can be computed efficiently via the Gershgorin circle theorem. Extensive experiments show that PRiSM improves several training-free baselines, with large gains when dealing with severe class imbalance and high numbers of classes.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces PRiSM, a plug-and-play class-prototype regularization method that improves training-free few-shot adaptation for VLMs under realistic class imbalance conditions, using a block Majorize-Minimize optimizer with efficient Lipschitz constant computation via Gershgorin circle theorem.
AI.motivation: Current training-free few-shot adaptation benchmarks for VLMs rely on unrealistic assumptions like class balance. The authors question these simplifying assumptions and introduce a more realistic benchmark using Dirichlet sampling to vary class balance and effective number of classes, revealing substantial performance drops in state-of-the-art methods.
AI.method: PRiSM is a class-prototype regularization module with a multi-term loss including: (1) an inter-class pairwise distance regularizer, (2) support-feature alignment, and (3) fidelity to baseline prototypes. It uses a block Majorize-Minimize optimizer with a valid blockwise Lipschitz constant computed efficiently via the Gershgorin circle theorem.
AI.result: PRiSM significantly improves several training-free baselines, with large gains especially under severe class imbalance and high numbers of classes. Performance drops are more pronounced when the number of labeled samples increases under the realistic setting.
AI.conclusion: PRiSM effectively mitigates performance degradation caused by class imbalance in few-shot VLM adaptation, serving as a plug-and-play module that boosts existing training-free methods without requiring additional training.

title: SEE: Structure-aware Exploring \& Exploiting for Long-horizon GUI Agent Trajectory Synthesis
comment: Accepted by ACM International Conference on Multimedia 2026 (ACM MM 2026)
summary: Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents powered by vision-language models hold promise for automating real-world mobile tasks. However, progress is limited by the lack of high-coverage, long-horizon interaction trajectories collected from element-rich and rapidly evolving apps. Existing pipelines often rely on costly human demonstrations or on-policy framework, which tends to over-sample common flows while missing rare transitions and complex multi-step procedures. To address this problem, we propose SEE, a two-stage data synthesis framework consisting of (i) an efficient exploration stage that builds an explicit UI transition graph over screens and elements, and (ii) a graph-based synthesis stage that composes diverse multi-step trajectories via planning and controlled sampling. This design yields reproducible and explainable data generation, while explicitly preventing spurious cycles and enabling long-horizon composition. Across multiple real-world apps, SEE produces trajectories with an average length of 14.8 steps while avoiding spurious loops, and agents fine-tuned on SEE achieve improved task success and generalization to unseen screens. We will publicly release our synthesis code and dataset.

AI.tldr: SEE is a two-stage data synthesis framework for GUI agents that builds UI transition graphs via efficient exploration and then generates diverse, long-horizon multi-step trajectories through graph-based planning and controlled sampling, achieving average 14.8-step trajectories without spurious loops and improving agent task success and generalization.
AI.motivation: Existing GUI agent data pipelines rely on costly human demonstrations or on-policy frameworks that over-sample common flows and miss rare transitions and complex multi-step procedures, limiting progress due to lack of high-coverage, long-horizon interaction trajectories from element-rich and rapidly evolving apps.
AI.method: SEE consists of two stages: (i) efficient exploration that constructs an explicit UI transition graph over screens and elements, and (ii) graph-based synthesis that composes diverse multi-step trajectories via planning and controlled sampling, preventing spurious cycles and enabling long-horizon composition.
AI.result: Across multiple real-world apps, SEE produces trajectories with an average length of 14.8 steps while avoiding spurious loops. Agents fine-tuned on SEE achieve improved task success and generalization to unseen screens.
AI.conclusion: SEE provides a reproducible and explainable data generation approach that addresses the coverage and diversity limitations of existing GUI data pipelines, and the authors will publicly release the synthesis code and dataset.

title: Consistent Feature Transport for Image Relighting
summary: Image relighting modifies illumination while preserving non-lighting content such as identity and geometry. Existing diffusion-based methods often suffer from unstable illumination changes or inconsistent content preservation under complex lighting, as they lack an explicit mechanism to learn feature transformations between images. We reformulate relighting as an illumination feature transport problem and introduce Consistent Feature Transport (CFT), a training principle that explicitly enforces illumination-consistent transport between source and target image distributions. Built upon rectified flow, CFT jointly models noise-to-image generation and illumination-consistent source-to-target transport through trajectory-level supervision. This dual-transport formulation encourages isolation of illumination-specific variations while preserving content-aligned features. To support complex lighting scenarios, we construct a large-scale portrait relighting dataset with diverse relighting effects. Experiments show consistent improvements over existing state-of-the-art relighting approaches and demonstrate that CFT can generalize to other editing tasks, including style transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/Dixin-Lab/CFT.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Consistent Feature Transport (CFT), a training principle that reformulates image relighting as an illumination feature transport problem using rectified flow, enabling stable illumination changes while preserving content. It shows state-of-the-art results on portrait relighting and generalizes to other editing tasks like style transfer.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based relighting methods suffer from unstable illumination changes and inconsistent content preservation under complex lighting, lacking an explicit mechanism to learn feature transformations between images.
AI.method: CFT reformulates relighting as an illumination feature transport problem using rectified flow, jointly modeling noise-to-image generation and illumination-consistent source-to-target transport through trajectory-level supervision with a dual-transport formulation.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over existing state-of-the-art relighting approaches; generalization to other editing tasks including style transfer.
AI.conclusion: The dual-transport formulation effectively isolates illumination-specific variations while preserving content-aligned features, enabling robust relighting and generalization across editing tasks.

title: SGN: A Similarity-based Generative Network for Data Generation under Distribution Shift
summary: Generative models trained on a source domain often produce samples that are poorly aligned with shifted target domains, limiting their effectiveness for target-domain data augmentation. Although target-specific adaptation can reduce this mismatch, it typically requires additional optimization and domain-specific parameters. We propose a Similarity-based Generative Network (SGN), a reusable framework that is trained once on labeled source data and applied to new target domains without parameter updates. SGN learns a latent space structured by label-induced pairwise similarities while preserving reconstructive information through an encoder-decoder architecture. At generation time, a small labeled representative set from the target domain is encoded and combined in the learned latent space, allowing the generated samples to inherit target-specific characteristics while maintaining class consistency. We further analyze the realizability and dimensionality requirements of the proposed similarity structure. Experiments on image and tabular datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of SGN for target-guided data augmentation under source-to-target distribution shifts.

AI.tldr: SGN is a reusable generative framework trained once on labeled source data that adapts to new target domains without parameter updates by using label-induced pairwise similarities in latent space and a small labeled target representative set to generate target-specific, class-consistent samples for data augmentation under distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: Generative models trained on a source domain produce samples poorly aligned with shifted target domains, limiting their effectiveness for target-domain data augmentation. Target-specific adaptation typically requires additional optimization and domain-specific parameters.
AI.method: SGN learns a latent space structured by label-induced pairwise similarities with an encoder-decoder architecture preserving reconstructive information. At generation time, a small labeled representative set from the target domain is encoded and combined in the learned latent space to produce target-specific, class-consistent samples without parameter updates.
AI.result: Experiments on image and tabular datasets demonstrate SGN's effectiveness for target-guided data augmentation under source-to-target distribution shifts.
AI.conclusion: SGN provides a reusable, parameter-free adaptation framework for target-guided data augmentation, with theoretical analysis of realizability and dimensionality requirements of the similarity structure.

title: Measuring and Improving Complex-Atomic Answer Consistency in Endoscopic VQA
summary: Endoscopic visual question answering (VQA) increasingly asks complex questions that combine several endoscopic answer components rather than isolated factual queries. Such complex answers may be scored as correct even when the same model fails on associated atomic questions. We introduce EndoCA, a paired complex-atomic answer consistency benchmark for evaluating whether complex answers remain consistent with same-image atomic answers. EndoCA contains two suites: EndoCA-Core evaluates compact question-complexity patterns commonly seen in practical endoscopic VQA, and EndoCA-Diagnostic supports controlled analysis across increasing question complexity. We evaluate 11 VLMs spanning open, medical, endoscopy-adapted, and closed-source models on EndoCA. Some VLMs achieve high complex-answer accuracy, yet their atomic-answer accuracy and complex-atomic answer consistency remain substantially lower. To reduce this complex-atomic inconsistency, we introduce Atomic-Support Reconciliation (ASR), a training-free mechanism that uses model-generated atomic answers as contextual premises for answer revision and consistency-guided selective answering. On four selected publicly available models, ASR-Revise improves paired complex-atomic correctness with modest changes in complex-answer accuracy, while ASR-Selective improves accuracy on answered cases by allowing the model to abstain from less reliable cases. Together, EndoCA and ASR provide a consistency-aware benchmark and a training-free mechanism for answer reconciliation and selective answering in endoscopic VQA.

AI.tldr: EndoCA is a benchmark for consistency between complex and atomic answers in endoscopic VQA, revealing that VLMs with high complex-answer accuracy often have low atomic-answer accuracy and consistency. ASR is a training-free mechanism that improves consistency via answer revision and selective answering.
AI.motivation: Endoscopic VQA increasingly involves complex questions combining multiple answer components, but models may score well on complex questions while failing on the associated atomic (component) questions, revealing inconsistency that undermines reliability.
AI.method: EndoCA benchmark (Core + Diagnostic suites) evaluates complex-atomic answer consistency across 11 VLMs. ASR (Atomic-Support Reconciliation) is a training-free mechanism using model-generated atomic answers as contextual premises for answer revision and consistency-guided selective answering.
AI.result: VLMs achieve high complex-answer accuracy but substantially lower atomic-answer accuracy and complex-atomic consistency. ASR-Revise improves complex-atomic correctness with modest accuracy changes; ASR-Selective improves accuracy on answered cases by enabling abstention on unreliable cases.
AI.conclusion: EndoCA and ASR provide a consistency-aware benchmark and training-free mechanism for answer reconciliation and selective answering, addressing the complex-atomic inconsistency gap in endoscopic VQA.

title: Sobek: Streaming Equivariant Tensor Product Convolutions
summary:
Equivariant graph neural networks repeatedly apply edge-conditioned tensor-product convolutions over graph edges. Conventional implementations materialize edge-specific weights, messages, and adjoints, causing tensor-product workspace and memory traffic to grow rapidly with graph size and operator width. This limits feasible workloads and can prevent larger problems from fully utilizing the GPU.
  We show that these edge-sized intermediates are artifacts of the execution schedule, not requirements of the equivariant operator. By reassociating radial projection, spherical-harmonic coupling, and graph aggregation, edge-local products can be consumed directly into bounded receiver-side state. The resulting streaming formulation preserves fully connected multiplicity mixing and extends through forward, backward, and double backward.
  We implement this formulation in Sobek, a generated-CUDA backend, and evaluate it across edge-scaling regimes and varied feature structures. Across two operator families and all three differentiation orders, Sobek is faster in all 75 capacity-matched comparisons, with speedups ranging from $1.2\times$ to $49.7\times$, and reduces peak allocated memory by up to 99\%. It also executes workloads up to two orders of magnitude beyond OpenEquivariance's capacity while retaining near-peak throughput. These results show that edge-scaled tensor-product workspace is a property of the conventional schedule, not of equivariant convolution itself.

AI.tldr: Sobek reformulates equivariant graph neural network convolutions to avoid materializing edge-sized intermediates, achieving up to 49.7× speedup and 99% memory reduction via a streaming approach that consumes edge-local products directly into receiver-side state.
AI.motivation: Conventional equivariant GNNs materialize edge-specific weights, messages, and adjoints, causing tensor-product workspace and memory traffic that grows rapidly with graph size and operator width, limiting feasible workloads and preventing full GPU utilization for larger problems.
AI.method: The paper reassociates radial projection, spherical-harmonic coupling, and graph aggregation to consume edge-local products directly into bounded receiver-side state (streaming formulation), preserving fully connected multiplicity mixing through forward, backward, and double backward passes. Implemented as a generated-CUDA backend called Sobek.
AI.result: Across 75 capacity-matched comparisons, Sobek is faster in all cases (1.2× to 49.7× speedups), reduces peak memory by up to 99%, and executes workloads up to two orders of magnitude beyond OpenEquivariance's capacity while retaining near-peak throughput.
AI.conclusion: Edge-scaled tensor-product workspace is a property of the conventional execution schedule, not an inherent requirement of equivariant convolution itself.

title: CaT-GS: Efficient 3DGS Rendering for Large Scale Scenes via Inter-frame Caching and Tile Scheduling
summary: Recent breakthroughs in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have advanced neural rendering with high fidelity and speed. However, its performance degrades significantly in large-scale scenes due to the computational burden of tile-based rasterization. Existing optimization efforts either require costly scene re-training or focus on narrow aspects of the pipeline, overlooking critical inefficiencies in real-world deployments. Through a comprehensive analysis, we identify three primary sources of redundancy and low GPU utilization: redundant inter-frame pre-processing, viewpoint-based occlusion redundancy, and severe tile-level load imbalance. To address these issues, we propose CaT-GS, a novel and efficient 3DGS rendering pipeline. CaT-GS introduces a speculative multi-frame preprocessing method to eliminate redundant computations across consecutive frames, and an inter-frame caching mechanism to eliminate viewpoint redundant rendering stages. Furthermore, it refactors rasterization tasks with a dedicated kernel to mitigate tile load imbalance, significantly boosting GPU utilization. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CaT-GS achieves a speedup of up to 10 times over the original 3DGS and up to 70% over previous state-of-the-art methods, establishing a new benchmark for high-fidelity, real-time rendering of large-scale scenes.

AI.tldr: CaT-GS is a novel 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipeline that achieves up to 10x speedup over original 3DGS and 70% over SOTA by addressing redundancy and GPU underutilization through speculative multi-frame preprocessing, inter-frame caching, and refactored rasterization for load balancing.
AI.motivation: 3DGS performance degrades significantly in large-scale scenes due to computational burden of tile-based rasterization; existing optimization efforts either require costly re-training or focus on narrow aspects, overlooking critical inefficiencies in real-world deployments.
AI.method: CaT-GS introduces: (1) speculative multi-frame preprocessing to eliminate redundant computations across consecutive frames; (2) inter-frame caching mechanism to eliminate viewpoint redundant rendering stages; (3) refactored rasterization with a dedicated kernel to mitigate tile-level load imbalance and boost GPU utilization.
AI.result: Achieves up to 10x speedup over original 3DGS and up to 70% over previous state-of-the-art methods, establishing a new benchmark for high-fidelity, real-time rendering of large-scale scenes.
AI.conclusion: CaT-GS effectively addresses three key inefficiencies (redundant inter-frame preprocessing, viewpoint-based occlusion redundancy, tile-level load imbalance) in 3DGS for large-scale scenes, setting a new performance standard for real-time neural rendering.

title: Generalised Bellman recurrence and three dualities in sequential decision-making
summary: What gives the Bellman equation its form? We show that the recursive properties of optimal value functions follow from three conditions: that the dynamics decomposes through sufficient statistics, that the return decomposes recursively, and that the aggregation of uncertainty is compatible with both. When all three conditions hold on a common state, the Bellman equation arises from their mutual consistency; when one fails, tractability can often be recovered by augmenting the state or by deforming return or dynamics. The same conditions are shown to give rise to three dualities: one between probability and return, one between return and aggregation, and one between aggregation and probability. Our framework reveals these dualities as arising from a single construction, unifying methods developed separately across reinforcement learning, control, and decision theory.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies three conditions (sufficient statistics, recursive return decomposition, compatible uncertainty aggregation) that give rise to the Bellman equation, and shows how failures can be addressed by state augmentation or deformation. It also reveals three dualities between probability, return, and aggregation.
AI.motivation: To understand the fundamental structural conditions that cause optimal value functions to satisfy the Bellman equation, and to unify seemingly disparate methods across reinforcement learning, control theory, and decision theory under a single framework.
AI.method: The authors derive three necessary conditions (dynamics decomposing via sufficient statistics, recursive return decomposition, and compatible uncertainty aggregation) and show that the Bellman equation emerges from their mutual consistency. They analyze cases where conditions fail and propose remedies (state augmentation or deformation of return/dynamics). They also construct three dualities between probability, return, and aggregation from a single underlying construction.
AI.result: The Bellman equation's form is explained by three conditions; three dualities between probability, return, and aggregation are uncovered; a unified perspective connecting reinforcement learning, control, and decision theory is provided.
AI.conclusion: The Bellman equation arises from three specific conditions on dynamics, return, and uncertainty aggregation; this framework unifies diverse methods across RL, control, and decision theory through a common set of dualities.

title: Leveraging Dissimilarity Invariance as a Robust Anchor for Learning with Noisy Labels
summary: Deep learning models excel in visual recognition but suffer severe performance drops when training labels are corrupted by noise. Under label noise prior work cannot learn accurate similarities and thus misguide the learning process. In this paper, we uncover a complementary and novel phenomenon, Dissimilarity Invariance, whereby semantic dissimilarity between unrelated samples remains stable despite label noise. Leveraging this insight, we propose NegScale, a plug-and-play framework that shifts focus from fragile similarity to robust dissimilarity. NegScale integrates: (1) Structured Negative Orthogonality Penalty (SNOP), enforcing subspace orthogonality for unrelated samples; and (2) Dissimilarity-Calibrated Similarity Adjustment (DCSA), suppressing spurious similarity using dissimilarity anchors. We also give theoretical analysis that proves Dissimilarity Invariance and the effectiveness of NegScale. Empirical results demonstrate that NegScale consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, establishing new benchmarks on CIFAR with synthetic noise and real-world datasets.

AI.tldr: NegScale leverages the novel phenomenon of Dissimilarity Invariance (where semantic dissimilarity between unrelated samples remains stable despite label noise) to improve learning under noisy labels, outperforming state-of-the-art on CIFAR and real-world benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Deep learning models suffer severe performance degradation when training labels are corrupted by noise; prior work under label noise cannot learn accurate similarities, misguiding the learning process.
AI.method: Proposes NegScale, a plug-and-play framework with two components: (1) Structured Negative Orthogonality Penalty (SNOP) enforcing subspace orthogonality for unrelated samples, and (2) Dissimilarity-Calibrated Similarity Adjustment (DCSA) suppressing spurious similarity using dissimilarity anchors. Theoretical analysis proves Dissimilarity Invariance and effectiveness.
AI.result: Consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, establishing new benchmarks on CIFAR with synthetic noise and real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: Shifting focus from fragile similarity to robust dissimilarity via Dissimilarity Invariance is an effective paradigm for learning under label noise.

title: SelectInfer: Selective Neuron Loading and Computation for On-Device LLMs
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities across a range of Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks, but their high computational and memory demands pose significant challenges for deployment on resource-constrained edge devices. Existing approaches to model compression and optimization often rely on coarse-grained pruning or quantization, which can compromise accuracy or require re-training and fine-tuning. In this work, we introduce SelectInfer, a neuron-level optimization framework that enables efficient LLM inference on edge devices through selective neuron loading and computation. By profiling and identifying both task-specific and general-purpose neurons using an offline LLM profiler, SelectInfer implements two key optimizations: selective loading, which reduces memory footprint by selectively loading a subset of neurons that were identified to be most important during the offline stage, and selective computation, which dynamically computes only the most relevant neurons at runtime. Evaluation across multiple datasets shows that SelectInfer achieves significant reductions in memory footprint and computation while preserving task performance, making it a practical step towards enabling LLM deployment on edge devices

AI.tldr: SelectInfer is a neuron-level optimization framework that enables efficient LLM inference on edge devices through selective neuron loading and computation, reducing memory and computation while preserving task performance.
AI.motivation: LLMs have high computational and memory demands that hinder deployment on resource-constrained edge devices, and existing pruning/quantization methods are coarse-grained, compromise accuracy, or require re-training.
AI.method: SelectInfer uses an offline profiler to identify task-specific and general-purpose neurons, then applies selective loading (loading only important neurons to reduce memory) and selective computation (dynamically computing only relevant neurons at runtime).
AI.result: Achieves significant reductions in memory footprint and computation across multiple datasets while preserving task performance.
AI.conclusion: SelectInfer is a practical step towards enabling LLM deployment on edge devices.

title: Locality-Aware Density Control for Efficient Gaussian-based Image Representation
summary: 2D Gaussian Splatting is an attractive direction for image representation due to its explicit formulation, fast rasterization, and favorable decoding efficiency. The representation quality of this paradigm depends on the proper allocation of Gaussian capacity to the demanding regions. However, existing methods fail to allocate Gaussian capacity efficiently during optimization: under-reconstructed content is often refined in a fragmented pixel-wise manner, while neighboring optimized Gaussians with similar attributes are redundantly retained. This inefficiency motivates the need for a density control framework that jointly addresses insufficient allocation in under-reconstructed regions and redundant allocation in over-reconstructed regions. Our key insight is that this framework should exploit two complementary forms of locality: the local continuity of reconstruction errors in image space for improved Gaussian allocation, and the local similarity of neighboring Gaussians in Gaussian space for redundant elimination. Based on this insight, we propose Locality-Aware Density Control (LocoADC), a plug-and-play framework that improves Gaussian capacity utilization through Region-wise Gaussian Densification (RGD) and Similarity-Driven Gaussian Merging (SDGM) strategies, together with a local color consistency constraint for more reliable merging. Extensive experiments on diverse datasets show that LocoADC consistently improves multiple baselines by enabling more effective local Gaussian allocation, including a 2.93 dB PSNR gain over GI on the CLIC dataset under the same 30k Gaussian budget. Code is available at: \textit{https://github.com/ChenJiaCong-1005/LocoADC}.

AI.tldr: LocoADC is a plug-and-play density control framework for 2D Gaussian Splatting that improves Gaussian capacity allocation by using region-wise densification for under-reconstructed areas and similarity-driven merging for redundant Gaussians, achieving consistent performance gains across multiple baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing 2D Gaussian Splatting methods fail to efficiently allocate Gaussian capacity: under-reconstructed regions are refined in a fragmented pixel-wise manner, while redundant Gaussians with similar attributes are retained, leading to suboptimal representation quality.
AI.method: LocoADC consists of two complementary strategies: (1) Region-wise Gaussian Densification (RGD) that exploits local continuity of reconstruction errors in image space for better allocation, and (2) Similarity-Driven Gaussian Merging (SDGM) that leverages local similarity of neighboring Gaussians in Gaussian space for redundancy elimination, along with a local color consistency constraint.
AI.result: LocoADC achieves a 2.93 dB PSNR gain over GI on the CLIC dataset under the same 30k Gaussian budget, and consistently improves multiple baselines across diverse datasets.
AI.conclusion: The proposed locality-aware density control framework effectively addresses both under-reconstruction and over-reconstruction in 2D Gaussian Splatting, serving as a plug-and-play module that substantially improves Gaussian capacity utilization.

title: Enhancing Rubric-based RL via Self-Distillation
summary: Rubric-based RL has recently shown promise in improving LLMs on open-ended tasks. A widely recognized limitation of rubric-based RL is limited exploration: criteria that no rollout manages to satisfy (Unexplored Criteria, UC) receive no optimization signal. Recent methods address this by incorporating rubric information as external guidance during rollout, yet they introduce a train-inference mismatch: the policy is optimized on rollouts produced under external guidance while this guidance is absent at inference time, causing error accumulation through autoregressive decoding. Moreover, these exploration-focused approaches overlook a fundamentally different failure mode that we term Suppressed Criteria (SC) -- criteria that are satisfied by some rollouts yet whose learning signals are lost during optimization because scalar reward aggregation assigns them non-positive aggregate advantages. Our analysis reveals that SC are remarkably prevalent: over 57% of samples exhibit this failure mode throughout training, with an average of 1.8 SC per sample. To simultaneously address both UC and SC without introducing training-inference mismatch, we propose Criterion-Distilled Policy Optimization (CriPO), which enhances rubric-based RL via on-policy self-distillation. For UC, CriPO constructs a criterion-injection self-teacher and computes a localized forward-KL loss to inject missing behaviors into the policy. For SC, CriPO employs a counterfactual self-teacher to locate criterion-relevant tokens in negative-advantage rollouts and flips their token-level advantages to positive values, preserving useful patterns that would otherwise be suppressed. Experiments on medicine and science benchmarks demonstrate that CriPO consistently outperforms rubric-based RL, achieving stronger final performance with approximately $2\times$ fewer optimization steps.

AI.tldr: CriPO addresses two failure modes in rubric-based RL for LLMs: Unexplored Criteria (UC) and Suppressed Criteria (SC). It uses on-policy self-distillation with a criterion-injection self-teacher for UC and a counterfactual self-teacher for SC, avoiding train-inference mismatch. Experiments show CriPO outperforms rubric-based RL with ~2x fewer optimization steps.
AI.motivation: Rubric-based RL for LLMs suffers from limited exploration (Unexplored Criteria) where criteria never satisfied receive no signal, and a newly identified failure mode Suppressed Criteria where satisfied criteria have their learning signals lost due to scalar reward aggregation. Existing methods addressing UC introduce a train-inference mismatch.
AI.method: CriPO (Criterion-Distilled Policy Optimization) enhances rubric-based RL via on-policy self-distillation. For UC, it uses a criterion-injection self-teacher with localized forward-KL loss. For SC, it uses a counterfactual self-teacher to locate criterion-relevant tokens in negative-advantage rollouts and flips token-level advantages to positive.
AI.result: Analysis reveals over 57% of samples exhibit SC throughout training with avg 1.8 SC per sample. CriPO consistently outperforms rubric-based RL on medicine and science benchmarks, achieving stronger final performance with approximately 2× fewer optimization steps.
AI.conclusion: CriPO effectively addresses both UC and SC failure modes without training-inference mismatch, demonstrating improved efficiency and performance over standard rubric-based RL approaches.

title: MuViSeg: Multi-View Segment Correspondences from Dense Geometry Priors
summary: Classical image correspondence is solved at the level of sparse keypoints or dense pixels, but the systems that consume these matches - object-level mapping, topological navigation, scene-graph maintenance - reason about whole objects. Recent work narrows this gap by matchng directly at the level of instance segments: a class-agnostic segmenter partitions each image, and per-segment descriptors are obtained by pooling features from large 3D foundation models over the masks. We build on this segment-level matching paradigm and propose three learned matching heads: a LightGlue-style attention head with DoubleSoftmax scoring on frozen MASt3R descriptors; a DPT-style multi-scale fusion module that exposes layered spatial detail from the VGGT foundation model before pooling; and - as our main contribution - a multi-view extension that performs joint self-attention over segments drawn from several views at once, recovering transitive correspondences that strictly pairwise matchers cannot reach. Under a stratified zero-shot protocol on Replica and Virtual KITTI 2 with controlled viewpoint baselines from 0 deg to 180 deg, the LightGlue-style head improves over a parameter-free Sinkhorn matcher on the same MASt3R backbone by +4.85 AUPRC on Replica and +25.9 AUPRC on Virtual KITTI 2. Dropped into the RoboHop topological navigation pipeline on the Habitat-Matterport 3D (HM3D) Instance Image Navigation benchmark without retraining, our multi-view variant raises success rate from 50% to 70%, and our LightGlue-style head raises SPL from 45.7 to 59.1.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes three learned matching heads for segment-level image correspondence: a LightGlue-style attention head, a DPT-style multi-scale fusion module, and a multi-view self-attention extension. The multi-view approach recovers transitive correspondences across multiple views, improving success rate from 50% to 70% on HM3D navigation and SPL from 45.7 to 59.1.
AI.motivation: Classical image correspondence operates at sparse keypoint or dense pixel levels, but downstream tasks like object-level mapping, topological navigation, and scene-graph maintenance reason about whole objects. This gap motivates segment-level matching using class-agnostic instance segmentation with pooled descriptors from 3D foundation models.
AI.method: Three learned matching heads are proposed: (1) LightGlue-style attention head with DoubleSoftmax scoring on frozen MASt3R descriptors; (2) DPT-style multi-scale fusion module extracting layered spatial detail from VGGT before pooling; (3) a multi-view extension performing joint self-attention over segments from multiple views to recover transitive correspondences. Evaluation uses stratified zero-shot protocol on Replica and Virtual KITTI 2 with controlled viewpoint baselines.
AI.result: LightGlue-style head improves over Sinkhorn matcher by +4.85 AUPRC on Replica and +25.9 AUPRC on Virtual KITTI 2. Multi-view variant raises HM3D navigation success rate from 50% to 70%; LightGlue-style head raises SPL from 45.7 to 59.1.
AI.conclusion: The proposed learned matching heads significantly improve segment-level correspondence and downstream navigation performance, with the multi-view extension enabling transitive correspondences beyond pairwise matching.

title: The Label Complexity of Class-Conditional Coverage under Distribution Shift
summary:
Standard evaluation of many recognition systems contains distribution shift by construction, since benchmarks place disjoint conditions in the training and test splits. Under such a shift, split conformal prediction keeps marginal coverage near the nominal level while per-class coverage fails silently: on a real cross-subject skeleton benchmark, marginal coverage stays near ninety percent, the worst action class is covered about seventy percent of the time, and ten of the sixty classes fall below eighty percent coverage.
  We characterize the cost of restoring per-class validity. First, an impossibility: once the shift acts jointly on the covariates and the labels, the target class-conditional score law is unidentified from source labels and an unlabeled target sample, so no label-free method attains per-class coverage that is at once valid and efficient. Second, we make the cost precise: per-class validity alone needs only a handful of target labels per class, while the label count necessary and sufficient for validity together with per-class efficiency grows as the inverse square of the efficiency tolerance and the logarithm of the number of classes, with matching upper and lower bounds. Third, within the evaluated prediction-powered inference family, even the most favorable use of the classifier's own pseudo-labels on an unbounded unlabeled target pool improves efficiency by at most a small constant factor where coverage collapses.
  Skeleton action recognition is our real-data case study. A per-class calibration using source labels alone recovers a substantial share of the per-class gap while the shift preserves marginal coverage, and stops helping exactly when marginal coverage itself breaks. Three real shifts of increasing severity trace this boundary, and the same collapse and recovery appears on a natural-image corruption benchmark, beyond any single modality.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the problem of per-class coverage collapse in conformal prediction under distribution shift, showing that (1) no label-free method can achieve valid and efficient per-class coverage when the shift acts jointly on covariates and labels; (2) per-class validity requires few target labels per class, but efficiency additionally requires labels scaling as inverse square of tolerance and log of class count; (3) prediction-powered inference yields at most a small constant improvement. Real-data case studies on skeleton action recognition and natural-image corruptions validate these findings.
AI.motivation: Standard conformal prediction maintains marginal coverage under distribution shift, but per-class coverage can fail severely (e.g., on a skeleton benchmark, marginal coverage stays ~90% while the worst class drops to ~70%). The paper aims to characterize the cost of restoring per-class validity and efficiency under such shifts.
AI.method: The paper provides theoretical analysis: (1) an impossibility result showing that when shift acts jointly on covariates and labels, the class-conditional score law is unidentified from source labels and unlabeled target data, making label-free per-class valid and efficient coverage impossible; (2) information-theoretic bounds on the number of target labels needed for per-class validity alone (few per class) vs. validity plus per-class efficiency (scaling as inverse square of efficiency tolerance and log of class count); (3) analysis of prediction-powered inference showing limited improvement from pseudo-labels. Empirical validation on skeleton action recognition (cross-subject benchmark) and natural-image corruption benchmarks.
AI.result: On a real cross-subject skeleton benchmark, marginal coverage stays near 90% while the worst class has ~70% coverage and 10/60 classes fall below 80%. Per-class calibration using source labels alone recovers much of the gap while marginal coverage holds, but stops helping when marginal coverage itself breaks. Three real shifts of increasing severity trace this boundary. The same pattern appears on a natural-image corruption benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Restoring per-class validity under distribution shift is fundamentally limited: no label-free method can achieve both validity and efficiency when shift is joint. However, per-class validity alone is inexpensive (few labels per class), while adding efficiency requires more labels following a precise scaling law. Prediction-powered inference offers only marginal gains. Practitioners should be aware that marginal coverage can be misleading under shift.

title: Exploration Matters for Escaping the Blur Trap in 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) employs Gaussian primitives for explicit scene representation, facilitating real-time, high-fidelity reconstruction and novel view synthesis of complex scenes. However, the explicit modeling inherent in 3DGS introduces a gradient bias during optimization, rendering its non-convex optimization process highly susceptible to convergence toward local suboptimal solutions. This constitutes a fundamental limitation in 3DGS optimization, which we term the Blur Trap. To address this limitation, we integrate simple explicit exploration into the 3DGS optimization framework. First, through rigorous mathematical analysis of the 3DGS optimization formulation, we identify the underlying optimization bias responsible for the Blur Trap and categorize it into two distinct subtypes: the Far-Side Blur Trap and the Near-Side Blur Trap. Subsequently, we propose two highly straightforward exploration strategies (Random Seeding and Random Splitting) to mitigate the far-side and near-side blur traps, respectively. Experimental validation demonstrates that the incorporation of these exploration operators effectively and complementarily overcome the Blur Trap, achieving high-quality rendering performance across multiple datasets. Project page: https://chengbo-wang.github.io/ExploreGS/

AI.tldr: The paper identifies and mitigates a fundamental optimization bias in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) called the Blur Trap, which causes convergence to suboptimal local minima. Through mathematical analysis, they categorize it into Far-Side and Near-Side subtypes, and propose two simple exploration strategies—Random Seeding and Random Splitting—to overcome them, achieving high-quality rendering.
AI.motivation: 3DGS optimization suffers from a gradient bias due to its explicit scene representation, making it prone to converging to local suboptimal solutions (Blur Trap). The paper aims to identify, analyze, and address this fundamental limitation.
AI.method: The authors mathematically analyze the 3DGS optimization formulation to identify two types of Blur Trap (Far-Side and Near-Side). They then introduce two straightforward exploration operators: Random Seeding to mitigate the far-side blur trap and Random Splitting to mitigate the near-side blur trap.
AI.result: Experimental results show that the proposed exploration operators effectively and complementarily overcome the Blur Trap, achieving high-quality rendering performance across multiple datasets.
AI.conclusion: Simple explicit exploration strategies can resolve the inherent optimization bias in 3DGS, improving its convergence behavior and rendering quality without complex modifications.

title: Empowering On-Device Model Adaptation with an Edge AI Inference Accelerator
comment: Accepted at the ITEM Workshop, held in conjunction with ECML-PKDD 2026. To appear in the ECML-PKDD joint post-workshop proceedings
summary: On-device model adaptation is essential to enable lifelong personalization on resource-constrained hardware, but compute, power, and memory limitations of such devices make end-to-end backpropagation impractical for modern deep neural networks. This work proposes a heterogeneous adaptation pipeline that repurposes a commercial edge AI inference accelerator, Hailo-8L, for frozen-backbone feature extraction during on-device training. The computational graph is partitioned so that the pre-trained backbone is quantized to INT8 and run on the accelerator, while only a lightweight FP32 classification head is fine-tuned on the host CPU, enabling frequent, energy-efficient in-field updates with most weights remaining fixed. Across multiple architectures and datasets, this pipeline achieves up to 15.4x faster wall-clock training time compared to a Raspberry Pi 5 CPU baseline, offers competitive throughput in favorable settings, and consistently reduces energy per sample. Post-training quantization restoration is shown to be crucial for preserving the quality of accelerator-generated features and mitigating accuracy loss in quantization-sensitive architectures. Overall, the results demonstrate a practical approach to efficient on-device adaptation using inference-oriented edge accelerators. The implementation is available at https://github.com/MatPiech/accelerator-training.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a heterogeneous on-device training pipeline that uses a commercial edge AI accelerator (Hailo-8L) for frozen-backbone INT8 feature extraction while fine-tuning only a lightweight FP32 classification head on the host CPU. This achieves up to 15.4x faster training, competitive throughput, and reduced energy per sample compared to a Raspberry Pi 5 CPU baseline, with post-training quantization restoration critical for accuracy preservation.
AI.motivation: On-device model adaptation is needed for lifelong personalization on resource-constrained hardware, but compute, power, and memory limitations make end-to-end backpropagation impractical for modern deep neural networks.
AI.method: A heterogeneous adaptation pipeline that partitions the computational graph: a pre-trained backbone is quantized to INT8 and runs on a commercial edge AI accelerator (Hailo-8L) for feature extraction, while a lightweight FP32 classification head is fine-tuned on the host CPU. This keeps most weights frozen and enables frequent, energy-efficient in-field updates.
AI.result: Up to 15.4x faster wall-clock training time vs. Raspberry Pi 5 CPU baseline, competitive throughput in favorable settings, and consistently reduced energy per sample. Post-training quantization restoration is crucial for preserving feature quality and mitigating accuracy loss in quantization-sensitive architectures.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate a practical approach to efficient on-device adaptation using inference-oriented edge accelerators.

title: Fine-Detail Monocular Geometry Estimation with Self-Guided Sparse Volumetric Refinement
summary: Monocular geometry estimation has recently achieved impressive performance across diverse scenes. However, state-of-the-art models still face notable distortion in local 3D structure, especially in fine details, like thin structures and small objects. We attribute this limitation to an architectural mismatch: most current models decode 3D geometry within a 2D parameterization, where feature interactions are governed by image-plane proximity rather than true 3D spatial relationships. This inadvertently mixes features from geometrically distant surfaces, resulting in over-smoothed geometry particularly around thin or elongated structure. In this paper, we propose a fine-detail monocular geometry estimation with Self-Guided Sparse 3D Refinement (SSR) that lifts monocular geometry modeling from 2D image space to 3D space for high-fidelity metric-scale point maps. Our model lifts the coarse point map from a foundation base model onto a sparse voxel shell and refines it via SSR. The SSR employs sparse convolutions that aggregate features based on 3D spatial locality, avoiding feature mixing across depth discontinuities. Extensive experiments on diverse datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing approaches in recovering fine detailed 3D geometry across both quantitative metrics and qualitative visualizations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Self-Guided Sparse 3D Refinement (SSR) to improve fine-detail monocular geometry estimation by lifting 3D geometry decoding from 2D image space to true 3D space using sparse convolutions on a voxel shell, avoiding feature mixing across depth discontinuities and significantly outperforming existing methods.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art monocular geometry estimation models suffer from notable distortion in local 3D structure (thin structures, small objects) due to an architectural mismatch: they decode 3D geometry within a 2D parameterization where feature interactions rely on image-plane proximity rather than true 3D spatial relationships, causing over-smoothed geometry around thin or elongated structures.
AI.method: The model first obtains a coarse point map from a foundation base model, lifts it onto a sparse voxel shell, then refines it via Self-Guided Sparse 3D Refinement (SSR). SSR employs sparse convolutions that aggregate features based on 3D spatial locality, preventing feature mixing across depth discontinuities.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on diverse datasets demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing approaches in recovering fine-detailed 3D geometry, both in quantitative metrics and qualitative visualizations.
AI.conclusion: Lifting monocular geometry modeling from 2D image space to true 3D space via sparse voxel refinement effectively resolves the architectural mismatch in current models, enabling high-fidelity metric-scale point maps with improved fine-detail reconstruction.

title: LLM-as-a-Coach: Experiential Learning for Non-Verifiable Tasks
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) on open-ended tasks compresses an LLM's rubric-based evaluation into a scalar reward, discarding rich textual feedback and conflating responses with distinct quality profiles. We propose Experiential Learning (EL), which repurposes the feedback model from an LLM-as-a-Judge into an LLM-as-a-Coach. The coach distills its assessment of each on-policy response into transferable experiential knowledge, which conditions a teacher model and is internalized by the policy through on-policy context distillation. Compared with scalar rewards, this higher-bandwidth feedback channel provides dense supervision and preserves fine-grained preferences among high-quality responses. Across two policy families, with feedback from the policy itself or a proprietary model, EL consistently outperforms rubric-based RL on held-out and unseen open-ended tasks. Notably, EL generalizes better beyond the training distribution, and mitigates reward hacking. These findings establish experiential knowledge as a richer and more generalizable learning signal for post-training on non-verifiable tasks.

AI.tldr: EL replaces scalar reward-based RL with experiential knowledge from an LLM-as-a-Coach, providing dense feedback that improves generalization and reduces reward hacking on open-ended tasks.
AI.motivation: Scalar rewards from rubric-based evaluation in RL discard rich textual feedback and conflate responses with different quality profiles, limiting learning signal quality.
AI.method: EL repurposes the feedback model into an LLM-as-a-Coach that distills assessment into experiential knowledge, which conditions a teacher model and is internalized by the policy via on-policy context distillation.
AI.result: EL consistently outperforms rubric-based RL on held-out and unseen open-ended tasks across two policy families, with better generalization beyond training distribution and reduced reward hacking.
AI.conclusion: Experiential knowledge serves as a richer and more generalizable learning signal for post-training on non-verifiable tasks compared to scalar rewards.

title: Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections for Parameter-Efficient Finetuning
summary: Most parameter-efficient finetuning (PEFT) methods adapt weights or activations, thus leaving one of the key Transformer components unchanged: residual connections. This paper investigates Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), a generalisation of residual connections, as a novel PEFT approach, wrapping frozen OLMo-2 backbones with learned residual routing modules. We find that mHC can finetune frozen Transformers, but that its role differs fundamentally from the original pre-training setting: in finetuning, fixing the residual mixing matrix to identity often improves performance. As a standalone PEFT method, mHC does not consistently outperform LoRA. However, at matched trainable parameter budgets, mHC+LoRA combinations improve language-modelling loss and show task-dependent benchmark gains at both 1B and 7B scale. Overall, our results identify residual routing as a distinct and promising novel PEFT axis.

AI.tldr: This paper explores Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), a generalization of residual connections, as a PEFT method for frozen Transformers. mHC alone underperforms LoRA, but combining mHC with LoRA yields improved language modeling loss and task-dependent benchmark gains at 1B and 7B scales, identifying residual routing as a novel PEFT axis.
AI.motivation: Existing PEFT methods adapt weights or activations but leave residual connections unchanged; this paper investigates whether modifying residual connections (via mHC) can serve as an effective PEFT approach.
AI.method: The authors propose Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC), which generalizes residual connections by wrapping frozen OLMo-2 backbones with learned residual routing modules. They evaluate mHC as a standalone PEFT method and in combination with LoRA at matched parameter budgets.
AI.result: Fixing the residual mixing matrix to identity during finetuning often improves performance. mHC alone does not consistently outperform LoRA, but mHC+LoRA combinations improve language-modeling loss and show task-dependent benchmark gains at both 1B and 7B scales.
AI.conclusion: Residual routing (via mHC) is a distinct and promising novel PEFT axis, particularly when combined with LoRA, rather than used as a standalone method.

title: HAS: Highlight-guided Attention Steering for Multimodal LLM Video Summarization
summary: Video understanding has become more and more important with the growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for video generation. Recently, Multimodal Large Language Model(M-LLM) has shown its capability in video understanding. Video summarization, a specific domain of video understanding, has proven its importance for efficient navigation and retrieval. Both video understanding and video summarization require a good selection of key frames in a video. Current video summarization methods heavily focus on the selected key frames and correlated segment captions. However, existing approaches overlook the perspective of treating the importance of the frames globally. We argue that using discrete selected frames for summarization will not only reduce the understanding coherence, but also lost important information in the video, as well as wasting the original capacity of the MLLMs. In this paper, we propose HAS, a Highlight-guided Attention Steering method for video summarization. We consider a challenging but practical setting where the video given to MLLMs for summarize should be continuous but with highlight guidance. HAS mainly consists of two parts: The first part is to find a continuous frame-level highlight distribution for the video globally. The second part is to apply the highlight distribution as an attention steering vector for the MLLM, targeting a better understanding of the video, and thus during the model inference time, putting more attention on the highlighted frames, while avoiding lost entire information on less highlighted frames through putting less attention instead of forgetting them. We evaluated HAS on a variety of benchmarks, and it has shown convincing performance in video summarization.

AI.tldr: HAS (Highlight-guided Attention Steering) is a method for video summarization that finds a continuous frame-level highlight distribution globally and uses it as an attention steering vector for MLLMs, enabling better video understanding by focusing more on highlighted frames while retaining information from less highlighted frames.
AI.motivation: Existing video summarization methods rely on discrete selected key frames and segment captions, which reduces understanding coherence, loses important information, and wastes MLLM capacity. The authors argue for treating frame importance globally and using continuous video input with highlight guidance.
AI.method: HAS consists of two parts: (1) finding a continuous frame-level highlight distribution for the video globally, and (2) applying this highlight distribution as an attention steering vector for the MLLM, putting more attention on highlighted frames while putting less (but not zero) attention on less highlighted frames during inference.
AI.result: Evaluated on various benchmarks, HAS shows convincing performance in video summarization compared to existing methods.
AI.conclusion: HAS addresses limitations of discrete frame selection by using continuous video input with global highlight-guided attention steering, achieving effective video summarization without losing information coherence.

title: Do Language Models Dream of Binding Molecules? Benchmarking LLMs under Spatial Constraints
summary: Structure-based drug design (SBDD) leverages the 3D structure of protein targets, often complemented by other spatial constraints, to generate candidate binding molecules. While diffusion models have dominated as a leading paradigm for high-quality 3D molecule generation, LLM-based methods are rapidly emerging in molecular design and have shown competitive performance in pocket-conditioned molecular generation. However, their ability to reason about physics and 3D spatial environments is largely underexplored. In this work, we systematically analyze whether current general-purpose LLMs are capable of navigating complex 3D constraints compared to established baselines such as specialized diffusion models. We consider 3D ligand generation conditioned on protein pockets together with ligand- and interaction-derived spatial constraints, including anchor fragments, pharmacophore points, and mandatory pocket-ligand interactions. To enable this evaluation, we introduce 3D-Fit - a token-efficient benchmarking strategy for assessing LLM performance on multi-conditioned spatial molecule generation. Our findings reveal a clear pattern in LLM spatial capabilities: while they still lag behind state-of-the-art approaches, they are promising and can handle multiple spatial constraints simultaneously, enabling scaling to heterogeneous setups.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates general-purpose LLMs on 3D structure-based drug design tasks with multiple spatial constraints, finding they lag behind diffusion models but show promise in handling heterogeneous constraints simultaneously.
AI.motivation: To systematically assess whether general-purpose LLMs can reason about physics and 3D spatial environments in pocket-conditioned molecular generation, a capability that remains largely underexplored despite LLMs' rapid emergence in molecular design.
AI.method: The authors introduce 3D-Fit, a token-efficient benchmarking strategy for evaluating LLMs on multi-conditioned spatial molecule generation, and compare LLMs against specialized diffusion models on tasks involving protein pockets, anchor fragments, pharmacophore points, and mandatory pocket-ligand interactions.
AI.result: LLMs lag behind state-of-the-art diffusion models but show promising spatial capabilities, particularly in handling multiple spatial constraints simultaneously and scaling to heterogeneous setups.
AI.conclusion: General-purpose LLMs have emerging but still limited 3D spatial reasoning abilities for SBDD; they are not yet competitive with specialized diffusion models but offer advantages in multi-constraint scenarios.

title: SAMRI-3D: Adapting SAM2 for 3D MRI Segmentation with Global Volume Tokens
summary: Foundation models such as Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) have transformed natural-image and video segmentation, and recent work has begun adapting them to medical imaging. These adaptations, however, are largely general-purpose models that treat MRI as one modality among many; large-scale, MRI-specific modelling and benchmarking remain limited, even though MRI's low soft-tissue contrast leaves many boundaries effectively invisible on individual slices. We present SAMRI-3D, a benchmark and method for 3D MRI segmentation with SAM2. The SAMRI-3D benchmark is the largest MRI-only evaluation to date - 10,392 volumes from 34 datasets (27 public, 7 in-house) spanning 12 anatomical domains and 10+ sequences, with explicit seen/unseen splits. Freezing the image encoder and fine-tuning only the lightweight decoder and memory modules raises mean Dice from 0.58 (zero-shot SAM2) to 0.76, surpassing recent SAM-based medical models (SAMed-2 0.69, Medical-SAM2 0.49, SAM-Med3D 0.37) with strong statistical significance. To target invisible boundaries, we introduce Global Volume Tokens (GVT): persistent memory tokens trained with a Truncated Signed Distance Field (TSDF) reconstruction objective that is discarded at inference (zero added cost). This full model, SAMRI-3D, attains the best accuracy (0.78) and lowest variance across all 34 datasets and, uniquely, shows no drop on 8 held-out datasets (0.79 unseen vs. 0.78 seen); per-sequence analysis confirms the TSDF objective helps most where per-slice contrast is weakest. We will release the benchmark, code, and models in this paper.
